example_value: With ±0.1 mm hole diameter and ±0.2 mm hole location, the hole edge can vary ±0.3 mm horizontally, while vertical variation is only ±0.1 mm from diameter alone.

subject: use of geometric tolerances (roundness) in addition to size
main_point: In addition to size limits, geometric form tolerances like roundness can be specified to prevent holes that meet diameter tolerance but are out-of-round (oval).
source_quote: Moreover, there are also tolerance that can indicate how round your hole should be such that is not an oval, i.e. one side that is -0.1mm while the other is +0.1mm.
example_value: A hole could meet a ±0.1 mm size tolerance yet be −0.1 mm on one side and +0.1 mm on the opposite, indicating ovality unless roundness is controlled.

subject: dimensioning strategy: datum-based locations vs direct hole-to-hole dimension
main_point: Locating two holes from separate references with their own tolerances causes their center-to-center distance to vary by the sum of those tolerances. Specifying the hole-to-hole distance directly constrains their spacing to that single tolerance and avoids this stack-up.
source_quote: For example the left hole can be placed with a tolerance of +/-0.2mm from the center line and the right hole with +/- 0.1mm. Hence, the distance between the two holes can vary with +/- 0.3mm. If you choose to define the distance between the two holes, the tolerance on this dimension is only +/- 0.2mm.
example_value: Left hole ±0.2 mm from centerline and right hole ±0.1 mm yields ±0.3 mm spacing variation; directly tolerancing the hole-to-hole distance at ±0.2 mm limits spacing to ±0.2 mm.

subject: bearing housing interference fit effect on bearing rotation
main_point: The bearings ran roughly only when pressed into the frame but rotated smoothly when removed, indicating the installed housing fit or alignment influenced their running smoothness.
source_quote: Ever since I bought it, most suspension pivot bearings run roughly when pressed into the frame. After the first 3 months I had the bike, I removed some of the bearings to inspect and found that the bearings ran fine when not in the frame.
example_value: On a Privateer 161 mountain bike, most pivot bearings were rough in the frame but fine once removed.
example_context: mountain bike suspension pivot bearings pressed into the frame

subject: hands-on evaluation of clearance fits using test holes and pins
main_point: Build intuition for fit tolerances by making holes at known clearances and testing how pins fit. Trying a range of gaps (from line-to-line up to several thousandths) lets you feel the transition from interference to loose clearance and informs tolerance choices.
source_quote: You to do things like drill and ream holes of different tolerances see how pins fit when the fit is 0.0000", 0.0002", 0.0005", 0.001", 0.002", and 0.005".
example_value: Clearance increments suggested: 0.0000, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.002, and 0.005 inches.

subject: clearance magnitude vs perceived fit on smooth metal parts
main_point: On smooth metal sliding fits, about 0.005 in clearance feels obviously loose and wobbly, while around 0.001 in slides easily without feeling tight. A non-wobbling sliding fit is roughly 0.0005–0.0001 in, and may require squareness or even an arbor press to assemble/disassemble due to jamming despite not being a true press fit.
source_quote: For smooth metal surfaces, 0.005" is visibly loose enough that you can feel it wobble with a lot of play and slide freely. 0.001" is not really wobbly loose but will slide easily and is by no means tight. A non-wobbling fit is located somewhere between 0.0005" and 0.0001" and is such that if it is something like a shaft sliding into a hole, you can't get it in or out without an arbour press even though it is not truly a press fit because the tolerances are so small it need to be square or it will jam.
example_value: Example context: a shaft sliding into a hole.
example_context: smooth metal sliding fits (e.g., shaft-in-hole)

subject: metal vs 3D-printed plastic for dimensional stability and surface quality
main_point: Machined metal parts generally provide smooth, flat, straight surfaces and exhibit low thermal/humidity-driven expansion, supporting tighter fits. 3D-printed plastics have poorer surface quality and dimensional stability, though their ability to flex can compensate in some assemblies.
source_quote: But I'm talking about metal which can hold nice smooth, flat, straight surfaces which don't expand much with temperature or at all with humidity. 3D printed plastic is terrible by comparison, but at the same time can give.
example_context: comparison of machined metal parts vs 3D-printed plastic parts for achieving reliable fits

subject: using a micrometer and gauges to develop feel for thousandths-inch clearances
main_point: Use a micrometer as a tactile/visual aid to understand thousandths-inch gaps: set it to target clearances and slide stock between the jaws to feel resistance. Supplement with feeler gauges, pins, or drill rod to calibrate your sense for clearance magnitudes when specifying fits.
source_quote: Get a micrometer then at least you'll be able to hold it up to the light and see what 0.001" or 0.005" looks like and stick pieces of stock in the jaws and see how easily it slides as you widen the jaws. You can stick feeler gauges, pins, drill rod, and other things in the jaws.
example_value: Demonstration clearances: 0.001 in and 0.005 in.

subject: off-the-shelf ball bearing nominal dimensions
main_point: Off-the-shelf metric ball bearings are often manufactured very close to their nominal ID/OD, leaving little or no inherent clearance for sliding fits if mating shafts are also near nominal. This can make nominal-on-nominal pairing too tight for easy assembly.
source_quote: These ball bearings are available in nominal mm sizes, and to the limit of my measuring tools, tend to be ground exactly to size.
example_value: User reports 15 mm ID and 24 mm OD bearings measure exactly 15 and 24 mm with their tools.
example_context: Off-the-shelf metric ball bearings for hobby/consumer applications measured with common shop metrology

subject: polishing shafts to achieve sliding fit
main_point: When a nominal shaft is too tight in a nominal bearing for a sliding fit, a practical workaround is to lightly polish down the shaft to create clearance, at the expense of the original ground finish.
source_quote: I have to polish the shaft down with sandpaper (destroying the nice finish) in order to get an bearing that can be assembled by sliding, such as for a bicycle hub axle.
example_value: For a 15 mm shaft in a bicycle hub bearing, the author sands the shaft to allow sliding assembly.
example_context: Nominal metric shafts and bearings for assemblies like bicycle hub axles where a close sliding fit is desired

subject: bearing inner race interference fit selection
main_point: When the shaft is the rotating member, choose an interference fit on the bearing’s inner race to prevent relative motion on the shaft. The housing side can generally be specified with a looser fit.
source_quote: Typically you want an interference fit on a bearing ID since the shaft is usually the element that's rotating and whatever the bearing OD goes into will have a looser fit.
example_context: rotating shaft applications where the bearing inner race is mounted to the shaft

subject: loose fit between rotating shaft and bearing ID
main_point: A rotating shaft with a loose fit in the bearing inner race can lead to shaft scoring and other problems. Specify sufficient interference on the ID to avoid fretting and wear.
source_quote: If your shaft is rotating and has a loose fit with the bearing ID it can start to score and cause a whole bunch of issues.
example_context: bearing inner race mounted on a rotating shaft

subject: thermal methods for assembling interference fits
main_point: Use thermal methods for assembling interference fits: heat the bearing or cool the shaft before assembly. The induced expansion or contraction provides temporary clearance to slip components together.
source_quote: Standard practice is to heat the bearing with a bearing heater, or cool the shaft, prior to assembly. The thermal expansion (or contraction) allows just enough clearance for assembly.

subject: bearing fit selection based on load and ISO clearances
main_point: Appropriate shaft-to-bearing fits depend on the bearing’s load and application, and are commonly selected using ISO clearance guidance. Fit choice should be tied to operating conditions, not just nominal sizes.
source_quote: Shaft fits are also dependent on the load and application of the bearing, usually based on ISO clearances.
example_context: bearing fit design guided by ISO clearance classes for specific loads and applications

subject: use of undersized dowel pins for sliding fits in bearings
main_point: As a practical option for achieving a sliding fit in standard bearings, consider using undersized dowel pins as shafts. These are commonly available and can provide the needed clearance.
source_quote: You can typically find undersized dowels which could work in your instance.
example_context: situations requiring an undersized  nominal shaft to fit a standard bearing ID with a sliding fit

subject: arbor press assembly for line-to-line or slight interference fits
main_point: For small bearings with line-to-line or slightly interfering fits, an arbor press can be sufficient for assembly. Heating or cooling may be unnecessary when the interference is minimal.
source_quote: For a 15 mm bearing with line to line fit or a little tighter you may be able to just use an arbor press and some elbow grease.
example_value: Example given for a 15 mm bearing with a line-to-line or slightly tighter fit.
example_context: small bearings around 15 mm ID with line-to-line or slight interference fits

subject: bearing shaft fit types
main_point: Bearing-to-shaft assemblies are typically designed as interference or transition fits, not sliding fits. Installation is done with applied force, preferably using a press or clamping tool.
source_quote: Shafts and bearings usually use interference or transition fits - they shouldn't slide and for installation you should use force - some kind of press or clamping tool would be best

subject: bearing installation impact damage
main_point: Striking a bearing directly during installation risks damaging it; if using a hammer, interpose a load-spreading material (e.g., wood) to distribute force evenly.
source_quote: you shouldn't hit the bearing directly to avoid damage, use something, for example piece of wood, to spread the force onto the whole bearing
example_value: Use a piece of wood between the hammer and bearing to spread the force.

subject: thermal expansion assisted assembly
main_point: To ease assembly of interference-fit parts, heat the mating component or cool the other to exploit thermal expansion and contraction.
source_quote: Alternatively, you can heat/cool one of the parts to make use of thermal expansion.

subject: hole-basis fits for bearings
main_point: Use a hole-basis fit: keep the bearing’s inner race at nominal in the H tolerance zone (never undersize), and select the shaft tolerance to achieve the desired fit—undersize for sliding, oversize for interference.
source_quote:
- the hole (in this case inner race of the bearing) is as close to nominal size as possible but never smaller (tolerance H)
- the shaft has tolerance selected for desired fit - so if you want sliding you would make it undersized, or if you want interference fit you would make them oversized

subject: shaft sizing for bearing fits
main_point: For proper bearing fits, do not rely on off‑the‑shelf shafts. Define the required fit and have a machinist make the shaft to that specification.
source_quote: This does not involve buying shafts off the shelf.  It involves setting the spec and having a machinist create the right sized shaft.

subject: bearing manufacturer fit recommendations
main_point: Bearing manufacturers publish application-specific interference/fit values that should be used to select shaft and housing dimensions.
source_quote: Bearing manufacturers will give values for interference based on the application.

subject: measurement accuracy for bearing fits
main_point: Achieving correct bearing fits requires measurement and machining accuracy on the order of micrometers.
source_quote: We are talking micrometers as the measurement accuracy required.

subject: bearing installation methods
main_point: Because some bearings cannot be installed with a press, alternative field installation techniques, including impact methods, are used.
source_quote: Not all bearings can be put on in a press, so field techniques also exist (yes, hammers are involved).

subject: industry practice for shaft sourcing
main_point: In pump and motor manufacturing, shafts are custom‑machined to meet fit specifications rather than sourced off‑the‑shelf.
source_quote: Pump and motor manufacturers make their shafts to the right specification, which is most certainly not by buying them off the shelf.
example_context: pump and motor manufacturers

subject: datum selection for tolerance measurement of linked parts with pin
main_point: For measuring a parallelism tolerance in a pinned linkage, define two datums: use the longitudinal axis of the linked parts and the line through the pin’s center. These two reference lines establish the measurement framework for the sliding interface.
source_quote: One is the longitudinal axis of the linked parts. The other one is the line through the center of the pin as shown below.
example_context: Assemblies with linked parts connected by a pin where parallelism is specified for sliding components.

subject: positional tolerance of flats relative to a datum
main_point: The positional tolerance calls for the flats to lie within a 0.100-unit radial band relative to datum A, constraining their radial location (and thus effective size/position) with respect to that datum. This defines how far the machined flats may deviate from the ideal geometry referenced to A.
source_quote: It says the flats shall be within 0.100 units of radial dimension positioned with reference to 'A'.
example_value: Flats must be within 0.100 units in radial dimension, referenced to datum A.
example_context: GD&T callout for flats on a circular rim specifying a 0.100 positional/radial tolerance relative to datum A.

subject: tolerance limiting feature size and position variability
main_point: A stated tolerance allows a small deviation from ideal geometry, and that bound directly limits how much a machined feature’s size and location may vary. The specified value (e.g., ±0.1) defines the allowable variation envelope.
source_quote: Some minor deviation from that precision (+/- 0.1 units) is permitted which limits the variability of size and position of the cut.

subject: small gear tooth profile tolerance
main_point: For small gears, typical tolerances on the actual tooth profile and corresponding inspection measurements are about 0.01 mm or tighter.
source_quote: Usually in the range of 0.01 mm or less for gears that size for actual tooth profile and inspection measurements.
example_context: small gears

subject: tile gaskets vs. bare MDF spoilboard for vacuum hold-down
main_point: Rubber tile gaskets often provide better hold-down than a bare MDF spoilboard because the gasket’s compliance and surface grip increase friction and sealing. This can improve workholding effectiveness on vacuum tables in many situations.
source_quote: I've used the tile gaskets and, in many situations, they seem to do a good job when compared to a bare MDF spoilboard. Part of that, of course, is due to the sponginess and grip of the gasket material.
example_context: CNC router vacuum tables using porous MDF spoilboards with rubberized tile gaskets

subject: MDF spoilboard porosity and vacuum leakage
main_point: Because MDF is porous, vacuum flows through it and will leak wherever the surface is not covered by parts or masks. As uncovered area increases, leakage degrades the effective hold-down.
source_quote: MDF is used for spoilboards due to its porosity - the vacuum essentially flows right through it, but leakage becomes an issue as soon as the entire spoilboard is not covered.
example_context: Porous MDF spoilboards on CNC router vacuum tables

subject: small-part vacuum hold-down without gasketing
main_point: Very small parts tend to be difficult to hold by vacuum alone without dedicated gasketing, particularly on porous MDF spoilboards. The limited area and leakage reduce effective clamping force.
source_quote: The biggest issue is the size of the part - 3"x3" parts are kind of hard to hold with no gasketing, especially on an MDF spoilboard.
example_context: Vacuum tables with MDF spoilboards holding ~3"x3" parts without gasket seals

subject: large-part vacuum hold-down effectiveness
main_point: Larger parts present enough area for vacuum to generate strong clamping force, making them easy to hold. Increased surface area compensates for leakage and boosts net downforce.
source_quote: An 8"x14" door panel is easy to hold with vacuum.
example_context: CNC router vacuum table holding an ~8"x14" door panel

subject: achievable vacuum pressure and resultant clamping force
main_point: With adequate vacuum capacity, achieving around a 10 psi pressure differential on a part is feasible, yielding substantial clamping force. On modestly sized panels, this translates to forces on the order of a thousand pounds.
source_quote: A decent vac pump can easily get 10psi on the part, resulting in over 1000 lbs of downforce.
example_value: At ~10 psi over an 8"x14" area, downforce exceeds 1000 lb.
example_context: CNC router vacuum system with a capable vacuum pump

subject: vacuum-only hold-down for machining soft metals on routers
main_point: Vacuum hold-down alone can be sufficient for machining softer metals such as aluminum and brass on a CNC router. The lower cutting forces compared to steel machining allow effective workholding by vacuum.
source_quote: Soft metals like Al and brass are easily machined on a router using vacuum only.
example_context: CNC routers cutting aluminum or brass with vacuum table workholding

subject: vacuum hold-down force vs exposed area
main_point: For vacuum workholding, the clamp force equals atmospheric pressure multiplied by the portion of the workpiece area actually open to the vacuum region; sealed areas contribute no force. This holds regardless of gasket island coverage—only the vacuum-connected area counts.
source_quote: It should always be atmospheric pressure x area exposed to the free space of the vacuum.

subject: porous materials/open-cell foam acting as breathers under vacuum
main_point: Porous media like MDF and open‑cell foam let air migrate through them, so vacuum can still communicate under a part via these materials. As a result, the effective vacuum‑exposed area is larger than the visible openings alone would suggest, reducing the apparent loss in hold‑down force.
source_quote: Incidentally, open-celled foams allow gas to pass through them so if these rubber tiles are made of open-celled foam, these would behave similarly. The area exposed to the free space of the vacuum would be reduced compared to if the materials were not there, but not as much as it might appear.
example_context: MDF spoilboards and open-celled foam tile gaskets used on vacuum tables

subject: closed-cell foam used as ad-hoc vacuum gasket
main_point: Using a full sheet of closed‑cell foam as a makeshift gasket under a vacuum lid can still achieve a working seal, even though closed‑cell foam isn’t expected to pass gas. In practice, the setup held, though seal strength wasn’t verified.
source_quote: However, I have had cases where I was too lazy to cut a proper ring gasket for vacuum pot lids and instead just placed a sheet of This was a closed cell foam (that should not have allowed gas to pass through) across the entire opening and placed the hard lid on top. I wasn't sure if this would work at first but it did, though I can't confirm if the seal was any weaker.
example_value: The author sealed a vacuum pot by placing a sheet of closed-cell foam over the entire opening and setting a hard lid on top; the seal worked.
example_context: Vacuum pot lid sealing with a sheet of closed-cell foam instead of a cut ring gasket

subject: datum selection for improvised shank grinding
main_point: When modifying an end mill shank without proper tooling, reference from the existing shank to maintain concentricity and avoid using the cutting edges as a locating surface to prevent damage.
source_quote: The datum you need to locate off is the current shank (take care to avoid using the cutting edges of the workpart)

subject: reducing shank diameter by machining below clamping zone
main_point: Clamp a sacrificial section of the shank, reduce the diameter below the clamping area, then cut off the clamped portion to end up with the newly sized shank without needing to grip the finished section.
source_quote: You can also spin it, and trim the workpart below where you hold. If you then chop off the piece you held, you will be left with the trimmed shank.

subject: using bearings/rollers to guide concentric rotation for grinding
main_point: A bearing sized to the shank can be mounted near the cutter to guide the part as it spins against the grinder for even material removal; alternatively, cradle the part between at least three rollers/bearings to achieve similar concentric rotation.
source_quote: If you get a bearing that fits the datum, you can affix the bearing relative to the cutter, install the workpart, and spin the workpart against the cutter to evenly trim the shank. You can get a similar effect with multiple (3 minimum) incorrectly sized bearings, installing them at an appropriate distance to fit the workpart between them.

subject: approximating round by successive flats when grinding a shank
main_point: When creating a round from flats using guide rails, continue adding facets until you reach at least six sides, then finish with very light passes to average out variations from cutter wear between passes.
source_quote: Keep making passes until the polygon has enough sides to be useful (at least 6) and then make one more set of passes removing a miniscule amount of material to minimize difference in the cutter (from wear) between passes.

subject: powered rotation of drill press with imbalanced arm
main_point: Do not power the drill press when using an arm attached to the spindle to spin a cutter around a fixed workpiece; the arm creates imbalance that makes powered rotation unsafe.
source_quote: (note that you should do so manually and not with the power of the drill press since there will be imbalance from an arm hanging off it)
example_context: Drill press setups where an arm is used to rotate a cutter around a stationary workpiece

subject: glued socket as temporary drill press chuck
main_point: A sized socket can be glued to the workpart and mounted in the drill press as a temporary chuck substitute, enabling slow rotation for grinding when a proper chuck is unavailable.
source_quote: Alternatively, with the press lined up, you could glue the workpart into a socket on the drill press. Such would work as a temporary chuck replacement, allowing you to spin the workpart in the drill press (preferably slowly).
example_context: Drill press workholding without an appropriately sized chuck

subject: excessive contact pressure disrupting centering in improvised grinding setups
main_point: Improvised methods for spinning and grinding a shank can only tolerate limited contact pressure; pushing too hard will disturb centering and introduce runout.
source_quote: Be aware that any of these (and most other) methods will have a limit on how much pressure you can apply between the workpart and cutter without screwing up the centering.

subject: light passes strategy for manual grinding
main_point: Use light pressure and take multiple small passes when grinding down a shank to maintain alignment and avoid upsetting concentricity.
source_quote: It is best to remove material very slowly and in multiple passes.

subject: outside edge fillet tooling (corner rounding end mill/radius cutter)
main_point: In metal machining, outside edge fillets are typically produced using a radius cutter, also known as a corner rounding end mill.
source_quote: However with metal it appears to be call a radius cutter or a corner rounding end mill.

subject: revolved cut to terminate partial-length fillets
main_point: To model a partial-length fillet, first create the fillet, then use a revolved cut to remove the end corners and form the termination arc. This workflow is supported in SolidWorks and can be replicated in Inventor using an equivalent revolved cut feature.
source_quote: You revolve cut the end corners
example_value: Author implemented the method in SolidWorks and notes the revolved cut feature should be available in Inventor as well.
example_context: SolidWorks or Autodesk Inventor CAD modeling using a revolved cut feature

subject: revolution axis orientation for revolved cut
main_point: When using a revolved cut to terminate a fillet, align the revolution axis perpendicular to the top face. This orientation ensures the cut is referenced correctly to the surface being trimmed.
source_quote:
Remember to keep the revolution axis 
normal to the upper face
.
example_context: SolidWorks or Autodesk Inventor CAD modeling using a revolved cut feature

subject: geometric limitation of revolved cut at very obtuse angles
main_point: With very obtuse corner angles, a revolved-cut termination cannot produce an end arc whose circle is exactly perpendicular to the external profile; the geometry prevents it. Expect a small deviation from a perfectly perpendicular circular line.
source_quote: In the case of very obtuse angles, like in the picture above, you won't exactly get the circular line perpendicular to the external profile, due to geometry:
example_context: Revolved-cut fillet terminations in SolidWorks/Inventor when the intersecting faces form very obtuse angles

subject: perceptibility of deviation near 90° angles
main_point: When the intersecting faces are close to 90°, the slight geometric deviation from the ideal perpendicular circular termination is hardly visible. The revolved-cut method yields acceptable visual results for near-right-angle cases.
source_quote: but as long as acute angles are nearly 90° this isn't very noticeable.
example_context: Revolved-cut fillet terminations in SolidWorks/Inventor when angles are near 90°

subject: depth per pass relative to end mill diameter
main_point: Limit depth of cut per pass to no more than half the cutter diameter; with sub‑millimeter tools this means making many shallow passes instead of a few deep ones.
source_quote:
As a general rule, your depth per pass should never exceed half the
diameter of your bit.
example_value: For a 0.8 mm bit, take about 0.4 mm or less per pass (e.g., five or more passes to reach ~2 mm).

subject: epoxy resin heat sensitivity during machining
main_point: Submerging a carbon‑fiber composite workpiece in water helps prevent heat buildup in the epoxy matrix, avoiding resin‑related complications during cutting.
source_quote: Performing the cut in a water bath probably resolves any heating of the epoxy which would certainly complicate the project.
example_value: The OP is cutting carbon fiber composite underwater to control heat.
example_context: Carbon fiber composite (epoxy matrix) machining with a water bath for cooling

subject: fixturing to prevent workpiece vibration
main_point: Rigidly secure the workpiece to a sacrificial board to eliminate workpiece vibration during cutting.
source_quote: Ensure that your work piece is well secured to the sacrificial sub-board. You very much do not want vibration on the work while cutting.

subject: double-stick tape workholding and heat-assisted release for CFRP
main_point: Double‑stick carpet tape is a common way to hold small carbon‑fiber composite parts; releasing the tape may require heat, which the composite can tolerate provided the epoxy is not overheated.
source_quote: Double stick carpet tape is a common substance and may require heating to remove without breaking the part, but carbon fiber composite can handle temperatures well enough as long as the epoxy resin is not damaged.
example_context: Workholding thin carbon‑fiber composite parts on a sacrificial board

subject: wood debris buildup on small end mills
main_point: When milling hard maple with a very small (0.8 mm) end mill, wood dust and resin can compact around the tool into a solid, soap-like disk. This accumulation can occur on the cutter during the cut.
source_quote: The end-mill accumulates a quite solid disk of wood debris. It has the consistency of soap and looks like a fine dust glued together with wood resin.
example_context: milling hard maple with a 0.8 mm end mill

subject: chip compaction from high speed and pressure
main_point: High cutting speed and pressure can compact chips together into a solid mass, similar to pellet formation during machining.
source_quote: Likely the speed and pressure is causing the chips to combine much like pellets are made.
example_context: machining operations where chips are subjected to high speed and pressure leading to compaction

subject: mitigating chip build-up with speed reduction and cleaning cycles
main_point: To prevent chip compaction on the tool, lower the cutting speed and include periodic cleaning stops to clear debris.
source_quote: Reduce the speed and stop for cleaning cycles.
example_context: situations where chips begin to accumulate on the tool due to compaction

subject: tool stick-out cross-section vs rigidity
main_point: Increasing the portion of a tool’s protruding length that remains at full shank diameter increases its strength and stiffness. A short cutting length on a full-diameter shank will be more rigid than having more reduced cross-section/fluted length extending from the holder.
source_quote: which would result in most of the stick out being full cross section which should help strength and rigidity.

subject: drill vs end mill flute geometry
main_point: Drill flutes are intended solely for chip evacuation. End mills have cutting edges and relief ground on their flutes, enabling them to cut on the side.
source_quote: Flutes of a drill bit are ground only for chip extraction, where as end mills take the chip extraction flute and grind an actual cutting edge on it ( b - c ) and some relief (c - d).

subject: adding side-cutting edges to drills cost impact
main_point: Adding side-cutting geometry to drill flutes would significantly increase manufacturing cost. This is a deterrent to making drills with end mill-like flute edges.
source_quote: And as far as grinding cutting edges on the flutes of a drill, for one it would make drills much more expensive to manufacture.

subject: resharpening practice for end mills vs small drills
main_point: Shops commonly resharpen end mills, but this author replaces any drill under 1/2 inch instead of resharpening. This practice reduces the handling cost/effort on small drills compared to sharpening.
source_quote: In manufacturing environments, end mills are generally re-sharpened, for me, any drill under 1/2" gets replaced.
example_context: Manufacturing environments; personal practice threshold at 1/2 inch drill diameter

subject: drill chuck limitation under side-milling forces
main_point: Drill chucks are not built to handle the radial loads from side milling. Adding side-cutting edges to a drill could encourage improper use that the chuck cannot safely withstand.
source_quote: Drill chucks are not designed to withstand the radial cutting forces of side milling so a cutting edge on a drill flute would give a false sense of acceptable practice.

subject: jobber-length drill deflection under side loads
main_point: The long length of cut of typical drills makes them radially weak. As a result, jobber-length drills deflect excessively and are unsuitable for side milling.
source_quote: That added LOC of a drill substantially weakens it in the radial direction. So standard, jobbers length drills would deflect far too much to be a usable side miller.
example_value: He contrasts a 1/2 inch end mill with about 1 inch LOC to a 3/16 inch drill cutting roughly 2 inches deep.

subject: flute-edge drills for materials that close up during deep drilling
main_point: Certain drills include a modest cutting edge on the flute to assist in materials that close up during deep drilling. This feature helps in alloys like bronze or copper that tend to pinch the tool as the hole deepens.
source_quote: Some drills have somewhat of a cutting edge ground into the flute, but from my experience, its for helping cut materials that tend to "close up" on you as you drill deep into a hole, bronze/copper/etc.
example_context: Deep-hole drilling in materials such as bronze or copper that tend to close up around the tool

subject: hardened toothed insert/washer to prevent sliding under clamp load
main_point: Use a hardened, double-sided toothed intermediate piece (e.g., a serrated washer/insert) clamped by the bolt to mechanically key the mating parts. The teeth bite into the titanium under preload, preventing sliding without needing precision-grooved surfaces.
source_quote: It might be easier to add a part that has teeth machined on to both sides of it from a hard material that under the clamping pressure of the bolt will dig the teeth into the titanium parts.
example_value: A toothed part on both sides, clamped by the bolt, that digs into the titanium surfaces.
example_context: bolted joints between Grade 4 titanium parts where sliding must be prevented

subject: cost of toothed insert/washer vs machining matched grooves
main_point: Adding a toothed insert/washer can be more economical than precision-machining matching grooves into both mating parts, since it avoids tight-tolerance features on multiple components.
source_quote: This might also be cheaper than trying to make properly toleranced grooves on both parts.
example_context: designs weighing precision machined mating grooves against a toothed insert/washer to resist sliding

subject: serrated/toothed washer biting action under tightening
main_point: Serrated/toothed washers create a mechanical interlock by biting into the mating surface when the bolt is tightened. This improves resistance to slip or relative motion at the joint interface.
source_quote: The solution I'm proposing is from a type of washer that digs into the material as you tighten the bolt.
example_context: use of toothed (star/serrated) lock washers in bolted joints

subject: adding a second bolt to increase joint clamping force
main_point: Using two bolts instead of one increases the total clamp load available in the joint, raising frictional resistance to shear and helping prevent slip. This is a simpler mechanical solution than adding interlocking surface features when geometry allows adding another fastener.
source_quote: You can also try adding a second bolt next to the first one if possible to increase the clamping force if possible, this will be simpler than what I propose in my other answer.

subject: using higher grade bolts to increase preload/strength
main_point: Selecting a higher-grade bolt increases fastener strength, allowing a higher achievable preload and thus greater clamping capacity for the joint. This can improve resistance to sliding without changing the bolt size or joint layout.
source_quote: If not possible, changing the grade of the bolt to a higher one to provide higher strength might work.

subject: triangular (60°) hole lattice in perforated sheets
main_point: Standard perforated sheets use equal-diameter holes arranged on a 60° triangular grid, with each hole equidistant to two holes in the adjacent row.
source_quote: Typical perforated sheets have regularly spaced equal diameter holes on a 60 degree spacing, that is the hole in one row is equidistant to two holes on the next row, which are also the same distance apart.

subject: uniform thickness reduction vs perforation (strength for equal weight saving)
main_point: For the same reduction in weight, uniformly thinning the plate yields a stronger plate than removing material via perforations.
source_quote: As you can see reducing the thickness gives a stronger plate for a given weight reduction.
example_value: Author compared strength ratios from a perforated-metal data source to a curve for uniformly reducing thickness.
example_context: mechanical strength of perforated sheet versus uniformly thinned solid plate from manufacturer strength curves

subject: strong vs weak direction in perforated sheets
main_point: In perforated sheets, the strong direction corresponds to failure across the rows of holes, while the weak direction corresponds to failure along a row of holes.
source_quote: Strong way involves breaking the plate across the rows of holes, whereas weak is breaking it along each row of holes.

subject: stress concentration in centrally located perforated region
main_point: If the perforated region is centered within a larger unperforated plate, that weakened region will carry the highest stresses and control failure.
source_quote: This ignores the rest of the plate which is unperforated, but assuming the perforated plate is in the middle of the larger one it will see the highest stresses.
example_context: larger plate with a centrally located perforated sub-plate under load

subject: Saint-Venant principle (insensitivity to remote boundaries)
main_point: Local stresses near applied loads are largely unaffected by details of distant boundaries, so far-field plate details have minimal influence on the loaded perforated region.
source_quote: That is, the remote boundary conditions have little effect on the stress field near the loads.

subject: strength loss disproportionate to weight saving in perforated/thinned plates
main_point: Weight savings can come with disproportionately large strength penalties; on the order of a 20% weight reduction accompanying roughly a 50% strength reduction.
source_quote: What is apparent is that even a small weight reduction implies a large strength reduction. 20% vs 50%, say.
example_value: Author references plotted strength-ratio curves for perforated sheets and a reduced-thickness plate.
example_context: strength-versus-weight curves for perforated metal and uniform thickness reduction from manufacturer data

subject: use FEA to evaluate perforation patterns and strength tradeoffs
main_point: Use finite element analysis to study and compare hole patterns and thickness strategies when you cannot perform physical tests.
source_quote: The best way to investigate this (other than physical testing) would be FEA.

subject: near-optimality of 60° hole spacing for strength/weight
main_point: Comparative strength-versus-weight curves suggest a 60° triangular spacing is close to optimal, especially at high weight reductions.
source_quote: The proximity of the curves at high weight reductions is what makes me think the 60 degree spacing is near optimal.
example_context: perforated sheet strength curves compared to uniform thickness reduction at high porosity

subject: uniform hole size and grid as baseline design
main_point: Start with equal-size holes on a uniform grid as a baseline; any further strength gains likely come from more complex, edge-sensitive layouts.
source_quote: It is intuitively obvious that the holes should be the same size, on a uniform grid, but there may be some complex arrangement that would improve the strength especially near the edges.
example_context: perforated plate designs where edge effects might motivate non-uniform patterns

subject: mass reduction depends on total removed area, not hole count
main_point: For a target mass reduction, only the total removed area matters; using few large holes or many small ones is equivalent in theory for weight.
source_quote: The size of the holes and the spacing result in a given mass reduction, but in theory it makes no difference whether the holes are few and large or small and  numerous. In theory.

subject: symmetrical periodic hole patterns (honeycomb/hex) for perforated sheets
main_point: Select symmetrical, connected, periodic perforation layouts when removing material from a subsheet S. Honeycomb/hexagonal perforations are a suitable pattern to implement this approach.
source_quote: You can use symmetrical, connected, periodic hole patterns such as Honeycomb / hexagonal perforations in S.

subject: square or staggered circular hole layouts with edge spacing control
main_point: Square or staggered circular perforation patterns are another viable option, provided you maintain careful edge-to-edge spacing between holes. Ensuring adequate spacing is a key design consideration for these layouts.
source_quote: You can also use Square or staggered circular holes with careful edge spacing.

subject: equivalent strip beam model for perforated plate
main_point: For a conservative design of a perforated plate, reduce the problem to a single intact strip and analyze it as a simply supported beam under a uniform line load. This provides a safe load path estimate when most material is removed except a strip.
source_quote: Model this strip as a simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed load along its length.
example_value: The answer assumes all plate material is removed except for one continuous strip that carries the load.
example_context: Conservative modeling of a perforated plate under uniform out-of-plane load by treating the remaining continuous strip as a simply supported beam.

subject: bending vs shear control and von Mises check
main_point: When sizing the remaining strip, expect bending to govern rather than shear, but still evaluate combined stresses with a von Mises criterion. This ensures you do not overlook shear contributions in a conservative check.
source_quote: Realistically, the bending stress will control over the shear stress, but for completeness' sake, you should consider both via the von Mises stress.
example_context: Beam-like analysis of a perforated plate’s remaining load path under uniform load.

subject: bending stress from moment and section modulus
main_point: Maximum bending stress in a beam is obtained by dividing the maximum bending moment by the section modulus. This is the standard relationship used for beam stress evaluation.
source_quote: Divide the maximum bending moment by the section modulus to obtain the maximum bending stress:

subject: strip width sizing against yield
main_point: Size the width of the remaining strip by checking calculated bending (von Mises) stress against the material’s yield; if it exceeds yield, increase the strip width. Iterate until the strip does not yield under the applied load.
source_quote: Compare this bending (von Mises) stress to the yield stress of your aluminum, and if the bending (von Mises) stress exceeds yield, then increase a (the width of the strip).
example_context: Design of an aluminum plate with a retained continuous strip under uniform load.

subject: preserving continuous strip as load path for perforations
main_point: After the continuous strip is sized to stay elastic, you may remove material elsewhere freely provided you do not perforate the strip. Keeping an unperforated load path maintains the design’s capacity.
source_quote: Once a (the width of the strip) is wide enough to not exceed yield, you are free to punch holes anywhere in the area as long as they do not overlap this strip.
example_context: Conservative design of a perforated plate under uniform load where one continuous strip carries the load.

subject: twist drill hole bottom geometry
main_point: Twist drills do not create flat-bottomed holes; their geometry leaves the bottom non-flat, so they are not suitable when a flat-bottomed recess is required.
source_quote: twist drills don't make flat holes

subject: tool choice for making flat-bottom counterbore holes
main_point: To create a flat-bottom recess for a bolt head, select an end mill or a counterbore tool rather than a standard twist drill.
source_quote: Use an end mill or counterbore.

subject: resharpening a twist drill to flatten a hole bottom
main_point: If dedicated tools aren’t available, you can regrind a twist drill to a flat-cutting geometry and use it to flatten the bottom after first drilling to depth.
source_quote: At a pinch, a drill can be re-sharpened to flatten a hole, pre-drill to depth then flatten.

subject: using washers to create a flat bearing surface in concave counterbores
main_point: If a twist drill leaves a concave-bottom recess instead of a flat counterbore, you can insert thick washers in the depressions so bolt heads bear on a flat surface. This provides a practical seating fix when you cannot produce a true flat-bottom counterbore.
source_quote: As a last resort, I could drill the countersink holes with a twist drill. Then fill the concave depressions with thick washers so the bolt heads would sit on a flat surface.
example_context: Bolted joints where counterbore/countersink recesses are drilled with a twist drill, leaving a concave bottom.

subject: using an end mill in a drill press
main_point: Milling with an end mill held in a drill press can produce severe vibration that rapidly dulls and chips the tool. This setup is not suitable for stable milling operations.
source_quote: I bought a 3/4-inch drill press chuck and a 1-inch endmill with 3/4-inch shank. But it didn't work very well. There was an incredible amount of vibration and it quickly dulled and chipped the endmill.
example_value: Tried a 1-inch end mill with a 3/4-inch shank in a 3/4-inch drill press chuck; the cut vibrated heavily and the end mill dulled and chipped quickly.
example_context: Drill presses used for milling operations with end mills

subject: drill press as milling machine
main_point: A drill press is a poor substitute for a milling machine and should not be expected to perform milling tasks effectively.
source_quote: It's not surprising that a drill press makes a poor milling machine.
example_context: Drill presses attempting milling operations

subject: PCB houses metal front panel fabrication capability
main_point: Many PCB fabrication vendors also offer metal front panel manufacturing, providing accurate hole machining and silkscreened graphics. This can be used as a precise faceplate for enclosures when small, accurately located holes are required.
source_quote: Several of the PCB manufacturing houses can make very professional metal panels with precision holes, silkscreen, etc.
example_value: Example vendor referenced: Beta-Layout (image source).
example_context: Front panel fabrication services offered by PCB manufacturing houses

subject: step drill for enlarging enclosure holes
main_point: When fitting a separate front panel, open up large clearance holes in the enclosure using a step drill. Step drills are well-suited for quickly creating clean, oversize holes in thin-walled enclosures.
source_quote: This gives you the option of drilling extra large holes in the box (a step-drill is great for this)
example_context: Drilling extra-large clearance holes in an enclosure to accommodate a separate front panel

subject: enclosure cutout leaving rim to support front panel
main_point: Instead of drilling many precise holes, you can remove most of the enclosure’s top and leave a perimeter rim to support a separate front panel. This creates a stable seat for a metal faceplate that carries all precise cutouts.
source_quote: or cutting out most of the box top and leaving enough to support the edges of the front panel.
example_context: Modifying a plastic or metal enclosure to mount a separate metal front panel

subject: cost of PCB-house-made front panels
main_point: In the author’s past experience, front panel services from PCB manufacturers were cost-effective relative to the quality delivered. This suggests such panels can be an economical choice for small runs.
source_quote: The last time I looked (a good few years ago) I thought the prices were reasonable for the quality of the product.
example_context: Pricing from PCB manufacturing houses offering metal front panel services, as seen a few years prior

subject: very fine thread taps
main_point: When working with very fine threads, taps tend to break very easily, making re-cutting such tiny threads risky due to tool fragility.
source_quote: recutting threads that fine is a pain. the taps are hard to find and very easily broken.
example_value: Attempting to re-tap eyeglasses screw threads around 1.4–1.5 mm.
example_context: very small thread sizes (around M1.4–M1.5), such as eyeglasses screws

subject: thread-locking adhesive vs buying a fine tap for repair
main_point: For repairing stripped tiny threads, using thread-locking adhesive is generally easier and significantly cheaper than sourcing and using a fine tap to re-cut the threads.
source_quote: @Rich's answer (using thread-locking adhesive) is your best bet: easy and cheaper by far than buying a tap.
example_value: Fixing a loose eyeglasses screw by applying thread-lock instead of re-tapping to 1.5 mm.
example_context: repairing very small threaded joints (e.g., eyeglasses screws around 1.4–1.5 mm)

subject: cutting tap predrill size vs chip removal
main_point: With a cutting tap, material is removed as chips, so the pilot bore can match the tap’s internal (minor) diameter without needing extra clearance for displaced material.
source_quote: When you are using a cutting tap, the tap removes material in the form of small chips. This means that the bore size can be the same size as the internal diameter of the tap.

subject: forming tap predrill size and material displacement
main_point: Forming taps displace rather than remove material, so the pilot hole must be larger than the tap’s internal (minor) diameter to provide space for the flowed material.
source_quote: When you are using a forming tap, no material is removed; it is displaced, which makes for a smoother thread. In this case the bore size would need to be larger than the internal diameter of the tap. There has to be space for that material to be moved into.
example_value: For M1.6×0.35, McMaster lists a 1.25 mm bore for a cutting tap vs 1.42 mm for a forming tap.

subject: forming tap failure in undersized bore
main_point: Attempting to use a forming tap in a bore smaller than the tap’s required internal/minor diameter will fail because there is insufficient space for displaced material.
source_quote: So I think that if the present bore is smaller than that of the forming tap you will not succeed.

subject: key/keyway anti-rotation function
main_point: A keyed shaft uses a longitudinal key and keyway so the key transmits torque and prevents the pulley from rotating relative to the shaft. This geometric interface locks rotation between the shaft and hub.
source_quote: key stock (square-profile steel) is inserted to prevent the pulley from rotating on the shaft
example_value: The user describes V-belt pulleys using keyed shafts.

subject: aviation shears starter hole for internal cuts
main_point: To cut an internal hole in sheet material with aviation shears, you must first create a starter hole to insert the shears into the workpiece.
source_quote: However, the shears would need a starter hole to be made

subject: circular shear-type hole cutter
main_point: Fabricate a circular shear-style hole cutter and drive it against a backing surface with a hammer or press to punch the hole cleanly. This tool-based approach is effective for cutting holes in lead sheet.
source_quote: Make a hole cutter like a shear against a surface and hit or press through.
example_value: The cutter can be made in required diameters such as 6", 9", or 12".
example_context: Cutting holes in lead sheet using a hammer or arbor press.

subject: lead sheet shearability
main_point: Lead is sufficiently soft that it can be readily sheared by a ring-like cutter, similar to how pastry cutters work.
source_quote: Similar to those pastry cutters, lead cuts easy enough.

subject: starter hole in sheet using hole or wad punch
main_point: When starting a hole in sheet material, consider using a hole punch or wad punch for the initial opening, provided the backing situation allows it.
source_quote: Depending on what's behind the sheet, you could use a hole punch (or wad punch, they're distinct) to put the initial hole through.
example_context: Sheet metal punching where the underlying support/clearance allows use of a hole or wad punch without damage or interference.

subject: hand nibbler chip form and debris generation
main_point: A hand nibbler removes material as a continuous ribbon, producing much less dust or small swarf than cutting methods that chip or grind.
source_quote: which will cut out a ribbon rather than produce dust or relatively small swarf.

subject: drilling debris generation
main_point: Proper drilling produces chips rather than airborne dust; dust generation typically occurs only when the tool is misused (e.g., inappropriate speed/feed).
source_quote: A drill won't kick up dust. It will produce cuttings, but not dust unless you're abusing it.
example_context: Drilling lead sheet

subject: drilling lead speed and feed selection
main_point: When drilling lead, use low spindle speed and a steady feed that maintains uniform chip thickness to produce manageable chips and keep temperatures low enough to avoid lead vapor.
source_quote: Drill at slow speed and a feed rate that ensures uniform chip thickness. It The chips will be easy to handle, and the temperatures will not lead to lead vapour.
example_context: Drilling lead sheet

subject: using steel hole punches on lead
main_point: For lead sheet, standard steel-rated hole punches are suitable, and using a press allows punching without a pilot hole.
source_quote: Punching it with hole punches made for steel should present no problem - and if you rig in a press you will not need a pilot hole.
example_context: Punching lead sheet on an arbor press

subject: manual holemaking with a chisel
main_point: You can create a hole by striking with a chisel and hammer, and using a narrow chisel gives better control so the hole size can meet the required tolerance.
source_quote: Use a chisel and hammer. A narrow chisel will allow you to make a hole within the tolerance you need.

subject: tool coating effects
main_point: Applying coatings such as TiN or TiCN to forming/cutting taps and drill bits increases tool life, reduces heat generation, and enables smoother drilling.
source_quote: I understand that the coating(Tin,Ticn),on forming/cutting taps,drilling bits etc,makes them last longer,run cooler,drill smoother.
example_context: TiN/TiCN coatings on forming/cutting taps and drilling bits

subject: self-tapping vs self-drilling screw selection
main_point: When a hole already exists, select a self-tapping screw (which cuts its own threads) rather than a self-drilling screw.
source_quote: The hole is already there. You're looking for a self-tapping screw - one which will cut its own threads.

subject: shoulder screw function in hinges
main_point: Replacing a shoulder-type hinge screw with a non-shoulder self-tapper removes the shoulder that prevents clamping, so tightening can pinch the hinge and cause high friction.
source_quote: You won't have the benefit of the shoulder on the screw to allow you to lock it down without pinching the hinge tight and running high friction on the hinge.
example_value: Eyeglass hinges commonly use shoulder screws to avoid binding when tightened.
example_context: hinge joints fastened by shoulder-type screws (e.g., eyeglass hinges)

subject: clearance hole enlargement when upsizing screws
main_point: Upsizing to a larger screw requires enlarging all related clearance holes in the mating parts so the fastener can pass and assemble properly.
source_quote:
- You'll need to enlarge the clearance hole in the top of the frame hinge screw entry point.
- You'll need to enlarge the clearance hole in the arm.
example_value: For an eyeglass hinge, both the frame’s hinge entry and the arm’s clearance holes must be opened up.

subject: selecting self-tapping screw by minor diameter relative to bore
main_point: To maximize thread engagement in a worn bore, choose a self-tapping screw whose thread minor diameter is smaller than the existing bore diameter.
source_quote: pick one with a thread minor-diameter < 1.4 mm. Then the threads will have maximum grip.
example_value: Minor diameter less than 1.4 mm in the eyeglass hinge case.

subject: clearance hole drill sizing to screw major diameter
main_point: Size the clearance drill to match the screw’s major thread diameter so the screw passes freely through the clearance holes.
source_quote: Take note of the major thread diameter and buy a drill bit to suit for the clearance holes.

subject: M1.6 metric tap drill size
main_point: The correct tap drill for an M1.6 thread is 1.25 mm, followed by tapping with an M1.6 tap. Use this drill size when re-tapping to M1.6.
source_quote: If you did drill out and re-tap the hole, you would use a 1.25mm drill (which is the tap drill size for a M1.6 screw) and then follow that with a M1.6 tap.

subject: hand drilling/tapping of micro holes
main_point: For very small features, avoid a power drill and instead use a pin vise to drill/tap by hand. Expect alignment to be more difficult with manual operation.
source_quote: And you would not use a power drill, because if you had an appropriate drill and setup you wouldn't have asked your post. You would use a pin vise and do it manually by hand but that makes alignment much more difficult.
example_value: Re-tapping a worn eyeglass screw hole around 1.4–1.6 mm.
example_context: Manual drilling/tapping of tiny holes (e.g., ~M1.6 in eyeglass frames or similar micro hardware).

subject: measurement of small diameters—micrometer vs calipers
main_point: Do not rely on calipers for high-precision measurement of very small diameters; use a micrometer instead for accuracy.
source_quote: For the precision you require and the diameters you are working with, caliper measurement should not be trusted.You would need a micrometer for that.
example_value: Verifying a nominal 1.4 mm screw/feature size.
example_context: Measuring ~1–2 mm diameters where tight fit and precision are critical (e.g., eyeglass hardware).

subject: pin retention by flaring ends
main_point: If a small press-fit pin won’t hold, flare both ends with a punch to mechanically capture it and keep it in place.
source_quote: If you can't get a press fit to work, then you cal also flare the pin on both ends of the pin with a punch to get it to stay in.
example_value: Using a flared pin instead of a tiny screw in a worn hole.
example_context: Repairing small assemblies (e.g., eyeglass hinges) by pinning when threads are no longer reliable.

subject: thread forming vs cutting for very small threads
main_point: For extremely small threads, thread-forming is likely more effective than cutting threads. This can improve outcomes in tiny, delicate features.
source_quote: Forming a thread does seem like it would work better than cutting a thread for something this small.
example_value: Using M1.4 self-forming screws in soft metal to reform threads.
example_context: Very small fasteners (around M1.4) in soft metals such as eyeglass frames.

subject: self-forming screw re-forming worn threads—removal risk
main_point: Reforming a worn thread with a same-size self-forming screw can lock the screw in, making later removal unsafe or damaging. Consider this irreversibility before attempting.
source_quote: I would try the M1.4 first to see if you can't just reform the thread. But it will probably not be removable safely after that.
example_value: Attempting to reform a worn M1.4 thread with an M1.4 self-forming screw.
example_context: Using small self-forming screws in soft metal components (e.g., eyeglass frames).

subject: alignment and breakage risk in micro drilling/tapping
main_point: In very small, short holes, manual drilling/tapping risks misalignment, cross-threading, or tool/part breakage. These features are unforgiving to setup errors.
source_quote: It's just so small and short your that the alignment is going to be off or something is going to cross thread or break.
example_value: Trying to drill and tap a tiny worn screw hole by hand.
example_context: Reworking micro-size threaded holes (e.g., ~M1.4–M1.6) in small assemblies like eyewear.

subject: availability of M1.4 self-forming screws for soft metal
main_point: Commercial M1.4 self-forming screws intended for soft metals are available from suppliers. These provide a thread-forming option at very small sizes.
source_quote: I did look at on McMaster-Carr and there are M1.4 "self-forming screws for soft metal".
example_value: Sourcing M1.4 self-forming screws via McMaster-Carr.
example_context: Fastener sourcing for tiny threads in soft-metal components.

subject: weight-relief cutouts in bicycle hub cage
main_point: The geometric center cutouts in the hub cage are not for structural purposes; they are primarily to reduce mass. Simple drilled holes can provide equivalent weight savings.
source_quote: No and yes. They add lightness!
example_context: bicycle hub/cage flange design for an internal gear hub

subject: spoke path over flat 90b0 flange edge
main_point: If the flange edges are changed to plain 90b0 angles instead of being conical or tilted, the outer spokes will bend sharply as they pass the edge. This produces a kink at the flange interface.
source_quote: That means the outer spokes will be kinked as they go over the edge.
example_context: bicycle wheel hub flange geometry

subject: hub conical profile alignment to rim centerline
main_point: Design the hubs conical/flange profile so the spoke line reaches the rims centerline. You should account for this alignment in any replacement part to avoid spoke misalignment.
source_quote: I don't know for sure but I imagine the real hubs conical profile will intercept the rim on its centreline. I think you need to address this.
example_context: bicycle hub design and spoke-to-rim alignment

subject: compound cross slide angular adjustment
main_point: On lathes equipped with a compound cross slide, you can rotate and feed the compound to cut faces at arbitrary angles, enabling angled flanges without complex multi-axis machining.
source_quote: The upper slide can rotate to any angle.
example_value: The response notes the OP can have the hub flanges tilted as desired using a lathe.
example_context: engine lathes with a compound cross slide

subject: bicycle spoke tension typical range
main_point: Bicycle wheel spokes carry substantial preload, commonly about 80–110 lbf, which imposes significant loads on the hub flanges.
source_quote: spokes are under quite a lot of tension (typically around 80-110 pounds).
example_context: bicycle wheel spoke tension and hub flange loading

subject: aluminum alloy and heat treatment for hub flanges
main_point: Given spoke tension loads, aluminum hub flanges should use high-strength alloys such as 6061 or 7075 and be heat treated to achieve adequate strength.
source_quote: To withstand that, the flanges do need to be pretty strong--if you're getting them made out of aluminum, you probably want something like 6061 or 7075 (and you probably want it heat treated as well).
example_context: aluminum bicycle hub flanges under spoke tension

subject: layered tamper-evident construction
main_point: Use a composite approach for tamper evidence: a hard, difficult-to-breach outer shell combined with a delicate inner liner that bears fine, hard-to-replicate features. Intrusion then requires breaching the tough exterior without damaging the fragile indicator, making undetected access far more difficult.
source_quote: Try an extremely tough material on the outside, and an very fragile material on the inside which contains microprint, or some other information not easily replicated.
example_value: Inner liner carries microprint or other information not easily replicated.

subject: material impenetrability
main_point: There is no truly impenetrable material; any substance can be breached by some method. Security should therefore be based on design strategies rather than relying solely on material resistance.
source_quote: No material is impenetrable, so the idea would be to make it very difficult to break the outside while being sufficiently gentle with the inside.

subject: anti-replication fragile liner
main_point: Design the fragile indicator liner so it embeds information distributed throughout its volume that is destroyed upon breach, preventing an attacker from replicating and replacing it to hide tampering.
source_quote: Assuming you succeed in that, you will then have to make sure the fragile indicating liner cannot be simply replicated and replaced. For that you will need it to contain some time of information throughout that is destroyed if the liner is destroyed.

subject: unknown internal information for tamper evidence
main_point: Embedding unknown information inside the container is essential, because an attacker can build a replica of the container to conceal entry; only altering or destroying hidden, unknown data upon opening provides reliable tamper evidence.
source_quote: Really, storage of unknown information within the container itself is the critical part here, because if we look at this as a thought experiment, it will generally be possible to replicate the container entirely, thus eliminating any evidence that it was opened.

subject: template jig with drill bushes for three-hole drilling
main_point: For a conventional part requiring three drilled holes, selecting a template jig equipped with appropriately sized drill bushings is a suitable approach. This is the author’s preferred jig choice in that scenario.
source_quote:
if it would have conventional product for drilling three holes, i would have chossen 
template jig
 and 
drill bushes of suitable dimension
example_context: Conventional products with three holes to be drilled

subject: use of additive plastic drill jigs based on tolerance
main_point: If part tolerances are permissive, 3D-printed plastic drill jigs can be a cost-effective choice. Choose them when precision requirements don’t demand a metal jig.
source_quote: Depending on your tolerances, it may be a reasonable case for some cheap additive plastic jigs.
example_context: Parts with moderate/loose tolerances where a plastic (additively manufactured) drill jig is acceptable

subject: avoiding cutter contact with plastic jigs
main_point: Design plastic drill jigs so the cutting edges do not contact the plastic to prolong jig life. Guide on non-cutting features instead.
source_quote: For long life of a jig try to avoid cutter contact with the plastic.
example_context: Plastic drill jigs and guides used to steer rotating cutting tools

subject: metal inserts in plastic jigs for heat management
main_point: Use metal inserts in plastic jigs to handle heat and reduce thermal damage or wear at guide interfaces.
source_quote: Metal inserts help with heat also!
example_context: Plastic (polymer) drill jigs that interface with rotating tools

subject: jig guiding on tool shank larger than cutter
main_point: When the tool’s shank is larger than the cutting diameter, design the jig to contact only the shank to reduce wear and extend jig life.
source_quote: If the shank is a larger diameter than the cutter, having the jig only youch the shank will extend the life of the jig.
example_context: Guided drilling with reduced-neck or small-diameter cutting tips where the shank diameter exceeds the cutting diameter

subject: adding bearings/collars/bushings to drill bits for guidance
main_point: Fitting drill bits with bearings, collars, or bushings provides non-cutting contact surfaces that protect the jig and maintain guidance.
source_quote: You can also add bearings, collars, or even bushings to bits to achieve the same or better effect.
example_context: Guided drilling operations where a plastic or soft jig would otherwise contact the cutting edges

subject: chip heat damaging plastic jigs
main_point: Hot, hard chips can damage plastic drill jigs if chip evacuation isn’t managed. Provide chip egress to prevent thermal/mechanical erosion of the jig.
source_quote: If the chips are hard and hot enough, they can damage a plastic jig.
example_context: Drilling metals with a plastic jig where chips are retained near the guide

subject: standard 2-flute drill walking and wearing jig
main_point: On irregular or unfriendly entry surfaces, standard 2‑flute drills tend to walk, which forces the cutter against the jig and gradually cuts into it.
source_quote: On that surface, a standard 2-flute drill point is going to want to walk. That equates to cutter forced against jig, cutting into it over time.
example_context: Using a twist drill with a guide on non-flat/angled/curved entry surfaces

subject: choosing alternative cutter to prevent drill walking/jig wear
main_point: Select a different cutter geometry to prevent walking and reduce jig wear, balancing the performance gain against added cost or complexity.
source_quote: You can solve that by using a different cutter, but may choose not to after weighing all costs.
example_context: Starting holes on challenging surfaces where a standard twist drill would wander and damage a guide

subject: motor bearing radial load capacity
main_point: When repurposing wheelchair motors to carry a wheel directly, confirm the motor bearings can handle the full wheel load; if they cannot, you should not load the wheel through the motor bearings. Instead, the wheel load must be supported by separate structure or bearings.
source_quote: it may be necessary if the wheelchair motors don't have bearings large enough to take the full load of the wheel.
example_value: The responder notes the OP’s external bearing approach may be necessary if the wheelchair motor bearings are undersized for the wheel load.
example_context: wheelchair drive motors used as wheel hubs on a rover robot

subject: misalignment accommodation between motor and wheel shaft
main_point: Use a compliant element between the motor and wheel shaft to tolerate misalignment. A flexible spider coupling or a belt drive are suitable options; alternatively, soft-mounting the motor can provide the needed compliance.
source_quote: You will probably want a spider coupler, or a belt between the wheel shaft and the wheelchair motor to handle any misalignment. Soft mounting the motors might also work.

subject: wheel hub-to-motor flange adapter design
main_point: If the motor bearings can support the wheel load, connect the wheel by making an adapter that matches the hub on one face and the motor’s bolt pattern on the other. Secure it to the hub with bolts (or a single large bolt through the shaft hole) and to the motor via its flange pattern; the adapter can be turned or 3D printed.
source_quote: If the wheelchair motors DO have strong enough bearings, you could make an aluminum adapter that attaches the motor flange to the hub. I would turn it on a lathe or 3D print it (you're probably going to want to learn it sometime). Basically make one side of it conform to the hub shape, and attach it with bolts, (or 1 large bolt through the shaft hole). The other face would have a hole pattern that matches the motor.
example_value: Adapter with a hub-conforming face bolted to the wheel hub and a motor-pattern face bolted to the motor flange; manufactured on a lathe or 3D printer.
example_context: wheelchair motors with sufficient bearing capacity used to directly mount wheels

subject: selection of cutting parameters
main_point: When setting drilling/turning/milling parameters, consider the work material, the cutting tool material, the relative cutting speed, and whether to use a cooling/lubricating medium.
source_quote:
Usually what happens when you are trying to determine parameters about drilling, lathing or milling a material you need to consider the following parameters:

- material that is being removed
- material of the bit that does the cutting
- the relative velocity between the material and the "bit".
- determine if a liquid medium is used to remove heat.

subject: primary considerations in machining
main_point: Across cutting operations, the two primary concerns are managing heat generation and ensuring rapid chip evacuation from the cutting zone.
source_quote:
There are two main considerations:

- heat developing due to removal of the material.
- quick removal of the material from the cutting area.

subject: tool life vs heat and speed
main_point: Excess heat rapidly degrades cutting tool properties, so running at high speed often shortens drill bit life.
source_quote: The concentration of heat is a parameter that affects the cutting bit and can lead to its very fast degradation of the properties. That is the reason that high speed is -in many cases- detrimental to the "life" of a drill bit.
example_context: Drilling and other metal-cutting operations where heat buildup at the tool–work interface is significant

subject: relation between speed, torque, and power in machining
main_point: Higher spindle speeds are typically associated with higher torque or power input from the machine.
source_quote: High speed is usually correlated (or driven) from high torque or high power input.

subject: heat mitigation via speed and feed reduction
main_point: To reduce heat-related problems in cutting, slow down by reducing spindle speed and feed rate.
source_quote:
Way to mitigate the problems caused by heat are:

- reducing rotational speed and feed rate

subject: use of water as coolant and corrosion risk
main_point: Using water as a cutting fluid can corrode the workpiece, so avoid plain water when corrosion is a concern.
source_quote: - introducing a lubricant for removing the excess heat as quickly (water should not be used because it might corroded the material).
example_context: Materials susceptible to corrosion (e.g., many ferrous alloys) during drilling/milling/turning

subject: tool geometry selection by material for chip evacuation
main_point: Choose cutting tool geometry to match the material (brittle vs. ductile, metal vs. plastic) so chips are evacuated as quickly as possible.
source_quote: The second issue (which is more common to drilling), is that you need to pick a geometry that for the type of material (e.g. brittle/ductile, metal/plastic) removes the excess material as quickly as possible.
example_context: Drilling different materials categorized by ductility (brittle vs ductile) and class (metal vs plastic)

subject: chip accumulation near cutting zone
main_point: Allowing chips to accumulate at the cutting region wastes time, dulls the tool, and can cause jamming.
source_quote: Keeping the material near the cutting region, is wasteful, it dulls the cutting bit, and can also lead to jams.

subject: feeds and speeds vary by material-tool-geometry combination
main_point: Optimal feed rates and spindle speeds depend on the specific combination of work material, tool material, and tool geometry.
source_quote: Different combinations of materials, cutting bits and cutting bits geometries have different optimal feed rates and rpms for drilling (but also for milling and lathing).

subject: drilling torque vs. material type (gray cast iron, aluminum, steel) at fixed RPM and feed
main_point: At identical RPM and feed, expected drilling torque ranks lowest for gray cast iron, low for aluminum, and medium to high for steel, with steel’s torque increasing with hardness. This provides a relative order of torque demand across these materials under equal cutting conditions.
source_quote: For the same RPM and feed ,the relative torque answer is; 1 . cast iron ( grey) = vey low, 2 aluminum = low ,3 steel medium to high depending on hardness.
example_context: Drilling operations run at the same RPM and feed across gray cast iron, aluminum, and steel, comparing relative torque.

subject: specific cutting force variability by material and treatment
main_point: The specific cutting force that governs drilling loads depends on the material, and also on its alloy composition and heat treatment. You cannot generalize by base metal alone; alloying and hardness significantly change cutting force.
source_quote: which varies by material.  Not just steel or aluminum - but what alloy (e.g. addition of lead acts as a lubricant and makes it easier to machine), and hardness treatment it has.

subject: specific cutting force typical values (Al, Fe, steel)
main_point: Typical specific cutting force values are on the order of 800 MPa for aluminum, 1500 MPa for iron, and 2500–3000 MPa for steel.
source_quote: In approximate terms: Aluminum 800 MPa, Iron 1500 MPa, Steel 2500-3000 MPa.
example_context: Common aluminum, iron, and steel alloys under comparable machining conditions

subject: relative torque requirement steel vs aluminum at equal parameters
main_point: At equal speed, feed, and tool geometry, expect roughly three times more power/torque to cut steel than aluminum due to higher specific cutting force.
source_quote: So very roughly 3x as much electricity or torque is required to cut steel vs aluminum (if same speed, feed, and geometry).
example_context: Comparing steel to aluminum at the same cutting speed, feed rate, and tool geometry

subject: specific energy (material removal) definition
main_point: Specific energy, expressed in J/mm^3, quantifies the energy needed to remove a unit volume of material during cutting.
source_quote: how much energy is required to remove a cubic millimeter.

subject: specific energy variation across steel and aluminum alloys
main_point: For certain alloy combinations, steel can require over 20 times the specific energy of aluminum to remove the same volume of material.
source_quote: According to Kalpajkian, the difference in specific energy can be more than 20x for some steel to aluminum alloys.
example_context: Some steel alloys compared to some aluminum alloys as reported by Kalpakjian

subject: leaded alloy machinability improvement
main_point: Adding lead to an alloy improves machinability because the lead acts as a lubricant during cutting.
source_quote: addition of lead acts as a lubricant and makes it easier to machine
example_context: Leaded steels or other leaded alloys

subject: pantograph belt
main_point: A pantograph belt is an appropriate mechanism to transmit rotation from a fixed drive to a moving wheel or tool within a plane. Use this linkage-driven belt system when the driven element must move while still receiving torque.
source_quote: you can use a pantograph belt.
example_context: Transmitting rotation to a tool or wheel that moves in a 2D plane relative to a fixed drive.

subject: pantograph belt industrial use
main_point: Pantograph belt systems are used in large machines to transmit rotation to a moving drill head, supporting motion paths such as cutting square shapes.
source_quote: They use them in large machines to transfer rotation to a moving drill to cut squares and what not.
example_value: Cutting squares with a moving drill driven via a pantograph belt.
