source_quote: HDPE is one lightest but toughest of all plastics in it's weight class, so idea for making your blades.
example_value: Cut the blades from commercially available HDPE sheet stock.
example_context: DIY windmill blades made from plastic sheet

subject: 1D element material/section orientation vector
main_point: Material orientation needs to be set explicitly for 1D elements; assign the section direction vector to <0 1 0> to define the orientation. Doing so ensures the model uses the intended material/section orientation.
source_quote: The material orientation matters. For 1D, give the  material(section) direction as <0 1 0>
example_context: MSC Patran 1D line/bar/truss elements (section orientation definition)

subject: SolidWorks 2021 view rotation behavior
main_point: In SolidWorks 2021, the default mouse-controlled view rotation snaps the model back to an upright orientation, removing the ability to hold arbitrary angles that earlier versions allowed.
source_quote: Currently in 2021, the model always returns to the upright position and this ability to rotate the model to any angle has been removed (at least in the default settings).
example_value: The asker notes that using the middle mouse in 2021 returns the model upright, unlike a 2019 example showing continuous rotation to any angle.
example_context: SolidWorks 2021 default mouse/viewport controls

subject: SolidWorks "Rotate About Scene Floor" rotation setting
main_point: In SolidWorks, the unusual rotation behavior is controlled by the "Rotate About Scene Floor" option; you can disable it by right‑clicking in the graphics area and unchecking that setting.
source_quote: I've found the setting which you inadvertently have selected - it's called "Rotate About Scene Floor" Simply right click off the model in the graphics area, and uncheck this option.
example_context: SolidWorks (graphics area UI setting)

subject: SolidWorks rotation behavior vs rendering packages when 'Rotate About Scene Floor' is enabled
main_point: Enabling "Rotate About Scene Floor" makes SolidWorks camera rotation mimic the behavior of some rendering packages, which users from those environments may prefer over the standard SolidWorks rotation.
source_quote: The reason one might choose this - is that it makes the camera rotation behave in a more similar way to some rendering packages. Users who are used to that environment will be as frustrated trying the 'normal way' as you were this way.
example_context: SolidWorks with 'Rotate About Scene Floor' enabled; users accustomed to rendering software controls

subject: axial load transfer and moment generation in pinned two-member joint
main_point: In this pinned, two-member leg, the applied top load is carried as axial forces in the connected members. The extension arm’s axial load goes directly to the bottom support, while in the other branch the vertical component continues down the vertical member and the horizontal component generates a base moment.
source_quote: The load at the top can transfer to both connected members just axially. The axial load in the extension arm is then directly transferred to the bottom support. The other axial load goes to the middle pin, where the vertical part continues axially along the vertical member and the horizontal part will induce a moment at the bottom load.
example_value: Top node with two members at angles carries load F as axial forces; horizontal component at the lower node induces a base moment.
example_context: Pinned two-member leg mechanism with an extension arm and a vertical member under a top load

subject: solving member axial forces via component equilibrium
main_point: Begin the analysis by writing equilibrium equations for the joint’s force components and solve for the unknown axial member forces from the applied load.
source_quote: $$F_c\cdot \cos(\alpha) -F_a\cdot\sin(\beta) = F$$
example_value: One component equation used is Fc·cos(α) − Fa·sin(β) = F.
example_context: Two angled members meeting at a loaded joint with angles α and β relative to axes

subject: base reaction moment from horizontal force component
main_point: The horizontal component of the axial force Fa produces a reaction moment at the base equal to Fa·cos(β) times the lever arm Lb.
source_quote:
Horizontal component of force 
$F_a$
 will create reaction moment 
$M_R$
:

$$M_R = F_a\cdot \cos(\beta)\cdot L_b$$
example_value: MR = Fa·cos(β)·Lb.
example_context: Pinned two-member leg with a base located a horizontal distance Lb from the joint carrying force Fa at angle β

subject: support reaction components from member force components
main_point: For this load path, the vertical support reaction equals the applied load (FRy = F), and the horizontal reaction equals the horizontal component of the member force (FRx = Fc·cos(α)).
source_quote:
Reaction force components are easy to calculate, 
$F_{Ry}$
 has magnitude of 
$F$
 and

$$F_{Rx} = F_c\cdot \cos(\alpha)$$
example_value: FRy = F; FRx = Fc·cos(α).
example_context: Pinned two-member leg mechanism where one member with force Fc makes angle α to produce a horizontal reaction at the base

subject: SolidWorks 'Up to Surface' end condition in linear patterns
main_point: In SolidWorks, linear-patterning an Extruded Cut that uses the Up To Surface end condition will make each patterned instance terminate on that same reference surface, so hole depths vary across the pattern when the surface is angled relative to the sketch plane.
source_quote: However, when I try to do this, each instance references the original end condition and so the depth of each hole created by the linear pattern is different due to the angle of the reference surface and the distance of the instance from the original "seed" feature.
example_value: A hole cut defined Up To Surface is patterned; because the target face is angled, instances farther from the seed end at different depths.
example_context: SolidWorks linear pattern of an Extruded Cut feature using 'Up to Surface' against an angled face

subject: SolidWorks merging feature behavior (Boss-Extrude)
main_point: In SolidWorks, when a boss-extrude is set to merge, any touching solids are combined into a single body.
source_quote: causes the two solids it touches to merge into one body.
example_value: The user's Boss-Extrude5 merged two solids into one body.
example_context: SolidWorks Boss-Extrude with Merge Result enabled, creating a feature pattern.

subject: SolidWorks non-merging feature creates new body
main_point: In SolidWorks, if a boss-extrude is not set to merge, it produces a new separate solid body instead of joining with existing geometry.
source_quote: You can see in the screenshot below it creates a separate solid body.
example_value: Boss-Extrude3 resulted in a separate solid body.
example_context: SolidWorks Boss-Extrude with Merge Result unchecked (non-merging).

subject: Enabling Merge Result to allow feature patterns
main_point: To successfully pattern a boss-extrude as a feature in SolidWorks, enable Merge Result so the feature merges with the existing body; leaving it non-merging prevents the pattern from succeeding.
source_quote: Checking this box 'fixes' your part, and allows the pattern to succeed as expected.
example_value: Toggling the Merge Result checkbox made the circular pattern work in the user's part.
example_context: SolidWorks circular feature pattern of a Boss-Extrude.

subject: Fully defining sketches in parametric CAD
main_point: As a best practice in parametric CAD modeling, fully define your sketches to ensure robust, predictable features and edits.
source_quote: to always fully define your sketches.

subject: SolidWorks pattern: switch from Features/Faces to Bodies
main_point: When a feature pattern fails in SolidWorks, change the pattern type to Bodies: deselect Features and Faces, select Bodies, and pick the solid body in the graphics area to successfully create the pattern.
source_quote: uncheck the Feature and faces then check the bodies check box.in graphic area select the body that yow wish to pattern
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling, Circular/Linear Pattern command using Bodies to pattern instead of Features/Faces

subject: SolidWorks geometry pattern limitation on merged features
main_point: In SolidWorks, attempting a Geometry Pattern on a feature whose faces merge with the main part body is not allowed and will fail with a patterning error.
source_quote: You cannot create geometry patterns of features that have faces merged with the rest of the part.
example_context: SolidWorks feature pattern (Geometry Pattern) behavior on merged-face features

subject: SolidWorks Simulation distributed bolt/pin/link connections large displacement limitation
main_point: In SolidWorks Simulation, the distributed connection features for bolts, pins, and links are not compatible with large-displacement analyses; attempting to use them when large displacements are present or enabled will produce an error.
source_quote: "Distributed connections based on bolts, pins, and links do not support large displacements."
example_value: While trying to hang a crane model using a link load, the solver stops with the stated error.
example_context: SolidWorks Simulation using distributed connections (bolts, pins, links) with large displacement behavior/option.

subject: SolidWorks inverse fillet modeling
main_point: To create an internal or concave "inverse fillet" feature in SolidWorks, use the Swept Cut tool instead of the Fillet feature. This produces the rounded removal (a groove) along a path rather than adding a round.
source_quote:
Use 
Swept Cut
example_context: SolidWorks CAD (e.g., SolidWorks 2024)

subject: flywheel stress maximum location
main_point: Standard stress equations for rotating flywheels predict that the maximum stress occurs at the center of the wheel. Any analysis or design assumption should recognize that the peak stress is at the center region.
source_quote: according to a flywheel's stress equation, the maximum stress occurs at the center of the wheel.

subject: FEA boundary conditions for rotating body (circumferential vs axial constraints)
main_point: In an FEA model of a rod/hub, constrain circumferential displacement on the rod’s cylindrical surface and constrain only the axial displacement at one or both rod ends. This keeps all nodes free to move radially (except those on the axis), avoiding over‑constraining radial motion.
source_quote: You could try to fix circumferential displacements at the cylindrical surface of the rod and then just fix axial displacement at one or both of the rod ends. This way, all nodes are able to freely move in radial direction (except the ones on the axis of course).
example_context: SolidWorks (or similar) FEA setup for a rotating flywheel/rod where boundary conditions must allow radial expansion

subject: cylindrical coordinate system requirement for circumferential displacement constraints (FEA)
main_point: To apply a circumferential displacement constraint in FEA, define a cylindrical coordinate system so the solver can reference the hoop direction.
source_quote: (You may need to ad cylindrical coordinate system to be able to fix circumferential displacements.)
example_context: SolidWorks Simulation or similar FEA tools when constraining circumferential DOF on cylindrical geometry

subject: SolidWorks tangency mate interpenetration
main_point: Using only a tangency mate to position a ball in SolidWorks allows the ball to rotate but does not prevent it from penetrating the other body; contact/collision is not enforced by that mate alone.
source_quote: I managed to do this through a tangency, but the ball “passes through” the second body.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly mates (tangent/contact behavior)

subject: Solidworks 'Thread Minor Diameter Inside' mapping to DIN 13-1 D1
main_point: In Solidworks Toolbox, the parameter labeled “Thread Minor Diameter Inside” corresponds to the DIN 13-1 D1 dimension, as inferred from predefined thread entries. This mapping helps align Toolbox fields with ISO thread standard dimensions.
source_quote:
I could get that the 
Thread Minor Diameter Inside
 is equivalent to 
D1
 in DIN 13-1 based on the values entered for already defined threads, such as M2x0.4.
example_value: The author compared predefined M2x0.4 data in Solidworks with DIN 13-1 values to deduce the equivalence.
example_context: Solidworks 2021 SP2.0 Toolbox thread data vs DIN 13-1 metric thread standard

subject: SolidWorks Thread Minor Diameter computation
main_point: In SolidWorks Toolbox/Hole Wizard for ISO metric threads, the Thread Minor Diameter is calculated as the Thread Minor Diameter Inside minus the g es tolerance offset from the standard.
source_quote:
Thread Minor Diameter
 = 
Thread Minor Diameter Inside
 - 
 g es
example_value: Author verified this relationship using an M2×0.4 example in a custom calculator.
example_context: SolidWorks Toolbox/Hole Wizard thread data fields using ISO metric thread definitions per BS 3643-1:1981 and DIN 13-1

subject: g es tolerance designation meaning
main_point: The symbol g es denotes the upper deviation (tolerance offset) for bolt threads as defined in BS 3643-1:1981.
source_quote:
g es
 = bolt thread g tolerance upper deviation offset in 
BS 3643-1:1981
example_context: ISO metric bolt thread tolerances per BS 3643-1:1981

subject: Thread Minor Diameter Inside mapping to DIN D1
main_point: In the SolidWorks thread data, Thread Minor Diameter Inside corresponds to the D1 dimension defined in DIN 13-1.
source_quote:
Thread Minor Diameter Inside
 = the D1 value you pointed out in DIN 13-1
example_context: SolidWorks Toolbox/Hole Wizard mapping of ISO metric thread parameters to DIN 13-1 dimensions

subject: g tolerance offset vs pitch
main_point: For ISO metric threads per BS 3643-1, the g tolerance offset (g es) varies directly with the thread pitch.
source_quote: The g tolerance offset value is directly related to the pitch (mm).
example_value: The author plotted g es versus pitch and fit a linear regression to build a calculator.
example_context: ISO metric bolt thread tolerances per BS 3643-1:1981

subject: parametric assembly relations controlling extrusion lengths
main_point: In SolidWorks, drive the frame with properly defined assembly relations so that changing the cabinet’s overall dimensions automatically updates the cut lengths of all extrusion members. This enables quick resizing without manually editing each piece.
source_quote: If you set the relations properly in your assembly you should be able to adjust the major dimensions of the cabinet and have all the extrusion lengths update automatically.
example_value: A cabinet model whose overall width/height/depth are changed will propagate new lengths to each frame extrusion through assembly relations.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies using parametric mates/relations

subject: master sketch or stub part driving frame assembly
main_point: Use a master sketch or a simple stub part to represent the cabinet’s final envelope, and mate the frame members to this driver so the assembly geometry updates from a single source. This simplifies controlling overall size and derived member lengths.
source_quote: I sometimes handle this by creating a master sketch, or a "stub" part representing the final dimensions of the cabinet.
example_value: Create a stub part that defines cabinet width, height, and depth, then constrain all frame members to it so resizing the stub resizes the frame.
example_context: Parametric CAD assembly modeling (e.g., SolidWorks)

subject: simplifying extrusion models to rectangular sections for planning
main_point: Simplify early design by modeling extrusions as rectangular sections rather than full profiles to quickly obtain accurate member lengths. Detailed fastening and profile-specific features can be worked out later.
source_quote: It might make sense to simplify the model by using rectangular extrusions instead of the the actual extruded profile.
example_value: Model frame members as simple rectangles to drive length calculations first, then add real profile geometry and fastener details afterward.

subject: Misumi SolidWorks extrusion plugin
main_point: Misumi provides a SolidWorks plugin that lets users insert aluminum extrusion profiles from Misumi’s catalog directly into a SolidWorks design. This streamlines selecting and placing catalog extrusions within that CAD environment.
source_quote: Misumi, a configurable components vendor, has a plugin that allows you to directly insert Aluminum extrusions from their catalog into solidworks:
example_value: Their RapidDesign plugin integrates Misumi catalog parts into SolidWorks via the linked service.
example_context: SolidWorks using Misumi RapidDesign or similar vendor catalog plugins

subject: Vendor-specific CAD plugin limitation
main_point: Vendor catalog plugins typically restrict you to using that vendor’s extrusion library, limiting part sources to what the plugin provides. Similar plugins generally impose the same constraint.
source_quote: You will have to use their extrusions, but that will most likely be the case for any plugin that functions similarly.
example_value: With the Misumi SolidWorks plugin, you are limited to Misumi’s extrusion profiles.
example_context: Vendor-supplied catalog plugins integrated into CAD (e.g., Misumi plugin for SolidWorks)

subject: web-based 3D builder for 80/20 extrusions
main_point: Crafty Amigo offers a free web-based 3D builder suited to assembling 80/20-style aluminum extrusion projects.
source_quote: it has a free web-based 3d builder that you can use to build your 8020 project.
example_context: Designing 80/20 aluminum extrusion assemblies using Crafty Amigo's web-based 3D builder

subject: Parco 3D Software design assistance
main_point: Parco provides free assistance to help users design their aluminum extrusion projects when using their software.
source_quote: If you need help, they will help you design it for free.
example_value: The author notes they have used the service a few times.
example_context: Parco 3D Software for aluminum extrusion design

subject: CAD software choice for aluminum extrusion assemblies
main_point: Autodesk Inventor is a viable CAD option for designing structures made from aluminum extrusions; the author uses it successfully for such projects.
source_quote: I use Autodesk Inventor for this (I built chests of drawers and HEPA filters from 2020 and 2040, and a sofa from 3030).
example_value: Built chests of drawers and HEPA filters from 2020 and 2040 extrusions, and a sofa from 3030.
example_context: Designing assemblies from T-slot aluminum extrusions (2020, 2040, 3030) using Autodesk Inventor.

subject: Availability of 3D models for aluminum extrusion profiles
main_point: 3D CAD models for common T-slot aluminum extrusion profiles can be obtained online or directly from manufacturers.
source_quote: Models for some 2020, 2040 etc profiles are available on the web (e.g. GrabCad) or from the manufacturers.
example_value: Example source mentioned: GrabCad.
example_context: T-slot aluminum extrusion profiles such as 2020 and 2040.

subject: SolidWorks Auxiliary View input limitation
main_point: In SolidWorks drawings, the Auxiliary View tool requires selecting an edge and does not accept a plane, so you cannot directly create an auxiliary view from a plane.
source_quote: You need to use the "Auxilliary View" tool, but, this is only able to accept an 'edge' as an input, so you can't use a plane.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing "Auxilliary View" tool

subject: Using a sketch edge to drive SolidWorks Auxiliary View
main_point: To create an auxiliary view when no suitable edge exists, draw a sketch entity perpendicular to the target feature and use that sketch edge to define the Auxiliary View; SolidWorks will then consume and hide the sketch line.
source_quote: The workaround for this is to create a sketch entity, set perpendicular to your holes, and use that to define the Aux View. The sketch line will be consumed by the Aux View and disappear.
example_value: Create a sketch line perpendicular to the holes and select it for the Auxiliary View.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing "Auxilliary View" tool

subject: SolidWorks Relative To Model drawing view
main_point: In SolidWorks, the Relative To Model drawing view lets you orient a drawing normal to a selected plane by manipulating the model in a separate window.
source_quote: This option will allow you to manipulate the 3D model in another window and select a plane to make the view normal to.
example_context: SolidWorks drawings using Insert > Drawing View > Relative To Model

subject: drawing view orientation for injection-molded parts
main_point: For injection-molded parts designed top-down with arbitrary part origins, orient drawing views to the mold pull direction using Relative To Model.
source_quote: I use this a lot with injection molded parts where the overall product is done with a top-down approach so that the origin of each individual part is at an arbitration location and orientation. Then for the drawing I make the views relative to the pull direction of the part.
example_value: Top-down product design yields parts whose individual origins are not aligned to meaningful manufacturing directions.
example_context: Injection-molded parts from top-down assemblies with arbitrary part origins

subject: saved view for drawing orientation
main_point: You can create a saved orientation in the model and place drawing views with respect to that saved view.
source_quote: Another option is to make a "saved view" in the model that has your desired orientation, and then do the drawing w.r.t. this saved view.
example_context: SolidWorks part/assembly models with saved view orientations

subject: Relative To Model view parametric updating
main_point: Relative To Model drawing views are parametric; when the model geometry changes, the drawing view reorients automatically.
source_quote: There are pros and cons to both. The "relative to model" option updates parametrically, so if something in your model changes, the view should re-orient automatically.
example_context: SolidWorks 'Relative To Model' drawing views

subject: Relative To Model view editability and reuse limitations
main_point: Relative To Model drawing views cannot be edited or inspected after creation and cannot be reused across drawings, limiting flexibility to copy/paste only.
source_quote: However it can't be "editted". You're stuck with the original definition and you can't even view what is was. It also can't be reused (other than by copy and paste).
example_context: SolidWorks 'Relative To Model' drawing views

subject: Saved view parametric behavior
main_point: Drawing views based on a saved view do not update with model changes; you must manually update the saved view when the model changes.
source_quote: The "saved view" option does not update parametrically, so you have to remember to manually update the "saved view" orientation if something about model changes such that the view orientation should be correspondingly updated.
example_context: SolidWorks saved view used for drawing orientation

subject: Editability: saved view vs Relative To Model
main_point: Saved-view–based drawing orientations can be edited by overwriting the saved view in the model, whereas Relative To Model views cannot be edited.
source_quote: But unlike the Relative-to-Model option, you can effectively edit/update this sort of view by overwriting the saved view in the part/assy model.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing views: saved view vs Relative To Model

subject: spherical snap-fit clearance vs undercut (y)
main_point: For spherical (circular) snap-fit joints, size the clearance to about half of the permissible deflection (undercut), i.e., clearance ≈ y/2. This provides an initial fit guideline tied to the designed snap deflection.
source_quote: You should also check for spherical joint clearance should be y/2.
example_context: spherical (circular) snap-fit joints

subject: material property inputs for snap-fit design
main_point: Proper snap-fit design requires using the material’s allowable strain limit (E) and its secant modulus evaluated at the relevant operating/assembly temperature. These values must come from material-specific data to size features and predict snap forces correctly.
source_quote: In order to use this formulas you need to consult material specific allowable strain limits (E) and secant modulus for appropriate temperature.

subject: permissible strain estimate for unreinforced plastics
main_point: For unreinforced plastics that exhibit a distinct yield point, a practical estimate for permissible strain in snap-fit design is about 70% of the yield strain (E ≈ 0.7·εy). This serves as a rule-of-thumb pending confirmation against specific design guidelines.
source_quote:
If your material has distinct yield point, I guess it will have if it's not reinforced with fiber 
$0.7\epsilon_{y}$
 can be taken.
example_context: unreinforced plastics with a distinct yield point used in snap-fit features

subject: measuring total length of multiple segments in SolidWorks
main_point: In SolidWorks, you can Ctrl-click each curve segment and the software will display the total length in the bottom-right corner of the interface.
source_quote: Okay, I've found out that I can just Ctrl-Click every segment and the total length will appear in the bottom-right corner.
example_context: SolidWorks 2023

subject: SolidWorks split feature child part update behavior
main_point: In SolidWorks, simply re-accepting the Split feature in the parent part (without changing anything) can trigger the software to automatically update the saved child parts generated by the split.
source_quote: I noticed that if I edited the split command and just clicked on the green tick without making any changes, then Solidworks updated the split files automatically.
example_context: SolidWorks part file using the Split feature to create linked child part files

subject: Recorded SolidWorks macro failing to update split children
main_point: A recorded macro intended to mimic re-accepting the Split feature did not cause the split child parts to update, even though doing the action manually did.
source_quote: but it didn't update the split files when I executed it
example_context: Recorded SolidWorks VBA macro attempting to force update of child parts by editing and accepting the Split feature

subject: SolidWorks external reference update conditions
main_point: For split-derived child parts to reflect edits made to the parent, SolidWorks must have the parent document open and the child must be rebuilt. Without both conditions, the change will not propagate to the child.
source_quote:
In order for the changes to propagate to the child, the following needs to happen:

1. The parent part must be open in SW
2. The child part must be rebuilt
example_context: SolidWorks part files with external references (Split feature creating child parts)

subject: Out-of-context child behavior after parent edits
main_point: Editing and saving the parent while children are closed will result in the child showing the old geometry when first opened, along with an out-of-context warning. The child must be brought back in context/rebuilt before it reflects the updated parent.
source_quote: If you have the child parts closed, you edit and then save the parent part, and then open the child parts to 'see if they have been updated', then they will appear with the old geometry. BUT they will also appear with a warning question mark showing that the reference is out of context.
example_context: SolidWorks parts with external references between parent and child (Split-derived parts)

subject: External reference requires parent in RAM
main_point: A child part cannot update its geometry from the parent unless the parent document is loaded into memory. External references only resolve while the parent is resident in RAM.
source_quote: The child can't pull any geometry from the parent part until it is loaded into RAM.
example_context: SolidWorks in-context modeling with parent–child external references

subject: Using Edit in Context to open parent quickly
main_point: To rapidly load the parent for an in-context update, right‑click the child and choose Edit in Context, then rebuild the child to see the propagated changes.
source_quote: The quickest way to open the parent part up is right clicking and using "edit in context".
example_context: SolidWorks parts with parent–child external references

subject: Auto-loading changed external references
main_point: Enable the SolidWorks option to automatically load changed external references into memory so child parts open in-context and reflect parent changes. Use the checkbox that loads them into RAM without adding separate windows.
source_quote:
So - to the solution: change your settings such that SW automatically loads any changed external references into RAM.
 There is a checkbox that sets them to load into memory only, and not clog up your "window" list.
example_context: SolidWorks options for handling external references between parent and child parts

subject: When to avoid auto-loading references
main_point: Disable automatic loading of external references if you work with very large assemblies, where manual loading reduces open times. This trades convenience for performance on heavy datasets.
source_quote:
The only reason to 
not
 have this enabled (and to therefore manually load references as needed) would be if you are working on very large assemblies, and need to speed up opening times.
example_context: SolidWorks large assemblies with external references

subject: drawing scale annotation mismatch
main_point: If a SolidWorks drawing’s scale is changed but the title block’s scale field is not updated, the stated scale can conflict with the actual drawing scale, creating inconsistent documentation and potential misinterpretation.
source_quote: The thing is, we use mainly SolidWorks to do our job, and sometimes it is easy to change the scale of a drawing without updating the relevant field that automatically shows the universal scale of the drawing. This obviously causes the true scale of the drawing to conflict with the scale provided in the relevant field in the title blocks.
example_context: SolidWorks mechanical drawings with a title block field that displays the sheet or universal drawing scale

subject: drawing scale inclusion
main_point: Always include the drawing scale on technical drawings. Even if it’s seldom consulted, omitting it can lead to later problems and it is trivial to provide.
source_quote: You should not ommit the scale. Even if no one seems to read it, it is still important information. The task is quite trivial, I don't see any reason why to remove the scale because it can cause several issue later on.

subject: regulatory audits and drawing documentation
main_point: In regulated environments, inadequate or incorrect drawing documentation can cause an organization to fail a regulatory audit.
source_quote: Since you are working for a medical device company and might be exposed to an audit from an quality organ, such as FDA or Tüv. They will look at everything and if it is not correctly documented the company might not pass the audit.
example_context: Medical device companies subject to FDA or TÜV audits

subject: missing drawing data and knowledge transfer
main_point: If information is missing from drawings, future staff will struggle to interpret past work, making retrieval and understanding of legacy data time-consuming.
source_quote: When a new employee has to look up old information, maybe you will no longer work there. It could become tedious to try and figure out what was done if data is missing from the drawing.

subject: SOLIDWORKS color settings reset
main_point: If SOLIDWORKS displays a black background or UI elements, reset the application’s color settings to defaults via the Colors tab in Options. This restores visibility by reverting any problematic custom color configuration.
source_quote:
1. Go to settings
2. Select colors tab
3. Reset colors to Defaults
example_value: Steps: Go to settings > Colors tab > Reset colors to Defaults.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS Options dialog, Colors tab (UI color configuration)

subject: SolidWorks drawing centerline creation
main_point: In SolidWorks drawings, create a centerline between two holes by entering sketch mode and using the Centerline sketch entity to draw between the holes.
source_quote:
Go in sketch, 
, select centerline, draw between holes.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing environment

subject: reference geometry via sketch entities
main_point: In SolidWorks’ part editor, create 2D/3D sketch entities (lines, arcs, points) and leave them in the part to visibly reference axes, vectors, and points while modeling.
source_quote: If you make sketches (2D or 3D) with these lines, arcs and points, you can just leave them in your part and they'll be displayed while you work.
example_context: SolidWorks part editor

subject: sketch annotations for labels
main_point: Avoid relying on sketch annotations for labels in SolidWorks (e.g., 2016); they tend to work poorly for this purpose.
source_quote: One caveat, there will be no labels. I have solidworks 2016, and maybe it's better in the future versions, but I find that adding annotations inside sketches does not work well. I wouldn't bother.
example_context: SolidWorks 2016 sketch environment

subject: dimensioning to center of mass
main_point: SolidWorks does not allow applying dimensions directly to the model’s center of mass, limiting direct parametric referencing to it.
source_quote: As far as I know you can't dimension to the center of mass, but you can show the coordinates, or a crude and simple way to locate relative to your part would be to zoom way in and place a point on it.
example_context: SolidWorks (circa 2016) center of mass referencing

subject: center of mass coordinates display
main_point: Instead of dimensioning to the center of mass in SolidWorks, display its coordinates to reference its location.
source_quote: you can show the coordinates,
example_context: SolidWorks center of mass display

subject: manual point placement at center of mass
main_point: To reference the center of mass in SolidWorks, zoom in and place a sketch point on it to create a dimensionable reference.
source_quote: a crude and simple way to locate relative to your part would be to zoom way in and place a point on it.
example_context: SolidWorks part editor when COM cannot be dimensioned directly

subject: SolidWorks editor suitability for illustrations
main_point: SolidWorks’ part editor is not intended for polished illustrations; achieving a beautiful presentation often requires post-processing in an external image editor (e.g., GIMP).
source_quote: The editor isn't really designed to create illustrations, so although I think you'll be able to come up with something workable, I likely will not be "beautiful" without some post processing in GIMP or similar.
example_context: SolidWorks part editor and external post-processing tools

subject: manual post-processing for arrows and labels
main_point: For a cleaner presentation, add arrows and labels manually (e.g., in post-processing) rather than relying on SolidWorks’ sketch tools.
source_quote: If I wanted this to look nicer I would draw the arrows on the ends of the lines by hand, and add labels. That should look decent.
example_context: SolidWorks outputs refined in an external graphics editor

subject: sketch text for labeling
main_point: If you need labels inside SolidWorks, inserting sketch text (like for engraving) can serve as a functional but inelegant labeling method.
source_quote: If I really needed a label I might insert some text in the sketch (as you would do for engraving), not elegant but it might work ok.
example_context: SolidWorks 2016 sketch environment

subject: planar references vs separate parts in SolidWorks assemblies
main_point: Creating a single planar reference by merging components lets SolidWorks solve and manipulate the assembly more robustly than trying to drive the motion with multiple independent parts. Giving the solver a plane simplifies the kinematics and avoids ambiguous constraints when mating a plate to two actuators.
source_quote: Merging the actuators forms a plane, which SolidWorks knows how to manipulate as opposed to three separate objects to manipulate.
example_value: Once the actuators are merged to define a plane, the circular plate can be mated to them reliably.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies (mates/merges and planar references)

subject: importance of mate/merge type and order in SolidWorks assemblies
main_point: To make a multi-part mechanism behave correctly without creating a shared plane, ensure the constraint operations are of the correct types and applied in the right order. Incorrect mate/merge selection or sequencing can prevent the assembly from solving to the intended motion.
source_quote: You could probably get it to work, but the merges would have to be the proper type and in the proper order.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies (choosing and sequencing mates/merges)

subject: parallelogram linkage side spacing change
main_point: When a parallelogram mechanism articulates, the perpendicular distance between its two parallel sides decreases. Designs that mimic a parallelogram must accommodate this reduction in side-to-side spacing during motion.
source_quote: However, when you flex it, the two actuator sides of the parallelogram come closer together, i.e. the distance between them (represented by a segment that is perpendicular to both sides simultaneously) shortens.
example_value: In the OP’s tilt platform, the two actuators function like the parallel sides of a parallelogram.

subject: over-constraint from fixed actuator spacing
main_point: If a mechanism prevents a pair of parallel actuators from moving closer together as it flexes, the system becomes over‑constrained and cannot achieve the intended tilting motion.
source_quote: In your mechanism, you have eliminated the possibility for the two parallel actuators to get closer to each other. This over-constrains your motion.
example_value: The tilt platform’s two actuators are mounted so their lateral spacing is fixed, which locks the parallelogram geometry.
example_context: Parallelogram-like mechanisms with two parallel actuators whose base spacing is fixed

subject: add horizontal translational DOF at actuator bases
main_point: Provide horizontal translational freedom at the actuator bases so the two bottom platforms can move toward each other, relieving the over‑constraint.
source_quote: To fix it, you should allow the two horizontal platforms at the bottom of the actuators to move closer to each other or something like this. For now they are fixed, but try to allow for a horizontal translational motion.
example_value: Redesign the actuator bottom mounts to slide laterally rather than being rigidly fixed.
example_context: Parallelogram-type tilt mechanisms using two parallel actuators

subject: modeling a bent tapered tube in Solidworks
main_point: In Solidworks, a more effective workflow for a bent, tapered tube is to first create the straight tapered tube with a revolve, then bend it using the Flex feature. This approach is recommended over directly trying to form the bent shape in one step.
source_quote: For the shape that you are attempting to create - it would be more effective to model the tapered tube in its unbent state using a revolve, and then use the Flex feature to bend it around.
example_value: A tapered tube that makes a U-turn.
example_context: Solidworks (v22) CAD modeling of a tapered tube that bends around a U-turn using the Flex feature.

subject: SolidWorks Intersection Curve tool
main_point: In SolidWorks, you can generate a 3D sketch of the intersection between components by using the Intersection Curve command found under Tools > Sketch Tools.
source_quote: I just found out how to make a 3D sketch outlining the intersection. Tools > Sketch tools > Intersection curve.
example_value: The user has two rectangular prisms in a subassembly and created a 3D sketch outlining their intersection using the menu path.
example_context: SolidWorks 2019 CAD: Tools > Sketch Tools > Intersection Curve

subject: SolidWorks Combine feature multibody requirement
main_point: To generate the intersected/common volume with SolidWorks' Combine tool, both solids must exist within a single multibody part; Combine cannot operate across separate parts in an assembly.
source_quote: In order to use the "Combine" feature, to create the volume that you want, you need to have a multibody part
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling using the Combine feature to create the common volume of two components

subject: Dynamic positioning of bodies in SolidWorks multibody parts
main_point: Within a SolidWorks multibody part, dynamic repositioning of bodies requires using Move/Copy Bodies with mates; bodies inside a part are not driven by standard assembly mates.
source_quote: In order to move the parts dynamically inside a multibody, you need to use mates with the "move/copy bodies" feature.
example_context: SolidWorks multibody part editing and positioning of bodies

subject: Move/Copy Bodies limitation on global variables
main_point: The Move/Copy Bodies mates in SolidWorks cannot be driven by global variables for translation or rotation, so those motions cannot be parametrically linked to globals and must be controlled by other means.
source_quote: It cannot accept a global variable for translate/rotate moves, which is a bit annoying.
example_context: SolidWorks Move/Copy Bodies feature when mating bodies inside a multibody part

subject: Mating to external references in SolidWorks assemblies
main_point: Because SolidWorks does not allow mating to external references in this setup, the assembly component positions must be driven by the multibody part's internal references rather than trying to drive the multibody from the assembly.
source_quote: You cannot mate to an external reference, therefore, the position of the parts in the assembly must be defined by the position of the parts in the multibody, not the other way around.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly referencing a multibody part used to compute an intersection

subject: 3D sketch controlling a body's six degrees of freedom in SolidWorks
main_point: A 3D sketch can fully control a body's pose in SolidWorks by governing all six degrees of freedom (three translations and three rotations).
source_quote: Adjusting the geometry of this 3D sketch can control all six degrees of freedom.
example_value: In the example, X/Y/Z are dimensioned and rotation is fixed by constraints; replacing constraints with angle dimensions would control rotation parametrically.
example_context: SolidWorks multibody part where a 3D sketch defines a component's position and orientation

subject: Parametric updates in SolidWorks multibody and Combine workflow
main_point: With this multibody-plus-Combine setup, model changes propagate dynamically: edits to body geometry or pose and feature additions update the intersected result automatically.
source_quote: Everything updates dynamically, you can change the shape/size/position/rotation of the bodies, you can add bosses or holes etc.
example_value: Changing body shape/size/position/rotation or adding bosses/holes updates the common volume.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly linked to a multibody part using a 3D sketch, Move/Copy Bodies mates, and the Combine feature

subject: SolidWorks Cavity tool intersection workaround
main_point: Because the Cavity feature cannot directly compute an intersection, you can emulate an intersected result by modeling one component as a mold of the target solid.
source_quote: Cavity doesn't do an intersection, but you can achieve that effect by modeling one of the parts as a "mold" of the solid you actually want.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly modeling using the Cavity feature

subject: Using SolidWorks Cavity to subtract one part from another in an assembly
main_point: For simple cases where you don't need to operate on individual bodies, the Cavity feature at the assembly level can subtract the volume of one part from another.
source_quote: you can use the cavity tool within an assembly to completely remove the volume of GreenPart from YellowPart.
example_value: Remove GreenPart’s volume from YellowPart using Cavity.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies with simple parts where body-level operations are not needed

subject: Saving assembly as multibody part to perform intersection
main_point: If you don’t need to maintain live parametrics, convert the assembly to a multibody part and use standard multibody features (e.g., Combine/Intersect) to generate the intersection.
source_quote: you can save-as the assembly as a multi-body part, and then use conventional multi-body operations to perform the intersection.
example_value: Combine, intersect, etc.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies where the final intersected shape is needed without parametric links

subject: 0-offset surface copy to transfer geometry between parts
main_point: In-context, use Offset Surface with zero offset to copy a body's faces from one part into another, then rebuild as a solid to enable multibody operations.
source_quote: offset surface command with an offset of 0 to make surface copies to get the geometry of a body in GreenPart into YellowPart.
example_value: Copy GreenPart’s body geometry into YellowPart via 0-offset surfaces.
example_context: SolidWorks in-context part editing within an assembly for multibody workflows

subject: Using three 3D sketch points to constrain inserted part location
main_point: Place three in-context 3D sketch points at known vertices to fully constrain an inserted part’s position and orientation by locking all six degrees of freedom.
source_quote: Within your assembly, create an incontext 3D sketch in YellowPart that contains three points that are located at easy-to-find vertices of    GreenPart. These will lock down the 6 degrees of freedom.
example_value: Three points on GreenPart’s vertices control YellowPart’s in-context alignment.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly context when preparing to Insert Part and maintain original placement

subject: Using Insert Part constraints to locate via 3D sketch points
main_point: When inserting a part, use the Constraints option to snap the part’s selected vertices to pre-made 3D sketch points to place it where it was in the assembly.
source_quote: Use the constraints option to locate the selected verticies of GreenPart where it was in the assembly via the sketch points in the 3d sketch.
example_value: Constrain GreenPart’s vertices to the 3D sketch points during Insert Part.
example_context: SolidWorks Insert Part workflow within an assembly using in-context 3D sketch references

subject: external references to align assembly sketch holes with STEP part holes in SolidWorks
main_point: To match and maintain alignment with holes in an imported STEP part, sketch circles and make the extruded cuts in the assembly, then edit the sketch and add external references from the circles to the STEP part’s hole geometry. This links your assembly holes to the STEP holes so they stay registered.
source_quote: The only other way to do this that I know of is to draw circles and extruded cut as usual to make the holes, then edit the circles in the assembly and create an external reference between your drawing and the holes in the STEP part.
example_value: In a SolidWorks assembly, cut the holes on the mating component, then edit the sketch and constrain the hole circles to the edges of the STEP part’s holes using external references.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies involving imported STEP parts where holes in a mating component must align with the COTS part’s holes.

subject: point-on-circle dimension reference
main_point: In SolidWorks, a reliable way to dimension from a line to a circle edge is to add a sketch point on the circle and place the dimension to that point. This makes the target explicit and tends to remain stable even if the line’s orientation changes.
source_quote: You can achieve this simply and quickly by adding a point to the circumference of your circle. I like this method because it's easy to see exactly where the dimension is going to, and it's robust in the case where the line become non-horizontal etc.
example_value: Add a sketch point at the circle’s circumference, then dimension from the line to that point for clarity and robustness.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch dimensioning within 2D sketches

subject: 'minimum' arc leader condition
main_point: SolidWorks offers an official method to dimension to an arc edge by setting the dimension’s leader to the 'minimum' arc condition in the dimension properties.
source_quote: You can achieve this more 'officially' by using the 'minimum' arc condition in the 'leader' tab of the dimension properties.
example_value: Use the dimension properties dialog and choose 'minimum' under the leader’s arc condition to drive the dimension from the circle edge.
example_context: SolidWorks dimension properties (Leader tab)

subject: manual dimension property edits
main_point: Avoid building workflows that depend on manually editing dimension properties, as this can be cumbersome and less robust. Favor approaches that don’t require per-dimension property tweaks.
source_quote: I don't like this method, because relying on manually altering dimension properties doesn't sit well in my personal workflow.
example_value: The author avoids the 'minimum' arc condition approach because it requires manual changes to the dimension’s properties.
example_context: SolidWorks workflows involving dimension property changes

subject: sketch dimensions matching manufacturing drawing
main_point: Dimension your sketches to reflect how the part will actually be manufactured. Aim for sketch dimensions that align with the dimensions you would place on the 2D manufacturing drawing.
source_quote: A more pertinent point, however, is that it's not good practice to dimension a part like this, since that's not how it will be manufactured. If possible, the dimensions in your sketches should match with those that would be desirable on the 2D manufacturing drawing.

subject: SolidWorks time rollback when editing earlier sketch
main_point: Editing an earlier sketch in SolidWorks rolls the model back to that point in the feature tree, temporarily hiding later features. This can make protrusions or other subsequent features seem to disappear while the earlier sketch is being edited.
source_quote: Your features disappear because solidworks "rewinds time" when you edit an early sketch and shows you the model as it looked when you made the sketch.
example_context: SolidWorks feature-based parametric modeling when editing an earlier sketch in the feature tree

subject: Selecting target sketch/feature from the FeatureManager tree
main_point: Use the FeatureManager tree to select and edit the specific sketch or feature you intend to change rather than invoking Edit Sketch from a model face. This helps ensure you modify the correct item, especially in complex models.
source_quote: I recommend selecting the sketch or feature you want to change from the list on the left, instead of using right click -> edit sketch like you're doing.
example_context: SolidWorks FeatureManager design tree workflow for editing sketches/features

subject: Editing sketches by clicking a face in complex SolidWorks parts
main_point: In complex SolidWorks models, a single face may be influenced by multiple features, so using Face -> Edit Sketch can open an arbitrary sketch, leading you to edit the wrong feature.
source_quote: As your part gets more complicated 1 face does not equate to 1 sketch, so when you click a face -> edit sketch, you're basically getting a sketch selected at random.
example_context: SolidWorks models with multiple features/sketches where faces are not uniquely tied to a single sketch

subject: face identity persistence across features (SOLIDWORKS)
main_point: In SOLIDWORKS, a face created by an earlier feature retains its identity even after later features modify its boundary. The system still treats it as the same face despite changes to its outline.
source_quote: Once the tab is added, this is still seen as the same face by SOLIDWORKS, even though its boundary has changed a bit
example_value: A base thin-extrude face remains the same face after adding a tab feature that alters the boundary.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS part modeling with multiple sequential features

subject: editing a feature's sketch via face selection (SOLIDWORKS)
main_point: To edit the correct sketch for a protrusion, select a face generated by that feature and choose Edit Sketch; this opens the sketch that defines that feature.
source_quote:
Clicking on this side face (which was 
created by
 the tab sketch) and clicking edit sketch, will allow you to edit the sketch you are interested in
example_value: Selecting the side face produced by the tab feature and choosing Edit Sketch lets you modify the tab’s sketch.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS part modeling; selecting a face created by the feature you want to edit

subject: editing sketches via FeatureManager design tree (SOLIDWORKS)
main_point: A straightforward method to edit a sketch is to locate the feature in the FeatureManager history tree and invoke Edit Sketch from there.
source_quote: The easiest way to do it, however, is to find the relevant feature in the history tree, and click edit sketch over there.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS FeatureManager design tree operations

subject: single-feature editing constraint in Solidworks
main_point: In Solidworks, you work on one feature at a time when making changes. To modify geometry, you must open and edit the specific feature (or its sketch) individually rather than multiple features simultaneously.
source_quote: I was told you can only edit one feature at a time.
example_context: Solidworks part modeling and feature editing

subject: editing a feature sketch via FeatureManager in Solidworks
main_point: To edit the geometry driving a protrusion in Solidworks, select the feature in the FeatureManager tree and choose Edit Sketch under the Extrude to open its sketch plane for modification.
source_quote: Next select that part on the left side and the click on edit sketch on level below the extrude, should bring up the sketch plan that you want to edit.
example_value: First click the part/feature to identify it, then select it in the tree and use Edit Sketch under the extrude feature.
example_context: Solidworks FeatureManager tree operations

subject: SolidWorks default templates contain projection symbols
main_point: SolidWorks’ standard ISO and ANSI drawing templates already include the projection symbols, so they are available without creating them from scratch.
source_quote: These symbols are built in to the default ISO and ANSI templates provided by SolidWorks,
example_context: SolidWorks drawing templates (ISO and ANSI standards)

subject: Reusing projection symbols from SolidWorks default templates
main_point: To add the projection symbol to a custom drawing template, copy and paste it from the default ISO/ANSI SolidWorks templates.
source_quote: you can copy/paste them from there into your own template.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing templates (ISO and ANSI standards)

subject: Manually drawing projection symbols in SolidWorks
main_point: You can manually create the projection symbol in SolidWorks since it consists of simple line and circle geometry, making it quick to draw.
source_quote: Alternatively, simply draw your own - it's just a few lines and circles!
example_context: SolidWorks drawings

subject: mechanical engineer vs drafter roles
main_point: In current practice, many mechanical engineers often handle both the engineering work and the drafting responsibilities traditionally done by a separate drafter.
source_quote: These days it seems most mechanical engineers (at least the ones I know) are really performing the role of both the drafter and the engineer.
example_value: The author notes this based on the mechanical engineers they personally know.
example_context: observations of the asker’s peers/industry context regarding modern mechanical engineering roles

subject: mechanical engineers' pre-CAD duties
main_point: Before CAD, mechanical engineers focused on designing components and performing the calculations to define materials, sizes, and other specifications.
source_quote: Engineers designed and sorted the calculations defining the components - material, size, etc.
example_context: Pre-CAD mechanical design workflows (before widespread CAD like SolidWorks)

subject: draftsmen's pre-CAD duties
main_point: In the pre-CAD era, draftsmen produced the engineering drawings by hand and prepared blueprint reproductions.
source_quote: Draftsmen did the drawing pencil on paper or ink, then did blueprints.
example_context: Pre-CAD mechanical design workflows (before widespread CAD like SolidWorks)

subject: auxiliary views via graphical projection rules
main_point: Before CAD, engineers used drafting projection rules to create auxiliary views so machinists could understand the part from any needed angle and make it to the drawing.
source_quote: Clever graphical rules were applied to the resulting drawings which permitted auxiliary views of the part to be generated so it could be viewed from any desired angle, as an aid to the machinists who made the part in accordance with the drawing.
example_context: Pre-CAD manual mechanical drafting (circa 1970s–1980s) in engineering offices.

subject: line weight conventions on manual drawings
main_point: Manual drafting used distinct line weights—thicker outlines, very thin dimension lines, and dark, thicker arrowheads—to improve drawing clarity and communication.
source_quote: The outlines of the part were drawn with one thickness of pencil line, dimension lines with a very thin line and arrowheads done thickly in softer pencil lead to produce a nice dark effect.
example_context: Pre-CAD manual mechanical drafting (circa 1970s–1980s) in engineering offices.

subject: tracking cumulative dimensions during manual drafting
main_point: Engineers manually tracked cumulative dimensions while laying out drawings, often using a handheld calculator to manage the running totals.
source_quote: Clipped onto that arm was a handy HP handheld calculator with which the engineer kept track of cumulative dimensions as he (all of them were "he") worked his way across the paper sheet.
example_context: Pre-CAD manual mechanical drafting (circa 1970s–1980s) in engineering offices.

subject: engineer–machinist collaboration to resolve interference issues
main_point: Interference issues were resolved collaboratively between engineers and machinists in the model shop rather than solely through analytical tools.
source_quote: parts interference problems were worked out in collaboration with the machinists in the model shop.
example_context: Pre-CAD manual mechanical design and prototyping in company model shops.

subject: hand calculations for stress analysis before CAD/FEA
main_point: Prior to modern software, engineers performed stress analysis by hand calculations rather than using computer-based FEA tools.
source_quote: Stress analysis was done by hand
example_context: Pre-CAD/FEA mechanical design workflows (circa 1970s–1980s).

subject: CAD/ERP tool necessity
main_point: In modern engineering and manufacturing, having CAD and ERP tools is a basic requirement to remain competitive. Organizations lacking these systems are at a structural disadvantage versus those that use them.
source_quote: Of course, CAD and/or ERP tools are a very important aspect, and you can't compete without them.
example_context: Modern engineering/manufacturing organizations operating in competitive markets

subject: process quality vs tool effectiveness
main_point: Engineering software alone cannot compensate for deficiencies in the overall process. Sustainable success depends on improving the end-to-end workflow and organization, not just adopting CAD tools.
source_quote: But as long as the working process as a whole has drawbacks, the CAD tools will not lead you to success by themselves.

subject: paper-based drafting change management
main_point: In manual, paper-based drafting, even minor design changes typically force you to redo large portions of the work, leading to repeated rework and lost productivity.
source_quote: You might spot at this point that the downside is that any small change and youll be redoing things. A lot.
example_value: The author recalls an older draftsman who produced one drawing per day and often had to start over the next day due to a trivial change.

subject: using paper sketches to counter MCAD design bias
main_point: Detail-focused MCAD tools can constrain how you think about solutions; using hand sketches during early design helps avoid being railroaded into limited approaches.
source_quote: The problem that raises with this is that it railroads you to thinking certain ways. Having paper sketches is a way to combat this thing.
example_context: MCAD tools like SolidWorks used primarily for detailed design work

subject: decline of drafting roles due to CAD
main_point: The adoption of CAD has largely eliminated the need for dedicated drafting roles in many organizations.
source_quote: It is true that the CAD application has in a way killed the drafing job.
example_context: Engineering organizations transitioning from manual drafting workflows to CAD-based workflows

subject: regional variation in drafting responsibility pre-CAD
main_point: Drafting responsibility has been culturally dependent; in some regions, engineers handled their own drafting even before CAD existed.
source_quote: in some parts of the world the engineers did their own drafting even before the advent of CAD applications.
example_context: Regional engineering practices prior to CAD adoption

subject: difficulty hiring draftsmen in Europe
main_point: Companies today often struggle to hire dedicated draftsmen, with this shortage perceived as especially pronounced in Europe.
source_quote: they can not easily find draftsmen (this is to my understanding much more a european problem).
example_context: European labor market for technical drafting roles

subject: headcount reduction from CAD adoption
main_point: Adopting CAD can eliminate multiple intermediary roles from the design-to-documentation pipeline, reducing the number of people involved by several positions compared to older workflows.
source_quote: So the CAD application really kills of 2-8 persons in the loop depending on how far back you look back.
example_context: Legacy workflows involving draftsmen and modelmakers replaced by engineers working directly in CAD

subject: outsourcing CAD changes vs self-modeling tradeoff
main_point: Routing design changes through another person can add roughly a day of delay, whereas modeling the change yourself can take under an hour but increases the likelihood of mistakes.
source_quote: The problem with having a extra person in the loop is that the change I want takes one day, while if im modeling myself it takes often less than a hour. But then i have more chances for screwups.
example_context: Author’s workflow comparing sending changes to a drafter versus doing the CAD work personally

subject: digitization dependency when working without CAD
main_point: Working entirely without computers can be viable, but it often requires a separate step where someone else converts the work into digital drawings for downstream use.
source_quote: There is really nothing wrong with doing it this way except that it neccesitates sometimes having somebody else make your drawings digital.
example_context: Paper-based design processes needing digital deliverables for collaboration or manufacturing

subject: low-fidelity physical prototyping for concept development
main_point: During early concept development, making quick physical mockups from simple materials (e.g., cardboard, clay, polyurethane) is an effective way to explore forms and ideas without CAD.
source_quote: you can bend sheetmetals out of cardboard, you can sculpt stuff out of modeling clay, or sand out of a block of polyurethane.

subject: CAD/FEA-enabled rapid functional analysis
main_point: Modern CAD tools like SolidWorks enable quick, reasonably accurate analyses of parts and assemblies to check functional performance early in design. This accelerates iteration compared to pre-CAD methods, provided the user understands how to set up and interpret the analysis.
source_quote: Nowadays with solidworks you can think something and you can do a very quick (and relatively accurate if you know what you are doing) analysis and see whether the part or the assembly you are building performs the function you intend.
example_value: Using SolidWorks Simulation to quickly evaluate whether an assembly will function as intended.
example_context: Modern CAD packages (e.g., SolidWorks) with built-in simulation/FEA capabilities

subject: 3D models replacing 2D drawings (model-based definition)
main_point: Some industries are transitioning from traditional 2D drawings to using 3D CAD models or STL files as the primary design and communication artifacts. This reflects a shift toward model-based definition for manufacturing and documentation.
source_quote: in many cases nowadays even the 2d drawings are being (slowly) replaced in certain industries by 3d models or stl files.
example_context: Industries adopting model-based definition that rely on 3D CAD models or STL files as the authority

subject: CAD tools as broad engineering and communication platforms
main_point: Modern CAD platforms like SolidWorks/Inventor serve as general engineering tools that support productivity and cross-disciplinary communication, beyond just drafting. Their value extends to analysis, collaboration, and overall workflow enablement.
source_quote: So, IMHO, Solidworks or Invertor isn't about drafting, is more about a generic tool that can help an engineer (manufacturing, electrical, mechanical, industrial) to achieve more and communicate better.
example_context: Use of SolidWorks or Inventor across engineering disciplines for design and communication

subject: weld access clearance
main_point: If a design does not provide enough clearance for a welder’s hand and torch, the weld operation may be impossible, so features must include adequate access space for welding.
source_quote: We'd often get comments from the drafters like "You cannot fit a hand plus welding torch in there."
example_value: A drafter pointed out a design area where there was no room to fit a hand and welding torch.

subject: drafter trade knowledge expectation
main_point: In some design offices, drafters are expected to understand fabrication trades such as welding and fitting so their drawings reflect practical build methods.
source_quote: In the offices I worked in, drafters were also expected to have a grasp of the trades required to build the thing they were drawing. They'd have some background in welding, fitting, and fabrication.
example_context: Mechanical design offices where drafters support welding/fitting/fabrication work

subject: engineering time allocation before CAD
main_point: Before modern CAD/CAE, engineers devoted more time to manual drawing and hand calculations rather than spending time learning and operating software tools.
source_quote: I guess we spent more time drawing and calculating, versus figuring out how to make software do it.
example_context: pre-CAD mechanical engineering workflows

subject: FreeCAD as alternative CAD starting point
main_point: For engineers without SolidWorks experience, beginning with FreeCAD is a practical way to create part models and produce files for workflows like 3D printing.
source_quote: Mechanical engineers that do not know about Solidworks yet in these days start from FreeCAD.
example_value: The author, with no prior SolidWorks experience, used FreeCAD to model parts and export STL files for 3D printing.
example_context: Engineers who do not know or do not have access to SolidWorks

subject: FreeCAD cost and platform support
main_point: FreeCAD is available at no cost and runs on Linux, making it an accessible CAD option for users without SolidWorks.
source_quote: FreeCAD that was free and able to run on my Linux.
example_value: The author selected FreeCAD specifically because it was free and compatible with their Linux system.
example_context: FreeCAD CAD software on Linux operating systems

subject: drafting clarity and role of draftsman
main_point: A drafter’s responsibility is to translate engineering intent into a drawing that is clear and unambiguous. This ensures design intent is communicated precisely for downstream use.
source_quote:
The draftsman's job was to 
render
 the engineer's intent in a drawing which is clear and unambiguous.
example_value: Clear drawings let the engineer confirm intent and the fabricator assess buildability.

subject: drawings as contractual arbiter of responsibility
main_point: The drawing is the authoritative basis for assigning responsibility when parts don’t work out. If a part conforms to the drawing, the engineer owns the mistake; if it does not, the fault lies with fabrication.
source_quote: if the part matches the drawing, the engineer pays, otherwise it was misfabricated.
example_value: The engineer and fabricator often work for different companies, so the drawing mediates accountability.

subject: delegation of CAD drafting workload
main_point: Even with modern CAD, detailed modeling and drawing work can be time-consuming, so retaining a drafting role can improve efficiency. Engineers may delegate CAD “fiddling” when short on time or inclination.
source_quote: There may still be a place for the draftsman, as the engineer may not have the time or inclination to do all that fiddling in Solidworks, which can be quite time-consuming even if it is faster than paper drafting.

subject: CAD tool capabilities for design verification
main_point: CAD systems support design work by enabling part definition, assembly fit/interference checks, and basic failure evaluation such as stress limit analysis.
source_quote: CAD tools can define parts, check they fit together, and check whether the design fails in some way (e.g. stress exceeds acceptable limits).

subject: CAD limitations in early-stage product definition
main_point: CAD tools are generally not used to determine product requirements or define what a design should do; they are more useful for evaluating concepts once those questions are answered.
source_quote: The other open-ended question a development engineer asks is "what should this do?" - and CAD is rarely involved in that question, even if it is very valuable in evaluating the answers.

subject: manual G-code speed vs CAD/CAM
main_point: For certain machining tasks, writing G-code by hand can be faster than creating a CAD model and generating the equivalent CAM output, so knowing G-code can reduce programming time in those cases.
source_quote: Because some programs for some operations can be written quicker than the time it takes to produce the equivalent CAD file.
example_context: operations where writing a simple CNC program is faster than modeling and CAM setup for the same feature

subject: parametric programming with variables
main_point: Use variables (parametric programming) to make CNC code reusable across part sizes; a single program can accept key dimensions as inputs, avoiding the need to create multiple CAD/CAM files and saving time.
source_quote: Also use of variables makes the program more useful ie a program to produce a cylinder can be written to take diameter as the controlling argument while producing many CAD files for various different diameters takes time.
example_value: A cylinder program takes diameter as an input parameter instead of maintaining separate CAD files for each diameter.
example_context: CNC controls that support macro variables/parametric programming

subject: G-code literacy for machine capability understanding
main_point: Learning G-code is useful pedagogically because it reveals the real capabilities and limitations of the machine that will execute the program. This understanding informs better decisions when operating or specifying CNC processes.
source_quote: At the very least as a teaching device it is useful to learn G-code to gain understanding of the capabilities and limitations of the machine tool which is going to be operated.

subject: manufacturing feedback in design optimization
main_point: Design optimization should integrate feedback from manufacturing to avoid unnecessary costs such as longer runtime, material waste, and accelerated tool wear. Considering process realities early leads to parts that are cheaper to produce.
source_quote: But I think more generally -- design optimization should include feedback from the manufacturing process so that a useful part can be produced without extra costs - costs including runtime, material waste, tool wear, etc.

subject: avoiding black-box CAD/CAM use
main_point: Treating CAD/CAM purely as a black box limits understanding of how G-code actually drives the machine. Engaging with the underlying details builds better appreciation of process behavior and constraints.
source_quote: Although CAD systems may be capable of abstracting away many of the details of how the G code would actually operate the machine I don't think you would be able to gain as much appreciation for these details if you only ever treated it as a black box.

subject: necessity of G-code knowledge for effective CNC control
main_point: A CNC executes code to generate motion, so understanding the G-code is necessary to effectively control and troubleshoot the machine. Without knowing the code, you can’t reliably make the machine do what you intend.
source_quote: The CNC machine moves based on the code. So if you don't know the code(s) then don't really understand how to make the machine work for you.

subject: software limitations in replacing engineering and manufacturing roles
main_point: CAD/CAM or other software cannot replace the distinct roles of drafting, engineering, programming, and machining. This limitation is particularly acute in job shops and when producing completely new parts.
source_quote: there is no software that can perform all those professions (especially for job shops & any shop that's looking to make something completely new to them)
example_context: job shops and shops producing completely new parts

subject: requirement for mechanical drawings in machining
main_point: Mechanical drawings are necessary to define and communicate manufacturing requirements for machining. Tooling and strategy choices make clear why a detailed drawing is required.
source_quote: Then you'll see why a mechanical drawing is required.

subject: need for programmers to integrate tools, strategies, and processes
main_point: Skilled CNC programmers are needed to coordinate tooling, strategies, and process details so the operation runs correctly. Relying solely on CAD/CAM output is not sufficient to make everything work together.
source_quote: And why you need programmers to figure out how to make everything work together.

subject: G-code snippets for setup tasks
main_point: Basic G-code literacy lets operators write small snippets to handle setup tasks like changing tools and setting work offsets without going back to CAM. This speeds routine setup and minor on-machine adjustments.
source_quote: Then it might be practical to be able to write short snippets to change tools, work coordinates etc.
example_value: Typing a command to load tool number 16 or to set a work coordinate.

subject: Reading G-code to debug/verify CAM output
main_point: To debug postprocessor-generated programs or verify them before running, you should be able to read G-code at least at a superficial level. This helps catch issues in CAM output quickly.
source_quote: In these cases you need to be able to read the g-code atleast superficially.

subject: Inserting program stops and simple automation edits
main_point: Editing G-code allows you to insert stops and inter-operation actions (such as cleaning a bore) and to make simple automation handoffs between programs. This avoids a full CAM re-post for small process tweaks.
source_quote: You might want to be able to add a stop in the program to clean up a bore between operations, make automation changes between programs etc.
example_value: Adding a stop to clean a bore between operations.

subject: On-machine edits vs returning to CAD/CAM for small changes
main_point: For small program tweaks, editing the G-code at the machine can be faster than leaving the shop floor to open CAD/CAM and re-post. Choosing on-machine edits reduces turnaround for minor adjustments.
source_quote: But that might mean leaving the shop floor opening the CAD or you might just type in the change then and there.
example_value: Typing a quick change at the control instead of reopening CAD/CAM.

subject: Using G-code to perform tasks not supported by CAM
main_point: When your CAM system lacks certain capabilities, writing direct G-code enables operations the CAM cannot produce, such as broaching or issuing robot commands. G-code extends capability beyond CAM limitations.
source_quote: You might want to do something your cam does not do. Like say a broaching operation or send commands to a tending robot.
example_value: Implementing a broaching cycle or sending commands to a tending robot via G-code.
example_context: CAM systems that do not support specific operations or external device commands.

subject: Parameterizing CNC programs with variables for reuse
main_point: You can reuse the same program for different part variants by parameterizing it with variables, reducing duplication and simplifying changes. Postprocessors can also be configured to output variables for this purpose.
source_quote: You may want to use same program for different parts so you might instrument it by variables.
example_context: CNC controls that support macro variables (e.g., Fanuc Macro B or equivalent).

subject: Importance of G-code literacy vs job variety
main_point: G-code reading skills grow in importance as job variety and changeovers increase. Frequent job changes demand more frequent program adjustments and verification.
source_quote: Being able to read g-code becomes more important the more different jobs you run during the course of a week.

subject: hand-written G-code vs CAD/CAM time-to-program
main_point: For some jobs, writing a simple G-code program directly is faster than creating a CAD model and generating code through CAM. Learning G-code lets you produce results more quickly when the full CAD/CAM workflow would add unnecessary overhead.
source_quote: Since certain projects for certain tasks can be composed speedier than the time it takes to create an identical CAD document.
example_context: quick/simple CNC tasks where full CAD/CAM setup would be slower than hand-coding

subject: parametric G-code with variables vs multiple CAD files
