main_point: Using variables to parameterize G-code allows one program to produce different sizes by accepting a key dimension as input. Creating and managing separate CAD files for each size takes more time and effort than maintaining a single parametric program.
source_quote: Likewise, utilization of factors makes the program more helpful ie a program to create a chamber can be composed to accept width as the controlling contention while delivering numerous CAD records for different various measurements requires significant investment.
example_value: Example given: a program to create a chamber that accepts width as the controlling parameter.
example_context: CNC controls/CAM workflows that support variables or parametric programming

subject: shop-floor G-code snippets for setup tasks
main_point: During machine and tooling setup, it’s practical to write short G-code snippets to handle tasks like tool changes and setting work offsets. Being able to code these directly speeds up adjustments without relying on the full CAD/CAM workflow.
source_quote: You have to arrange the machine and apparatuses every once in a while. At that point it may be functional to have the option to compose short pieces to change instruments, work organizes, and so on
example_value: Author’s example: a simple command like loading tool number 16.

subject: reading G-code to debug/verify CAM-posted programs
main_point: When CAM postprocessors generate code or when you need to verify a program, you must be able to read G-code at least at a basic level. This enables you to troubleshoot issues or confirm what the program will do before running it.
source_quote: You might be in a circumstance where you have to troubleshoot code created by the postprocessor of your CAD/CAM application. Or on the other hand, you have to check a program. In these cases, you should have the option to peruse the g-code at least cursorily.
example_context: using CAD/CAM systems with postprocessors to generate CNC code

subject: inserting program stops for in-process interventions
main_point: Operators should know how to insert program stops to pause execution for in-process tasks. This allows cleanup between operations (e.g., removing a burr) or making automation-related changes before continuing.
source_quote: You should have the option to include a stop in the program to tidy up a drag between activities, make computerization changes between programs, and so on
example_value: Adding a stop to clean up a drag between operations.

subject: on-machine G-code edits vs returning to CAD/CAM
main_point: For small edits, it can be more efficient to modify the G-code at the machine rather than leaving the shop floor to adjust the CAD/CAM file and repost. Knowing G-code enables quick, in-place changes that minimize downtime.
source_quote: You may need to roll out a little improvement to the program. Sure you can return to the scoundrel application. Yet, that may mean leaving the shop floor opening the CAD or you may very well sort in the change without even a moment's pause.
example_context: shop-floor situations where minor program tweaks are needed during machining

subject: SolidWorks sketch lines vs model features in drawings
main_point: In SolidWorks, a standalone sketch line cannot be turned into a model feature, so it will not appear in a drawing via model-derived annotations. To have geometry propagate to the drawing, it must exist as a feature rather than just a line in a sketch.
source_quote: Obviously, it's impossible to generate a feature from a line. And without a feature, you can't propagate the line into the drawing.
example_value: The author notes a free-hanging line is illegal and would need to be converted into a slot to create the feature properly.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling and drawing generation

subject: laser cutting path length vs cost
main_point: Replacing a single line cut with a slot doubles the laser cut length, which increases cutting time and therefore cost.
source_quote: But doing that means I end up cutting twice as much and paying more.
example_value: Using full cutouts with a width of about 1 mm instead of single-line cuts.
example_context: Laser cutting jobs where pricing scales with cut length/time

subject: B-Rep nonmanifold edges in CAD models
main_point: Solid B-Rep models cannot represent one-dimensional cut lines as features because those would be nonmanifold edges; a single-line cut cannot exist as a valid solid feature.
source_quote: Well the main problem is that a B-Rep model can not end up producing nonmanifold edges.

subject: laser kerf and CAD representation of cuts
main_point: Because lasers have kerf and CAD models the finished geometry, a cut is represented as a finite-width slot; even with zero kerf the operation yields a bounded cavity, not a 1D line.
source_quote: The thing is a laser obviously has a kerf and your CAD application is intended to model the end result after cutting. Even a cut without a Kerf would produce a cavity with 4 sides.

subject: CAM responsibility for optimization
main_point: Path and process optimization for cutting should be handled in CAM, not forced into the CAD model geometry.
source_quote: Obviously optimization like this is the CAM modules job.

subject: sketch lines included in 2D export for laser cuts
main_point: To convey single-line laser cuts without creating solid features, draw them as separate sketch entities and include those lines directly in the 2D export.
source_quote: But if you must like to suggest an alternative approach just make the individual line cuts as a separate sketch entity and then include the lines in your final 2D export.
example_context: SolidWorks 2D export for laser cutting drawings

subject: using categories/layers for dashed bend guides
main_point: Indicate bend guides by assigning lines to a distinct category (layer/color) rather than drawing literal dashed segments, and rely on the downstream CAM operator to map categories to operations.
source_quote: As for dashes who cares just make the line a different category and let whoever is downstream worry what different lines mean. Data is still going to go to a CAM operator (even if its you).
example_context: Laser-cutting workflows where CAD output is interpreted by CAM operators

subject: service policies and standards for one-line cuts
main_point: Many laser-cutting services prohibit single-line (nonmanifold) cuts; since standards don’t define such lines, you’ll be forced to add ad-hoc explanations and may face significant QC issues.
source_quote: Note that some operators like say LaserBoost actually tell you bluntly that you are not allowed to do these one line cuts. This also makes sense, there is really no provision in technical drawing standards for what the nonmanifold line would mean. So you would need to explain things anyway, and have huge problems if you for some reason have QC problems.
example_context: Laser cutting service providers (e.g., LaserBoost) and adherence to technical drawing standards

subject: treating SolidWorks as indirect/parametric modeler
main_point: Do not approach SolidWorks as a direct modeler; treat it as an indirect/parametric modeling system rather than trying to encode manufacturing minutiae in the solid.
source_quote: Thing is your treating soldworks as a direct modeller, don't. Its an indirect modeling engine.
example_context: SolidWorks parametric modeling workflows

subject: CAM handles cut sequencing and direction
main_point: SolidWorks does not specify cut job start points or per-line cutting directions; such sequencing is handled downstream by CAM or the operator.
source_quote: Your also not expecting to define starting point of cut job, cutting direction of each line in the model etc. in solidworks so there's still a lot that gets done by something/someone downstream.
example_context: SolidWorks-to-CAM laser cutting process

subject: dash style mangling during CAD/CAM translation
main_point: If dashed lines are represented as actual segmented geometry, intermediate translation steps can mangle them into many dash segments, which is undesirable for downstream processing.
source_quote: This way if worst comes to pass nothing in-between mangles your dashes to actual dash segments which is bad indeed.
example_context: Export/import steps between CAD and CAM for laser cutting

subject: progressive mating strategy in SolidWorks assemblies
main_point: For mechanism layout in SolidWorks, begin by over-constraining parts with angle and distance mates to explore and stabilize the configuration, then progressively remove those mates as true interconnections are added. This trial-and-error approach helps you find workable geometry before finalizing realistic constraints.
source_quote: I tend to use SolidWorks assembly to trial and error these types of assemblies, then worry about how to make it work.  Constrain (Angle and Distance) the crap put of components to start and remove them as components are interconnected.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies for mechanism layout using mates

subject: removing angle mates to restore kinematic freedom
main_point: After using angle mates to construct the structure, delete those angle constraints so the assembly retains only the true joints and can move as a basic mechanism.
source_quote: Remove all angle mates and you should have the basic mechanics.
example_context: SolidWorks mechanism assemblies where angle mates were used for construction

subject: origin-to-origin mating to anchor an assembly
main_point: Anchor the mechanism by mating a component’s origin to the assembly origin, ensuring that origin lies on the faces being mated so the relationship is valid.
source_quote: Mate one of the lower arm origins to the assembly origin.  Origin must be on mated faces.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies using origin and face mates

subject: consistent orientation of repeated subassemblies
main_point: Keep repeated components oriented consistently during assembly to avoid mirrored or inconsistent kinematics.
source_quote: Make sure all  upper arms are in the same direction.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies of multi-arm mechanisms

subject: using point mates as a simplification
main_point: As a simplification during layout, you can temporarily mate components to a reference point instead of modeling the full, realistic joint.
source_quote: You can see I cheated and mated them to a point.
example_context: SolidWorks mechanism assembly where platform is temporarily mated to a point

subject: SOLIDWORKS subassembly flexibility with layout sketches
main_point: In SOLIDWORKS, any subassembly that contains a layout sketch cannot be set to Flexible; it is forced to remain Rigid.
source_quote: subassemblies with layout sketches must be kept rigid
example_value: The user attempted to make the Robotic Arm subassembly flexible within the Robotic assembly but was blocked by this limitation.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS assemblies that include layout sketches within a subassembly

subject: fillet feature order of operations (SolidWorks)
main_point: Apply the smaller fillet first before creating adjacent larger fillets to prevent a sharp cusp where the fillets intersect. Sequencing fillet features matters for achieving smooth blends.
source_quote:
You need to do the yellow fillet 
first
, in order to avoid the "sharp point where the two fillets meet" which you mentioned in your comment.
example_value: The 1 mm (yellow) fillet was created first to avoid a cusp, then the larger radii were added.
example_context: SolidWorks fillet features on intersecting edges where multiple radii meet

subject: removing existing fillets from imported geometry using Delete Face
main_point: When working from imported/featureless geometry, use the Delete Face command to strip existing fillets and return to an unfilleted solid so you can rebuild the blends correctly.
source_quote: I removed both of these using the "delete face" command to give a true 'blank slate',
example_value: The previously applied yellow and red fillets in the provided model were removed to start fresh.
example_context: SolidWorks surface/solid editing of imported STEP models lacking feature history

subject: using variable radius fillet to combine multiple radii
main_point: Create multiple differing corner radii in one operation by using a variable radius fillet after establishing the initial fillet, which helps produce a smoother blend.
source_quote: before adding both red and orange together using a variable radius fillet.
example_value: After the 1 mm fillet, both the 5 mm (red) and 2.3 mm (orange) radii were applied together as a variable radius fillet.
example_context: SolidWorks variable radius fillet feature for blending adjacent fillets

subject: SolidWorks tessellation of curves for graphics and STL export
main_point: In SolidWorks, both the on-screen graphics and STL export represent curved geometry by tessellating it into straight line segments. Each has its own resolution settings, so a smooth spline can appear faceted if either setting is too coarse.
source_quote: there are separate settings for the SW graphic window and STL export which both approximate the curve as a series of straight lines.
example_context: SolidWorks graphics window and STL export settings

subject: Diagnosing faceted curves via STL export settings (SolidWorks)
main_point: If a mathematically smooth spline looks faceted in a 3D print or exported mesh from SolidWorks, first attribute the issue to STL export tessellation settings rather than the spline itself. Check and adjust those STL settings to eliminate the faceting.
source_quote: Your problem is in your STL export settings
example_context: SolidWorks STL export for 3D printing/additive workflows

subject: DWG import duplicate contours from stacked path layers
main_point: Importing a DWG (exported from Illustrator) into a SolidWorks sketch can result in two stacked path layers that create duplicate contours, which in turn cause sketch/extrude errors.
source_quote: Using Repair Sketch, I found the issue to be that there are just 2 layers of paths stacked on top of each other, and this is what caused the duplicate contours.
example_value: The user imported an Illustrator-generated DWG for an engraving sketch; extrude failed until Repair Sketch revealed two stacked path layers creating duplicates.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch import from Adobe Illustrator DWG export

subject: Effect of Illustrator stroke width on DWG duplicate layers
main_point: Setting stroke width to zero in Illustrator does not prevent the creation of separate duplicate layers/contours when the DWG is imported into SolidWorks.
source_quote: I used 0 stroke in Illustrator, but this still created the separate layer as shown.
example_value: Despite using a 0 stroke setting in Illustrator, the imported DWG still produced an extra overlapping path layer in the SolidWorks sketch.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch import from Adobe Illustrator DWG export

subject: Illustrator Image Trace duplicate paths on DWG export
main_point: Image Trace output in Illustrator can contain two coincident paths merged as one object, which export as two separate paths in a DWG even though Illustrator does not flag duplicates.
source_quote: The end product of the module creates two separate paths that are joined as one, so although Illustrator doesn't identify it, it still results in 2 paths when exported into DWG.
example_value: Exporting the Image Trace output to DWG produced two overlapping paths in the DWG file.
example_context: Adobe Illustrator Image Trace module exporting to DWG

subject: Excluding non-image paths to avoid duplicate DWG entities
main_point: To prevent duplicate paths when exporting a traced graphic to DWG, exclude all non-image paths and keep only the paths that define the image.
source_quote: The workaround for this is to make sure to exclude all paths except for the ones pertaining to the image, and this seemed to work.
example_value: Keeping only the image-related paths avoided the doubled paths after export.
example_context: Adobe Illustrator Image Trace module exporting to DWG

subject: comment syntax in SolidWorks equations text files
main_point: In SolidWorks external equations/global variables text files, start a comment with an apostrophe (VBA-style). This lets you append comments after a variable or equation on the same line.
source_quote: It works the same way as VBA - just add an apostrophe, so, for example:
example_value: "Length" = 5mm 'Comment
example_context: SolidWorks external equations/global variable definition text files (Equation Manager input), circa 2021

subject: visibility of comments in SolidWorks Equation Manager
main_point: Comments added in the SolidWorks variables/equations text file appear in the Equation Manager’s Comments column.
source_quote: This will then be visible in the "Comments" column within the Equation Manager, too.
example_context: SolidWorks Equation Manager UI behavior for external equations/global variable files

subject: uniform surface pressure equivalent to a torque on a circular face
main_point: A uniform pressure applied over a circular face to generate a target torque Mt relates by Mt = (2/3)·π·q·R^3, so the required constant pressure magnitude is q = (3/2)·Mt/(π·R^3). This follows from integrating the torque contribution of annular rings under constant pressure across the radius.
source_quote:
Then the magnitude of the constant pressure 
$q$
 should be:

$$q= \frac{3}{2}\frac{M_t}{\pi  R^3}$$

subject: STL editability and IP protection
main_point: The STL format is not intended as an intellectual property protection mechanism and STL files are editable using mesh editors such as Meshmixer.
source_quote: No. Intellectual property isn't relevant, and STLs are definitely "editable" - I use Meshmixer to edit them directly.
example_value: The author states they edit STL files directly in Meshmixer.

subject: STL interchange purpose
main_point: The STL format is designed for broad compatibility and predictable viewing/usage across devices, analogous to how PDFs are intended for consistent display.
source_quote: It is meant to make a file safe to open on pretty much any device with predictable results, similar to a PDF.

subject: STL data content
main_point: STL files encode geometry by storing mesh vertex data rather than parametric features or analytic surfaces.
source_quote: STL's store the vertices.

subject: BREP vs mesh surface representation
main_point: BREP CAD geometry represents a cylinder as a single smooth surface, while an STL export approximates it with many flat polygons spanning between mesh vertices.
source_quote: You will notice that a cylinder created in SOLIDWORKS is a single smooth surface, where a cylinder saved as an STL is made up of numerous flat polygons, which bridge the gaps between the vertices.

subject: STL facet size tradeoff and export control
main_point: STL mesh resolution is set at export, controlling the facet size and thus the tradeoff between file complexity and geometric accuracy to the original BREP.
source_quote: The size of these facets (and so the tradeoff between STL complexity and accuracy to the ideal geometry) is determined during export from BREP to Mesh.

subject: SOLIDWORKS STL import default behavior
main_point: Dragging and dropping an STL into SOLIDWORKS imports it as a graphic body by default rather than an editable mesh/solid.
source_quote: When you drag/drop an STL into SOLIDWORKS, by default, it imports as a graphic body.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS (circa SW2020) mesh import behavior

subject: Initial SOLIDWORKS workflow for STL editing
main_point: After importing an STL into SOLIDWORKS, first convert it to a mesh body and remove the graphic bodies so only the editable imported bodies remain.
source_quote: Your first step should be: INSERT -> FEATURES -> CONVERT TO MESH BODY. Select everything, hit OK, and then delete all graphic bodies from the feature tree, leaving only "Imported" bodies.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS (SW2020) mesh tools workflow

subject: Splitting multi-part STLs
main_point: To separate parts in a multi-body STL, handle it in the slicer or delete unwanted imported bodies in SOLIDWORKS, optionally using Delete/Keep Bodies for a non-destructive approach.
source_quote: Splitting multi-part STLs is usually handled directly in the slicing software. You can simply delete the "Imported" bodies that you don't want, or use a "Delete/Keep Bodies" feature to do so non-destructively if you prefer.
example_context: 3D printing workflows and SOLIDWORKS body management

subject: SOLIDWORKS mesh body editing methods
main_point: In SOLIDWORKS, mesh bodies can be edited either via surface operations (such as Surface Cut or Split) or by interacting with another mesh body using the Combine tool.
source_quote: There are two main ways you can interact with Mesh bodies. These are with surfaces (e.g. Surface Cut, Split, etc.), or with another mesh body, using the "Combine" tool.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS mesh editing (SW2020)

subject: Adding features to mesh bodies in SOLIDWORKS
main_point: To add geometry to an STL in SOLIDWORKS, model the new feature, convert it to a mesh at the desired resolution, then use Combine with the Add option to merge it into the existing mesh.
source_quote: So, to Add a feature to your mesh, you can model said lump as normal, use "Convert to Mesh Body" to create a mesh, with whatever resolution you require, and then use "Combine" and "Add" to join these together.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS mesh operations workflow (SW2020)

subject: Cutting features from mesh bodies in SOLIDWORKS
main_point: Use Combine with the Subtract option to remove geometry from an STL in SOLIDWORKS to control mesh resolution, or make a surface from a protruding tool and perform a surface cut.
source_quote: To Cut a feature from your mesh, it's best to use the same process with the "Subtract" option, as this gives you control over the resolution. Alternatively, if the cutting tool sticks out of the original mesh, you can delete one face of the solid to make a surface, and use surface cut.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS mesh operations workflow (SW2020)

subject: Moving features in mesh models
main_point: Relocating features in an STL is often easier in dedicated mesh editors like Meshmixer or Blender rather than inside SOLIDWORKS, depending on the model's specifics.
source_quote: Moving a feature is a little trickier, and may be best handled, again, with mesh-specific software such as Meshmixer or Blender, depending on your specific model.
example_context: Mesh editing with Meshmixer/Blender vs. SOLIDWORKS

subject: STL limitation for parametric face operations
main_point: Because STL meshes lack the topological and parametric face data of BREP models, they cannot support operations like 'move face' that rely on surrounding faces adapting to fill gaps.
source_quote: STL files simply do not contain the data of where their faces are in the same way, and cannot afford this functionality.

subject: Mesh vertex/face moves causing deformation
main_point: Directly moving STL faces or vertices in mesh editors often deforms adjacent polygons, creating geometry that typically needs subsequent repair steps.
source_quote: In a Mesh editing specific software, you would be able to select the STL faces/vertices directly and move these around, but this would likely leave deformed polygons either side of the moving feature - which requires additional steps to fix anyway!

subject: Converting mesh to BREP in SOLIDWORKS
main_point: SOLIDWORKS can convert an STL mesh into a solid BREP composed of many planar facets.
source_quote: You can convert the mesh to a solid BREP made of lots of flat surfaces.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS mesh-to-solid conversion (SW2020)

subject: Recommendation against general mesh-to-BREP conversion
main_point: Converting STL meshes to BREP solids in SOLIDWORKS is generally discouraged and should be reserved for very simple models.
source_quote: and is not recommended except on the simplest of models.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS mesh-to-solid conversion (SW2020)

subject: Scan-To-3D remodeling workflow
main_point: Using SOLIDWORKS Scan-To-3D can accelerate sketch creation from a mesh, but you still have to remodel the part from scratch rather than obtaining a fully featured SLDPRT.
source_quote: You still need to model the part 'from scratch', but sketch generation is considerably sped up.
example_context: SOLIDWORKS Scan-To-3D add-in usage (SW2020)

subject: fillet application to part edges
main_point: In CAD workflows, a fillet feature targets edges that belong to a single continuous body/part, not edges spanning multiple separate parts. This is the typical way fillet operations are defined.
source_quote: Fillets are generally applied to edges of one homogenous part.
example_context: 3D solid modeling CAD systems (e.g., Solidworks)

subject: lack of shared edge prevents fillet between parts
main_point: If two components are separate bodies that do not share a common edge, a fillet cannot be created between them. The absence of a shared topological edge is a hard limitation for fillet features.
source_quote: You can't because the two parts don't share an edge.

subject: merging parts to enable cross-part fillet
main_point: To create a fillet across the interface of two components, first combine them into a single body (or otherwise create a shared edge). Once merged, the fillet can be applied as a normal single-part edge feature.
source_quote: You need to merge the two parts somehow.
example_context: Creating a fillet across the interface of two CAD parts/components

subject: conceptual limitation of filleting separate objects
main_point: The inability to fillet between two separate parts is conceptual rather than a software shortcoming: fillets are defined on a single object's edges, so applying one across independent objects is not a meaningful operation.
source_quote: It's not a limitation of the software. It's that filleting two separate objects doesn't make sense.

subject: SolidWorks multibody combine-subtract to propagate fillet between parts
main_point: To create a fillet that spans two assembly parts and propagate it to one part in SolidWorks, edit one part and temporarily convert it to a multibody by inserting the other part. Duplicate the host body, merge the bodies, apply the fillet, then use Combine-Subtract with the copied host body to remove the inserted part, leaving the fillet on the host part.
source_quote:
Use insert part, to add the yellow part, making this a multibody

Use move/copy bodies to make a copy of the grey part in the same place

Merge the grey and one of the yellow parts using combine tool

Apply fillet

Subtract the yellow part using combine tool, with the copied body as a subtract source.
example_value: Example: insert the yellow part into the gray part, copy the gray body, combine/merge, fillet, then subtract the yellow using the copied gray body as the subtract tool.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling workflow using Insert Part, Move/Copy Bodies, and Combine features within a multibody part

subject: temporary geometry to create inter-part fillet
main_point: A practical way to create a fillet between two separate parts is to add temporary extrusions to the target part so the fillet can be formed across the interface, then remove those temporary features afterward. This leverages sacrificial geometry to allow the fillet operation and preserves the final part shape by cutting the dummies off.
source_quote: This is similar to Johnathan's answer, but I would add some dummy extrudes to the grey part, apply the fillet, and then cut off the extrudes.
example_value: Add dummy extrudes to the gray part, apply the fillet across the interface, then cut away the dummy extrudes.

subject: direct modeling of fillets via extrude/revolve
main_point: For typical situations, it’s often faster to directly model the fillet as a simple extrude or revolve from a sketch on the part rather than constructing a complex inter-part fillet. This manual approach simplifies the operation and avoids extra steps.
source_quote: In most practical cases I would probably just extrude or revolve a simplified fillet onto the gray part by manually drawing it.

subject: equation-driven helix definition
main_point: You can generate a 3D helical curve in Solidworks by defining an Equation Driven Curve with x(t)=2t·cos(3t), y(t)=2t·sin(3t), and z(t)=4t.
source_quote:
Try using the following equations

- X(t) = 2* t* cos(3*t)
- y(t) = 2* t* sin(3*t)
- z(t)= 4 *t
example_value: Parameter t drives a helix whose radius grows with t and whose height increases linearly with t.
example_context: Solidworks Equation Driven Curve feature for 3D parametric curves

subject: helix radial growth parameters
main_point: In the parametric helix x(t)=a·t·cos(b·t), y(t)=a·t·sin(b·t), the coefficients on t and the angle (the “2” and “3” in the example) control how quickly the helix’s radial circle grows as t increases.
source_quote: 2s and the 3s in the first two will change the rate that the circle of the  helix grows
example_value: Using x=2t cos(3t), y=2t sin(3t) produces a faster-growing radius than smaller coefficients.
example_context: Solidworks Equation Driven Curve with x=a·t·cos(b·t), y=a·t·sin(b·t) formulation

subject: helix axial spacing parameter
main_point: In the parametric helix z(t)=c·t, the coefficient multiplying t (the “4” in the example) sets the axial spacing of the helix; changing it changes the spacing.
source_quote: 4 will change the spacing of the helix
example_value: With z(t)=4t the turns are spaced farther apart than with z(t)=2t.
example_context: Solidworks Equation Driven Curve using z(t)=c·t for axial advance

subject: SolidWorks reference planes for applying forces in Motion Study
main_point: In SolidWorks Motion Study, when the target surface is curved or non-flat, define reference planes (perpendicular to an axis or parallel to a surface) and apply forces relative to those planes to control force direction/type.
source_quote: you can create planes perpendicular to any axis or parallel to any surface. if the surface is not flat as in your case these planes can then be used to apply forces of different types in motion study
example_value: For a mechanism with non-flat contact surfaces, create auxiliary planes and use them as the basis to apply forces in different directions within Motion Study.
example_context: SolidWorks Motion Study on assemblies/parts with curved or non-flat surfaces

subject: STEP export of PCB from Altium to SOLIDWORKS
main_point: Exporting a PCB from Altium to STEP loses silkscreen and trace detail, resulting in a plain block-like model in SOLIDWORKS rather than a realistic PCB.
source_quote: since silk-screen printing and tracks on the PCB are not drawn. The PCB itself is just like a block, very unrealistic.
example_context: Exporting a PCB from Altium Designer to STEP and importing into SOLIDWORKS

subject: 3D PDF import into SOLIDWORKS solids
main_point: Importing a PCB via 3D PDF into SOLIDWORKS yields only graphics bodies, and attempting to open it as a solid or surface can cause the software to hang.
source_quote: 1. The board opens in the form of Graphics bodies, if you open it as a solid body or surface, then the solid simply hangs and that's it.
example_context: Importing a 3D PDF exported from Altium Designer into SOLIDWORKS

subject: 3D PDF unit scaling on import
main_point: When importing a 3D PDF, the model scale may be incorrect due to improper unit translation between metric and imperial, leading to major dimensional errors.
source_quote: There should be a length of 100 mm, and it is 9 with something, that is, the point is not in the correct translation of inch-centimeter-meter-millimeter.
example_value: A board expected to be 100 mm imports at about 9.x mm.
example_context: Importing a 3D PDF of a PCB into SOLIDWORKS

subject: Manual recoloring to restore imported PCB appearance
main_point: Manually assigning colors/materials to imported PCB geometry in SOLIDWORKS can restore a good-looking drawing, but it is time-consuming and duplicative effort.
source_quote: You can manually sit to paint all the conductors and radioelements, set the material for them. Yes, it works, after painting, the model can be drawn very well, but it is long and wrong to sit and paint what I have already painted in another program.
example_context: After importing a PCB (e.g., via 3D PDF) where colors are lost in SOLIDWORKS drawings

subject: SolidWorks limit mate
main_point: In SolidWorks assemblies, use Advanced Mates—specifically a Limit Mate—to constrain a component’s motion so it stops at a defined limit or within a set range.
source_quote: Have a look at some of the advanced mates. For example limit mates :
example_context: SolidWorks assembly mates (Advanced Mates, Limit Mate)

subject: SolidWorks path mate
main_point: For more complex constrained motion, use a Path Mate in SolidWorks to force a component to move along a defined trajectory.
source_quote: Or you can get even fancier by defining a mate along a path.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly mates (Path Mate)

subject: SolidWorks sidebar visibility control for solid bodies
main_point: In SolidWorks, expand the FeatureManager sidebar and open the Solid Bodies folder to hide bodies individually. This enables per-body visibility control instead of hiding the entire part.
source_quote: See below - expand the side bar and the solid bodies folder, to then individually hide solid bodies.
example_context: SolidWorks FeatureManager Design Tree and Solid Bodies folder

subject: SolidWorks sidebar visibility toggles for reference geometry and sketches
main_point: The same SolidWorks sidebar can quickly toggle visibility of reference geometry and sketches such as Sketches, Planes, and Axes. You can show or hide these entities from the tree without affecting other items.
source_quote: You can use the same side bar to quickly toggle visiblity of Sketches, Planes, Axes etc., too
example_context: SolidWorks FeatureManager Design Tree visibility controls

subject: SolidWorks mesh body conversion enabling Boolean operations
main_point: In SolidWorks, convert an imported graphics body (e.g., from STL) to a mesh body to enable Boolean operations with other mesh bodies. This conversion lets you modify the mesh using standard Boolean tools.
source_quote: You can convert it from a graphic body to a mesh body (use the command search at the top right of the screen), and then you can use the Boolean tools to affect it using other mesh bodies.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD with an imported STL that initially appears as a graphics body

subject: Sketching on mesh bodies in SolidWorks
main_point: In SolidWorks, you cannot sketch directly on a mesh body’s “face” because meshes are composed of vertices/triangles rather than analytic faces. This imposes a limitation on face-referenced sketching for mesh geometry.
source_quote: You will not be able to "sketch on the face", since by their very definition, mesh bodies are made up of vertices, not faces.
example_context: SolidWorks mesh bodies imported from STL

subject: Creating sketch planes from mesh triangle vertices
main_point: When you need to sketch relative to mesh geometry in SolidWorks, define a reference plane using three vertices from a mesh triangle, then sketch on that plane as a substitute for a face.
source_quote: If you need to sketch on a face, You can use the three vertices of any triangle to define a plane, and sketch on that.
example_context: SolidWorks workflows involving mesh bodies (e.g., imported STL) where direct face sketching is not supported

subject: SolidWorks 'Save As' and mirror workflow for mirrored part creation
main_point: To create a mirrored counterpart as its own file in SolidWorks, duplicate the model with Save As, open the new file, mirror the geometry, and remove the original body if needed. This yields a separate mirrored part you can reuse.
source_quote:
You can 
Save as
 a new part, then in the new part mirror (and delete the old).
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling

subject: SolidWorks multi-body approach for mirrored component
main_point: When the relative placement is fixed, create a second solid body within the same SolidWorks part to represent the counterpart, and insert that body into assemblies like any other component. This avoids building a separate part file.
source_quote:
If the distance is fixed and the orientation You can create another body within the same part. (This is something people sometimes forget)

Then you can insert that body as you would normally do
example_context: SolidWorks multi-body parts and assemblies

subject: SolidWorks first feature labeling (base vs boss)
main_point: In SolidWorks 2020, the first feature in a new part appears labeled as a boss feature rather than a base feature.
source_quote: but rather it alway shows as a boss feature
example_value: The feature tree shows Boss-Extrude1 for the initial extrude.
example_context: SolidWorks 2020 part modeling feature tree

subject: SolidWorks base vs boss feature definition
main_point: In SolidWorks terminology, a base feature is the initial feature of the part, while a boss feature refers to subsequent features built from it.
source_quote: a "base feature" represents the starting feature and a "boss feature" represents any features built off of that
example_context: SolidWorks feature terminology and documentation

subject: base vs boss extrude equivalence in SolidWorks
main_point: In SolidWorks, there is no functional distinction between a base extrude and a boss extrude; they are the same operation. Only cut extrudes are different in function.
source_quote: There's no difference at all - an extrude is an extrude is an extrude (unless it's a cut)
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling features

subject: SolidWorks extrude tools vs other CAD
main_point: SolidWorks exposes Boss and Cut as separate tools, whereas some other CAD systems use a single extrude command with an add/remove (Boolean) toggle.
source_quote: SolidWorks differs from some other CAD in that Boss and Cut are separate tools - others have just one extrude tool with a Boolean toggle in the feature manager
example_context: Comparison of SolidWorks to other CAD systems’ feature tool design

subject: feature naming in SolidWorks feature tree
main_point: Rename features in the SolidWorks FeatureManager tree to clearly represent their role or intent; use names like "Base" if that improves clarity.
source_quote: You can (and should for your own sanity) rename features in the tree to better represent what they are to you.
example_context: SolidWorks FeatureManager design tree and feature naming

subject: SolidWorks cavity cut at assembly level
main_point: When trimming one part by another at the assembly level in SolidWorks, the resulting cut feature resides in the trimmed part’s feature tree, while the part’s position continues to be controlled by the assembly constraints.
source_quote: The cut must be added to the feature tree of the part to be trimmed, but the location of the body remains defined within the assembly.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies using the Cavity feature or in-context edits to trim one part with another

subject: Using assembly-level inter-part references in SolidWorks
main_point: Avoid using assembly-level inter-part trimming as a general practice because it creates many interlinking references that complicate the model.
source_quote: I wouldn't usually recommend this as best practice, however, since there are a lot of interlinking references.
example_context: SolidWorks in-context features and assembly-driven references between parts

subject: Suppression/deletion limitation for Cavity cutting tool component in SolidWorks
main_point: A component used as the cutting tool for a Cavity feature in a SolidWorks assembly cannot be suppressed or deleted because the Cavity depends on that reference.
source_quote: You can't suppress or delete it, as the cavity feature is referencing it.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly modeling using the Cavity feature to trim one part with another

subject: Procedure to trim a part by another using SolidWorks Cavity feature
main_point: To trim a part against another at the assembly level in SolidWorks, edit the target component, insert a Cavity feature, and select the cutting component as the tool body.
source_quote:
1. In the assembly, click Edit Component for the part to be cut
2. Insert - Feature - Cavity
3. Select the part that you wish to do the cutting with.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly workflow for inter-part trimming using the Cavity feature

subject: SolidWorks drawing border line weight adjustment
main_point: To reduce border line thickness in a SolidWorks drawing, enter Edit Sheet Format to select the border entities, then use the Lines toolbar to change their line weight to a thinner value.
source_quote:
1. Right click in the drawing area, and then click "Edit Sheet Format", to allow you to select the lines you want to adjust
2. Open the Lines Toolbar - you can search for it if you don't have it visible
3. Change the line weight using the relevant tool
example_value: Workflow: right-click the drawing area > Edit Sheet Format; open the Lines Toolbar; adjust the selected lines’ weight to a lighter thickness.
example_context: SolidWorks drawings using Edit Sheet Format and the Lines Toolbar

subject: SolidWorks Smart Fasteners hardware stack
main_point: In SolidWorks, the Smart Fasteners capability for adding associated hardware is called a "hardware stack," and it is an officially documented feature with setup guidance.
source_quote: This is known as a hardware stack, and the official SW help pages provides a clear explanation regarding setting these up:
example_context: SolidWorks Smart Fasteners feature

subject: online SolidWorks platform for file format conversion
main_point: Use a free online SolidWorks platform to convert SolidWorks files into another desired format.
source_quote:
I found one way and that is to use free 
online solid-work platform
 to change those tile format to desired new format:
example_context: Web-based SolidWorks services/tools for file conversion

subject: IGES/STEP exchange format import to FreeCAD
main_point: To get SolidWorks models into FreeCAD, export them to a neutral exchange format like IGES or STEP and then import those files in FreeCAD. This avoids relying on native SLDPRT/SLDASM support.
source_quote: As mentioned before, you could use an exchange file format such as IGS or STEP and import this file into FreeCAD.
example_value: Examples of neutral formats mentioned are IGS (IGES) and STEP.
example_context: Transferring SolidWorks part/assembly geometry into FreeCAD via neutral CAD exchange formats (IGES/STEP).

subject: Onshape import and conversion of SolidWorks files
main_point: You can use Onshape to import SolidWorks files and then convert/export them to other formats for use in different CAD tools. This provides a free path to translate SLDPRT/SLDASM into neutral formats.
source_quote:
Onshape
 that lets you import SolidWorks files for free and you could convert it to another file format.
example_context: Using the Onshape cloud CAD platform to import SolidWorks files and export alternative formats.

subject: SolidWorks to FreeCAD file conversion via STL
main_point: To use SolidWorks part/assembly files in FreeCAD, have someone with SolidWorks open them and export to STL, which FreeCAD can import.
source_quote: you could send them your SLDPRTs and SLDASMs and they could import them and send them back to you as STLs which you can import into FreeCAD.
example_context: Interoperability between SolidWorks (.sldprt/.sldasm) and FreeCAD by exporting from SolidWorks to STL and importing into FreeCAD

subject: Onshape browser-based parametric CAD
main_point: Onshape runs in a web browser and provides parametric modeling capabilities, offering an online CAD option.
source_quote: It is a browser based parametric modelling software.

subject: transition from SolidWorks to Onshape vs other CAD
main_point: For a SolidWorks user evaluating alternatives, moving to Onshape can be easier than switching to Inventor or Creo.
source_quote: I've also tried a couple of others like Inventor and Creo. However, the transition to Onshape has been the smoothest.
example_value: The author used SolidWorks for over 10 years, tried Inventor and Creo, and found Onshape the smoothest transition.
example_context: Users migrating from SolidWorks to other CAD systems (Onshape, Inventor, Creo).

subject: eDrawings SolidWorks viewer
main_point: eDrawings provides a no-cost, lightweight way to view SolidWorks part and assembly files. It is suitable as a viewer when you only need to open and inspect these formats.
source_quote: It is a free lightweight viewer for Solidworks files and assemblies.
example_context: eDrawings viewer for SolidWorks (.sldprt, .sldasm) files

subject: eDrawings Linux support
main_point: eDrawings likely does not offer a native Linux version, limiting Linux users from running it directly on their systems.
source_quote: The only problem is that probably there is no option for linux.
example_context: Linux desktop OS support for eDrawings

subject: Running eDrawings on Linux via Android emulator
main_point: As a workaround for the lack of a Linux version, you can run the eDrawings mobile app under an Android emulator on Linux.
source_quote: Unless you use an android emulator and you download the mobile version.
example_value: Install an Android emulator on Linux and use it to run the eDrawings mobile app.
example_context: Linux users needing to view SolidWorks files without native eDrawings support

subject: methods to transform moment of inertia to a new axis
main_point: To obtain inertia about an arbitrary axis from data at the center of mass, apply the Parallel Axis Theorem and rotate the inertia tensor to the desired orientation. These two operations together handle translation of the axis and reorientation of the principal axes.
source_quote:
You probably need the following two for the generic solution

- Parallel axis Theorem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_axis_theorem
- Rotation of the inertia tensor https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_of_inertia#Inertia_tensor_of_rotation

subject: computability of MOI about arbitrary axis from CG data
main_point: If you know the moment of inertia about the center of mass, you can compute the inertia about any other axis. This requires appropriate translation and rotation of the inertia tensor.
source_quote: Given the Moment of inertia with respect to the center of gravity you can calculate the moment of inertia with respect to a new axis.

subject: operation order in inertia tensor translation and rotation
main_point: When transforming inertia to a new axis, performing rotation and parallel translation in the wrong order can yield incorrect results. Ensure the sequence of operations is applied correctly.
source_quote:
you need to be 
careful
 about the order to rotation and parallel translation though.

subject: spline profile variety
main_point: Industry uses a wide variety of shaft/spline interface profiles, including square and hex shapes, multi-spline counts (6, 8, and higher), and “lemon” shafts, which are commonly seen in agricultural applications.
source_quote: Many "spline" designs around in industry - load dependant etc start with square, then hex, splines 6, 8 and upward, also "lemon" shafts - lots of those used in the agricultural branch.

subject: spline specification parameters
main_point: To identify or specify a spline for replication, provide key parameters such as inner and outer diameters, spline count, length, whether it is a sliding joint, and the intended application.
source_quote: You need to give some more info : diameter inner and outer, no of splines, length, sliding joint, application etc.

subject: spline specification baseline parameters
main_point: Regardless of spline type, drawings should specify major and minor diameters, number of teeth, the class of fit, and the spline form (e.g., involute or flat) as baseline identifiers.
source_quote: Some of them are pretty straightforward and will be needed regardless of the type of spline, such as physical diameters (major and minor), number of teeth, the class of fit and spline shape (involute, flat, etc.)

subject: flat-side spline dimensioning
main_point: Flat-side (parallel-sided) splines can be fully defined using only major and minor diameters, tooth count, and the spacing between two parallel tooth flanks.
source_quote: For the most basic splines I work with, we can define it with only a major and minor diameter, the number of teeth, and the distance between two parallel tooth edges, because it's a flat side spline.
example_context: flat side splines

subject: involute spline required parameters
main_point: Involute splines require additional defining parameters—pitch diameter, pressure angle, effective tooth width, and specified pin-measurement distance—to be properly defined for manufacturing and inspection.
source_quote: However, something like an involute spline requires more information, such as a pitch diameter, pressure angel, effective tooth width, and distance between pins of a given size.
example_context: involute splines

subject: involute spline measurability limitation
main_point: Because involute tooth geometry cannot be directly measured in a practical, meaningful way, drawings must provide both theoretical design dimensions and separate measurable dimensions for inspection.
source_quote: This is because the complex shape makes it impossible to directly measure the spline geometry in a meaningful way, so we require both design dimensions and measurable dimensions.
example_context: involute spline inspection and dimensioning

subject: spline table on machining prints
main_point: Include a complete spline dimension table on machining drawings so the defining dimensions and inspection values are readily available.
source_quote: I would include a table like this on any spline machining print so that you have the information readily available.

subject: referencing ANSI B92.1 splines on drawings
main_point: When using an ANSI B92.1 spline, reference the standard on the drawing and include only the identifiers needed to find it in the table (pressure angle, fit class, and either tooth count or pitch diameter); the standard supplies the remaining data or calculation methods.
source_quote: If you are using a standard spline, such as a spline defined by ANSI B92.1, you could refer to it on a customer print as just the ANSI standard spline with only the information necessary to locate it in the standards table (should be pressure angle, class of fit, and either number of teeth or pitch diameter.) Then the standard will provide all other information, or the methods to calculate the information necessary to manufacture the spline.
example_context: splines defined by ANSI B92.1

subject: SolidWorks dimension name reset breaking variable pattern references
main_point: In SolidWorks, updating the model can reset a user-assigned name on an angle dimension that defines a plane; if a variable pattern table references that named angle, the reset breaks the reference and the pattern stops working.
source_quote: whenever I update some part of the part, it seems, the name I've given to the angle resets.  this is a problem because I'm referencing the name of that angle in the pattern table for a variable pattern.
example_value: A sketch was created on a plane defined by an angle; the angle’s user-given name was used in a variable pattern table. After updating the part, the angle’s name reset and the pattern no longer worked.
example_context: SolidWorks variable pattern tables that reference a user-named angle dimension defining a plane

subject: SolidWorks design table scaling workflow
main_point: In SolidWorks, scaling a part via a design table is typically done by exposing all sketch dimensions to the table and creating alternate configurations that drive those dimensions to different values.
source_quote: scaling in solidworks with design tables usually involves providing the table with all the dimensions of the sketch, then producing alternate configurations within the table.
example_context: SolidWorks parts using design tables to manage configurations and dimensions

subject: SolidWorks global variables in Smart Dimensions
main_point: In SolidWorks, typing ="R" in a Smart Dimension creates a global variable R, which you can reference in other dimension equations to drive and rescale geometry.
source_quote: When you are Smart Dimensioning, if you enter ="R", SW will create a global variable "R", which can be used in equations to redimension as required as long as you use "R" in the new dimensions as formulas.
example_value: A second circle dimensioned with ="R"*2 scales with the base variable R; changing R to 40 updates both circles.
example_context: SolidWorks Smart Dimension and Equations/global variables

subject: SolidWorks equation-driven dimension indicator
main_point: SolidWorks marks equation-driven dimensions with a sigma symbol to show they are controlled by equations.
source_quote: SW puts sigma before the dimension to indicate it is a equation:
example_context: SolidWorks Smart Dimension and Equations/global variables

subject: Accessing SolidWorks Equations manager
main_point: You can open and manage the Equations manager by right-clicking the Equations item in the FeatureManager tree.
source_quote: Right mouse click on Equations and you can manage Equations.
example_context: SolidWorks Smart Dimension and Equations/global variables

subject: Scaling models by driving key variables
main_point: To scale models efficiently in SolidWorks, define a small set of key global variables and drive dependent dimensions from them; adjusting those variables scales related features. Keep the setup simple.
source_quote: This is how I handle scaling.  Usually I adjust a fey key variables and I get good results.  Start simple.
example_value: Changing the single variable R scales multiple circles dimensioned from R and its multiples.
example_context: SolidWorks Smart Dimension and Equations/global variables

subject: Solidworks Simulation FFEPlus solver support for inertia relief with large displacement
main_point: In Solidworks Simulation, the FFEPlus iterative solver cannot run a study that combines Inertia Relief with Large Displacement; to use that combination you must switch to the Direct Sparse solver.
source_quote: Inertia Relief with Iterative solver is not supported by Large Displacement. Please use the Direct Sparse Solver.
example_value: Attempting to start a study with both Inertia Relief and Large Displacement enabled returns an error directing the user to use the Direct Sparse Solver.
example_context: Solidworks Simulation using the FFEPlus iterative solver

subject: SolidWorks design table A2 'family' requirement
main_point: When formatting a SolidWorks design table, the Excel A2 cell must be labeled "family" per SolidWorks’ requirements.
source_quote: the A2 cell must be named "family", as described here
example_context: SolidWorks design tables (Excel-based)

subject: SolidWorks standard vs mechanical mates robustness
main_point: In SolidWorks assemblies, Standard mates tend to be more robust than Mechanical mates. Prefer Standard mates wherever possible to achieve more reliable assembly behavior.
source_quote: The "Standard" mates are more robust than the Mechanical mates, and should be used wherever possible.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly mates and constraints

subject: cam profile continuity in SolidWorks
main_point: When modeling cams in SolidWorks, make the cam profile a single continuous face. Use the Fitspline tool to create a continuous edge from segmented geometry.
source_quote: A cam should have one continuous face, you can use the fitspline tool to create this.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD sketching/modeling of cam profiles

subject: imported sketch connectivity causing shared extrusion
main_point: If entities in an imported DWG are connected, SolidWorks interprets them as a single sketch region, so attempting an Extruded Boss/Base will extrude both shapes together.
source_quote:
The reason these two shapes are extruding together, is, because in the .DWG file, they 
are connected to each other
example_value: Zooming into the imported geometry revealed the two shapes were subtly connected, causing them to extrude as one feature.
example_context: SolidWorks extruded boss/base using geometry imported from an AutoCAD DWG

subject: workflow for fixing problematic DWG imports
main_point: To resolve bad or connected imported geometry, either correct the DWG itself or recreate the sketch natively in SolidWorks using the DWG only as a tracing/reference.
source_quote: What you need to do in this instance, is either fix your original .DWG file, or simply use the .DWG as a reference for a new SolidWorks sketch.
example_value: The author suggests repairing the DWG or rebuilding the sketch in SolidWorks instead of trying to extrude the flawed import directly.
example_context: SolidWorks workflow when importing AutoCAD DWG sketches for extrusion

subject: coradial/concentric relation requiring shared center
main_point: If two imported circles are not exactly concentric, SolidWorks will not allow a coradial-type relation between them.
source_quote: I was unable to use coradial for both circles, because, they don't exactly share a centrepoint!
example_value: The circles from the DWG were slightly off-center relative to each other, preventing application of the coradial relation.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch relations applied to geometry imported from DWG

subject: fixing misaligned circle centers via coincidence constraint
main_point: To correct slight misalignment that prevents applying a circle relation, constrain the inner circle’s center coincident with a reference point to force proper alignment.
source_quote: I set the inner circle coincident to one of the points to fix this.
example_value: Instead of using coradial, the author aligned the inner circle by making its center coincident to a point, resolving the relation issue.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch cleanup after importing DWG geometry

subject: reference planes/axes defined early in feature tree
main_point: Create reference planes and axes at the beginning of the model so they are stable drivers for downstream features and dimensions throughout the history tree.
source_quote: Always define your planes or axes as early in the history tree as possible.

subject: using infinite centerline to enable diameter dimensions in revolve sketch
main_point: Using an infinite-length centerline in a revolve sketch lets you apply diameter dimensions directly, avoiding extra steps like dividing global variables by two.
source_quote: I started with an infinite length centreline - this allows us to use diameter dimensions, rather than needing to divide the global variables by 2.
example_context: SolidWorks revolve feature sketches and dimensioning practice

subject: helix tool equation input limitation and workaround
main_point: Because the Helix feature does not accept equations directly, first enter a placeholder numeric value, then assign the intended parameters through the Equation editor.
source_quote: You can't type equations directly into the helix tool (like you can with regular dimensions), so you need to just type a starting point, before moving to the Equation editor to add values as shown in my first image.
example_context: SolidWorks Helix/Spiral feature with global variables and Equation Manager

subject: Merge result option to create separate bodies
main_point: Disable Merge result during the sweep so the swept antenna remains a separate solid body from the cone.
source_quote: Uncheck 'Merge result' in the options to keep this as a separate body from the cone.
example_context: SolidWorks Sweep feature creating multibody parts

subject: helix height overshoot for smooth runout
main_point: Make the helix taller than the final part height by two pitches so you can trim back to height and achieve a smooth runout at the end.
source_quote: the height of the final object, plus 2x the pitch. This allows it to be cut to height and have a smooth runout - I hope this is correct.
example_context: SolidWorks helix-driven sweep on a conical antenna trimmed with planes

subject: driving feature height via reference plane position
main_point: Drive the feature’s height by an offset reference plane rather than a sketch dimension so the plane location controls the model height.
source_quote: Note that the "Height" is not dimensioned here, it's driven by the location of the plane.
example_context: SolidWorks parametric modeling with a 'Max Height' plane offset from a base plane

subject: defining global variables up front
main_point: Define global variables at the outset so dimensions and features can reference them consistently throughout the model.
source_quote: Set up your global variables before you start modelling.
example_context: SolidWorks Equations/Global Variables driving parametric features

subject: driving dependent sketch angle from master profile dimensions
main_point: Define the antenna profile’s angle by referencing the cone profile sketch so it updates automatically from the max/min diameter parameters.
source_quote: Note how the angle of this is defined by the Cone Profile sketch, which is in turn driven by the Max/Min diameters.
example_context: SolidWorks conical antenna model with a master cone profile sketch controlling dependent features

subject: aligning helix start angle by choosing sketch plane
main_point: Place the cone profile on a plane that makes a 0° helix start line up with the profile, simplifying the sweep’s start alignment.
source_quote: I put my Cone profile on the right plane so that a start angle of 0 deg will be coincident with the Cone Profile Sketch.
example_context: SolidWorks Helix feature start angle alignment using the Right plane for the cone profile sketch

subject: SolidWorks variables and equations
main_point: In SolidWorks, parameterize your model by defining variables and driving relationships with equations, then reference those variables or their equations directly in drawings. This lets you control and update geometry and documented dimensions consistently from a single set of parameters.
source_quote: You can define variables in the Solidworks model, and use them (or equations derived from them) in your drawings.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD models using the Equation Manager and global variables

subject: SolidWorks hole table CSV line breaks for complex holes
main_point: SolidWorks hole table CSV exports can split a single complex hole entry across multiple lines using a CR-CR-LF sequence. Parsers must account for this multi-line record behavior when handling tapped or counterbored holes.
source_quote: complex holes (tapped and counterbore, for example) are split by CR-CR-LF.
example_value: Complex holes such as tapped and counterbore are affected.
example_context: SolidWorks hole table CSV export formatting for complex holes (tapped, counterbore).

subject: VBA preprocessing to join CR-CRLF-split CSV records
main_point: When parsing SolidWorks hole table CSVs in VBA, you can reconstruct complex hole records by replacing the CR-CRLF sequence with a space (or other separator). This normalizes multi-line entries back into a single line for easier parsing.
source_quote: a = Replace(strFileContent, vbCr & vbCrLf, " ")
example_value: Read the entire CSV into a string and perform a Replace on vbCr & vbCrLf to a space before further parsing.
example_context: VBA-based parsing of SolidWorks hole table CSV exports containing CR-CRLF within records.

subject: SolidWorks hole table CSV newline characters in callouts
main_point: SolidWorks hole table CSV exports can embed newline characters inside the hole callout text, causing a single hole’s data to be split across multiple lines instead of one. This makes straightforward row-by-row parsing unreliable unless the embedded newlines are handled.
source_quote: The problem is that the CSV export is including the new line characters that are part of the hole callout.
example_value: An entry like A1,2.07,9.78,<MOD-DIAM> .257 THRU followed by 5/16-18 UNC  THRU appears on two lines but represents one hole.
example_context: SolidWorks hole table CSV export

subject: Preprocessing embedded newlines in SolidWorks hole table CSV for parsing
main_point: Preprocess the CSV by replacing pairs of embedded newline characters in hole callouts with a unique placeholder delimiter so each hole remains a single parsable record. This simplifies downstream parsing logic that expects one hole per line.
source_quote: You can perform a string replace of any pair or new line characters with some delimiter of your own (say, {new-line}) to make parsing easier, and you can get data like this:
example_value: Replace double newlines with "{new-line}", yielding lines like A1,2.07,9.78,<MOD-DIAM> .257 THRU{new-line}5/16-18 UNC  THRU.
example_context: SolidWorks hole table CSV export with multi-line callouts

subject: SolidWorks helix sketch requirement
main_point: In SolidWorks, you cannot generate a helix directly from an existing sketch; you must create a new sketch specifically for the helix feature.
source_quote: a helix can't be created from an existing sketch,  you have to create a fresh sketch just for it.
example_context: SolidWorks Helix/Spiral feature creation

subject: SolidWorks curve driven pattern surface requirement
main_point: For a Curve Driven Pattern in SolidWorks to function, the helical path must lie on the same surface that the patterned feature is normal to.
source_quote: in order for the curve driven pattern to work, the helical path -must- be on the surface to which the object to be patterned is to be  normal...
example_context: SolidWorks Curve Driven Pattern along a helical path on a cylindrical surface

subject: un-merged solid loft as cut tool
main_point: In SolidWorks, create the loft as an unmerged solid body so it can later serve as the cutting tool for subtractive operations or patterning. Keeping the loft separate enables using it directly in cut/subtract features.
source_quote: Make your loft into an un-merged solid, that can be used as a cut tool later.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling of loft-based cuts and subsequent patterning or subtract operations

subject: body pattern vs feature pattern reliability
main_point: In SolidWorks, body patterns generally regenerate more reliably than feature patterns, so prefer patterning bodies rather than features for repeated geometry.
source_quote: Pattern bodies instead of features, this is always more reliable
example_context: SolidWorks CAD modeling when creating patterned geometry along paths or arrays

subject: using helix feature directly as path
main_point: In SolidWorks, the Helix/Spiral feature can be referenced directly as the path for operations like curve-driven patterns or sweeps, eliminating the need to create a separate 3D sketch of the helix.
source_quote: Another thing to note - you can use the helix feature directly as your path, there's no need for a 3D sketch.
example_context: SolidWorks operations that require a path reference (e.g., Curve Driven Pattern or Sweep) along a helical path

subject: SolidWorks sweep patterning workaround by connecting sweeps via a solid surface
main_point: To resolve patterning issues with swept features in SolidWorks without creating an assembly, connect the sweeps with a solid surface and sketch the sweep’s end profile on that surface; this enables the operation to succeed within the part file.
source_quote: creating a solid surface with which to connect all the sweeps, then sketching the end profile of the sweep on the solid surface fixes the problem, and no assembly is necessary.
example_value: The poster connects all sweeps using a solid surface and sketches the end profile on that surface, after which the patterning works in the part.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling involving sweeps, mirrors, and circular patterns

subject: SolidWorks patterning requires merging features
main_point: SolidWorks will refuse a pattern operation and report an error if the selected features do not merge; patterning is limited to merging features.
source_quote: ordinarily when I try to do this I get the error "only merging features can be patterned".
example_value: Attempting to circular pattern two mirrored sweep features that share some volume triggered the error message.
example_context: SolidWorks circular pattern of features in a part model

subject: sizing bendable sheet-metal flaps to load
main_point: Bendable sheet-metal flaps should be dimensioned based on the expected applied load rather than using a generic standard geometry. Because load requirements vary by application, there is no single standard cutout that fits all cases.
source_quote: They will need to be sized appropriate to the load that will be applied, which means that they are not “standard”.

subject: fatigue life and strength of bend area in sheet-metal flaps
main_point: Design the bending section of the flap to have adequate strength and service life, especially if it will be flexed frequently. Account for repeated flexing so the feature does not fail prematurely.
source_quote: You need to make sure the part that bends is sufficiently strong and will have sufficient life when it is flexed often.

subject: using Move Face to rotate a feature
main_point: Model the geometry orthogonally first, then rotate the required portion into position using Move Face about an existing connecting edge. This avoids creating extra angled planes and provides a direct way to set the final angle.
source_quote: You can model the part at 90 degrees, and then use the Move Face tool to rotate the feature about the top connecting edge.
example_value: The 'notched' plate is extruded normal to a base plane, then rotated into position about the top connecting edge.
example_context: SolidWorks Move Face tool within a feature-based parametric model

subject: Move Face selection options
main_point: The Move Face tool supports selecting an entire feature as the entity to move, not just individual faces. This enables operations to reference a feature rather than specific faces.
source_quote: N.B. You can select features (as well as single faces) when picking which faces to move.
example_context: SolidWorks Move Face tool

subject: feature-level selection for robust updates
main_point: When using Move Face, select the upstream feature as the input rather than individual faces to preserve robustness under later edits. Feature-level selection keeps the Move Face operation valid even if the feature gains holes or loses slots.
source_quote: Selecting the Extrude feature (made in step 3) as the input for the Move face (step 4) means that even if you edit the extrude to have extra holes or to remove a slot, the move face will still work.
example_value: Choosing the extrude feature for the notched plate as the Move Face input continues to work after adding extra holes or removing a slot.
example_context: SolidWorks Move Face applied to an extruded feature

subject: topology change causing face-reference failure
main_point: If you manually select individual faces for a Move Face operation, later topology changes (added or removed faces) can cause the feature to fail. Prefer feature-level references to avoid this failure mode.
source_quote: Manually selecting the faces may cause this feature to fail as new faces appear or old faces are removed.
example_context: SolidWorks Move Face referencing individual faces

subject: helicoid non-developability (flattening)
main_point: Because a flat helix (helicoid) is not a developable surface, it cannot be flattened without distortion. Any attempt to create a flat pattern will run into geometric error relative to simple unrolled calculations.

subject: using middle fiber radius for helicoid flat pattern estimation
main_point: When estimating a helicoid’s flat pattern by hand, use the middle-fiber radius to improve agreement with CAD-generated flattening. This neutral-fiber approximation typically yields closer results than edge-based radii.
source_quote: Try using the middle fiber radius and compare the hand calc to the software and see if they aren't a lot closer.
example_context: Estimating unrolled dimensions for a flat helix (helicoid) when comparing hand calculations to CAD flattening.

subject: Abaqus Standard vs Abaqus Explicit selection
main_point: When selecting Abaqus, choose between the Standard and Explicit solvers based on the nature of the problem. Solver choice should be matched to problem type rather than picked arbitrarily.
source_quote: I would suggest Abaqus Standard or Abaqus Explicit (depending on the type of problem you are trying to solve).
example_context: Selecting between Abaqus Standard and Abaqus Explicit for FEA analyses

subject: High-end FEA software annual licensing cost
main_point: High-end commercial FEA tools can cost on the order of $20,000 per year for licensing. Budgeting for such software should account for this recurring annual expense.
source_quote: Cost will be around $20000 per year.
example_context: Annual licensing for commercial FEA packages such as Abaqus or Ansys Workbench

subject: major FEA package capability for orthotropic analyses
main_point: Mainstream FEA packages such as Nastran, Abaqus, Ansys, Adina, and Comsol support the requested orthotropic-material static analysis capabilities (including relevant failure criteria).
source_quote: Any of the major FEA systems (Nastran, Abaqus, Ansys, Adina, Comsol, etc) can do this.
example_context: Major FEA packages (Nastran, Abaqus, Ansys, Adina, Comsol)

subject: FEA software selection for limited analysis requirements
main_point: When your needs are limited (for example, linear statics with orthotropic materials), select the lowest-cost entry-level or student license from a vendor that includes orthotropic material models.
source_quote: If you have a fairly limited requirements (e.g. only linear statics), look for the vendor with the cheapest entry-level or student-level version of the code which includes orthotropic material models.
example_context: Users needing only linear statics and orthotropic material models; entry-level or student license tiers of FEA software

subject: drawing scale validity on printed copies
main_point: Resizing a drawing when printing (e.g., changing paper size) invalidates the stated scale, so notes like "Do not scale drawing" instruct readers not to rescale printed copies. If the sheet is printed at a different size, the indicated scale (such as 1:8) will no longer be accurate.
source_quote: This is information to be shown on the printed copy - it is telling the reader to please not print this A1 drawing sheet on A4 paper, or else the information you have highlighted "Scale 1:8" would not be true any more.
example_value: Printing an A1 drawing on A4 will make the label "Scale 1:8" incorrect.

subject: scaling measurements from drawings
main_point: The note "Do not scale drawing" instructs that you should not take physical measurements off the printed drawing to make the part; rely on the stated dimensions instead.
source_quote: not to measure the drawing using a 6" machinist scale, and use those measurements to fabricate the part
example_value: For example, do not use a 6-inch machinist scale to read sizes from the drawing for fabrication.

subject: parametric CAD design intent
main_point: In parametric CAD, identify the critical dimensions and structure the model so they are controlled in a single sketch; changes to those values should propagate automatically to update the rest of the model.
source_quote: What dimensions are the critical ones? You want to be able to change those in one sketch and then have the rest of the model update if you need to change things.

subject: modeling approach selection in CAD
main_point: For a given part, multiple CAD modeling methods can work; choose the approach that aligns with your design intent so future edits affect the right aspects of the model.
source_quote: There are so, so many ways to model the shape you're after, and which one is best will depend on your design intent.

subject: SolidWorks Pack and Go for single parts/assemblies
main_point: In SolidWorks, the straightforward method to duplicate a single part or assembly is to use the Pack and Go feature.
source_quote: For a single assembly or part it would be a simple case of using the "Pack and Go" feature of solidworks,
example_context: SolidWorks CAD users duplicating a single part or assembly

subject: isolated machine check for CAD assembly external links
main_point: To confirm a cloned CAD project is truly self-contained, open the copy on a separate, isolated computer. Any lingering external references will fail to resolve there, revealing broken links.
source_quote: I would make a copy onto a USB stick then, at best, check that on a separate computer - any broken links should show up.
example_value: Copy the project to a USB stick and open it on a different computer to see if any links break.
example_context: CAD assemblies with external file references (e.g., SolidWorks) where a clean clone must not reference original directories.

subject: using separate user account to isolate CAD link resolution
main_point: If a second computer is unavailable, test the clone under a different user account that lacks access to the original user directories so the software cannot silently resolve links to old files.
source_quote: If you don't have separate computer then a new account may do the same - as long as it does not get access to your user file directory.
example_value: Create a new OS user and ensure it cannot access your existing user file directory before opening the cloned project.
example_context: Workstations running CAD (e.g., SolidWorks) where user directory access controls can prevent access to original project paths.

subject: OS path substitution for CAD project relocation
main_point: You can avoid updating CAD file references after relocating a project by using OS-level path substitution so the new location appears at the original path, making the software see unchanged paths and requiring no further changes.
source_quote: Most operating systems can substitute the path so that after the operation another path looks like another. So from the softwares perspective it is the same path even if it is not. This is a very easy way out as you dont need to change anything at all.
example_context: Operating systems that support path substitution/mapping (e.g., symbolic links, junctions, mount points) for applications that reference files by path.

subject: SolidWorks Explorer for moving files and updating references
main_point: Use SolidWorks Explorer to move or restructure SolidWorks files so it updates file-level changes and maintains references, reducing the risk of broken links.
source_quote: This said solidworks includes a tool called solidworks explorer that will handle updating file level structure changes.  Use that for the moving of files.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD assemblies and parts that are being moved or renamed.

subject: Using PDM to clone projects for traceability
