main_point: Prefer handling project duplication and restructuring through a PDM system rather than manual file copying, because PDM preserves links between versions for traceability and downstream operations.
source_quote: Ideally, instead of copying disk level items, you would have let your PDM handle this, as this leaves a link between versions for traceability and other operations.
example_context: CAD environments using a Product Data Management (PDM) system such as for SolidWorks projects.

subject: Version control system for CAD when no PDM
main_point: If a PDM system is not in use, consider setting up a version control system to manage iterations and maintain history for CAD project files.
source_quote: In this kind of cases i might be tempted to just set the stff up for a vrsion control system.
example_context: CAD teams without PDM seeking basic versioning and traceability.

subject: 'Package Master' top-level assembly for Pack and Go
main_point: Create a temporary top-level “Package Master” assembly that simply contains all sub-assemblies (without mating them) to gather the entire project into one structure before cloning. This simplifies running Pack and Go so all references are captured in one operation.
source_quote: If this were my project, I would create a 'Package Master' top level assembly that contains your 40 assembly files as sub-assemblies. No need to mate them to each other, just have them there contained within the file.
example_value: A single top-level assembly that contains the 40 assemblies as sub-assemblies, with no mates applied.
example_context: SolidWorks multi-assembly projects prepared for Pack and Go cloning

subject: Select/Replace-driven version renaming to avoid filename collisions
main_point: Use the Select/Replace tool to strip old version identifiers from filenames and apply the new version across the clone. This prevents filename collisions and avoids confusion when different parts would otherwise share the same name.
source_quote: I always use the Select/Replace tool to remove the previous 'version number', and update with the latest one, so that you never get in trouble with two different parts having the same filename, and either windows or a user getting confused between these.
example_value: Replace the prior 'version number' in filenames with the latest during Pack and Go.
example_context: SolidWorks Pack and Go workflow using Select/Replace for batch renaming

subject: duplicate CAD part filenames
main_point: If two different parts share the same filename, the system or users can confuse them, leading to errors in selecting or referencing the correct file. Avoid duplicate filenames during cloning and renaming.
source_quote: so that you never get in trouble with two different parts having the same filename, and either windows or a user getting confused between these.
example_context: Windows-based SolidWorks file management and Pack and Go cloning

subject: Pack and Go inclusion options
main_point: Explicitly enable Pack and Go options to include related drawings and suppressed components as needed, ensuring the clone is complete. Selecting these options prevents missing documentation or parts in the copied project.
source_quote: Make sure you tick the 'Include Drawings', 'Include Suppressed Components' etc. boxes at the top left of the Pack and Go dialogue according to your needs.
example_context: SolidWorks Pack and Go options during project cloning

subject: removing temporary Package Master after cloning
main_point: After the Pack and Go completes successfully, remove the temporary 'Package Master' from the cloned directory if it’s no longer needed. This keeps the target set clean of temporary scaffolding files.
source_quote: You can delete the 'Package Master' from the target directory once everything has gone through, if you don't need it any more.
example_context: SolidWorks project cloned via Pack and Go using a temporary master assembly

subject: SolidWorks file format (2015+)
main_point: Starting with the 2015 release, SolidWorks changed its file format so it is no longer based on Microsoft’s Compound File Binary (MS-CFB) structure. Post-2015 SolidWorks files therefore cannot be analyzed as CFB containers.
source_quote: Since version 2015 the files are no more based on MS-CFB (Compound File Binary File Format).
example_context: SolidWorks versions 2015 and newer file formats

subject: SolidWorks Projected View tool
main_point: In SolidWorks drawings, add an additional view by invoking Projected View from an existing view. Select a current view and use the Projected View command to generate the desired orthographic projection.
source_quote: You can use the "Projected View" button to add another view, by selecting an existing view.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing environment

subject: drawing view count
main_point: Avoid adding extra drawing views; include only as many views as needed to fully define the part’s geometry. Minimizing redundant views improves clarity and conciseness of the drawing.
source_quote: You should bear in mind, however, that you should avoid adding unnecessary views if you can fully define the geometry of the object with only a few.

subject: bulkhead-style fitting mounting holes
main_point: For bulkhead/through-wall style fittings, you typically use a clearance hole rather than tapping; the fitting is secured by a nut on the opposite side of the wall.
source_quote: The hole does not need to be tapped, just a clearance hole for the fitting to pass through, the nut then goes on the other side of the wall, holding the fitting in the wall.
example_context: bulkhead or through-wall fittings that clamp with a nut through a panel/wall

subject: bulkhead fitting wall thickness limit for nut clamping
main_point: For the specified bulkhead-style fitting, walls thicker than 1.25 in cannot be secured with the standard through-wall nut and require the wall to be tapped to hold the fitting.
source_quote: Per the drawing, if the wall is thicker than 1.25", then you will have to tap the wall to hold the fitting.
example_context: as specified on the manufacturer’s drawing for this particular bulkhead/through-wall fitting

subject: missing thread specification on vendor drawing
main_point: When a drawing requires a tapped feature but does not specify the thread size, obtain the thread information directly from the manufacturer.
source_quote: If that's the case, you will have to contact the MFG for the thread size as its not annotated on the drawing.
example_context: vendor-supplied drawings for proprietary fittings lacking thread callouts

subject: SolidWorks Simulation free body force output
main_point: In SolidWorks Simulation, you can obtain the total lifting force on a selected housing surface by using List Result Forces and choosing Free Body Force; the software then displays the total F_Kab.
source_quote:
To get the lifting force 
$F_{Kab}$
 I right click the simulation results and pick “list result forces”. And now I choose “free body force”, klick the appropriate housing surface and klick the update-button. Now SolidWorks shows me the (total) lifting force 
$F_{Kab}$
.
example_context: SolidWorks Simulation post-processing (List Result Forces > Free Body Force on a selected housing surface)

subject: preload loss due to embedding (Fz) in bolted joints
main_point: In bolted joint analysis, Fz denotes the reduction in preload caused by embedding (settlement) during operation.
source_quote: $F_z$ is the loss of preload as a result of embedding during operation

subject: base-excited SDOF high-frequency transmissibility
main_point: For a base-excited mass–spring–damper system, the transmitted motion to the mass diminishes at high excitation frequencies, effectively isolating the mass from the base. At sufficiently high frequency ratios, the mass behaves as if it is nearly disconnected due to the dynamic stiffness dominating the response.
source_quote: Consider a mass attached to a base by a spring and a damper. If the base is shaken then at high frequencies the response of the mass falls off, it is as if there is nothing connecting the mass and the base at high frequency.

subject: base-displacement excitation high-frequency response
main_point: With constant base displacement excitation, a structure’s response amplitude remains roughly constant at high frequencies (mass-dominated behavior), except near resonances that couple energy into modes.
source_quote: In other words, for a constant base amplitude, the tip amplitude of your tuning fork will also be approximately constant at high frequencies, except when there is a resonance that affects the motion of the system.
example_value: For the tuning fork, the tip displacement stays about constant at high frequency for a fixed base amplitude, aside from resonant peaks.

subject: force scaling under fixed-displacement excitation
main_point: For a fixed displacement input, the required excitation force rises with the square of frequency (outside resonances), because acceleration scales with ω² for a given amplitude.
source_quote:
Note that if you apply a fixed displacement, the 
excitation force
 will increase for higher frequencies (and except where there is a resonance in the displacement response) it will be approximately proportional to the frequency squared.

subject: constant-force excitation displacement behavior
main_point: Under constant force excitation, displacement amplitude decreases as frequency increases, but will diverge as frequency approaches zero if the structure is unconstrained (rigid-body mode).
source_quote:
If you applied a constant 
force
, you would see the displacement falling as the frequency increased, but unless the structure is constrained in some way, the displacement amplitude will increase to infinity as the frequency gets close to zero.

subject: inertia-dominated high-frequency dynamics
main_point: At excitation frequencies well above a structure’s resonances, inertia dominates and stiffness can be neglected in the equations of motion, simplifying the response to mass-matrix relations.
source_quote: In that situation the elastic forces are small compared with the inertia forces, so we can ignore the stiffness term in the equation of motion

subject: SolidWorks Measure tool
main_point: In SolidWorks, the Evaluate > Measure tool provides measurements such as point‑to‑point distance and can also report area, diameter, and perimeter. After launching it, selecting two points returns their distance.
source_quote: 'Evaluate>Measure'. Now a dialogue box appears. now select two points to know the distance. This tool can be used for measuring area, diameter, perimeter etc
example_value: Invoking Evaluate > Measure and selecting two points shows the distance between them in the dialog.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD software, using the Evaluate > Measure command

subject: Move/Copy Bodies translation vs constraints
main_point: When positioning inserted bodies in SolidWorks, prefer simple translations in the Move/Copy Bodies tool rather than adding constraints, because translations are unaffected by downstream geometry changes and thus lead to fewer errors.
source_quote: Once in the Move/Copy Tool, you can click the "Constraints" button to get a rudimentary version of the Assembly Constraints environment, but, I'd stick to translation where possible, since this then will not be affected by geometry changes, giving fewer errors.
example_context: SolidWorks Move/Copy Bodies tool within SLDPRT files

subject: Breaking link on inserted part in SLDPRT
main_point: In a SolidWorks part document, an inserted part’s external reference link can be broken during insertion, avoiding any need to convert the geometry to another format to make it inert.
source_quote: You can also choose to break the link to the part that you inserted at this point, so for a .SLDPRT file, you don't need to do any conversion.
example_context: SolidWorks SLDPRT files when inserting another part via Insert > Part

subject: Saving assemblies as SLDPRT for insertion
main_point: To use an assembly as inert geometry in a part environment, first save the assembly as a SLDPRT file.
source_quote: For assemblies, you will need to save as a .SLDPRT.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies being prepared for insertion into SLDPRT files

subject: All Components option when saving assembly as part
main_point: When saving an assembly as a part, enable the All Components option to ensure all geometry is included in the resulting file.
source_quote: Make sure you select "All Components" while saving, if you want all the data to be present.
example_context: SolidWorks Save As from SLDASM to SLDPRT with save options

subject: Methods to position inserted part in SLDPRT
main_point: A part inserted into a SolidWorks part file can be positioned by enabling Locate part with Move/Copy during insertion or by moving it later with the Move/Copy Bodies tool.
source_quote: When you insert the part (Insert --> Part), you can either check the box labelled "Locate part with Move/Copy feature", or simply use the Move/Copy Bodies Tool (Insert --> Surface --> Move/Copy) to move the object afterwards.
example_context: SolidWorks SLDPRT environment using Insert > Part and Move/Copy Bodies

subject: creating a 'dumb' SolidWorks assembly via Save As SLDPRT
main_point: To insert an inert version of an assembly into another assembly in SolidWorks, save the assembly as a single .SLDPRT part file. This produces a non-parametric “dumb” part suitable for reuse in higher-level assemblies.
source_quote: In order to insert a 'dumb' copy of an assembly into another higher level assembly, you can save the assembly as a .SLDPRT File.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies and parts; using Save As to create a part from an assembly

subject: Save As SLDPRT geometry inclusion options
main_point: When saving an assembly as a part in SolidWorks, choose the Save As options to control how much geometry is included so the exported part has only the needed detail.
source_quote: Make sure to select the correct amount of geometry to save, according to your needs from the options in the 'Save As' dialogue.
example_context: SolidWorks Save As options when converting an assembly to a part (.SLDPRT)

subject: independence and composition of SLDPRT created from assembly
main_point: A part (.SLDPRT) saved from an assembly in SolidWorks is independent of the source assembly and consists of internally stored IGES bodies.
source_quote: This .SLDPRT will be completely independent from the original assembly, being made up of internally saved .IGES components.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies saved as parts (.SLDPRT)

subject: inserting and mating the dumb SLDPRT in an assembly
main_point: After creating the inert .SLDPRT, insert it into the top-level assembly and apply mates just like any normal part.
source_quote: You can then simply insert this new part into your high level assembly, and mate it as normal.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly workflows with an inserted dumb part

subject: No External References toggle to avoid accidental external refs
main_point: When editing within an assembly in SolidWorks, enable “No External References” to avoid unintentionally creating external references to the inserted dumb part (e.g., from sketch snaps).
source_quote: if you ever use the 'Edit Component' Function inside the Assembly environment, you can toggle "No External References", which will prevent you from accidentally creating references to the 'dumb assembly', e.g. by accidentally snapping a sketch point to it.
example_context: SolidWorks Assembly environment using Edit Component with a dumb inserted part

subject: half-arc revolve profile (SolidWorks)
main_point: Use a semicircular (half-arc) sketch profile to create the half-dome; with that profile, a revolve about the center axis will work correctly.
source_quote: The basic problem is that it should be a half arc; then it should (and in my case did) work properly with the revolve tool and the center axis.
example_value: The author reports that after changing the profile to a half arc, the revolve with the center axis worked in their model.
example_context: SolidWorks revolve feature using a center axis

subject: revolve sketch axis as construction line
main_point: When preparing a revolve feature, begin the sketch by adding the axis of revolution as a construction line within that same sketch. This clarifies the revolve setup and reduces ambiguity during feature creation.
source_quote: Whenever you are sketching a profile to be revolved in any CAD package, you should start by drawing your axis of revolution into that sketch as a construction line.

subject: revolve sketch geometry kept to one side of axis
main_point: For revolve profiles, keep all sketch geometry on a single side of the centerline/axis. This avoids ambiguous or self-crossing profiles and produces a clean revolve feature.
source_quote:
Then, keep 
every
 other line to one side of that axis.

subject: SolidWorks diameter dimensions from centerline-based revolve sketch
main_point: In SolidWorks, organizing a revolve sketch around a centerline so geometry lies on one side enables using diameter dimensions instead of radii, which can be preferable for cylindrical features.
source_quote: In SolidWorks, this gives you the added benefit of being able to dimension diameters, rather than radii, which may be more appropriate.
example_context: SolidWorks part sketches used for revolve features

subject: master sketch to define axis and sketch plane for revolves
main_point: When a revolve’s orientation changes, create a master sketch that defines both the revolve axis and the target sketch plane. This centralizes control of the geometry and setup for downstream features.
source_quote: If you wanted to revolve your dome in the other direction, then you need to create a 'master' sketch to not only define the axis, but also the plane on which the sketch should be created.

subject: equation-driven dependent sketch dimensions (master modeling)
main_point: In a master-modeling workflow, drive dimensions in dependent sketches with equations that reference the master sketch. This ensures updates propagate automatically and keeps the model consistent.
source_quote: All the dimensions in this sketch should be equation driven, since you've already defined all the geometry elsewhere.

subject: SolidWorks Delete Face with Delete and Patch to extend/patch surfaces
main_point: To remove an unwanted overhang, use Delete Face with the Delete and Patch option; SolidWorks will remove that face and extend the adjacent cylindrical surface to meet the dome, eliminating the overhang without manual trimming.
source_quote: Simply delete the face underneath the overhang, with "delete and patch" selected, and SolidWorks will extend the Cylinder face up to meet the dome.
example_context: SolidWorks surface/solid editing using the Delete Face tool with Delete and Patch

subject: failure of multi-face delete-and-patch when faces meet at a single vertex
main_point: Attempting to delete and patch multiple overhang faces simultaneously can fail when those faces meet at a single vertex; the kernel cannot resolve the patch in this topology, so delete them one at a time.
source_quote: Deleting both at once will not work due to the way both overhang faces meet at a single vertex causing the maths to fall over.
example_context: SolidWorks Delete Face with Delete and Patch on adjacent faces sharing a single vertex

subject: master modelling approach (driving sketches + equations)
main_point: Master modeling—using a separate driving sketch and equations to control the build geometry—is a powerful approach and often the best method for complex models, enabling automatic updates across features.
source_quote: The fundamental concept of master modelling (defining geometry in a sketch that isn't actually used to build the model, and referring to that using equations in order to allow automatic updating of the built geometry) is extremely powerful, however, and in other more complicated examples, it is absolutely the best way to work.

subject: 3D Sketch Spline for hose routing
main_point: For routing a flexible hose in SolidWorks, use a 3D Sketch Spline rather than projected curves. It better represents the hose’s natural shape under perpendicular end constraints at the inlet and outlet.
source_quote: I'd recommend using a 3D Sketch Spline for creating your hose - this will more accurately model the natural shape that the hose would assume given the boundary conditions of perpendicular to the grey transparent block at the in/out positions.
example_value: Ends constrained perpendicular to a block at the hose in/out positions.
example_context: SolidWorks hose path modeling with perpendicular end constraints at inlet/outlet.

subject: IR camera temperature calibration using a reference object
main_point: Include a known-temperature reference object in the same scene when capturing IR images, then use it to map image colors to approximate actual temperatures. This in-scene reference allows you to calibrate the thermogram for more reliable temperature estimation.
source_quote: For your IR camera, you need an image of a known object at a known temperature in the same environment as a temperature reference , then when you have the IR image you can cross-reference the colours to approximate the temperatures.
example_value: Author suggests looking at building thermal images as an illustration of color-referenced thermograms.

subject: OEM-supplied CAD model fidelity limits
main_point: Vendor-provided CAD for commercial products can be missing or simplified features, making it too inaccurate for detailed CFD or thermal analysis. This often happens because manufacturers remove information to protect intellectual property.
source_quote: The model may not be accurate enough for your need. They may have ripped some data out to protect their IP
example_context: OEM-supplied CAD models of servers used as a basis for CFD/thermal simulations

subject: over-detailed geometry hindering simulation workflow
main_point: Overly detailed CAD in areas irrelevant to the analysis can clutter the model and impede setup and solution of the CFD. Excess geometry detail can become a time-consuming obstacle rather than a benefit.
source_quote: It may be too accurate in places that are of no interest for you. And mostly the data is just in your way.
example_context: Using detailed OEM geometry of server internals for CFD pre-processing and meshing

subject: missing material and heat-generation data in CAD for CFD
main_point: Geometry-only CAD from a supplier may be unsuitable for CFD because it lacks essential inputs like material properties and internal heat generation. Without these, you cannot properly define boundary conditions or source terms for thermal analysis.
source_quote: The model may be unsuitable for your task. So its geometry but your cfd needs the material info and heat generation info.
example_context: Importing OEM CAD of a server chassis into SolidWorks Flow/CFD for thermal studies

subject: abstracted CAD models for faster CFD
main_point: Create a suitably abstracted CAD model tailored to the physics you need; such simplified geometry typically solves faster than importing heavy, detailed models. Building this abstraction is doable and can deliver better simulation throughput.
source_quote: That said modeling a suitably absteacted version that simulates faster than imported models is not necceserily  a huge job.

subject: model abstraction level for CFD
main_point: Focus on simplifying the geometry to only what affects the flow and heat transfer; avoid modeling unnecessary detail. This reduces preprocessing effort and improves solver performance without sacrificing relevant accuracy.
source_quote: Concentrate on abstracting things as much as you can. Do you really need every detail?

subject: 3D scanning utility for reverse-engineering CAD for CFD
main_point: 3D scanning typically does not directly solve the need for clean, simulation-ready solids, but it can accelerate measurement by providing a digital reference to check dimensions. This is most helpful when the physical hardware isn’t always available at the bench.
source_quote: Would scanning help? In my experience not really, though it might speed up data gathering, as you now have a digital model to check against.
example_context: Using 3D scanning of server internals to support creating Solidworks solid models for CFD

subject: 3D scanning workflow complexity
main_point: Incorporating 3D scanning introduces additional workflow complexity that can offset its benefits. Plan for added processing, cleanup, and integration steps if you choose to scan.
source_quote: However, scanning is another can of worms as a work process.
example_context: Adding a scan-to-CAD workflow for modeling server internals

subject: thermal IR imaging measures band-limited radiance and depends on emissivity
main_point: A thermal camera does not measure heat generation directly; it measures radiance in a specific spectral band, which depends on material emissivity and surface condition. Without correcting for these factors, apparent temperatures and inferred heat sources can be misleading.
source_quote: Also note thermal camera does not directly neasure what you want it measures how much things radiate at a specific band which varies by material and its surface quality.
example_context: Thermal IR cameras (MWIR/LWIR) used to infer component heat loads in electronics

subject: silicon transparency in typical thermal IR bands
main_point: Silicon can be transparent in the spectral ranges used by many thermal IR cameras, causing measurements to miss or misrepresent underlying heat sources. Material spectral properties must be considered when interpreting IR images of electronics.
source_quote: worse some materials like the silicon in your chips are transparent at typical infrared camera ranges.
example_context: Electronics components imaged with typical thermal IR camera ranges (e.g., LWIR)

subject: need for convective heat transfer data in thermal modeling
main_point: For meaningful thermal modeling, you must quantify how materials transfer energy to the air (e.g., via convection). Source terms or boundary conditions require more than surface temperatures to capture heat exchange correctly.
source_quote: You still need to know how much the materials transfer energy to air.

subject: using thermal imaging to validate CFD models
main_point: Use thermal camera measurements as validation targets for your CFD/thermal model rather than as the sole source for heat inputs. Comparing predicted and measured temperatures provides a practical check on model fidelity.
source_quote: That said the thermal camera is a good validator target for your model.

subject: SolidWorks assembly instance coloring via material edit
main_point: In SolidWorks 2014, editing a component’s color via Material > Edit in an assembly propagates the color to all identical part instances, not just the selected one.
source_quote: When I change the colour of the first one to green (material...edit) they all become green even though only the first one is selected.
example_context: SolidWorks 2014 (SP2) assembly with multiple identical instances of the same .sldprt

subject: SolidWorks appearance manager copy/paste behavior
main_point: In SolidWorks 2014, using Copy/Paste Appearance replaces the existing appearance on a component instead of adding an additional appearance layer.
source_quote: Also I couldn't persuade the appearance manager to understand what I want as the "copy/paste Appearance" features seem to overwrite the Appearance rather than adding new ones.
example_context: SolidWorks 2014 (SP2) appearance manager operations

subject: SolidWorks appearance application to selected components
main_point: In SolidWorks, you can assign a chosen appearance to specific components by selecting them in the feature tree and pasting the appearance onto that selection to set their color.
source_quote: Right click your selection and click "Paste Appearance"
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies using the Appearances tab and feature tree selection

subject: appearance attribute retention when editing color
main_point: When you edit the color of a newly applied appearance in SolidWorks, the existing transparency and overall material look are preserved.
source_quote: It should maintain transparency & general material appearance
example_context: SolidWorks Appearances editing workflow

subject: blind extrude on a hollow tube
main_point: Using a blind extrude on a hollow tube will create material that spans into and fills the bore, making it unsuitable for adding an external flange without altering the interior void. An alternative approach is required to avoid closing off the inside.
source_quote: In my real world example, this is actually a tube, so I can't blind extrude, because it will also fill the inside void.
example_value: The author’s tube model would have its interior void filled if a blind extrude were used from the exterior surface.
example_context: SolidWorks 2012 modeling of a hollow tube where an external flange is needed

subject: isometric projection angle
main_point: The depicted view is an isometric projection using a 30-degree angle for the axes.
source_quote:
This is a simple isometric projection
The angle is, by the picture 30.

subject: auxiliary sections for complex parts
main_point: For complex geometries, add auxiliary section views in addition to the standard three orthographic views to make dimensioning practical and clear.
source_quote: You probably need some auxiliary sections as well as the three basic views.
example_context: technical drawings of cylindrical parts with complex nonline/non-arc rib features

subject: sectional views for straight rib dimensioning
main_point: A mid-height section looking down the axis allows straightforward dimensioning of straight ribs on a cylindrical part.
source_quote: For example if you draw a section at mid-height looking down the axis, you can easily dimension the "straight" ribs.
example_context: cylindrical parts with axial straight ribs

subject: rib cross-section dimensioning via normal section
main_point: Use a section cut normal to a curved rib to dimension its cross-section; if ribs are uniform, that section defines all of them.
source_quote: If you draw a section normal to one of the curved ribs, you can dimension the cross section of that rib, and presumably they are all the same.
example_context: cylindrical parts with repeated curved ribs of uniform cross-section

subject: tolerancing non-critical ribs
main_point: When ribs are non-critical and not load-carrying, a general note stating they follow the cylinder contour with an approximate square cross-section is sufficient, instead of tight, detailed dimensions.
source_quote: Since the dimensions of the ribs don't look very critical (presumably only the top part is actually load-carrying) just conveying the message that "this rib follows the contours of the cylinder and its cross section is approximately $x$ inches square" is probably as much information as anyone needs in real life.
example_context: cosmetic or cooling ribs on a cylindrical motor mount where only the top region carries load

subject: radial hole pattern as alternative to complex rib cutouts
main_point: To replicate the function of ventilating/lightening ribs on a cylinder, machine a hollow cylinder and drill a radial pattern of through-holes instead of complex cutouts.
source_quote: Unless you really want it to look like that for aesthetic reasons, a way to machine something with the same functionality would be make to a hollow cylinder, and then drill a pattern of holes through it radially.
example_context: cylindrical parts requiring heat dissipation or weight reduction without aesthetic constraints

subject: operation sequencing for thin-walled cylinders
main_point: For thin-walled cylinders, drill radial blind holes while the part is still solid, then bore the interior; this sequencing simplifies drilling and stabilizes the workpiece.
source_quote: Since the cylinder is thin, it might be easier to drill a pattern of radial blind holes into the solid cylinder before you bore out the interior.
example_context: thin-walled cylindrical components needing radial holes

subject: internal fillet radius limited by cutter radius
main_point: When milling internal corners, the achievable fillet radius is limited to the cutter radius; you cannot make an internal corner radius smaller than the milling tool.
source_quote: (The fillets radii would be the same size of the milling tool, of course.)

subject: purpose of auxiliary views and dimensions for manufacturing
main_point: Auxiliary views and dimensions on a drawing should communicate how to set up the machine; once set up, the tooling and process inherently control the resulting dimensions of the remaining features.
source_quote: With either of those options, it's more obvious what you need to include on the drawing - the purpose of the auxiliary views and dimensions is to tell the operator how to set up the machine tool, and the tool itself will "automatically dimension" everything else.

subject: referring to solid model for undimensioned geometry
main_point: You can control complex, non-critical geometry by referencing the CAD model on the drawing and applying a profile tolerance (e.g., 0.020 in) to any unspecified surfaces, rather than dimensioning them explicitly.
example_value: A standard drawing note allows using the solid model and sets all unspecified surfaces to match the model within 0.020 in via a GD&T profile tolerance.
example_context: Drawing practices that leverage the CAD model as authority (model-based definition) with GD&T profile tolerance for unspecified surfaces

subject: dimensioning for design intent and inspection
main_point: Include only those dimensions on a drawing that communicate design intent and provide a clear basis for inspection; full explicit dimensioning of every surface is not required.
source_quote: You only need to put the necessary dimensions on a print so that the design intent is clearly conveyed and there is a standard by which the part can be inspected.

subject: dimensioning critical interfaces and strength features
main_point: Avoid dimensioning non-critical features; instead, dimension all interfaces with mating parts and any features required for part strength, and ignore complex rib shapes unless they are critical to the design.
source_quote:
Therefore, I would advise that you 
don't
 dimension any features that aren't critical to the design intent. 
Do
 dimension every feature that interfaces with your motor and other parts of your spinning top and 
do
 dimension every feature that must be made correctly for part strength, but don't stress about the angles and curves of your ribs unless those dimensions are critical to your design.
example_value: Interfaces with the motor and other spinning-top parts should be fully dimensioned; rib angles/curves need not be unless critical.

subject: STEP file exchange interoperability
main_point: Sharing CAD data via STEP file translation is a widely adopted industry method and generally provides reliable interoperability between different CAD systems.
source_quote: I disagree, step file translation and exchange is industry standard works great..
example_context: Multi-CAD environments exchanging 3D CAD models via STEP (ISO 10303).

subject: undimensioned drawings practice
main_point: It is common industry practice to provide drawings without full dimensions, relying on other sources (e.g., the model) rather than fully dimensioning every feature.
source_quote: Undimensioned drawings are common practice...

subject: terminology for partially dimensioned drawings
main_point: Partially dimensioned drawings are commonly referred to as Critical Feature Drawings or Limited Dimension Drawings.
source_quote: Partial dimensioned drawings are also called "Critical Feature Drawings" or "Limited Dimension Drawings".

subject: Autodesk vs Solidworks product focus
main_point: Autodesk spans a broad suite that includes graphics/animation tools like Maya and Mudbox, while Solidworks concentrates on engineering and manufacturing. This difference in portfolio focus can drive perceptions about each brand’s strengths in surface modeling versus mechanical design.
source_quote: This may be the fact that the Autodesk brand covers quite a broad range of software including more graphics orientated products like Maya and Mudbox which are intended for things like animation whereas Solidworks is more narrowly focused on engineering and manufacturing applications.
example_context: Autodesk suite (e.g., Maya, Mudbox) versus Solidworks

subject: artistic mesh modeling vs parametric solid modeling
main_point: Artistic surface-modeling tools emphasize editing complex meshes to create organic shapes, whereas mechanical CAD focuses on building precise, dimension-driven solids. These tool categories are optimized for different geometry-creation goals.
source_quote: Typically the more 'artistic' surface modelling software is focused on manipulating complex meshes eg for creating realistic face and figure models and is much more geared towards creating complex organic surfaces rather than building up solids according to specific dimensions.
example_value: The author likens Mudbox to digital clay modeling, contrasted with assembling carefully dimensioned parts.
example_context: Artistic mesh-based modeling tools (e.g., Maya, Mudbox) versus parametric solid CAD for mechanical design

subject: Autodesk Inventor capabilities for mechanical design
main_point: Autodesk Inventor supports mechanical part and assembly design and also provides integrated tools: basic FEA, weldment and sheet-metal environments, standard hardware/sections, and automated drawing and parts list generation.
source_quote: Having said that the Autodesk stable does include things like Inventor which very capable for designing mechanical parts and assemblies and includes things like basic finite element analysis and specific environments for welded and sheet metal assemblies as well as tools for things like threaded fasteners, holes as well as standard section materials (I beams etc) as well as the ability to easily generate projected drawings, parts lists etc from models and assemblies.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor mechanical CAD environment

subject: Autodesk Suite vs SolidWorks product scope
main_point: Do not compare SolidWorks to the entire Autodesk Suite; compare SolidWorks to Autodesk Inventor, which is the Autodesk package with roughly equivalent parametric solid modeling capabilities. The Autodesk Suite is a collection of different tools, not a single product.
source_quote: First of all, the comparison you suggest isn't really valid since SolidWorks is really a parametric solid modeling software package, while The Autodesk Suite encompasses several different software packages, one of which, Inventor, is roughly the functional equivalent to Solidworks.
example_context: CAD platform families (SolidWorks vs Autodesk Suite/Inventor)

subject: Location of Autodesk surface modeling tools relative to Inventor
main_point: Within Autodesk’s ecosystem, most advanced surface modeling capabilities reside in Autodesk packages other than Inventor; Inventor is not the primary vehicle for those surfacing tools.
source_quote: The surface modelling functions that Autodesk offers are primarily part of other Autodesk software packages and not Inventor.
example_context: Autodesk product lineup, distinguishing Inventor from other Autodesk surfacing-focused tools

subject: CAD tool selection criteria (interoperability, legacy data, customer compatibility)
main_point: When choosing between Autodesk and SolidWorks, prioritize how each integrates with PLM/PDM systems, handles legacy data, and aligns with your customers’ software environments.
source_quote: From my perspective, the choice between one or the other comes down to interoperability with other engineering software like Product Lifecycle Management/Product Data Management tools, how they deal with legacy data and, in many cases, interoperability with the customer's software.
example_context: Selecting between Autodesk Inventor and SolidWorks based on enterprise integration and customer ecosystem

subject: surface modeling characteristics (surface-only, no material properties, not parametric)
main_point: Surface modeling represents only the geometry’s skin; it typically omits material properties and is not driven by parametric solid features.
source_quote: surface modeling is just that, modeling of just the surface. There's no material properties and the models aren't parametrically driven.
example_context: General CAD workflows distinguishing surface modeling from parametric solid modeling

subject: surface modeling primary use cases (appearance/visualization)
main_point: Surface models are best suited for appearance-focused outputs such as renderings, marketing collateral, and animation rather than engineering analysis or parametric design.
source_quote: Their real application is in things where apprearance is the primary goal (think artist's renderings, sales brochures or animation).
example_context: Design visualization and marketing/animation deliverables

subject: detent mechanism naming
main_point: The knob interface that provides indexed positions is called a detent.
source_quote: So to answer the question the interface is called a detent.

subject: detent element and mating cavity
main_point: A detent typically consists of a protruding element (pin, ball, pawl, or bump) engaging a matching cavity to create indexed positions.
source_quote: a pin, ball, pawl or bump that fits against a mating cavity.

subject: spring-loaded detent behavior
main_point: In spring-loaded detents, the spring lets the detent element release from its cavity once sufficient force is applied during rotation, producing the characteristic clicking feel.
source_quote: Usually there is some kind of spring to allow the detent to disengage when enough force is applied. This gives the familiar click as a knob is rotated.
example_context: spring-loaded detent mechanisms in rotary knobs and indexed controls

subject: press nut preformed hole requirement
main_point: Self-clinching press nuts require a pre-made hole in the sheet; they are not self-drilling. The hole can be produced by drilling, punching, or laser cutting before insertion.
source_quote: Yes the nuts I want to use need holes drilled/punched/lasered into the sheet before insertion.
example_context: self-clinching press nuts (e.g., PEM) installed in sheet metal

subject: press nut hole size relative to clinching end
main_point: For press nuts, the installation hole is specified slightly smaller than the clinching end diameter so the nut can be forcefully inserted and retained. This interference ensures proper clinching into the sheet.
source_quote: This end is to be forcefully inserted into sheet metal with a hole slightly smaller in diameter than the nut's end.
example_context: self-clinching press nuts (e.g., PEM) installed in sheet metal

subject: SolidWorks Smart Components/Smart Features
main_point: In SolidWorks, Smart Components/Smart Features provide a way to link a hardware part to the CAD features it requires on mating parts. This lets you manage the component and its associated holes/cuts together.
source_quote: This technique will associate parts with features.
example_context: SolidWorks Smart Components and Smart Features

subject: press nut terminology
main_point: Some practitioners refer to these fasteners as "press nuts" or more generally as "press hardware," providing useful search terms when working with this type of sheet‑metal insert.
source_quote: As for the naming, we call those "Press Nuts", or more generically "Press Hardware"
example_context: Terminology used in some English-speaking shops for sheet‑metal insert fasteners

subject: SolidWorks Hole Wizard placement workflow
main_point: In SolidWorks, use the Hole Wizard to create correctly sized holes and place them by switching to the Positions tab, selecting a face, and clicking to drop holes to the chosen specification.
source_quote: Go to the hole wizard, pick the size hole you want, then go to the "Positions" tab, click a face and you're able to drop holes of the spec you chose wherever you want.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD Hole Wizard feature

subject: press nut hole requirement
main_point: Press nuts for sheet metal are generally installed into a single prepared hole in the sheet.
source_quote: That said, as far as I know, all of those nuts have you drill one hole in the sheet.
example_context: PEM press nuts for sheet metal

subject: PEM catalog hole size and tolerance specification
main_point: For press nuts, consult the vendor’s catalog page and use the “Hole Size in Sheet” values to call out the required hole diameter and tolerance to the fabricator.
source_quote: look at any of the pages on the site you linked, for a specific nut, you can see the hole size and tolerance you need to specify to the sheet metal fabricator. It's that big column labeled, "Hole Size in Sheet."
example_context: PennEngineering (PEM) press nut catalog pages

subject: Hole Wizard custom hole size and tolerance
main_point: SolidWorks Hole Wizard supports defining custom hole sizes and tolerances beyond its standard presets.
source_quote: You can specify a custom hole size and tolerance when you're in the hole wizard.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD Hole Wizard feature

subject: Hole Wizard saving custom hole settings
main_point: Save custom hole definitions in SolidWorks Hole Wizard so you can reuse them without retyping parameters each time.
source_quote: add the custom hole settings to the wizard to save those settings.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD Hole Wizard feature

subject: construction geometry for alignment in SolidWorks sketches
main_point: Use construction geometry to control alignment of sketch entities. In SolidWorks, create a centreline or convert a line to construction to provide reference geometry for aligning circles or other features.
source_quote: But search for centreline (a construction line) or right click on a normal line to give you some geometry to align the top two circles with.
example_value: Aligning the top two circles of a plate sketch using a centreline.
example_context: SolidWorks 2D sketching and relations

subject: Fillet tool for rounded edges
main_point: To create rounded edges in a model, use the Fillet feature rather than manually sketching arcs. This applies to adding radii on edges in CAD workflows.
source_quote: A filet is what you want for the rounded edges.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling/features

subject: SolidWorks sketch constraint indicators (green boxes)
main_point: Green boxes in a SolidWorks sketch indicate applied relations (constraints), which can include unintended constraints like enforced verticality. Reviewing and managing these relations is necessary to control geometry.
source_quote: Also the green boxes are constraints,  and I can see you have some you don't want, like the left and right uprights have been forced to be vertical.
example_value: Left and right uprights were unintentionally constrained to be vertical.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch relations UI

subject: Adding sketch constraints via context menu
main_point: Add sketch relations directly from the graphics area by right‑clicking the entities and choosing the needed constraint. This speeds up applying constraints without opening separate dialogs.
source_quote: To add constraints, right click on the parts you want to constrain and select what you need.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch relations workflow

subject: Deleting unwanted sketch constraints
main_point: Remove unwanted sketch relations by selecting their green relation indicators and pressing Delete. Cleaning up incorrect constraints helps ensure the sketch defines as intended.
source_quote: To delete them, click on the green squares and press delete
example_context: SolidWorks sketch relations UI

subject: Anchoring sketches to origin/geometry
main_point: Avoid leaving sketches "floating" by anchoring key geometry to the model origin or other reference geometry. For example, select the origin and a circle and apply a concentric relation to lock the sketch location.
source_quote: Also your sketch is currently floating in space, not fixed to the geometry like it should be. To fix this, select the origin and a circle (hold shift) and select make concentric.
example_context: SolidWorks sketch constraint practices

subject: Color feedback for fully defined sketch entities
main_point: SolidWorks provides visual feedback: fully defined sketch entities are shown in black. This indicates that dimensions and relations fully constrain the entity.
source_quote: When a line is fully defined, it will turn black.
example_context: SolidWorks sketching visual status

subject: Sequencing: fully define sketch before feature creation
main_point: Complete sketch definition before creating 3D features. In SolidWorks, once the sketch is fully defined, proceed to Features and create the solid with Extruded Boss/Base.
source_quote: When the whole sketch is fully defined, you can move on, go to the features toolbar, and select extruded boss/Base.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling workflow

subject: Proceeding with underdefined sketches
main_point: Proceeding to features with an underdefined sketch risks accidental geometry shifts because unconstrained entities can be dragged without notice. This leads to downstream problems that are difficult to diagnose and correct.
source_quote: If you move on without fully defining the sketch, you can accidently drag lines out of place without knowing. Which is the worst to try to hunt down and fix.
example_context: SolidWorks parametric sketching behavior

subject: SolidWorks non-uniform scaling of drawing views
main_point: SolidWorks cannot scale drawing views independently in X and Y; non-uniform scaling is not supported because it would distort the model, so alternate methods are required for clarity.
source_quote: No this is not possible, as it would distort the part.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing views

subject: using Broken Views to shorten long spans in drawings
main_point: Use Broken Views to remove long, featureless spans so the entire long beam remains legible on the sheet while still showing all key features.
source_quote: - Broken Views- These would allow you to cut out the long sections between the flanges allowing one to visualize the whole beam.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing views

subject: hiding lines to declutter zoomed-out drawing views
main_point: Hide interior or merging lines in a zoomed-out view so only the outer edges are shown, improving readability while keeping the overall view to scale.
source_quote: - Hiding lines - with a zoomed out view you can hide the lines that are blending together to only show the outer edges of the w. This allows you to show the entire beam to scale.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing views

subject: angled end view without perspective to mimic changed aspect ratio
main_point: To mimic a changed aspect ratio, disable perspective, start from an end view, and rotate slightly; this makes the beam appear with a different aspect ratio but clearly looks like an angled view.
source_quote: - An angled view- If you turn off perspective and view the beam from the end, then rotate by a small angle you can effectively get a changed aspect ratio, but it will be obvious that it is an angled view.
example_context: SolidWorks drawing views

subject: aluminum beverage can wall thickness
main_point: Typical wall thickness for US aluminum soda cans is about 0.1 mm.
source_quote: Most soda cans in the US are on the order of 0.1 mm thick
example_value: This figure is used to benchmark the plausibility of a 0.25 mm wall thickness in a lightweight aluminum design.
example_context: aluminum beverage cans in the United States

subject: order-of-magnitude comparison
main_point: When comparing your design to reference ranges, don’t assume similarity based on overlapping extremes; consider the scale of the range. Large order-of-magnitude differences (e.g., tens of times) make such comparisons misleading.
source_quote:
This means you need to be 
very
 careful looking at those ranges and saying "oh that means my measurement is about tin foil." Understanding orders of magnitude is a very important engineering principle.
example_value: The cited foil thickness range spans 0.006–0.2 mm (a 33× spread), so using its upper bound to equate with a 0.25 mm wall is not a sound comparison.

subject: default curve rendering detail in SolidWorks
main_point: SolidWorks intentionally displays curves with reduced tessellation by default, so circles may look faceted on-screen even though the underlying geometry is exact. This is normal behavior to limit display detail below the monitor’s maximum capability.
source_quote: By default, SolidWorks renders curves on the screen using less than the highest possible level of detail that your monitor is capable of displaying.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD display/image quality settings

subject: curve detail vs. redraw performance in SolidWorks
main_point: Increasing curve display detail increases redraw time, which can make SolidWorks feel sluggish on some hardware. Higher tessellation trades visual smoothness for reduced interactive performance.
source_quote: The more detailed the curve, the longer it takes to redraw the screen; depending on your hardware, this could make the software feel unresponsive or "laggy" and make it harder to use.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD viewport performance when increasing curve tessellation

subject: SolidWorks Image Quality slider and chordal deviation
main_point: In SolidWorks, the Image Quality slider sets display resolution, and the Deviation field sets maximum chordal deviation; these two are linked inversely—higher slider settings reduce chordal deviation and vice versa.
source_quote:
The slider controls the image quality resolution, and Deviation is the
  maximum chordal deviation in effect. Move the slider or type a value
  in Deviation. The slider setting and deviation value are coupled and
  are inversely proportional.
example_context: SolidWorks Document Properties > Image Quality settings for curve rendering

subject: when to avoid increasing SolidWorks image quality
main_point: Avoid raising the Image Quality setting just to verify a circle’s true geometry, because higher settings degrade performance. Keep lower display detail unless smoother visuals are genuinely needed.
source_quote: If all you're concerned about is confirming that your circle is actually a circle even when it is rendered with corners, you may not want to increase this setting, as it will have a negative impact on performance.
example_context: SolidWorks CAD display/image quality settings and performance trade-off

subject: adjusting SolidWorks Image Options for curve detail
main_point: To make on-screen curves appear smoother in SolidWorks, increase curve detail via Image Options in Document Properties.
source_quote: You can adjust the Image Options in the Document Properties tab to render curves with more detail
example_context: SolidWorks Document Properties > Image Quality configuration

subject: Creo student vs professional file compatibility
main_point: Files created in Creo’s professional edition can contain additional data that the student edition cannot interpret, leading to failures to open or convert those parts in the student edition.
source_quote: The "professional" version has more features, so the parts have extra information that the student version won't be able to read or convert.
example_context: PTC Creo professional vs student editions

subject: Opening Creo professional parts with the student edition
main_point: Use the professional edition to open complex Creo parts; the student edition may only succeed with very simple geometry such as basic prismatic shapes.
source_quote: So, You will need the "professional" version - at least for complicated parts. If it was just a simple bar it would likely open.
example_value: A simple bar may open in the student edition, but complicated parts require the professional edition.
example_context: PTC Creo professional vs student editions

subject: CAD vs CAM responsibility for manufacturing details
main_point: Use Creo to capture product design while delegating manufacturing-specific layouts/details to a downstream CAM module. Separating these responsibilities keeps design definition in CAD and production details in CAM.
source_quote: In general Creo is meant for making design details and manufacturing details should be handled by a CAM module downstream.
example_context: PTC Creo for design with a downstream CAM module handling manufacturing details

subject: design vs manufacturing lifecycle and scheduling needs
main_point: Design artifacts tend to persist longer, whereas manufacturing details need to be re-sequenced and optimized to fit changing shop priorities. This lifecycle and scheduling difference justifies separating design documentation from manufacturing instructions.
source_quote: Well the design usually has a longer time span than the manufacturing detail, and manufacturing floor might want to interleave it with different jobs at different times and optimize for different needs.
example_context: Manufacturing environments where design data is maintained long-term while production is scheduled and optimized job-to-job

subject: secondary assembly layout to generate drawings
main_point: Instead of creating a standalone sketch, build a secondary assembly to arrange the components and generate the drawing from that assembly.
source_quote: A secondary assembly that lays out the components and make a drawing out of that.
example_context: Creo Parametric: create a secondary assembly for layout and produce the drawing from it

subject: using exploded state for assembly layout in drawings
main_point: When the parts all belong to the same design, create the required layout as an exploded state in the assembly rather than building a separate construct.
source_quote: If all the parts go to the same design you may do this layout as a explode state.
example_context: Creo assembly drawings leveraging exploded states for layout

subject: CAM-driven layout of parts for manufacturing
main_point: Prefer to have the CAM module arrange the layouts, as this maximizes manufacturing flexibility and can enable automatic optimization of placement.
source_quote: Let the CAM module lay them out (this is best as it gives manufacturing much more flexibility, also most likely it can be auto optimized)
example_context: Using a downstream CAM module after Creo design to arrange part layouts

subject: associativity of manufacturing instructions to CAD models
main_point: Keeping manufacturing instructions tied to the CAD models (rather than as standalone drawings) preserves associativity, so updates to the design propagate to the instructions.
source_quote: the benefit of this is that the instructions are associative with the actual designs and not a self contained drawing
example_context: Creo models with downstream CAM or assembly-driven drawing workflows that reference live CAD

subject: off-center keyway load simplification
main_point: For a keyed torque joint, you can simplify the load calculation by ignoring the slight off-center line of action during the force derivation. Compute the force magnitudes first, then apply them at their true non-radial locations in the model.
source_quote: I would ignore the fact that the keyway makes the actual forces slightly off-center at least when calculating the forces themselves. The forces can be placed at their true locations once they are calculated.
example_value: Engineer calculates force magnitudes assuming centered action, then maps those forces onto the actual keyway contact faces in the FEA model.
example_context: FEA of torque transmission via a key/keyway in a hub or adapter where the keyway contact is slightly off the radial line of action.

subject: key/keyway contact load distribution assumption
main_point: Model the keyway contact as a continuous distribution that is zero at the center and increases toward the outer edge. This assumption is reasonable if tight tolerances or deformation equalize contact across the key length.
source_quote: I would also assume that the load is continuously distributed from the center to the outer edge. This assumes that the key is machined with a tight enough tolerance (or deflects/deforms enough) to equalize the distribution. This also assumes that a given amount of rotation produces more force at the extremes of the key than at the center (where it is zero).
example_value: Assume pressure varies from zero at the midline of the keyway to a maximum at the outer radius, reflecting higher force at the extremes under rotation.
example_context: FEA of torque transfer through a keyed connection where contact along the key length is intended to be uniform due to tight fit or elastic/plastic accommodation.

subject: maximum force per unit length under torque (keyway model)
main_point: Under the stated distribution assumptions, the maximum line load at the end of the keyway is w_max = T / ((2/3) R^2). Use this to set the peak force per unit length before mapping it to the actual contact geometry.
source_quote:
$P = \frac{1}{2}\frac{T}{\frac{2}{3}R} \
and \\
P = \frac{1}{2}R *w_\text{max}\\
gives:\\
w_\text{max} = \frac{T}{\frac{2}{3}R^2}$
example_value: Derivation relates torque T and radius R to peak distributed load w_max at the outer edge of the keyway.
example_context: FEA of a keyed torque joint using a continuous load distribution that increases from the center to the outer radius.

subject: FEA result sensitivity to load placement
main_point: In many structural FE models, small differences in exact load placement do not materially change the final results, but sensitivity varies by case. Validate whether your model’s results depend on precise load placement before relying on simplifications.
source_quote: Note also that I am used to working with models where the finer details of the exact load placement does not affect the final results, so I may be making assumptions that are not correct for your model.
example_value: Analyst notes prior experience where outcome metrics were insensitive to exact application points of loads.
example_context: Structural FEA where global response (e.g., overall stiffness/strength) dominates and local load application details have limited influence.

subject: adapter plate fabrication via CNC
main_point: Engine-to-gearbox swaps typically require a bellhousing adapter plate, and fabricating that plate is straightforward with CNC equipment. The adapter itself is not the difficult part of the conversion.
source_quote: A plate between the flywheel housing on the engine and the bell housing of the gearbox would almost certainly be required to mount the gearbox. This would be no problem to produce with a CNC machine.
example_context: fabricating a bellhousing adapter plate to mate a non-original manual gearbox to an engine

subject: transmission swap interface checks
main_point: Before fitting a different gearbox, verify all critical interfaces and packaging: clutch clearance and actuation, input shaft engagement and spline compatibility, shifter location/clearance, transmission tunnel fit, underbody clearances, crossmember/mount compatibility, and driveshaft alignment, connection/slip, and length.
source_quote: Will the gearbox obstruct the clutch assembly in any way? Will the gearbox imput shaft engage in the clutch? Will the splines of the imput shaft mate and be driven by the clutch? Will the clutch release mechanism operate the clutch successfully? Will the gearshift lever enter the cab? Will the gear shift lever be obstructed in anyway when shifting gear? Will the gearbox casing fit in the transmission tunnel? Will the gearbox effect the underbody position of things like the exhaust system or fuel tank? Will the gearbox cross member accept the new gearbox mountings? Will the propshaft alignment be in alignment? Will the propshaft connect to the gearbox and allow a sliding joint? Will the propshaft length now be too long or too short to connect to the differencial?
example_value: The post enumerates checks for clutch obstruction, input shaft engagement, spline match, clutch release function, shifter entry/obstruction, case fit in tunnel, exhaust/fuel tank interference, crossmember mount compatibility, propshaft alignment/connection/sliding joint, and propshaft length to the differential.
example_context: converting a vehicle to a different manual gearbox than originally fitted

subject: custom gearbox swap cost viability
main_point: Because the vehicle was built around its original drivetrain, reconciling all the mismatches to fit a different gearbox often makes the project uneconomical in time and money. The cumulative integration work can render the swap not viable.
source_quote: When your vehicle was first built it was with its present configuration. You would need to reconcile each every difference from that first build. In time and expense terms it would be highly unlikely to be a viable undertaking.
example_context: retrofitting a non-original manual gearbox to a vehicle

subject: SAE #3 bolt pattern compatibility
main_point: Engines with an SAE #3 transmission mount pattern will not directly match most common transmissions, so off-the-shelf mating options are limited. The uncommon bolt pattern is the reason few transmissions bolt up without adaptation.
source_quote: If I read the specs right, it has an SAE #3 transmission mount bolt pattern. This is why you won't find many trannies which will mate directly to it.
example_value: The Nissan SD33T engine is cited as having an SAE #3 mount pattern, explaining the limited direct-fit transmission options.
example_context: Engines with SAE #3 transmission mount bolt patterns (e.g., industrial/forklift-derived engines like the Nissan SD33T).

subject: flywheel spacer use with transmission adapter plates
main_point: When adapting an automotive transmission to a non-automotive engine, the solution often includes both an adapter plate and a flywheel spacer to compensate for required geometry and spacing.
source_quote: They make adapter plates to mate automotive transmissions to non-automotive engines (they also make the spacers for the flywheel to compensate).
example_value: Commercial kits include the adapter plate plus a flywheel spacer as part of the solution.
example_context: Automotive transmission to non-automotive (industrial) engine adaptations.

subject: buy vs build adapter plate decision
main_point: Prefer purchasing an existing adapter solution for engine-to-transmission mating because it arrives much faster than designing and machining a custom adapter; only consider DIY if cost pressures outweigh time-to-solution.
source_quote: Unless cost is a factor, something already exists to mate your engine to a different tranny, so why try to machine something up your self. Phoenix has what you need and can get it to you a lot faster than you can re-engineer something to fit in.
example_value: A vendor like Phoenix Casting & Machine offers ready-made adapters that can be obtained quicker than fabricating one via CNC/waterjet.
example_context: Engine/transmission adaptation projects where commercial adapter kits are available.

subject: drivetrain swap cost tradeoff
main_point: Evaluate swapping to a different engine/transmission combo as a potential cost-saving alternative to custom adapters, as local availability and choices can make a full swap cheaper overall.
source_quote: Consider putting a different engine/tranny combo into your vehicle. Depending on what you might choose, this may actually be a cheaper option, especially considering the area of the States you are located.
example_context: Vehicle drivetrain modifications where regional availability and pricing influence total project cost.

subject: helicoil tang interference with bolt
main_point: In most helical wire insert installations, the break-off tang remains at the bottom of the hole and the mating bolt does not contact it. As a result the tang typically does not affect thread engagement or operation even if left in place.
source_quote: The tang is usually either left or broken off at the very bottom of the hole and causes no problem as it is not normally reached by the bolt.
example_context: Helical wire thread inserts (Helicoil) with break-off tangs used for thread repair

subject: upsizing fastener instead of using helicoil
main_point: When the part can be safely drilled and re-tapped, upsizing the thread and using a larger bolt can be a better repair than installing a helical insert. This avoids insert installation constraints and restores strength with a simpler joint.
source_quote: If you can drill it and tap it ready for the helicoil, you may be better off just putting a larger bolt in.
example_context: Repairing a stripped threaded hole where sufficient wall/material exists to accept a larger thread

subject: using washer or flanged bolt to cover enlarged hole
main_point: If installing an insert enlarges the entry face, use a washer or a bolt with an oversized/flanged head to cover and support the larger opening. This helps restore bearing area and appearance without modifying the part further.
source_quote: If you install the helicoil from the correct side - could you add a washer or one of the bolts with a wider head to cover the larger hole?
example_context: Fastener joints where the outer face was opened up to install a helical insert from the correct side

subject: through-bolt with nut to bypass stripped internal thread
main_point: You can bypass a stripped internal thread by using a longer bolt as a through-fastener with a nut on the far side. This provides clamping without relying on the damaged tapped hole, albeit with aesthetic tradeoffs.
source_quote: Another possibility may be to use a longer bolt and put a nut over the top of the clamp, - ugly though...
example_context: Assemblies where the fastener path can be converted from a tapped hole to a through-hole with external nut access

subject: plugging and re-tapping a damaged threaded hole
main_point: A robust repair for a stripped hole is to bore it oversize, fit a solid plug tightly (optionally welded), secure it with adhesive, then re-drill and tap the new threads and re-profile the exterior as needed. This restores full thread integrity when inserts or upsizing aren’t feasible.
source_quote: Edit, so now after seeing the pictures I would drill the old threaded hole a bit larger and then make a blank to fit in that hole tightly (welding it up is a good suggestion) and cement it in place, then re-drill and tap it - cutting the outer profile to fit.
example_context: Repairing a damaged threaded hole in a clamp or similar component with limited surrounding material

subject: weld-fill and re-tap repair for stripped hole
main_point: If a helicoil repair isn’t feasible or fails, a shop can weld-fill the damaged hole and then it can be drilled and tapped back to the original thread size as an alternative restoration method.
source_quote: You could take it to an engineering company and get them to fill the hole using a welder, then re-drill and tap to the original size if your helicoil doesn't work.
example_value: For a stripped clamp hole, have a machine shop weld the hole closed, then re-drill and tap to the original size instead of using a helicoil.
example_context: repairing a stripped threaded hole when a helicoil cannot be installed or is unsuccessful

subject: embedded round nut thread repair
main_point: A stripped threaded hole can be repaired by partially enlarging the damaged side, inserting a round steel nut as an internal insert, and securing it—optionally with adhesive—to restore usable threads without through-drilling.
source_quote: You could partially enlarge the hole (where the tread stripped). Place a round steel nut into the enlarged part. You could also fix the nut with glue

subject: helicoil tang orientation when installed from wrong side
main_point: Installing a helicoil from the opposite side leaves the drive tang at the entry face, which can interfere with bolt engagement and is difficult to remove from that side.
source_quote: From what I read, it seems that primary problem in installing the helicoil from the wrong side is that the tang would be left on the entry side of the helicoil.

subject: improvised backward helicoil insertion in aluminum
main_point: To avoid the tang issue or access constraints, install the helicoil backwards; in soft aluminum you can manually thread the insert using improvised tools (e.g., pliers) if the standard insertion tool can’t be used.
source_quote: How about just installing the helicoil backwards? Depending on the insertion tool this may require some improvising to get it installed, but aluminum is so soft you could probably thread it in even with just pliers.
example_context: helicoil installation into aluminum parts when standard insertion access/tools are unavailable

subject: tangless threaded inserts with screwdriver slots
main_point: An alternative to tang-type helicoils is using tangless threaded inserts driven by a screwdriver, eliminating the need to break off a tang.
source_quote: There are also threaded inserts that do not have a tang, instead having slots for a screwdriver,
example_value: Example product: E-Z Lok tangless inserts.

subject: M7 stem bolt head diameter vs M6
main_point: Some M7 bicycle stem bolts have relatively small heads, potentially close to M6 head diameters, which may avoid the need to enlarge the counterbore or clearance for the head.
source_quote: The ones pictured (meant for stem bolts)appear to have a smaller head in proportion to the thread than metric screws usually have.  They may well be near enough the same head diameter as a standard M6.
example_value: The answer references stem/post bolts marketed for bikes that have smaller-than-typical heads for their thread size.
example_context: Bicycle stem or seatpost clamp bolts sold as M7

subject: Clamp clearance hole oversize
main_point: Clamp clearance holes are often slightly oversized, so a slightly larger bolt head may already fit or require only minimal enlargement of the head recess.
source_quote: you might need to open out the head hole a touch, but you might have enough room as the clearance holes are often a bit oversized in clamps.
example_value: The comment follows an example of an M7 bolt with an  11 mm head possibly fitting a clamp originally for M6.
example_context: Bicycle-style clamps with clearance and head recess holes

subject: tap selection for threading
main_point: While having both taper and bottoming taps is preferable, you can often complete the job using only a taper tap when conditions allow.
source_quote: A set of taper and bottoming taps would be good, but you could get away with just a taper tap.
example_value: In the discussed repair, the hole is not blind, so a taper tap alone may suffice.
example_context: Tapping non-blind (through) holes such as a bike clamp repair

subject: quick-release skewer with angled welded washers
main_point: As an alternative to rethreading, retrofit the clamp by welding angled aluminum washers to both sides and using a quick‑release skewer to apply clamping force, yielding a neat and safe repair.
source_quote: Get a quick-release skewer.  Fit (grind) an angle on a thick aluminum washer so that the skewer applies correctly.  Solder fitted washers to both sides of your clamp with argon welder.  That'll be neat and safe solution.
example_value: Grind an angle on a thick aluminum washer so the skewer bears correctly, then weld fitted washers to both sides of the clamp.
example_context: repairing an aluminum bicycle clamp with stripped threads where a helicoil/drill approach is impractical

subject: upsizing damaged threads in an aluminum bike clamp
main_point: Avoid re-tapping a damaged clamp to a larger diameter; in this application it can fail under load, leading to the seat dropping or a crash.
source_quote: Please don't rerun your damaged thread with larger diameter. I've been thru exactly the same situation personally. You don't want to share experience of your seat drop or fall off when you're busy pedalling or soaring down the slope, believe me!
example_value: Author reports personal experience of a seat dropping or falling off while pedaling or descending after upsizing threads.
example_context: bicycle seat/clamp repair in aluminum where the original threads have stripped

subject: tapping technique in aluminum from reverse side
main_point: When threading aluminum from the reverse side, advance the tap in very small increments (about 10–15 degrees), back off to break chips, and repeat with light oil for lubrication.
source_quote: But, if you will, aluminum alloys generally would take the backwards thread application. Just do a step by step, rotate 10-15 degrees max, then back, then repeat.  Apply light oil.
example_context: thread cutting in aluminum alloys (e.g., reverse-side thread application)

subject: wedge shims to align bolt head and nut on non-parallel faces
main_point: When a threaded repair isn’t feasible on a non-parallel clamp, you can use a longer through-bolt with wedge-shaped shims on both sides. Hand-cut triangular shims from bar stock are sufficient; the critical requirement is setting the shim angle so the bolt head and nut bear on parallel faces.
source_quote: You could put a longer bolt through if there were wedge-shaped shims on either side. You could cut and shape these just from some bar stock by hand - no precision is needed, just a hole big enough to fit the bolt and the key thing is getting the triangle angle correct so the bolt head and nut have parallel sides.
example_value: Make triangular shims from bar stock with a clearance hole and use a longer bolt to clamp across angled sides.
example_context: retrofitting a clamp with angled sides where thread repair (e.g., helicoil) isn’t practical

subject: wood prototypes for wedge shims
main_point: Prototype the wedge shims in wood to quickly dial in the angle and fit, since timber is easy to shape by sanding. Use metal for the final parts, as wood may not withstand the required bolt tightening force.
source_quote: You could even trial it by cutting them from timber, which has the advantage of being easier to shape by sanding, but may not be hard enough for the degree you need to tighten the bolts.
example_context: fitting wedge shims to align a through-bolt on angled clamp faces

subject: helicoil installed from opposite side
main_point: Installing a helicoil from the opposite side of a through hole can be a viable, straightforward repair on an aluminum clamp when front-side access is limited. Successful execution involves standard steps (drill, tap, install, break tang) with attention to depth control and tang removal.
source_quote: Well, I did it, and it was one of the most straightforward fixes possible.
