Although i have not tested this yet, there is a new tool/website that let you convert 3D Models (can be imported from Fusion as well as an STL) to URDF.
Maybe its worth giving it a try.
example_value: The suggested tool is https://lever-robotics.github.io/URDF_creator/ and it claims to accept Fusion and STL inputs for URDF generation.
example_context: Lever Robotics URDF_creator web tool for converting Fusion or STL models to URDF

subject: auto-generated reference coordinate systems in SolidWorks URDF exporter
main_point: Using the SolidWorks URDF Exporter with the "Automatically Generate" reference coordinate systems option can complete the export but yield incorrectly located joint axes.
source_quote: If I select the option "Reference Coordinate system - Automatically Generate" then the exporter works but the axis generated are at incorrect locations.
example_value: In the reporter’s model, enabling Automatically Generate allowed export to proceed, but the produced axes did not align with the intended locations.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter in SolidWorks when using "Reference Coordinate system - Automatically Generate"

subject: URDF exporter error about missing sketch in SolidWorks
main_point: The SolidWorks URDF Exporter can report a Property Manager/sketch-missing error even when the referenced sketch actually exists.
source_quote: the plugin throws an error stating there is a issue in property manager and sketch doesn't exist. However the sketch does exist
example_value: The user had mates and a coordinate system defined, yet the exporter complained that a sketch did not exist.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter in SolidWorks assemblies with mates and defined coordinate systems

subject: assembly axes without sketches
main_point: If the axes are created as assembly features without an underlying sketch, SolidWorks will correctly report an error that no sketch defines those features.
source_quote:
you've created those axes as an 
assembly
 feature, in which case I believe your error is correct in that there is not actually a 
sketch
 that defines those features,
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter setups where reference axes were created as assembly features rather than sketch-defined features

subject: reference sketches for joint axes
main_point: Create a sketch in each relevant part to define the joint’s axis of rotation for both input and output joints.
source_quote: I would open each part and create a sketch in those parts that defines the axis of rotation for the input and output joints.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies being prepared for URDF export and joint definition

subject: accessing child sketches in assembly
main_point: In the assembly, expand each part to access its child sketches and select sketch features to drive the assembly constraints.
source_quote: Then, when you're in the assembly, you can expand the parts to get access to their child sketches, and you can select features from those sketches for the constraints.
example_context: SolidWorks assembly constraints selection workflow

subject: subassembly vs part-level reference sketches
main_point: Place reference sketches either at the subassembly level or the individual component level, then expand the subfeature trees to access the needed sketches.
source_quote: you can make sketches at the subassembly level or still at the individual component level, and you would just expand those subfeature trees as necessary until you get to the reference sketches you need.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies with multiple subassemblies and component feature trees

subject: FreeCAD STEP-to-Collada export capability
main_point: FreeCAD can be used to convert STEP geometry into Collada (.dae) while letting you tune meshing parameters to control the resulting polygon mesh.
source_quote: FreeCAD can import STEP files and export Collada .dae files with good control over the mesh parameters.
example_context: Using FreeCAD to convert STEP models to Collada (DAE) with configurable mesh settings

subject: SolidWorks-to-FreeCAD via STEP for meshing
main_point: Export your model from SolidWorks as STEP to retain exact geometry, then perform the meshing step in FreeCAD where you have more control.
source_quote: Exporting STEP from Solidworks preserves the exact geometry and then you can work on the mesh in FreeCAD.
example_context: SolidWorks models exported as STEP and meshed in FreeCAD

subject: Blender CAD import limitation
main_point: Blender is limited to importing mesh formats, so attempting to bring in non-mesh CAD formats like STEP will not work.
source_quote: I believe it only can import mesh formats,
example_context: Blender import capabilities (no native STEP/BREP import)

subject: SolidWorks-to-Blender via STL
main_point: To use Blender when only mesh imports are supported, export an STL from SolidWorks and import that into Blender.
source_quote: exporting a STL out of Solidworks and importing into Blender is also an option.
example_context: Workflow to move SolidWorks geometry into Blender by meshing as STL first

subject: pycollada requirement for Collada export on Windows
main_point: While some guidance recommends installing pycollada for Collada export, on Windows this extra library may not be needed.
source_quote: Some forum posts suggest you need to install the pycollada library but I don't think that's required on Windows.
example_context: FreeCAD Collada export behavior on Windows platforms

subject: Multi-tool pipeline for URDF visual meshes
main_point: A multi-stage toolchain (converting, meshing, and editing across several apps) can produce URDF visuals that are smooth, colored, and with manageable polygon counts.
source_quote: I've used pipelines as complex as STEP->FreeCAD->Meshlab->Blender->URDF before to get nice looking, smooth visuals with colors and not too many polygons!
example_value: STEP -> FreeCAD -> Meshlab -> Blender -> URDF
example_context: Preparing URDF visual meshes using FreeCAD, Meshlab, and Blender

subject: STEP-to-DAE conversion workflow (CAD Assistant -> GLTF -> Blender)
main_point: A practical path to produce Collada (DAE) and STL from a STEP model is to convert the STEP to GLTF with Open Cascade CAD Assistant, then import the GLTF into Blender to process and export as Collada and STL.
example_context: Using Open Cascade CAD Assistant and Blender to convert CAD models to Collada (DAE) and STL.

subject: Model size reduction and reorientation via Blender during conversion
main_point: Despite requiring multiple steps, using Blender after converting to GLTF is an effective, easy way to reduce file size and correct model orientation before exporting.
source_quote: It's a bit cumbersome, but for reducing the size and orienting the object correctly I've found this to be the easiest way..
example_context: GLTF imported into Blender for cleanup and orientation prior to exporting to Collada/STL.

subject: feature-induced property mismatch in URDF export
main_point: While tracing mass mismatches between the URDF Exporter and Solidworks Mass Properties, the user found a specific modeling feature (Thicken) that caused the discrepancy, indicating certain features can disrupt exported mass calculations.
source_quote:
Repeat this process until finding a feature that results in a mismatching mass.

I did this until I found my first feature that is causing an issue. It is a Thicken feature on the back cover plate.
example_value: In the base_link assembly, a Thicken feature on the back cover plate was identified as triggering the mismatch.
example_context: Solidworks 2019 SP5 with URDF Exporter 1.5.1; base_link assembly including a Thicken feature.

subject: URDF Exporter vs Solidworks Mass Properties mass/COM discrepancy
main_point: The URDF Exporter and Solidworks Mass Properties can report slightly different mass and center-of-mass values for the same selected components.
source_quote: Note the small differences in the Mass and Center of mass on the Mass Properties vs the Inertial Origin in the Exporter. (e.g. mass = 0.54812303 vs 0.54821, and x = -0.00412774 vs -0.0041336).
example_context: Solidworks 2019 SP5 with URDF Exporter 1.5.1; base_link assembly.

subject: URDF Exporter moments of inertia mismatch with Solidworks
main_point: Even when mass and center of mass agree, the URDF Exporter can output inertia tensor values that do not match the matrices reported by Solidworks Mass Properties for the same link.
source_quote: The Inertial Origin matches the Center of mass as calculated by Solidworks Mass Properties as does the Mass (0.045216 kg). The Moment of Inertia in the Exporter looks nothing like any of the matricies given in the Mass Properties of Solidworks.
example_value: For Link_WheelLeft, mass matched at 0.045216 kg while MOI values differed significantly.
example_context: Solidworks 2019 SP5 with URDF Exporter 1.5.1; Link_WheelLeft in a two-wheel robot assembly.

subject: overridden mass/inertia properties support in URDF exporter
main_point: The SolidWorks URDF Exporter does not honor overridden mass or inertia properties. If a model relies on overridden values, the exported mass and inertia will not reflect them due to this tool limitation.
source_quote: the exporter does not support overridden properties, and it would be difficult to support that with the current workflow of the tool.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter for generating URDF from SolidWorks models

subject: mass property parity between SolidWorks and URDF exporter
main_point: If you export the exact same set of components without any overridden properties, the exported link’s mass properties should match SolidWorks. A mismatch in this case likely indicates a bug.
source_quote: it would be an unknown bug if the combined mass properties of a selected group of components (with no overridden properties) in SolidWorks does not match the same list of components in a link once exported.
example_context: Comparing SolidWorks Mass Properties to SolidWorks URDF Exporter outputs with no overridden properties

subject: reference coordinate system selection for mass properties
main_point: When comparing mass and inertia to the exporter, set the reference coordinate system in SolidWorks’ Mass Properties dialog to the intended frame. Otherwise, values are taken about the global origin, causing apparent discrepancies.
source_quote: make sure that you set the reference coordinate system in the mass properties dialog, otherwise the properties will be in reference to the global origin in SolidWorks.
example_context: SolidWorks Mass Properties dialog settings when validating URDF exporter inertia

subject: exporter inertia reference frame (inertia origin at COM)
main_point: The URDF exporter reports inertia about each link’s inertia origin located at its center of mass, aligned with the link’s joint origin. Comparisons must use the same reference frame to match values.
source_quote: The inertia properties in the exporter dialog are always in reference to the link's inertia origin, which is the center of mass and aligned with the link's joint origin.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter link inertia display and reference frames

subject: including hidden and skin components in link selection
main_point: Include both internal (hidden) parts and skin (visual) parts in each link’s component selection to make the exported mass properties match those computed in SolidWorks.
source_quote: You are correct that you will need to include both the hidden components and the skin components as the components in your link in order for the mass properties to match the solidworks components.
example_context: Preparing component selections for links in the SolidWorks URDF Exporter

subject: organizing per-link subassemblies for export
main_point: Organize each link’s parts (including skin) into a single SolidWorks subassembly before exporting. This simplifies selection and improves the likelihood of correct mass and inertia aggregation.
source_quote: The advice I give everyone when exporting from SolidWorks is to put all the parts and assemblies for each link into a single SW subassembly, which would include skin parts.
example_context: SolidWorks model organization for URDF export

subject: single-part link handling for export
main_point: If a link consists of only one part, export it directly without creating a subassembly. Creating a subassembly is unnecessary in this case.
source_quote: If a link is just a single part, then you can leave it as a part.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter workflow for simple single-part links

subject: assembly mates representing link DOF
main_point: Set assembly mates so each link’s assembly reflects the intended degree of freedom for that link in the robot. This ensures the assembly behaves and exports consistently with the robot’s kinematics.
source_quote: Also make sure that you set the mates so that the link assembly has the representational degree of freedom of the link in your robot.
example_context: SolidWorks assemblies prepared for URDF export to reflect kinematic DOF

subject: selection list ambiguity with many components
main_point: Selecting a large number of components for a single link can make the exporter ambiguous about user intent, increasing the likelihood of misinterpreting which items define the link.
source_quote: If you include many components in the selection list for a link, it's harder for the exporter to know what you want.
example_context: Selecting components for a link in the SolidWorks URDF Exporter

subject: potential bugs with multiple components in selection list
main_point: There may be unresolved bugs triggered when multiple components are included in a link’s selection list, which can lead to incorrect export behavior or results.
source_quote: It may also be possible that there are still bugs when there are multiple components in the selection list.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter behavior when multiple components are selected for a link

subject: ROS TF NaN transform values
main_point: In ROS TF, a transform is ignored if any component contains NaN values. If your broadcaster publishes a transform with NaNs in the translation or rotation fields, TF will drop it.
source_quote: [ERROR] [1542609991.430536188]: Ignoring transform for child_frame_id "link1" from authority "unknown_publisher" because of a nan value in the transform (-nan -nan -nan) (-nan -nan -nan -nan)
example_value: Log shows TF ignoring transform for child_frame_id "link1" due to NaN values in both translation and quaternion.
example_context: ROS TF (tf/tf2) transform broadcasting on ROS Kinetic

subject: ROS TF invalid quaternion
main_point: ROS TF rejects transforms that have an invalid orientation quaternion. If the quaternion is invalid (e.g., contains NaN values), the transform will be ignored.
source_quote: [ERROR] [1542609991.430645045]: Ignoring transform for child_frame_id "link1" from authority "unknown_publisher" because of an invalid quaternion in the transform (-nan -nan -nan -nan)
example_value: Error indicates TF ignoring the "link1" transform because the quaternion values are all NaN.
example_context: ROS TF (tf/tf2) orientation handling on ROS Kinetic

subject: URDF joint axis property
main_point: When building a URDF, verify that each joint’s axis property is correctly defined; if not, you should correct it. Misdefined or unset joint axes are a common source of problems and should be checked and fixed during model setup.
source_quote:
First issue: some of the 
joint
s don't have their 
axis
 property set correctly (
this one
 for instance). That would be something to check and fix.
example_value: The responder points to a specific joint in the provided URDF as an example where the axis property was not set correctly.

subject: sw2urdf unit conversion and inertia zeroing
main_point: The sw2urdf plugin outputs in MKS units, and for very small models the computed inertia values can be so tiny that the plugin writes them as zeros. This is a limitation observed when exporting small-scale designs.
source_quote: sw2urdf plugin exports all the units is mks unit, as a ressult if the model is very small or say the intertia tensor values are very small than as i've seen the plugin calculated them as zero since the vale is very small.
example_value: Exporting a very small SolidWorks model via sw2urdf resulted in all inertia tensor values being 0.
example_context: SolidWorks to URDF export using the sw2urdf plugin for small-scale models

subject: manual entry of inertia values from SolidWorks mass properties
main_point: To avoid zero inertias from sw2urdf on small models, compute the mass properties in SolidWorks, convert them to MKS, and manually enter those inertia values during URDF export.
source_quote: u can use evalute->mass property to calulate those values and than convert it to mks units and than put it manually while exporting to urdf.
example_value: Use Evaluate -> Mass Properties in SolidWorks, convert results to MKS, then type the inertia into the URDF exporter fields.
example_context: SolidWorks to URDF export using the sw2urdf plugin when automatic inertia comes out as zero

subject: URDF mesh formats and recommended usage
main_point: URDF supports STL and Collada mesh formats, and a common practice is to use STL for collision geometry and DAE for visual geometry. This separates simple collision meshes from richer visual meshes with materials.
source_quote: I know that URDF files only support .stl and collada (.dae) files and that I should use .stl files for the collision tag and .dae for the visual tag.
example_context: ROS URDF models (visual and collision tags) used with Gazebo/ROS Kinetic

subject: SolidWorks2URDF exporter Collada support limitation
main_point: The SolidWorks2URDF exporter does not generate Collada (.dae) meshes, so URDFs produced by it will reference STL meshes (for both visual and collision) unless meshes are converted by another tool.
source_quote: because the exporter doesn't export any collada (.dae) files.
example_context: SolidWorks2URDF (sw_urdf_exporter) plugin for SolidWorks

subject: STEP AP214 support for colors vs appearances
main_point: STEP AP214 carries color information but does not include full appearance/texture data. Choosing AP214 preserves colors without appearances when converting.
source_quote: format 214 so that it also has colors but not appearances
example_context: STEP (ISO 10303) AP214 file format for CAD data exchange

subject: Gazebo visual mesh path resolution
main_point: In Gazebo, a white cube rendering indicates the URDF visual mesh file path is incorrect; correcting the mesh path resolves the issue.
source_quote: When a white cube appears on Gazebo that means that the path to the visual mesh in not well specified.
example_context: Gazebo/ROS URDF visual mesh file references

subject: Using absolute paths to debug URDF mesh references
main_point: If a package-based mesh reference fails in Gazebo, try using an absolute filesystem path to verify the mesh loads, then switch back once the path issue is corrected.
source_quote: when I used the full path the tree appear and everything seemed to be fine.
example_context: Gazebo/ROS URDF visual mesh file references

subject: SolidWorks2URDF COLLADA export limitation and alternative
main_point: Because SolidWorks2URDF does not export COLLADA (.dae), use a separate tool like SimLab Collada Exporter to generate the visual meshes.
source_quote: The SolidWorks2URDF (link: http://wiki.ros.org/sw_urdf_exporter) plugin works  just fine but doesn't export COLLADA models, which means you have to get them through another plugin, which is the SimLab Collada Exporter.
example_context: SolidWorks model export for ROS/URDF and Gazebo visuals

subject: SimLab Collada Exporter appearance export limitation
main_point: The SimLab Collada Exporter cannot export SolidWorks appearances to COLLADA; only flat RGB colors are carried over.
source_quote: Keep in mind that this plugin can't export any appearances to a COLLADA file, only normal colors, i.e., the RBG combinations.
example_context: SimLab Soft Collada Exporter for SolidWorks

subject: STEP export lacks appearances
main_point: Appearances cannot be exported to STEP (.stp); STEP will not include SolidWorks appearance data.
source_quote: (I also discovered that it is not possible to export appearances to a STEP (.stp file), which was something that I also tried when trying to work my problem around).
example_context: Exporting SolidWorks models to STEP (e.g., AP214) for use in other tools

subject: SimLab Collada Exporter version support
main_point: SimLab Collada Exporter supports SolidWorks versions 2013 and newer.
source_quote: The SimLab Collada Exporter (https://www.simlab-soft.com/3d-plugins/SolidWorks/Collada_exporter_for_SolidWorks-main.aspx) is supported on SolidWorks 2013 and more recent versions.
example_context: SimLab Soft Collada Exporter compatibility with SolidWorks versions

subject: SW2URDF automatic joint generation
main_point: The SW2URDF exporter’s automatic joint generation can silently fail, providing no warning or error. Users should anticipate that this step may not complete successfully even though no message is shown.
source_quote: In essence it seems that the automatic generation of joints fails without giving any warning or error.
example_context: SolidWorks to URDF exporter (SW2URDF) for ROS

subject: Manual joint definition to bypass auto-generation
main_point: Manually defining joints in SW2URDF allows you to bypass the failing automatic joint-generation step and proceed with export. This avoids the silent failure during auto-generation.
source_quote: Luckily you can define the joints yourself and effectively skip this part of the process.
example_context: SolidWorks to URDF exporter (SW2URDF) for ROS

subject: mesh origin alignment for RViz visualization
main_point: If an STL appears offset in RViz, you can fix it by resetting the mesh’s origin to the object’s coordinate system in Blender; RViz will then visualize the model centered as intended.
source_quote: So in Blender as AndyZe said, I changed the origin to my object coordinate system and everything works for now, and i can visualize object in rviz with origin in center of object.
example_value: The author changed the STL’s origin in Blender and afterward the mesh appeared in RViz with its origin at the object center.
example_context: ROS RViz using visualization_msgs::Marker with MESH_RESOURCE for an STL exported from SolidWorks; Blender used to set the STL’s origin to the object’s coordinate system.

subject: SolidWorks export origin control
main_point: In SolidWorks, define a reference Coordinate System and, during Save As, choose it as the Output Coordinate System so the exported mesh uses that origin instead of the model’s default. Access this via the Save As Options dialog.
source_quote: You can explicitly create a coordinate system as reference geometry and tell Solidworks to export the part with respect to that coordinate system to take out the guess work. There is an options button at the bottom of the Save As window which brings you to another window that lets you set the "Output Coordinate System".
example_context: SolidWorks STL export using Save As Options -> Output Coordinate System

subject: changing mesh origin in Blender
main_point: If a mesh’s origin is not where you need it, open the model in Blender and adjust the object’s origin there; a Gazebo tutorial explains the steps.
source_quote:
You can change the origin with Blender. See 
http://gazebosim.org/tutorials?tut=guided_i2
example_context: Editing mesh models in Blender for Gazebo use (per Gazebo tutorial)

subject: fit tolerance selection without standards in low-volume work
main_point: For one-off or low-volume parts, the author advises not relying on formal fit standards and instead determining the fit experimentally. In non–mass production work, choose slip/press fit values by testing and adjusting.
source_quote: I think, unless you are planning for mass production, you need not search for any standards.you can experiment and decide the values yourself.
example_context: single components or non-mass production jobs

subject: use of IT grades in mass production fits
main_point: In mass-production hole–shaft assemblies, IT tolerance grades are employed to handle the fact that parts cannot all be machined precisely identical. The grades accommodate part-to-part variation inherent in large runs.
source_quote: But from what I learnt IT grades are used in mass production of hole shaft assemblies because machining cannot be done precisely and identically for all the parts.
example_context: mass production of hole/shaft assemblies

subject: material thermal expansion variability
main_point: Different materials (e.g., wood, plastics, and metals) have widely differing thermal expansion/contraction coefficients, so their dimensions change differently as temperature varies. This variability directly affects how a fit behaves across temperatures.
source_quote: it can be anything from wood/plastic/steel or bronze or whatever with very different expansion/retraction coefficients depending on temperature.

subject: service-condition fit testing
main_point: Test the fit under realistic service conditions, not just at standard lab conditions. A part that measures perfectly at around 1 atm and 20 C can still fail in its actual operating environment.
source_quote: The simplest answer is already given test...you can manufacture it to perfection at 1 atm air pressure and 20 Celsius just to fail where it should be used...
example_value: A fit verified at 1 atm and 20 C may not hold in the intended use environment.

subject: over-constrained boundary conditions near contact edges
main_point: Over-constraining a model or imposing uniform radial stiffness at the contact edges can skew the local contact response. Review and relax boundary conditions near edges to avoid artificial stiffness and edge artifacts.
source_quote: from the proximity it seems that you might be over constrained or at least to have uniform radial stiffness near the edges.
example_context: ANSYS structural contact analyses (e.g., interference fit models) where edge constraints influence contact pressures/displacements

subject: Normal-Projected Normal contact setting
main_point: Enable the Normal-Projected Normal contact option to potentially improve contact behavior and result smoothness. This setting adjusts how contact normals are treated to reduce artifacts.
source_quote:
Another option for might be to turn on the 
Normal-Projected Normal
 option
example_context: ANSYS Workbench contact settings for interference/contact simulations

subject: contact formulation selection for smoothing results
main_point: Experiment with different contact formulations to improve the smoothness of contact pressure/displacement results. A single default formulation may not yield the best behavior for a given model.
source_quote: To get smooth results you need to try out different contact formulations also,
example_context: ANSYS contact analyses where formulation choice (e.g., penalty, augmented Lagrange) affects result smoothness

subject: limits of smoothness in contact pressure results
main_point: Perfectly smooth contact pressure distributions are unrealistic; expect some spatial variation. A practical best-case is on the order of about 10% deviation from the average pressure.
source_quote: in my experience you will never get 100% smooth. The best I have ever achieved is pressure results within 10% of the average.
example_context: ANSYS contact/interference fit simulations assessing contact pressure smoothness

subject: contact interface mesh conformity
main_point: When meshing a contact interface, align the element divisions on both mating edges so their meshes are similar, ideally matching the number of divisions along the line.
source_quote: Try to make meshes at the interface similar (number of divisions along the line).
example_context: finite element contact interfaces (e.g., interference fits)

subject: using virtual cells to merge split lines for meshing
main_point: If a contact edge is segmented, merge the segments into a single line using virtual cells so you can apply consistent mesh divisions along the interface.
source_quote: If the line is split into multiple, you can combine into one using virtual cells.
example_context: ANSYS Workbench meshing (virtual cells feature)

subject: transition fit vs clearance fit consistency
main_point: Compared with loose clearance fits, transition fits yield tighter positional consistency of assembled parts, improving overall product consistency.
source_quote: A transition fit actually makes the end product more consistent than the clearance fit.

subject: transition fit assembly method
main_point: When a transition fit results in slight interference, assembly can typically be done with a mallet rather than requiring a press or thermal shrink, simplifying installation.
source_quote: Also, if interference occurs, we don't need to used press fit or temperature based shrink fit. We can simply use mallet for transition fit.

subject: transition fit selection for high-accuracy components
main_point: Designers should prefer transition fits for high-accuracy components to achieve precise location without resorting to full interference or loose clearance.
source_quote: This makes transition fit a preferable choice in case of the higher quality grade equipment such as Gears (cycloidal), Hubs, driven bushes where more accuracy is needed.
example_value: Cited applications include cycloidal gears, hubs, and driven bushes that demand higher accuracy.
example_context: high-accuracy components such as cycloidal gears, hubs, and driven bushes

subject: transition fit for accurate location
main_point: Transition fits are primarily chosen to accurately locate mating parts, providing a compromise between clearance and interference behaviors.
source_quote: Transition fit is mostly used for accurate location, a compromise between clearance and interference.

subject: clearance fit-induced vibration in cycloidal gears
main_point: Using a clearance fit on cycloidal gear/shaft interfaces can reduce location accuracy and lead to increased vibration.
source_quote: Here, a clearance fit my cause less accuracy resulting in more vibrations in cycloidal gears.
example_value: Two cycloidal gears that require exact center distance between shafts experience vibration when a clearance fit reduces accuracy.
example_context: cycloidal gear pairs requiring exact center distance

subject: interference fit serviceability risk
main_point: Interference fits on gear–shaft assemblies can make replacement difficult and risk damaging the shaft during removal.
source_quote: While the interference fit my cause the replacement of the gear difficult as shaft can be damaged while replacing the gear.
example_value: In the cycloidal gear example, an interference fit complicates replacement and may damage the shaft during disassembly.
example_context: gear mounted on shaft with interference fit (e.g., cycloidal gear application)

subject: selective assembly via size sorting
main_point: In high-volume production of mating parts, you can sort components by measured size and selectively pair them to achieve very tight fits even if each part was made to relatively loose (cheaper) tolerances. This practice can justify specifying a transition fit, relying on post-process binning to control the assembled clearance/interference.
source_quote: use sorting machines to sort the parts (small, medium, large, etc.) to get really tight fits between parts that were made with loose tolerances (i.e. cheap)?
example_value: Examples mentioned include 2-liter bottle caps and flat-pack furniture parts assembled by customers.
example_context: High-volume consumer products with many mating parts where automated sizing/sorting equipment is available.

subject: clearance fit retention under vibration
main_point: In the presence of vibration, a push-fit/clearance that is too loose risks the component working its way out over time. Ensure sufficient interference or a retention method when vibration is expected.
source_quote: There isn't much load on the plunger or part, but there is vibration that could make the plunger work its way out if it is too loose.
example_value: The designer notes minimal load but vibration on a 3 mm plunger and worries that a loose hand-fit could let it work out.

subject: clearance hole diameter for pass-through bolts
main_point: For a bolted joint where the screw passes through a part, the specified dimension is the clearance hole diameter—the hole size that allows the screw shank to pass through freely.
source_quote: IF I understand your question correctly what you are looking for is the clearance hole diameter. I.e. how big to make the hole to be able to let an M3 bolt to pass through.
example_value: The post refers to an M3 bolt passing through a part as the case in question.

subject: M3 clearance hole diameter range
main_point: Standard tables give M3 clearance holes in the range of about 3.2 to 3.9 mm, with the exact size chosen based on the desired clearance fit.
source_quote:
you can find a lot of tables like the following in the internet, where you can see that the clearance hole is between 3.2 and 3.9 mm 
depending on the fit
 that want to have.
example_context: Metric M3 screws; selection based on desired clearance (fit class).

subject: press-fit assembly deformation
main_point: Assembling a press/snap-fit coupling inherently requires temporary deformation of at least one of the mating parts. This elastic deformation enables the interference engagement during mounting.
source_quote: During mounting of the coupling, the parts will have to deform.

subject: slotted female component for assembly compliance
main_point: Introduce slots in the female component to increase compliance so the press-fit can be mounted more easily and with less risk of damage. Added flexibility reduces assembly force for interference joints.
source_quote: If you make slots in the female part, this will be easier.

subject: thermal expansion effect on reamed hole size (cooled workpiece)
main_point: Reaming a hole while the workpiece is cold (with a room‑temperature reamer) will yield a final hole that ends up larger at room temperature, because the material expands as it warms after machining.
source_quote: If you cool the workpiece and the reamer is at "normal" temperature then your final hole will be larger.

subject: heating workpiece before reaming reduces final hole size after cooling
main_point: If the workpiece is heated before reaming, the final hole will measure smaller once the part cools to room temperature due to thermal contraction.
source_quote: So if you heat the workpiece and it cools down after reaming then the final hole will be smaller...

subject: bearing OD measurement prior to reamer selection
main_point: Measure or otherwise verify the actual bearing outside diameter before selecting a reamer to achieve the intended fit.
source_quote: You need to know the size of the bearing before purchasing the correct reamer.

subject: thermal assembly without a press (heating housing and freezing insert)
main_point: Lacking a press, heating the cylinder head to roughly 200°C and freezing the valve guides allowed them to slide in easily due to differential thermal expansion.
source_quote: I fitted new valve guides into a cylinder head once - not having a press I heated the cylinder head to about 200 deg C and put the guides in the freezer. They slid in a treat...
example_value: Valve guides were installed into a cylinder head by heating the head and freezing the guides, eliminating the need for a press.
example_context: Installing valve guides in a cylinder head without a press, using heat (~200°C) on the head and freezing the guides.

subject: trial reaming on scrap to verify bearing fit
main_point: Prototype the operation on scrap: ream a test hole to the target size and trial-fit the bearing before machining the actual part. This lets you confirm the fit and adjust your approach without risking the real workpiece.
source_quote: I think your best bet, since you're not sure would be to get a scrap piece of stock and ream the 24mm hole and see if the bearing fits.
example_value: Ream a 24 mm hole in scrap and check if the 24 mm OD bearing fits.

subject: equal nominal sizes yield no clearance fit
main_point: A bearing with the same nominal OD as the hole diameter will not provide a clearance; it typically will not go in. Equal nominal dimensions do not produce a slip fit.
source_quote: If the bearing is 24mm it won't fit

subject: easing a tight bore with emery cloth on a lathe
main_point: If the reamed hole is slightly too tight for the bearing, you can lightly polish and open it using emery cloth on the lathe. This provides a controlled way to ease the fit without re-cutting.
source_quote: but you can emery the hole, easy to do on a lathe.

subject: temperature-controlled reaming
main_point: If you try to control hole size by chilling or heating during reaming, you must keep the entire workpiece at that temperature throughout the cut and account for heat added by the reamer. This requirement imposes a significant limitation on using temperature to achieve size while machining.
source_quote: and maintain the complete piece of metal at that temperature for the whole time it takes to ream the hole - and allowing for the heat generated by the reamer itself, of course.
example_context: Reaming an aluminum part on a lathe while attempting to use thermal expansion/contraction to hit size

subject: aluminum thermal expansion affecting hole size
main_point: A diameter change of about 0.01 mm on a 24 mm aluminum feature requires approximately a 20°C temperature change due to thermal expansion.
source_quote: To change the diameter of a 24mm in aluminum by 0.01mm, you need to change the temperature by about 20 degrees C,
example_context: Aluminum workpiece with a 24 mm diameter hole or boss

subject: reamer size selection for target hole diameter
main_point: To achieve a specific hole size (e.g., 23.99 mm), select and use a reamer ground to that exact size rather than relying on thermal tricks or undersizing methods.
source_quote: If you want to make a 23.99mm diameter hole, just use the correct size reamer to do the job. Problem solved!

subject: boring vs reaming for hole sizing
main_point: For sizing holes to a specific diameter, you can use a single-point boring bar on a lathe or a boring head on a mill instead of a reamer. This approach lets you bring the hole to size without relying on a fixed-size reamer.
source_quote: If you are using a lathe, you can use a single point boring bar/tool instead of a reamer to bore the hole to the size. If on a milling machine, you can also just use a boring head/tool.

subject: reaming for speed on multiple holes
main_point: When producing many holes under time pressure, choose a reamer because it is the faster method for reaching size across multiple parts or features.
source_quote: If you have to make multiple holes and time is of the essence, then, go with a reamer.

subject: self-clinch nut installation embedment
main_point: For self-clinching nuts that have a spiked outer diameter, correct installation requires the spiked diameter to be fully embedded in the parent material; visible spikes indicate improper installation.
source_quote: the 'spiked' diameter should be fully embedded in the bulk material.
example_context: self-clinching nuts (e.g., TR Fastenings 'Self Clinch Non-Locking Mini Squeezed Nut')

subject: press-fit or captive nuts
main_point: The fasteners in question are known as press-fit (also called captive) nuts, which is the correct terminology for identifying this hardware type.
source_quote: Those are "press fit" or "captive" nuts.

subject: sourcing press-fit/captive nuts from McMaster-Carr
main_point: McMaster-Carr is a likely source for purchasing press-fit/captive nuts, so checking their catalog is a practical way to obtain replacements.
source_quote: Mcmaster Carr should have whatever your looking for.
example_context: Sourcing standard fasteners from McMaster-Carr

subject: test coupons for laser-cut holes
main_point: When targeting a specific fit in laser-cut acrylic, make test coupons with varied hole sizes and cut profiles and verify them using pin gauges or the actual shaft. This lets you dial in process settings to achieve the desired interference more reliably than relying on nominal dimensions.
source_quote: If your project allows for creating test pieces, consider to use a variety of hole sizes and cutting profiles, testing your holes with pin gauges or with the shaft to determine correct settings.
example_value: Prepare multiple holes of different diameters and profiles and check each with pin gauges or the 5 mm shaft to find the correct settings.
example_context: laser-cut holes in ~5 mm acrylic (PMMA) for interference fit

subject: cast vs extruded acrylic behavior
main_point: Cast and extruded acrylic do not behave the same, so cutting and fit outcomes can differ depending on which type is used. Material form should be considered when planning hole sizing and interference fits.
source_quote: Cast acrylic behaves differently from extruded acrylic.
example_context: PMMA (acrylic): cast vs extruded sheet

subject: laser power vs travel speed impact
main_point: Laser power influences allowable cutting speed, and those speed differences alter hole characteristics. Expect different hole quality and dimensions when cutting with higher- versus lower-power lasers.
source_quote: High power lasers are able to use higher travel speeds than lower powered lasers, changing the characteristics of the hole.
example_context: laser cutting acrylic or similar plastics

subject: laser slowdown on curves/corners
main_point: Controllers reduce feed on circular and curved paths (and at sharp corners), which alters the cut profile and surface finish. Small circular holes are therefore prone to speed-induced variation affecting fit.
source_quote: Laser cutters typically slow for circles and curves and especially for right angle corner cuts. This changes the profile of the cut and the surface rendered by such a cut.
example_context: laser cutter motion control during curves/circles

subject: kerf compensation for inside dimensions
main_point: You can tune kerf compensation in the laser software to tighten inside dimensions, but running test cuts is often the simpler path to hit the target fit. Favor empirical test pieces over relying solely on kerf settings.
source_quote: Kerf settings in the software that create the laser job can be adjusted to provide more precision for inside dimensions, but I suspect the tests would give you simpler results.
example_context: laser job/CAM software for laser cutters

subject: beam divergence in thick stock
main_point: When cutting thick acrylic with a low-power laser, the beam can diverge near the bottom surface, producing a tapered/non-cylindrical hole. This geometric deviation can compromise interference-fit assumptions based on a nominal cylindrical hole.
source_quote: With such a thick material, a low power laser may have some divergence as it nears the lower edge of the material and may create a non-cylindrical hole.
example_context: low-power CO2 laser cutting ~5 mm acrylic sheet

subject: laser cutting tolerances and surface finish
main_point: When producing holes for an interference fit, laser cutting often lacks the tolerance and surface finish needed, leading to unreliable fits or assembly issues.
source_quote: laser cutting may well not provide good enough tolerances or surface finish to reliably produce the fit you need
example_context: laser cutting holes in acrylic (PMMA) for an interference fit

subject: drilling after laser pilot marking
main_point: Use the laser only to mark or pilot, then drill to final size to achieve the precision and finish required for a reliable fit.
source_quote: you woudl probably be better off drilling the holes, possibly using the laser to create a reference mark or pilot hole.
example_context: fabricating precise holes in acrylic sheets when both laser cutting and drilling are available

subject: acrylic/polycarbonate interference fit cracking
main_point: Interference fits in polycarbonate or acrylic generate stresses that often lead to cracking, with risk heightened if hole edges are not polished and chamfered; clearance is generally preferred.
source_quote: Secondly poly-carbonate and acrylic don't really like this sort of interference fit and the advice is generally to give holes decent clearance as the stresses involved tend to cause cracks, especially if the holes aren't polished and chamfered.
example_context: interference-fitting shafts into polycarbonate or acrylic (PMMA) components

subject: adhesive with clearance hole for shaft retention
main_point: Instead of an interference fit in acrylic, drill a clearance hole and bond the shaft with adhesive to secure it without inducing stress cracks.
source_quote: You would probably be better off drilling a hole with adequate clearance and using an adhesive to secure the shaft.
example_context: assembling a metal shaft into acrylic or polycarbonate parts

subject: 2020 extrusion slot profile variation
main_point: Within the 2020 aluminum extrusion category, slot profiles can differ significantly between variants or suppliers, so interchangeability of hardware (like T-slot nuts) should not be assumed solely from the "2020" designation.
source_quote: Again, the profile of the slot varies considerably.
example_value: The OP found multiple 2020 profiles online whose slot shapes differed markedly from each other.
example_context: 2020 aluminum extrusions from different suppliers

subject: M5 nut compatibility with a specific 2020 extrusion profile
main_point: For the specific 2020 extrusion profile the OP sourced in Bangkok, standard T-slot nuts do not fit; only regular M5 hex nuts are compatible with the slot.
source_quote: As ericnutsch states, in his answer, only regular hexagonal M5 nuts will fit.
example_value: The OP’s Bangkok-sourced 2020 extrusion accepted regular hex M5 nuts but not T-slot nuts.
example_context: A particular 2020 aluminum extrusion profile available in Bangkok for a Wilson II 3D printer build

subject: T-slot nut compatibility with OpenBuilds V-Slot 2020 extrusions
main_point: Generic T-nut hardware sourced from AliExpress has been found to fit and function with OpenBuilds V‑Slot 2020 extrusions. This suggests common T-nuts are compatible with that 2020 profile in practice.
source_quote:
I use 
openbuilds v-slot
 on a lot of my projects (its 2020 designed for perpendicular v rollers) and all the 
aliexpress t-nut hardware
 I have bought works fine.
example_value: Author reports using OpenBuilds V‑Slot 2020 extrusions with multiple AliExpress T‑nuts without issues.
example_context: OpenBuilds V‑Slot 2020 aluminum extrusions using generic AliExpress T‑nuts

subject: Using regular nuts as substitutes for T-nuts in aluminum extrusion slots
main_point: If matching T‑slot nuts aren’t available for a given aluminum extrusion, standard hex nuts can be used in the slot as a functional substitute. They are less convenient to use but will still work.
source_quote: Worst case, you can use regular nuts with the aluminum rail you have access to; they are not as convenient but will work fine.
example_value: In absence of compatible T‑nuts for an aluminum rail profile, the author recommends inserting regular nuts in the slot.
example_context: Aluminum T-slot extrusion systems (e.g., 2020 profiles) when proper T-nuts are unavailable

subject: shrink fitting interference requirement
main_point: Shrink fitting works by designing the shaft and collar to have a cold-state interference fit; heating/cooling is used only to temporarily ease assembly, not to make up for an undersized interference.
source_quote: Shrink fitting depend on the fact that you have a shaft and collar which are sized to an interference fit when cold.

subject: aluminum heating window before anneal/melt
main_point: When heating aluminum for a thermal fit, the allowable temperature range is narrow; overheating risks annealing the part and, with further heat, melting it.
source_quote: One problem with aluminium is that you have a fairly narrow window for heating it before it first anneals and then melts.

subject: aluminum thermal expansion at ~200C
main_point: Heating aluminum to around 200 C typically produces only a few thousandths of an inch diameter growth, which is often insufficient to overcome sizable clearance or interference gaps.
source_quote: A rough calculation  suggests that that change in diameter with heating to 200C is in the order of thousandths of an inch which is somewhat less that the tolerance of your part (although this is back of the envelope stuff so I may be wrong but is suspect that its not too far out).
example_value: The author estimates that at ~200 C the thermal expansion is only on the order of thousandths, less than the clearance needed for the OP’s fit.
example_context: aluminum parts heated to approximately 200 C for attempted shrink fit assembly

subject: adhesive bonding for mounting knobs on shafts
main_point: For attaching a knob to a shaft, using an epoxy or bearing-retaining adhesive is a preferable, strong, and more convenient solution than attempting a heat/shrink fit.
source_quote:
In any case I think that for a knob you will be much better off using an adhesive,  epoxy or a 
bearing retaining adhesive
 should be plenty strong enough and a lot more convenient.
example_context: attaching a knob onto a small shaft where mechanical expansion/shrink fitting is impractical

subject: aluminum thermal expansion limits for interference-fit sizing
main_point: Relying on thermal expansion to grow an aluminum spacer’s ID by about 8.7% is not feasible: it would require a temperature rise on the order of 4000 °C, so the part would melt before reaching the needed expansion.
source_quote:
the thermal expansion coefficient of aluminum is ~ 22 10^-6/C, so to expand that much you need to heat to

0.087/(22 10^-6) or ~4000C

ie You will melt the aluminum long before it expands that much.
example_value: Expanding a 0.115 in ID to 0.125 in requires 0.087 strain; with aluminum’s ~22×10^-6/°C CTE, ΔT ≈ 0.087 / 22e−6 ≈ 4000 °C.
example_context: Aluminum components (CTE ~22×10^-6/°C) such as an unthreaded spacer being heated to fit a 0.125 in shaft

subject: using tolerance spread to achieve fit without machining
main_point: If the specified ID tolerance range includes your target size, buying multiple parts can yield one at the high end that fits without modification.
source_quote: Note the drawing tolerance is -0/+0.01, so maybe buy a bunch and you will get lucky :-)
example_value: A nominal 0.115 in ID with a -0/+0.01 tolerance could be as large as 0.125 in, potentially fitting a 1/8 in (0.125 in) shaft.
example_context: McMaster-Carr 92510A422 aluminum spacer with nominal 0.115 in ID and -0/+0.01 in tolerance

subject: using a split tube (slotted sleeve) as an adapter
main_point: Use a split tube (slotted sleeve) as an alternative adapter to bridge the size difference instead of attempting a heat-fit expansion.
source_quote: Hunt around for a split tube..

subject: gear tooth profile scaling
main_point: For meshing gears, tooth size and profile must remain constant regardless of gear diameter; simply scaling a complete gear model to change diameter alters the tooth geometry and will not mesh correctly.
source_quote: It is important to remember that, when you design a set of meshing gears you need to keep the size and shape of the teeth the same, irrespective of the diameter. There is a temptation to design a gear template and simply scale the whole thing to get the diameter you want but this does not work.

subject: integer tooth count constraint on gear diameter
main_point: For a given gear design (fixed tooth size/profile), allowable gear diameters are quantized by integer tooth counts; you cannot choose a diameter that implies a non-integer number of teeth.
source_quote: One implication of this is that for any particular design the range of available diameters available to you is limited by the need to have an integer number of teeth. For example if you start with a gear with diameter D=10 and N = 10 teeth then if you are locked into that ratio so you can't have a  diameter of 20.5 as that would imply 20.5 teeth and you can't have half a tooth.
example_value: Starting from D=10 with N=10, a diameter of 20.5 would imply 20.5 teeth, which is impossible.

subject: gear module
main_point: Using the gear module concept is a common way to simplify the gear design process.
source_quote:
The concept of 
module
 is widely used to simplify this design process

subject: diametral pitch matching for gear meshing
main_point: Two gears must have the same diametral pitch to mesh; if their diametral pitches differ, the teeth will not engage properly and the gears will not mesh.
source_quote: Gears will only mesh together when they both share the same Diametral Pitch.

subject: slip fit clearance starting value
main_point: A clearance around 0.010 inch is a reasonable starting point for a slip fit, though tighter clearances may still function depending on the application.
source_quote: 0.01" is probably a decent place to start as a slip fit, though you can certainly go tighter.
example_context: general slip-fit assemblies intended for easy hand assembly/disassembly

subject: fit choice for telescoping sections that must stay extended
main_point: If a telescoping assembly needs to stay extended on its own, a pure slip fit is inadequate; design in controlled friction so it holds position yet can be moved by hand.
source_quote: You say it's for an antenna, and if you want it to extend and stay extended on its own like other collapsible antennae, a slip fit probably won't accomplish that. You'll need something that creates some friction but not so much that it can't be overcome by a person pulling on it.
example_context: telescoping antenna sections that must remain extended without external latches

subject: importance of tolerances vs nominal dimensions
main_point: Specifying appropriate tolerances is more critical than nominal sizes, because as-built parts will not exactly match nominal dimensions, particularly at thousandth-inch resolution.
source_quote: In any case, what's potentially more important than the actual dimension is the tolerance. Those nominal dimensions will not be what you actually get, especially when you call out things down to the thousandth of an inch.

subject: slip fit tolerance scheme (equal nominals with OD + tol and ID - tol)
main_point: To control a slip fit’s maximum clearance, set equal nominal diameters for mating parts, then apply a + tolerance to the OD and a − tolerance to the ID; with ±0.005 inch on each side, the clearance will be at most 0.010 inch.
source_quote: For a slip fit, how I would actually dimension it is to make the nominal dimensions the same for the inner and outer, and then create a plus tolerance (e.g. +0.005"/-0) on the OD and a minus tolerance on the ID. Using 5 thousandths on each end will get you a 10 thousandths slip at most.
example_value: +0.005 inch on OD and −0.005 inch on ID yields at most 0.010 inch clearance

subject: achievable tolerance by good machine shops
main_point: A total tolerance band of about 0.005 inch is generally achievable for a good machine shop, but material behavior—especially plastics like Delrin—may affect how readily it can be held.
source_quote: 0.005" isn't that tough for a good machine shop, though I'm not sure how workable that plastic is, I'm more used to dealing with steels and cast irons.
example_context: general-purpose shops machining steels and cast irons; plastics may be more variable

subject: difficulty of making non-standard holes vs shafts
main_point: In typical machining practice, producing a non-standard diameter is generally more difficult for holes than for shafts, implying it is often easier to vary a shaft diameter than a hole diameter.
source_quote: I've heard that it is typically harder to make non-standard holes than non-standard shafts
example_value: The designer needs one plate to have an interference fit and another a clearance fit on the same pin, with diameter differences of only tens of microns.
example_context: General metalworking of steel pins and plate holes with tight fit differences on the order of tens of microns.

subject: interference fit member stiffness
main_point: In designing an interference fit, it is generally preferable for the shaft to be significantly stiffer than the plate (hole member) so the joint maintains a reliable interference. Greater shaft stiffness helps ensure the hole deforms to grip rather than the shaft yielding.
source_quote: Normally for an interference fit, you'd the shaft to be a lot stiffer than the plate in which the hole is, to ensure a good interference.

subject: reaming holes vs turning shafts for fine fit control
main_point: When the required difference between fits is very small, achieving tolerance by drilling/reaming the hole is typically easier and more reliable than turning a stepped shaft, making a hole-basis preferable even if it requires a special reamer.
source_quote: Having said that, and given that the difference in diameter is very small (0.01-0.02m), I would have thought that it easier/more reliable to drill/ream a hole in a plate of the right size with the right tolerance, than to turn down a shaft to the right diameter, even if this means buying a specialised reamer. So my vote is for the hole-based system.
example_value: The author prefers drilling/reaming to size rather than turning a shaft step, and would buy a specialised reamer to do so.
example_context: Very small fit differences (on the order of a few tens of microns) where a clearance and an interference fit must be achieved on the same nominal pin across different plates.

subject: availability of standard H7 reamers limits hole size options
main_point: If you do not make custom tooling, you are constrained to standard reamer sizes for holes; common H7 sizes like 8 mm are readily available, while odd sizes like 7.38 mm H7 are not off-the-shelf. This imposes a practical limit on achieving specific fits by varying hole size.
source_quote: If you are not going to fabricate special tools for your project, you will be limited to standard hole sizes - meaning you will easily find a 8 mm H7 reamer but would never find a 7.38 mm H7 reamer on the shelves.
example_value: Readily available: 8 mm H7 reamer; Not available on the shelf: 7.38 mm H7 reamer.
example_context: common workshops without custom hole-making tools (standard H6/H7 reamer availability)

subject: standard lathe accuracy across a range of shaft diameters
main_point: A standard lathe can hold tight tolerances across many shaft diameters, providing the same precision at both standard and nonstandard sizes within its capacity. This makes varying shaft diameter a flexible way to achieve different fits.
source_quote: The manufacturing capability of a standard lath machine (turning machine) should provide you a greater flexibility, since it offers a great accuracy for a wide range of shaft sizes.
example_value: Example given: if the machine holds +/- 0.001 mm up to 15 mm diameter, it can achieve the same accuracy on 8 mm and 7.38 mm shafts.
example_context: standard engine/turning lathes within their specified diameter/tolerance capability

subject: sliding/transition fit selection for shaft–hub
main_point: For a motor shaft–hub connection, target a sliding or transition fit rather than a loose clearance to ensure proper engagement without play.
source_quote: You probably want a sliding fit or transition.
example_context: Motor shaft to hub coupling

subject: acceptable clearance magnitude for shaft–hub fit
main_point: A 0.2 mm clearance between a motor shaft and hub is excessively loose for this application; a much tighter fit is required.
source_quote: 0.2mm clearance is far too much
example_context: Motor shaft to hub coupling

subject: H7/g6 fit recommendation and clearance range
main_point: An H7/g6 fit is appropriate for a shaft–hub connection, yielding a hole 0.005–0.029 mm larger than the shaft to achieve a controlled sliding/transition fit.
source_quote: H7g6 sounds about right, hole is 0.005-0.029 mm bigger than the shaft.
example_context: Motor shaft to hub coupling using ISO fits

subject: tool selection for tight hole tolerances
main_point: To achieve the tight tolerance required for a sliding/transition fit hole, use a reamer or a D-bit rather than relying on a drilled finish.
source_quote: You'll need to use a reamer or a D bit.
example_context: Producing precise holes for H7/g6 sliding/transition fits

subject: sliding fit looseness and jamming tendency
main_point: Looser clearances in sliding mechanisms tend to increase the likelihood of jamming compared to tighter clearances. In practice, sliding components with more play are more prone to bind or cock during motion.
source_quote: A loose drawer or loose sliding parts in general jam more easily than ones with tighter clearance.
example_context: mechanical sliding components such as drawers and loose sliding parts

subject: minimum clearance calculation for shaft–hole fits
main_point: Minimum clearance in a toleranced shaft–hole fit is found by subtracting the largest permissible shaft diameter from the smallest permissible hole diameter; this value may be negative, indicating interference. In other words, use the worst-case extremes (max shaft, min hole) to compute minimum clearance.
source_quote: The minimum clearance occurs when the largest possible shaft meets the smallest possible hole.
example_value: Example: a 50.02 mm shaft in a 50.00 mm hole gives a clearance of -0.02 mm.

subject: bottom clearance for threaded holes
main_point: Provide a relief at the bottom of a blind threaded hole or reduce the specified full-thread depth to allow tool clearance. Without it, you risk ending up with less thread length than specified or causing tool drag/breakage at the hole bottom.
source_quote: You need clearance at the bottom of the threaded hole or shorten the depth of the thread. This is to allow for the machining process and clearance for the cutting tool. Otherwise your thread will not be a long as you specified(because the machinist needed clearance, or the machinist will break a tool or drag the tool at the bottom of the hole if they are not careful.

subject: clearance amount rule-of-thumb under threads
main_point: A practical rule of thumb is to allow a bottom clearance about two thread pitches to safely accommodate the threading tool.
source_quote: If I interpret your picture correctly, then I think 4mm(equal to 2 x thread pitch) would be sufficient/safe.
example_value: For M55 x 2.0, 4 mm clearance (2 × 2.0 mm) was suggested as sufficient/safe.
example_context: M55 x 2.0 milled thread per the OP’s pictured geometry

subject: clearance dependence on threading tool choice
main_point: Consult the shop about the specific threading tool (single-point vs. thread mill), since the required bottom clearance depends on the tool they will use.
source_quote: Ultimately, talk to the machine shop and ask what tool will be used to cut the thread. A single point tool or a thread-mill? That will show you how much clearance below the thread you need.
example_context: Thread cutting with either a single-point tool or a thread mill

subject: single-point thread mill bottom clearance requirement
main_point: A single-point thread mill’s geometry necessitates extra space at the bottom of a blind hole so the cutter can clear during exit, so a relief below the last thread is required.
source_quote: See below what a single point thread mill looks like and you will see how the tool requires clearance at the bottom due to geometry of the tool
example_context: Single-point thread milling tools

subject: manual tubing cutter performance on thin-wall stainless tubing
main_point: A manual tubing cutter produced burr-free results reliably over more than 200 cuts, but required about 60 seconds per cut. This reflects a slow yet consistent option for cutting thin-wall stainless tubing.
source_quote: The cutter has been reliable for 200+ cuts, has no bur, and takes approximately 60 seconds per cut when working quickly.
example_value: 200+ cuts; ~60 seconds per cut; burr-free results
example_context: Ridgid manual tubing cutter on 3/8 inch and 1/2 inch 316 stainless steel tubing with 0.035 inch wall

subject: cordless copper tubing cutter used on stainless steel
main_point: A cordless copper tubing cutter can cut stainless quickly (about 20 seconds per cut) but shows wear and declining cut quality after roughly 50 cuts, and it is limited to 1/2 inch capacity.
source_quote: It is showing some wear and cut quality issues at 50+ cuts. It takes about 20 seconds per cut and it only works for 1/2" tubing.
example_value: 50+ cuts before wear/quality issues; ~20 seconds per cut; 1/2 inch capacity
example_context: Milwaukee M12 cordless copper tubing cutter used on 1/2 inch 316 stainless steel tubing, 0.035 inch wall

subject: bandsaw blade wear with thin-wall tubing
main_point: Very thin-wall tubing is a challenging application for bandsaw blades, tending to be hard on the teeth and accelerating wear or damage.
source_quote: very thin wall tubing is hard on bandsaw blade teeth.

subject: stacking thin-wall tubes for bandsaw cutting
main_point: Stacking thin-wall tubes to distribute tooth load during bandsaw cutting can still lead to significant chatter. The load-sharing benefit does not eliminate vibrational instability in this setup.
source_quote: Cutting the tubes in stacks may help distribute the tooth load but would probably still have lots of chatter.
example_context: Bandsaw cutting of thin-wall tubing bundled or stacked to share tooth load

subject: plasma cutting thin stainless edges
main_point: For thin stainless, use a plasma cutter with a fixture that rotates the workpiece during the cut; it yields a smooth, glassy, burr‑free edge that requires no finish sanding.
source_quote: I would recommend a plasma cutter and a fixture that rotates the workpiece as the cut occurs. When cutting thin stainless (like a metal sink for example) the plasma cutter produces a completely smooth, glassy edge with no burrs and no need for finish sanding.
example_value: Example given: thin stainless like a metal sink.
example_context: thin stainless steel

subject: abrasive air-jet machining suitability vs work-hardening materials
main_point: Consider abrasive machining that uses compressed air to propel fine grit at the kerf; it performs especially well on materials that do not work‑harden.
source_quote: You might also try abrasive machining, where a jet of compressed air propels fine abrasive grit at the cut kerf. This works extremely well for materials that do not work-harden.
example_context: materials that do not work-harden

subject: enclosure punctures and water resistance
main_point: To preserve water resistance, avoid creating new holes or penetrations in the enclosure; non-penetrating mounting methods are preferable.
source_quote: The easiest way to maintain water resistance is to not puncture the enclosure.

subject: using built-in mounting holes
main_point: When an enclosure includes dedicated through-holes for mounting, prefer using those features rather than adding new penetrations to maintain enclosure integrity.
source_quote: It looks like the box has holes extending through the cover down to the bottom, I'm guessing these are specifically for mounting? (The 2 large holes). Use those if you can.
example_value: The box appears to have two large holes running from the cover to the bottom intended for mounting; use them.
example_context: enclosures that provide purpose-built through-hole mounting features

subject: mounting with bottom against plate and outside-in screws
main_point: If you can’t use through-cover mounting, position the enclosure with its bottom against the plate and drive screws from outside into the existing top-to-bottom holes to mount without making new holes.
source_quote: The next best option would be to attach the box so that the bottom is against the plate, and screws come in from the outside into the screw holes that extend from the top of the box to the bottom.
example_value: Screws inserted from the outside engage holes that run from the top of the box to the bottom while the bottom sits against the plate.
example_context: enclosures that have continuous holes from top to bottom suitable for external screw insertion

subject: internal mounting with sealing screws and flat sealing surface
main_point: For internal screw mounting of a sealed enclosure, locate holes where the interior surface is flat and use sealing screws to maintain a watertight seal.
source_quote: Another option is to attach the plate with screws from the inside. Place the holes so the inner surface around the hole is flat, and then use sealing screws.
example_value: Screws are installed from inside; holes are placed on flat interior regions and sealed with sealing screws.
example_context: water-resistant enclosures mounted with screws from the inside where sealing is required

subject: angle bracket mounting with downward-facing screw holes
main_point: Using angle brackets to orient screw holes downward can reduce water ingress; while not fully waterproof, this orientation sheds water and improves resistance to rain or splashes.
source_quote: Depending on how water proof you need the box to be, it might also be viable to just mount the box using angle brackets so the screw holes are facing the ground. Although not fully waterproof, water would be unlikely to get in that way.
example_value: Mount the box on angle brackets so the screw holes face the ground to limit water entry.
example_context: enclosures in wet or outdoor environments where partial water resistance (not full waterproofing) is acceptable

subject: Inventor chamfer tool parameterization
main_point: In Autodesk Inventor LT 2021, the chamfer feature only accepts two fixed distances or one fixed distance plus an angle measured from a selected face, which constrains how a chamfer can be defined.
source_quote: The tool requires either fixed distance on both faces or a fixed distance on one face and an angle from that face.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor LT 2021 chamfer tool

subject: variable rim width on angled pipe cut
main_point: When a pipe is cut at an angle, the resulting rim face around the opening does not have constant width; it varies around the circumference due to the angled intersection.
source_quote: The problem is the width of the top face varies ever so slightly due to the angled cut through the piped.

subject: revolve operation limitation for noncircular paths
main_point: A revolve feature cannot create geometry that follows a non-circular path; it requires rotational geometry about an axis, so it is unsuitable for features that do not have circular symmetry.
source_quote: I initially was going to revolve it, but that does not work as the path it need to follow is not circular.

subject: helix vs angled pipe cut path mismatch
main_point: A helical (coil) path does not match the geometry of a pipe cut at an angle, so using a helix cut will not reproduce the angled cut’s edge path.
source_quote: I just forgot, I also tried a helix (coil) cut, but the path of the helix is not the same as the angled cut through the pipe.

subject: sweep profile twist along path
main_point: When sweeping a profile along an edge/path, the profile can rotate (twist) relative to its original orientation as it follows the path, affecting the resulting cut.
source_quote: It was as if the triangle did not remain in its original horizontal position but got twist as it followed the path.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor LT 2021 sweep along part edge

subject: blended-surface method to model a constant-angle chamfer on an angled pipe
main_point: To model a constant-angle chamfer on an angled pipe end, create a surface by blending between two guide lines set at the target angle and use the pipe’s end edge as the blend path; then use that surface to cut the solid or extrude it and subtract.
source_quote: Cut with a surface which is a blend between 2 lines which both are tilted 15 degrees from the horizontal. The edge of the pipe end is the blending path. Or instead of cutting extrude the blending result and subtract.
example_value: Guide lines set to 15 degrees relative to horizontal.
example_context: CAD surface-modeling workflow when a standard chamfer feature cannot maintain a fixed angle on an angled pipe end.

subject: accuracy limitations of two-line surface blend for constant-angle chamfer
main_point: A simple two-line surface blend does not yield an exact, uniformly angled chamfer; keeping error under about 1 degree requires adding more intermediate guide lines, and even then the result may not be exact in some CAD programs.
source_quote: Cutting the pipe and measuring revealed that more intermediate lines are needed for less than 1 degree error. To make the error smaller one can insert intermediate lines as many as he likes, but this blending idea doesn't lead to an exact result, not at least in this program.
example_value: Error less than 1 degree required adding more intermediate lines.
example_context: Surface blending tools in certain CAD programs when creating a constant-angle chamfer on an angled pipe end.

subject: alternative blend-and-split approach accuracy versus simple blend
main_point: A blend-and-split workflow can yield better accuracy than a simple two-line blend and avoids the need for numerous intermediate guide lines.
source_quote: Here's another approach (also blending and splitting with the blending result) which seems to give better accuracy without numerous intermediate steps
example_context: CAD modeling using blended surfaces and splitting operations to form the chamfered pipe end.

subject: measured uniformity of resulting chamfer angle across cross-sections
main_point: Cross-sectional measurements of the modeled chamfered pipe end indicated the top surface maintained a consistent tilt (e.g., 16 degrees) relative to horizontal.
source_quote: I cannot prove it in math, but making a couple of cross-sections and measuring the angle showed it's the same (=16 degrees from the horizontal):
example_value: Measured 16 degrees from the horizontal on multiple cross-sections.
example_context: Verification by cross-section measurement of a CAD model produced with the alternative blend-and-split approach.

subject: chamfer feature definition
main_point: A chamfer is parameterized relative to a reference surface, specified either by an angle or by a setback distance from that surface.
source_quote: Chamfer is an angle or distance from a surface.

subject: chamfer on varying-angle surface
main_point: If the target face changes orientation relative to your reference plane, applying a standard chamfer as done (fixed angle/distance from that plane) will not yield the intended geometry.
source_quote: Since your surface varies in angle to the horizontal, you will not get the desired results the way you did it.

subject: move distance for creating angled chamfer via surface modeling
main_point: After offsetting the pipe surface, translate the outer surface along the pipe axis by the offset distance multiplied by tan(desired chamfer angle) to generate the chamfer surface (e.g., 15°).
source_quote: Then use Move Body to shift by (the offset distance from the thicken) * tan(15deg) along the pipe axis.
example_value: For a 15° chamfer, move the surface by offset * tan(15°) along the pipe axis.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor surface modeling using Thicken/Offset and Move Body (or similar CAD with equivalent tools)

subject: surface-first modeling workflow for angled pipe with chamfer
main_point: Model the pipe as surfaces first (trim to the slant, then thicken, move the outer surface, patch, and stitch) so the 15° chamfer surface is inherently created before adding subsequent cuts and fillets.
source_quote: If instead of revolving the solid, you started your pipe as a surface of 36 mm diameter, trimmed it to your 8 mm slant (extruding a line can make a surface to trim to), used thicken by 4 mm, moved the outer surface body, made a couple of patches at top and bottom, and stitched the four into a pipe, the 15 degree "chamfer" surface would already be there prior to cutting the 40 mm feature and filetting.
example_value: Start as a surface, trim to the slant, thicken by wall thickness, move the outer surface, patch top/bottom, and stitch into a solid; the chamfer surface exists before later features.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor (or similar CAD) using surface modeling, Thicken/Offset, Patch, and Stitch

subject: order of fillet and pocket operations in FreeCAD
main_point: If fillets and pockets interact poorly in a FreeCAD model, try changing the feature order: apply the fillet before creating the pocket. Reordering features can eliminate geometry artifacts at their intersection.
source_quote: As a workaround have you considered performing the fillet first then pocketing out the hole.
example_context: FreeCAD parametric feature modeling (fillet and pocket features)

subject: Baud and Thum-Bautz fillets under dual envelope constraints
main_point: Baud and Thum-Bautz fillet profiles are effective when only one dimension (X or Y) is constrained, but they perform poorly when both X and Y envelope limits must be met simultaneously. Their suitability degrades under combined dimensional constraints.
source_quote: I have looked into Baud Fillets and Thum-Bautz fillets, but I find that although these fillets work fantastically for a desired y height OR a desired x height, these don't work well when one has constraints on both of these dimensions.
example_value: The author evaluated these fillets for cases with a single desired X or Y height versus cases with both X and Y constrained.
example_context: Fillet geometry selection with simultaneous X-length and Y-height envelope limits for steps in tubing (ID/OD).

subject: Scaling optimized fillet shapes to fit envelopes
main_point: Simply scaling a fillet profile along one axis to meet an envelope often performs poorly and can yield higher stresses than using a simple circular fillet. Axis scaling can degrade the effectiveness of optimized fillet shapes.
source_quote: Furthermore, it seems scaling the fillet shape along the axis does not work well, in many cases ending up worse than a circular fillet.
example_value: When trying to fit within both X and Y limits, scaled profiles sometimes performed worse than a circular fillet.
example_context: Fillet design under simultaneous X and Y envelope constraints for ID/OD step transitions in tubing.

subject: fillet geometry selection under simultaneous X and Y constraints
main_point: When formulas target only a single dimension, evaluate two candidate fillets by running FEA with just the X constraint and with just the Y constraint, then pick the option that yields the lower stress. This comparative approach can extract the best performance from one-dimensional fillet formulas when both dimensions are bounded.
