source_quote: By definition you will have more backlash in a train with more gears, as you need to account for some runout and thermal expansion in each mesh to avoid binding. This will limit your shaft positional tolerances and gear runout. If they become too tight it may just be impossible to manufacture what you need.

subject: multi-stage vs two-gear ratio precision and tooth wear
main_point: A multi-stage train can deliver an exact overall ratio while keeping individual meshes non-integer so tooth contacts “hunt” and wear distributes, whereas a single two-gear exact 8:1 pairs the same teeth repeatedly unless you offset the ratio slightly.
source_quote: With more gears you can achieve a more precise ratio without losing bending/wear resistance. For 2 gears having an exact 8:1 ratio the same tooth on the pinion will always mesh with the same teeth on the gear. To work around this you would need something like 7.96:1 or 8.04:1. With multiple gear meshes you can achieve 8:1 exactly and still have even tooth wear.
example_value: For 2 gears having an exact 8:1 ratio the same tooth on the pinion will always mesh with the same teeth on the gear. To work around this you would need something like 7.96:1 or 8.04:1.

subject: spur gear mesh efficiency and losses
main_point: Each additional gear mesh reduces overall efficiency; spur meshes peak around 98% efficiency, so multi-stage trains can incur noticeable energy losses in continuous operation.
source_quote: You'll have more losses due to friction for more gears. Spur gear meshes are about 98% efficient at a maximum. On a small scale that might not mean much but if you have several of these running 24/7 those losses start to add up.

subject: gear train noise with more meshes
main_point: Increasing the number of gear meshes raises noise levels, which may violate workplace or local noise limits and constrain the design.
source_quote: Noise. More gears in mesh = more noise. Depending on the environment you may need to limit the noise of the gear train/machinery for OSHA, local ordinances, etc.
example_context: environments subject to OSHA or local noise ordinances

subject: packaging flexibility: two-gear vs multi-gear layouts
main_point: A single two-gear layout fixes the relative shaft locations, while a multi-stage layout allows non-collinear centers and can fit the drivetrain into a smaller footprint.
source_quote: Available center distance. With layout A you are locked where your input to the pinion and output from the gear can be located. With layout B the centers of rotation do not all need to be in line, you could conceivably fit them in a much smaller footprint.

subject: lubrication requirements under high contact pressure
main_point: High gear contact pressures can demand specific lubrication; lubrication breakdown is a leading cause of machine failure, so incorrect or inadequate lube selection is a major risk.
source_quote: This might also dictate what lubrication you need if the contact pressure is high enough. Lubrication breakdown is the main cause of machine failure.
example_context: gear meshes with high contact pressure

subject: sun+ring teeth sum divisibility by planet count
main_point: In a planetary gear set, if (sun teeth + ring teeth) divided by the number of planets is an integer, the planets can be positioned at equal angular spacing (e.g., 120° for three planets).
source_quote: As long as the number of teeth of the sun plus ring gear divided by the number of planet gears is an integer, they will be equally spaced (120 deg for 3 planets).
example_value: Example: with three planets, equal spacing is 120°.

subject: planet-sun mesh load phasing
main_point: Equal angular spacing synchronizes the peak tooth loads of the planet–sun meshes so their forces balance, which reduces vibration in the gearbox.
source_quote: When they're equally spaced the planet-sun meshes will all be hitting the highest tooth loads at the same time. These forces will balance out, minimizing vibration.

subject: out-of-phase planet load vectors
main_point: If the planet gear load vectors are out of phase, one will dominate at a time, which excites vibration in the system.
source_quote: If they're out of phase, you'll always have one vector contributing more magnitude than the others, inducing vibration in your system.

subject: cyclical gear loading
main_point: Gear tooth loading varies cyclically; synchronized planets can be considered as in-phase sinusoidal load contributions.
source_quote: The loading of gears is cyclical, so think about all 3 loads having the same sine function for intensity.

subject: AGMA 6123 planetary gear design standard
main_point: Consult AGMA 6123 as a reference standard when designing planetary (epicyclic) gear systems.
source_quote: AGMA 6123 is a helpful standard.
example_context: Planetary/epicyclic gear design standards and guidelines (AGMA 6123).

subject: rackmount equipment external envelope usage
main_point: Modern rackmount equipment may occupy space outside the basic chassis envelope near the rack posts to maximize internal volume. Older racks may need additional clearance around the posts to accommodate such overhangs.
source_quote: To get the most volume possible, modern equipment uses that space outside the "box"
example_value: The author notes a Dell SAN as an example where equipment uses space outside the nominal "box".
example_context: modern rackmount servers and SANs in legacy racks

subject: slide rail minimum collapsed length
main_point: Telescoping rack slide rails have a minimum collapsed length, so in shallow or short-depth racks they may not shorten enough to reach the rear supports. This can prevent direct installation of modern rails in legacy racks.
source_quote: Additionally, the modern rails are longer, so won't collapse short enough to reach the rear supports.
example_value: In the author's rack, the modern rails would not collapse short enough to reach the rear supports.
example_context: modern slide rails used with older shallow server racks

subject: managing live cables during cutting operations
main_point: When cutting with a grinder near energized cables, there is a risk the cables could swing into the cutting zone; tape or secure them out of the way to prevent contact.
source_quote: Also notice the live power cables taped out of the way so they wouldn't swing into the cutting area.
example_value: While cutting welds inside a server rack, the author taped live power cables aside to keep them from swinging into the grinder path.
example_context: Hand grinder cutting inside a server rack with equipment still powered

subject: retaining flanges for structural strength during modifications
main_point: When modifying rack posts for clearance, preserve the flange to maintain structural strength and relocate it to eliminate interference.
source_quote: The flange was left in place for added strength, but I swapped the sides so it was no longer in the way.
example_value: During rack post trimming, the author kept the flange for strength and moved it to the opposite side to clear server rails.
example_context: Steel server rack posts being cut/trimmed for rail clearance

subject: zinc primer on bare steel after cutting/grinding
main_point: After drilling and grinding expose bare steel, deburr and prime the exposed areas with a zinc spray to protect the metal.
source_quote: Drilled holes were deburred, weld was ground flat, and all bare metal was primed with zinc spray paint.
example_value: Post-modification, the author deburred and zinc-primed all newly exposed steel on the rack.

subject: angle grinder orientation affecting spark direction and ease of cut
main_point: Angle grinder orientation in tight spaces affects spark direction and cutting ease; positioning that directs sparks downward tends to be easier than cuts that force sparks upward.
source_quote: Left side was easier, the sparks were flying down, but on the right side the sparks went up because the grinder wouldn't fit in the other way.
example_value: While trimming a rack flange, one side allowed the grinder to throw sparks downward and was easier; the opposite side forced sparks upward and was harder due to tool fitment limits.
example_context: Angle grinder trimming of a flange in a constrained rack interior

subject: grinding dust tracking contamination
main_point: Metal grinding generates pervasive dust that adheres to footwear and can be tracked indoors, creating a major cleanliness issue; avoid grinding near clean areas or plan containment/cleanup.
source_quote: Finally, grinding metal is dirty.  Very dirty, and the dust likes to stick to your shoes and be tracked inside.  Not recommended.
example_value: After grinder work on the rack, the author noted dust sticking to shoes and being tracked inside.

subject: overcutting risk when removing welded joints
main_point: If you overlook an existing weld while cutting out components, you can accidentally cut into an adjacent structural rail and damage it.
source_quote: I missed a weld and managed to cut clean through the corner of one side rail.
example_value: During weld removal on the rack, a missed weld led to cutting through the corner of a side rail.
example_context: Cutting welded joints on a steel server rack with a cutoff wheel

subject: assembly-driven clearance limit on flange (foot) width
main_point: The required insertion path under the registration pins constrains the support feet to remain narrow. Widening the feet would create interference with the cross-member underneath during assembly.
source_quote: Because of the way I need to "scoop" the panel in from below so that the oval slots maneuver under the pins and up into them, I can't make the feet especially wide, to avoid contact with the support member underneath.
example_value: Feet width is limited to avoid contacting the support member during a “scoop-in” insertion under pins.
example_context: Sheet-metal panel with oval slots engaging registration pins; cross-member underneath; panel inserted by scooping from below.

subject: bend line width limited by reliefs around adjacent folds
main_point: Relief features required by nearby folds prevent the bend line from spanning the full flange width. As a result, the effective bend length is reduced relative to the foot width, limiting support at the bend.
source_quote: Because of the need for relief around other folds in the area, I also can't make the bend line the full 10mm width of the foot; it's only 5.2mm wide.
example_value: Foot is 10 mm wide but the bend line is only 5.2 mm long.
example_context: Sheet-metal part with adjacent fold reliefs that interrupt the bend line across a flange (foot).

subject: beam flexure formula
main_point: In elastic beam bending, the flexure formula relates bending stress to bending moment and section properties: σ = M·y/I. This allows you to compute stresses from geometry and applied moments for beams and cantilever features.
source_quote: M/I=sigma/y

subject: cantilever load redistribution under tip deflection/contact
main_point: When a cantilevered flange’s free end deflects upward into contact, the load path shifts toward the fixed/root region, increasing support and reducing the likelihood of catastrophic failure. This makes the overload behavior more benign as deformation progresses.
source_quote: However the failure mode is benign, as the tip is forced upwards more of the load will be applied to the root of the beam, and it will be supported there.
example_context: cantilevered sheet-metal flange/foot that can deflect into contact with its supporting structure near the root

subject: rebate feature aiding alignment and jigging
main_point: Including a rebate (rabbet) in the frame is beneficial for assembly because it improves part alignment and simplifies jigging during build. Designing these locating features reduces assembly variability and effort.
source_quote: You've also got a rebate in the wooden frame, this will help with both alignment and jigging during assembly.
example_context: panel seated into a wooden frame that includes a rebate/rabbet feature

subject: off-the-shelf two-point latch width
main_point: Commercial two-point latch mechanisms typically package to about 2 inches in width, which is a common size constraint when considering off-the-shelf solutions.
source_quote: Off-the-shelf two-point latch systems are around 2" wide.
example_context: Off-the-shelf two-point latch systems

subject: fine-pitch UNF thread installation
main_point: Using UNF (fine-pitch) threads for user-installed components can increase the risk of cross-threading during assembly and requires more rotations to seat, slowing installation, even though they may offer higher strength.
source_quote: UNF while provides the strength could present issues with installment because the customer could cross thread AND it also takes longer to thread.
example_context: UNF (fine) threads used in customer-installed handpiece standoffs or similar attachments

subject: threaded joint misalignment
main_point: Cross-threading typically happens because the mating parts are not aligned properly when starting the thread engagement.
source_quote: People cross threading joints is usually due to alignment
example_context: manually assembled threaded joints

subject: alignment sleeve for thread engagement
main_point: Add a guide sleeve or alignment feature so parts are aligned before the threads engage to reduce cross‑threading during assembly.
source_quote: consider a sleeve to control alignment then engage the thread.
example_context: manually assembled threaded joints

subject: pool cue joint designs (Uni-Loc)
main_point: Some joint designs used in pool cues (e.g., Uni‑Loc) are made so they cannot be cross‑threaded and are useful references for anti‑cross‑threading mechanisms.
source_quote: Check out the types of joint used in pool cues - uniloc etc that cannot be cross-threaded.
example_context: pool cue joints (e.g., Uni‑Loc)

subject: pre-thread alignment feature for threaded joints
main_point: Providing a short, non-threaded lead-in that mates with a complementary feature on the mating part can give users tactile alignment feedback before the threads engage, helping them align parts and avoid mis-starts.
source_quote: Not 100% sure, but it seems to give the user some extra tactile feedback about alignment before the threads engage.
example_value: A milk jug cap uses a short plain cylinder on the neck that mates with a groove in the cap before its triple-start threads engage, giving alignment feel.
example_context: threaded closures like blow-molded milk jug caps with triple-start threads

subject: through-holes in sealing surfaces
main_point: Placing through-holes in a sealed joint provides leak paths and compromises sealing integrity. Avoiding through-holes in the sealing interface reduces the risk of leakage.
source_quote: through holes create leaks

subject: multiple small fastener holes in gasket area
main_point: Populating the sealing face with many small fastener holes weakens gasket integrity and often forces heavy reliance on RTV to achieve a seal.
source_quote: many small holes in the middle of the mating/sealing surfaces lead to weak gaskets or a mass application of RTV.

subject: thin large plates bolted with many screws
main_point: Thin, large-diameter plates fastened with many screws are prone to warping if torque sequence and levels are not strictly controlled during assembly and maintenance.
source_quote: Large diameter, thin plates fixed by many screws tend to get warped unless tighening sequences and torques are strictly adhered to during assembly and maintenance.

subject: removal of rusted bolted plates using heat
main_point: In dirty, rust-prone service, freeing a bolted plate commonly requires heavy localized heating, which can warp the plate.
source_quote: Removal of plates this way after prolonged use in dirty environments -- ie. rusted -- is a nightmare almost guarenteed to need the application of substantial localised heating which inevitably results in warping.

subject: overtightening small countersunk screws
main_point: Small countersunk screws are easy to over-torque, increasing the risk of stripping the threads during assembly.
source_quote: it is far too easy to overtighten and strip such small screws

subject: interference fit analysis using Lam equations
main_point: An interference fit of a tube in a bore can be modeled as a concentric tube-in-tube shrink-fit using Lam thick-cylinder equations to compute elastic deformation and stresses.
source_quote: This problem can be simplified to a shrink-fit of tube in tube using Lam equations for thick cylinder elastic deformation.

subject: effect of outer member stiffness on interference fit stresses
main_point: In an interference fit, increasing the stiffness of the surrounding plate raises the stresses in the inner tube; a conservative bound is an infinitely stiff, effectively infinite plate (zero far-field radial stress).
source_quote: The inside tube stress will be the higher the more stiff the plate will be. You can assume, that the worst case scenario is plate with infinite outside diameter, where the radial stress is zero,

subject: relative stress in bore vs tube for interference fit
main_point: For the analyzed tube-in-plate interference fit, the bore (plate) experiences much lower stress than the inner tube at the mating surface.
source_quote: A good thing is, that bore stress is much smaller than tube stress.
example_value: Calculated stress distributions show the bores tangential stress at the inner surface is much lower than the tubes when using the provided material properties.
example_context: Interference fit of a tube into an effectively infinite plate with bc=0.3 for both, E(inner)=200 GPa, E(plate)=118 GPa.

subject: thermal assembly of interference fits by cooling
main_point: You can assemble an interference fit without hammering by cooling the tube to take advantage of thermal contraction; the required temperature drop depends on the materials coefficient of thermal expansion.
source_quote: There is also cooling which you would require to fit the tube without hammer for coefficient of thermal expansion 11e-6 K^{-1} (minimum same temperature fitting force could be calculated using radial contact stress, coefficient of friction and contact area):
example_value: Using b1 3 11d710^-6 K^-1 (typical of steel), cooling the tube provides the clearance needed for slip-fit assembly.
example_context: Steel or similar metals with coefficient of thermal expansion around 11d710^-6 K^-1.

subject: tightness requirement for interference fits
main_point: Achieving a leak-tight interference fit requires continuous contact with adequate contact pressure, which in turn demands precise machining and control of the interference.
source_quote: For tightness, you need continuous contact with some contact pressures, which would require precision to achieve.

subject: axial scratches degrading tightness after disassembly
main_point: Disassembling the fit can create axial scratches in the bore that act as leak paths, making it significantly harder to achieve tightness on reassembly.
source_quote: This may be even harder after first disassembly, when the bore surface may get damaged with axial scratches, which are the worst for the tightness.

subject: axisymmetric model limitations causing uneven stress
main_point: An axisymmetric analysis will not capture geometric or stiffness asymmetries; departures from axisymmetry (especially in plate shape near the bore) cause uneven circumferential stress relative to the model.
source_quote: Presented model is axisymmetric, so any deviation from that will lead to deviations in reality. This will be probably most pronounced in plate shape around the bore, which will lead to uneven stress distribution around tube circumference.

subject: clocked feature orientation vs threaded stem
main_point: When a feature must be clocked to maintain the orientation of a through-hole relative to a rod, adding a threaded stem is not feasible because tightening the thread would change the orientation. For clocked parts, threads can conflict with required angular alignment.
source_quote:
Threading the stem on the knobs isn't feasible due to the clocking of
the pre-drilled hole relative to the rod that is supposed to pass
through them.
example_value: The handrail knob has a pre-drilled hole that must be oriented relative to the handrail rod, so threading the knob’s stem would disturb that orientation.
example_context: clocked handrail knobs with a pre-drilled hole that must align to a through-rod

subject: tapping very small holes in tiny parts
main_point: Creating a female thread with an extremely small tap in a tiny part risks damaging the part because of the small hole size and fragility involved. Ultra-small tapping operations can be impractical on miniature components.
source_quote:
Tapping the base of the knob stem for a female thread
will require an extremely small tap and the hole might damage the
knob due to it's small size.
example_value: The small brass handrail knob would need an extremely small tap in its base, raising the risk of damage.
example_context: tapping extremely small holes in small brass knobs or miniature components

subject: press-fit effects on nickel-plated parts
main_point: A metal-to-metal press fit complicates later removal and risks damaging a nickel-plated surface during insertion. Press-fitting plated components can mar the finish and reduce serviceability.
source_quote: Metal-to-metal press fit isn't really desirable either because it makes removal difficult but not impossible and I also might damage the nickel plating that will eventually be on the knobs during insertion, but I'll do it if no other good options are out there.
example_value: Press-fitting the nickel-plated handrail knobs into the brass smokebox could make removal difficult and scratch or damage the nickel plating.
example_context: assembly press-fit of nickel-plated knobs into a brass body

subject: metric pillow block standard sizes
main_point: Metric pillow blocks are commonly available in standard bore sizes of 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, and 20 mm, making intermediate diameters like 14 mm less commonly available.
source_quote: However, the common size pillow blocks are 8, 10 ,12, 15, 17, 20mm, etc.
example_context: metric pillow blocks for shaft/lead screw support

subject: leadscrew end machining for mounting
main_point: Industrial practice for mounting leadscrews is to machine the screw end to create proper features for retention and alignment rather than relying on simple clamping methods. This provides a robust, purpose-made interface for supports.
source_quote: I think in industry, machining the end would actually be what is done and looking at the various machine tools in the shop that seems to be true.
example_context: Industrial machine tools using acme leadscrews

subject: set screws on acme-threaded leadscrews
main_point: Avoid fixing an acme-threaded leadscrew by driving a set screw into its threads; it's poor practice compared to purpose-machined ends.
source_quote: Set screw going into an acme thread just sounds like a bad idea to me.
example_context: Acme leadscrews retained with set-screw pillow blocks

subject: 14 mm acme leadscrew size availability
main_point: A 14 mm diameter is a non-standard size for acme leadscrews, so matching off‑the‑shelf mounting hardware is harder to source.
source_quote: Either way, 14mm seems to be an oddball size for acme screws.
example_context: Acme screw size standards and available mounting components

subject: avoiding non-standard parts without machining capability
main_point: Do not choose non‑standard component sizes if you lack the machining capability to adapt them; odd sizes typically require custom machined features or mounts.
source_quote: If you can't machine things then don't use oddball parts.

subject: using clamping shaft collars as flange mounts
main_point: Instead of a pillow block, a clamping shaft collar can be repurposed as a flange by drilling bolt holes and fastening it to a mating face to mount a leadscrew.
source_quote: But you could forego the pillow block and just drill holes into the collar and bolt it to the face of something as if it were a flange.
example_value: Using a 14 mm clamping collar on a 14 mm leadscrew when a matching pillow block size is unavailable.
example_context: Repurposing 14 mm shaft clamping collars for leadscrew mounting

subject: oversizing and locating holes in flexible clamping collars
main_point: When using clamping collars as flanges, account for collar and hole flex by drilling oversized clearance holes and locating them with transfer punches for proper fit-up.
source_quote: Since they are clamping collars they will flex as will any holes on their face holes so drill them large enough for clearance and transfer the holes with locating transfer punches.
example_context: Drilling bolt holes in repurposed clamping collars used as flanges

subject: blind bearing removal holes
main_point: Provide three tangential holes around a blind bearing bore so a drift can be used to tap the bearing out for service. This design feature enables removal of a seated bearing from a closed-end housing.
source_quote: Consider putting 3 holes tangential to the bearing to tap the bearing out with a drift.

subject: thin cylinder galling in steel-on-steel fits
main_point: Thin-walled cylindrical parts can misalign during removal or installation and gall the mating surface, which makes inserting a replacement bearing difficult. This failure mode is especially likely with steel-on-steel interfaces compared to dissimilar materials or plastics.
source_quote: Thin cylinders tend to get cockeyed and gall up the surface, then you would have difficulty inserting a new replacement bearing, more applicable for steel on steel, than steel bearing on a dissimilar metal(or plastic).
example_context: steel-on-steel cylindrical fits with thin-walled parts during bearing removal/installation

subject: anti-seize to prevent galling in press fits
main_point: For tight steel press fits, apply an anti-galling anti-seize to reduce the risk of galling and ease future disassembly. Copper-based or molybdenum anti-seize compounds are suitable options.
source_quote: In that situation I used to use a anti-galling anti-seize compound, typically copper powder in a oil binder, but molybdenum anti-seize compounds also exist.
example_value: In tool and die work with tight press fits between inserts and a die block made from steels like D2 or O2.
example_context: tight press fits between tool steel inserts and die blocks (e.g., D2/O2)

subject: sheet metal cylinder flattening seam
main_point: When modeling a cylindrical sheet‑metal part for a flattened pattern, include a longitudinal gap/seam so the model can be unwrapped and flattened.
source_quote: Note the gap at the rear to allow the sheet metal flattening.
example_value: The example pipe model includes a small rear gap before using the sheet‑metal flatten feature to generate the flat pattern.
example_context: OnShape sheet‑metal modeling of a cylindrical tube to create a flat pattern

subject: angled reference plane definition using line and point
main_point: To position an angled cut/extrusion for intersecting cylinders, define a reference plane using a construction line and a point.
source_quote: Note that Plane 1 is defined by the construction line at the bottom right and the point visible above the pipe intersection.
example_value: In the intersecting pipe model, an auxiliary plane (Plane 1) is created from a bottom‑right construction line and a point above the intersection.
example_context: OnShape CAD modeling of intersecting pipes and angled cuts

subject: planet gear angular spacing formula
main_point: The angular spacing between adjacent planet gears can be computed as d = 360 × floor((s + r) / n) / (s + r), where s is sun teeth, r is ring teeth, and n is the number of planets.
source_quote:
d = the number of degrees between planet gears

d = 360 * floor((s + r) / n) / (s + r)
example_value: With r = 47, s = 15, n = 3, the formula gives d ≈ 116.129°.

subject: integer condition for equal planet spacing
main_point: Perfectly equal angular spacing of planet gears occurs only when the sum of sun and ring teeth divided by the number of planets is an integer.
source_quote: In the case where (s + r) / n is an integer, the spacing will be equal.

subject: bellows isolation for alignment stability
main_point: Placing a bellows between a heated duct and an emitter–detector instrument can decouple duct thermal growth so that duct movement minimally disturbs the instrument’s alignment.
source_quote: I am using bellows to create a cushion between the duct and the instrument - the idea is that as the duct heats up, the movement of the duct will minimally interfere with the alignment of the instrument.
example_value: Using bellows as a cushion between the duct and instrument to mitigate thermal expansion effects on alignment.
example_context: Emitter–detector gas concentration instrument mounted to a process duct that heats up

subject: minimally invasive mounting and data reliability
main_point: Previous minimally invasive mounting approaches, including directly attaching the instrument to the duct, did not provide continuous, reliable data, indicating the need for a more robust support design.
source_quote:
This is my third design iteration, and the previous two "minimally invasive" designs failed in giving 
continuous
 reliable data. At first, I had mounted the instrument directly to the duct, without any support structures, etc.
example_value: Initial design mounted the instrument directly to the duct without any support structures and it failed to deliver continuous reliable data.
example_context: Emitter–detector gas concentration instrument installed on process ducts

subject: tube-to-base plate weld continuity
main_point: Use a continuous, all-around weld to join the square tube to the base plate to ensure a robust connection.
source_quote: I would weld all around the tube to the base plate
example_value: Recommended for the instrument support post-to-baseplate connection.
example_context: welded square tube column to base plate for an instrument support

subject: torsional stress check for post
main_point: When torsion is significant in the post, compute stress using σt = (Ft·e)/J and verify it remains below yield strength.
source_quote:
If you have significant torsion, please check the torsional stress against yield by the formula 
$\sigma_t = \dfrac{F_t*e}{J}$
example_context: square steel tube post for instrument support under torsional loading

subject: polar moment for 3x3 square tube (given)
main_point: For the specified 3x3 tube section, use J = 4.28 in^4 in the stress calculation.
source_quote:
$J = 4.28 in^4$
 for the 3x3 tube.
example_context: 3x3 square steel tube section proposed for the support post

subject: 2x2x3/16 square tube flexibility at 90 in height
main_point: A 2x2x3/16 square tube used as a 90-inch-tall post is too flexible, so a larger section is required to control deflection.
source_quote: Note: this is an update from the previously suggested 2x2x3/16, which will be too flexible for its height (90").
example_value: The author revised an earlier 2x2x3/16 recommendation because at 90 inches it would be excessively flexible.
example_context: 90-inch-tall instrument support post

subject: baseplate sizing for anchor bolt installation
main_point: Increase the baseplate size if needed to make anchor bolt installation easier.
source_quote: You may consider a larger baseplate for the ease of anchor bolt installation.
example_context: installing anchor bolts for a column baseplate in constrained locations

subject: indoor-only design limitation
main_point: The proposed support design details are intended only for indoor use and may not be suitable for outdoor environments.
source_quote: This is valid for the INDOOR application only.
example_context: instrument support structures located indoors

subject: lateral tie bracing for slender posts
main_point: Provide a lateral tie to brace the post and improve stability.
source_quote: A Lateral tie is recommended.
example_context: slender vertical support posts for instruments in indoor installations

subject: resonance between pipe and support post
main_point: If the support post’s natural frequency aligns with the pipe’s vibration, resonance can amplify motion and corrupt measurements. Avoid frequency overlap to prevent instrument reading errors.
source_quote: But the vibration of your hot pipe could resonate with that of the post and throw all the readings off.
example_value: A vibrating hot pipe can excite the post at resonance, disrupting the instrument’s readings.

subject: support natural frequency separation from source vibrations
main_point: Identify the pipe/support system’s natural frequency and design the instrument post so its natural frequency is sufficiently separated to avoid resonance with the pipe.
source_quote: so we need more information about your pipe section, its supports, and the natural frequency of those to design the post with a natural frequency away from that.

subject: dynamic load factor for preliminary sizing
main_point: As a preliminary rule of thumb for dynamic conditions, size components by applying a factor of three to the static load to account for vibration and dynamics.
source_quote: and we could multiply loading by 3 as a dynamic load factor and be done with it.
example_context: Preliminary sizing of support structures and fasteners subject to dynamic loads or vibration

subject: square keyway/shaft torque joint strength
main_point: A gear with a square keyway mated to a matching square shaft provides a high-strength torque-transmitting joint between the gear and shaft.
source_quote: The ratchet gear in the video has a square keyway and the rotating bar is cut square as well, giving a high strength joint.
example_value: In the referenced video, the ratchet gear uses a square keyway and the rotating bar is cut square.

subject: shrink fit assembly requirements
main_point: Shrink-fit joints require precision-machined mating dimensions and enough thermal differential to assemble; without suitable machining capability and adequate heating/cooling, a shrink fit is not practically achievable.
source_quote: A shrink fit is possible, but do you have the mill or lathe to make the appropriate dimensions and then sufficient heating and/or cooling?

subject: available temperature differential for shrink fitting with household equipment
main_point: Using a household freezer and oven for shrink fitting provides roughly a 300 deg C temperature differential; liquid nitrogen is another potential cooling method.
source_quote: Liquid nitrogen is a possibility, but a household freezer is about -18 deg C and a household oven about 280 deg C, which means a delta T of 300.
example_context: DIY shrink-fit assembly using a household freezer (~-18 deg C) and oven (~280 deg C).

subject: brazed joint strength vs welding
main_point: When executed correctly, brazed joints can achieve strength close to welded joints, making brazing a viable high‑strength joining method for metals like bronze.
source_quote: Brazing is a very strong joint if done properly (nearly as good as welding).

subject: drilled round keyways for torque transmission
main_point: A practical alternative to a milled/broached keyway is to drill one or more holes to form a round keyway, providing a torque‑transmitting feature between gear and shaft.
source_quote: You could also drill, tools permitting, a round keyway or keyways.

subject: stock steel/HSS tolerances vs assembly fit
main_point: Commercial steel and HSS stock are supplied to dimensional and geometric tolerances, not to an assembly "fit." You select from size/form/orientation tolerances on the stock; the mating clearance (fit) only arises when paired with another part.
source_quote:
In the above context, when you buy a metallic bar/HSS section there is usually no fitbe no 
fit
. E.g. only tolerances of the diameter of the bar, or other types  of tolerances (orientation, location, form etc), are relevant.
example_context: Commercial steel bar and hollow structural section (HSS) stock supply

subject: large-quantity custom manufacturing for specified tolerances
main_point: To obtain stock made to your specific tolerances, buy in large quantities and work directly with the manufacturer. With sufficient volume, economies of scale make custom tolerance production feasible.
source_quote: If you can order a much larger quantity (economies of scale), you can contact directly the manufacturer and have them produce the product in your specific tolerances.
example_context: Direct procurement from manufacturer with large order quantities

subject: tolerance classes for interchangeable components
main_point: Standardized interchangeable components (e.g., bearings and bolts) are sold off-the-shelf in defined tolerance classes, allowing you to choose the precision grade without custom manufacturing.
source_quote: This particular type of products, are so common and yet specialized that you can buy them into classes of tolerances.
example_value: SKF has for its bearings a class tolerance Normal, P6, P5 and it goes to P4 and below in what it calls "super-precision" bearings.
example_context: Standardized interchangeable components such as bearings and bolts

subject: fit as clearance determining functional relationship
main_point: Fit is the clearance between mating parts, and its magnitude dictates function: larger clearances permit relative movement, while small or negative clearances create temporary or permanent joints.
source_quote: In engineering terms, the "fit" is the clearance between two mating parts, and the size of this clearance determines whether the parts can, at one end of the spectrum, move or rotate independently from each other or, at the other end, are temporarily or permanently joined together.

subject: telescoping steel tubing availability
main_point: Telescoping steel tubing can be purchased off the shelf from industrial suppliers like McMaster-Carr, eliminating the need for custom manufacturing for sliding tube pairs.
source_quote:
McMaster-Carr
 is also a reliable source for materials and this link points specifically to telescoping steel tubing.
example_value: Supplier catalog pages list mating steel tube sizes designed to telescope.
example_context: McMaster-Carr catalog offerings of telescoping steel tubing

subject: telescoping tube clearance using standard sizes
main_point: Pairing adjacent standard tube sizes can yield enough diametral clearance for one tube to slide within another without binding.
source_quote: This is quite close to 2.75 inches, another common diameter. This provides a clearance of 0.13 inches, allowing for sliding without slop.
example_value: Using 3.00 inch OD tubing with 0.058 inch wall gives a 2.884 inch ID that fits over a 2.75 inch OD tube, for about 0.13 inch diametral clearance.
example_context: Standard 4130 steel tubing sizes and common 0.058 inch wall thickness

subject: rectangular/square tubing sourcing
main_point: Sourcing specific sizes or tight-fit options for rectangular and square tubing typically depends on what manufacturers and their representatives provide; distributors seldom have exact sizes for precise fits available from stock.
source_quote: For rectangular or square you are pretty much limited to the manufacturer and his reps.
example_value: The author notes that a distributor might by chance have the size you want, but it’s not reliable.
example_context: rectangular and square metal tubing procurement

subject: round tubing customization by distributors
main_point: Compared to rectangular or square tubing, round tubing is more readily customized by distributors, who can draw down or expand existing stock to achieve custom diameters, though it adds cost.
source_quote: Round tubing is different because some distributors will be able draw down or expand inventory to produce custom sizes; for a price.
example_context: round metal tubing supply and value-added services

subject: swaging round tube ends for telescoping fit
main_point: For round tubing, some suppliers can swage (reduce) the end diameter so it fits inside another round tube, enabling a telescoping-style fit without machining.
source_quote: Also , with round , some distributers can swage down an end to fit into another round.
example_context: round tubing forming/swaging services from distributors

subject: gear and bearing noise in small reduction drives
main_point: In a compact reduction drive, even if the motor is quiet, the worm gear meshes and associated bearings can become the dominant noise sources, producing significant sound on their own.
source_quote: My first try was to use a 2-step worm reduction, but I noticed that although the motor itself was silent, the gears and the bearings their axles were on started producing large noise.
example_value: A 2-step worm reduction produced large noise, overpowering the otherwise silent motor.
example_context: small-scale 2-step worm gear reduction driven by a quiet computer fan motor

subject: frictional retention in freely rotating joints
main_point: Do not rely on interference fits or other friction-based connections to retain a pin if the joint must rotate freely. Frictional retention will compromise free rotation, so it is unsuitable for true pivot joints.
source_quote:
Interference fit or other types of frictional connections are 
not
 an option if you are after a freely rotating joint.

subject: pin retention methods for rotating joints
main_point: To prevent a freely rotating pin from falling out while preserving rotation, use a mechanical retainer such as a split (cotter) pin or capture the pin by forming/peening it like a rivet. These methods secure the pin axially without relying on frictional clamping.
source_quote:
- some type of safety pin or split pin

- using rivets

subject: lock pin rotational limitation due to interference
main_point: Using a lock pin as a cross-pin to secure rotating members will mechanically interfere after about 180 degrees of rotation, so it cannot provide near-full rotation. If the design requires almost a complete turn, a lock pin will block motion.
source_quote: The issue is that lock pins only allow a rotation of 180 degrees before impeding and this needs to rotate almost a full rotation.
example_value: In the described assembly, the cylinders must rotate almost a full turn, making a lock pin unsuitable.
example_context: Cross-pinning two perpendicular cylindrical members (e.g., a sliding cylinder on a rotating axle) with a lock/detent pin.

subject: swivel joints and screwdriver joints
main_point: Swivel joints are standard components for making rotating connections, while "screwdriver joints" are used for fixed joints; these are common categories with many available examples.
source_quote: If you search on the internet on swivel joint for the rotating joint and under screwdriver joints for the fixed joint you will find manny examples.

subject: small DIY/desktop CNC suitability for production
main_point: Small DIY/desktop CNC machines typically require many hours of tuning, may never achieve acceptable quality, and even when they do, they cut slowly. They are a poor choice for producing a short pilot run compared to outsourcing.
source_quote: Those are cool and fun, but you will have to dick around with it for dozens of hours, and it may never produce good results, and if it does, it will be slow.
example_context: small desktop/DIY CNC machines and kits

subject: low-volume custom machining cost benchmark
main_point: A $25-per-set quote is considered inexpensive for custom machined parts at low volumes. This indicates that outsourcing the pilot batch can be cost-effective.
source_quote: 25 bucks a set for parts is actually quite cheap for custom machined stuff.
example_context: low-volume custom machined parts

subject: outsourcing pilot run vs DIY investment
main_point: When per-unit machining quotes are low, paying a few thousand dollars for a limited run is a straightforward way to validate a product. Unless budget is extremely tight, outsourcing the pilot batch is likely the best option.
source_quote: You could just bite the bullet and spend $2500 bucks to test the idea. That's simple and straight forward and unless you're on a shoe-string budget probably the best option.
example_context: pilot batch around 100 sets at ~$25 per set

subject: redesigning for laser cutting to reduce cost
main_point: Redesign parts for laser cutting to lower cost while keeping a clean appearance. Laser-cut parts are typically inexpensive and look good for prototyping.
source_quote: An alternative I might consider is to re-design the parts for laser cutting. Laser cuts are nice because they're cheap, and the parts look good.
example_context: laser cutting flat sheet parts

subject: laser-cut sheet part limitations
main_point: Laser-cut sheet parts have limited strength and constrain designs to flat geometries. If your parts must carry load or have 3D features, laser cutting may not be suitable.
source_quote: The downside is they're not very strong and your parts have to be flat.
example_context: laser cutting of flat sheet materials

subject: 3D-printed drill jigs for hole placement
main_point: Use 3D-printed drill jigs to accurately locate and guide screw holes during secondary operations. This provides consistent hole placement without complex fixturing.
source_quote: You can 3d print drill jigs to for the screw holes.

subject: acetone vapor smoothing of ABS FDM prints
main_point: Print parts in ABS on an FDM printer and post-process them with acetone vapor to greatly improve surface smoothness. This technique relies on ABS being soluble in acetone.
source_quote: For a smoother look, you could fdm 3d print the parts in ABS, then smooth them with acetone vapor.
example_context: FDM 3D printed ABS parts

subject: SLA/pro service vs FDM surface finish
main_point: Professional 3D printing processes (e.g., SLA) typically produce a smoother surface finish than desktop FDM printers. Using a service bureau can improve cosmetic quality for prototypes.
source_quote: They have a variety of 3d printing methods that will give a better surface finish then a FDM printer.
example_context: SLA and service bureaus (e.g., Shapeways) compared to FDM printers

subject: silicone mold resin casting tradeoffs
main_point: Silicone-mold resin casting is complex and finicky, so it should be avoided unless achieving an injection-molded appearance is critical. For most prototypes, simpler methods are preferable.
source_quote: it's a complex and finicky process. I wouldn't recommend it unless the injection molded appearance is a top priority.
example_context: silicone mold and resin casting for short-run parts

subject: hybrid prototyping process selection
main_point: Use a hybrid approach by combining manufacturing methods to balance cost, strength, and appearance. Assign each part to the process that best suits its requirements.
source_quote: The best bet is probably to combine these methods as necessary.
example_value: SLA print the brackets and stand arms, and laser cut the stand base.

subject: local sourcing of sheet materials to reduce cost
main_point: Contact local plastic suppliers to source material more cheaply than online. Even if you must buy a full 4x8 sheet, the total and per-part cost is likely lower.
source_quote: Try calling around to local plastic supplies, they might force you to buy a 4x8 sheet, but it will probably be much cheaper.
example_context: local plastics (and metals) distributors vs online retailers

subject: outsourcing laser/waterjet to Big Blue Saw
main_point: Use an online service like Big Blue Saw for laser and waterjet jobs; the author endorses them based on repeated positive experience. Outsourcing these cuts can accelerate prototyping without in-house equipment.
source_quote: Edit: for laser and water jet cutting, try "Big Blue Saw". I use them all the time and really like them.
example_context: outsourcing laser and waterjet cutting to job shops

subject: operation count minimization
main_point: Design parts so they require as few manufacturing operations as possible; minimizing steps improves manufacturability by reducing handling, setups, and complexity.
source_quote: Ideally, a part should have as little steps to produce as possible

subject: DFM mental simulation of manufacturing
main_point: During design, mentally simulate the manufacturing process: consider toolpaths, cut direction, workholding, fixtures/jigs, assembly, and mold-related needs like pull direction, draft, and minimum radii to ensure the part is manufacturable.
source_quote: When designing a part I always imagen that I am the machine that has to manufacture it, you have to imagen the tool paths, cut direction, how you're going to hold it, fixtures, jigs, assembly, and if applicable things like pull direction, drafts, minimum radii etc.

subject: flat-pack design for shipping efficiency
main_point: Designing parts as a flat-pack assembly can significantly reduce packing volume and logistics costs, at the tradeoff of requiring user assembly; countersinks and similar features can be cut during fabrication so parts arrive ready to assemble.
source_quote: machines now can even cut counter sinks so all of the parts would be ready to go and have the advantage of being 'flat pack' requiring the user to assembly but massivly reducing packing.
example_value: The author suggests laser/water cutting components with countersinks so they ship as a flat pack and assemble later, reducing packing volume.

subject: injection molding/die casting cost drivers (undercuts, side pulls, parting line)
main_point: For small runs, injection molding or die casting can be economical if the design avoids undercuts and side pulls and uses a flat parting line; with such features controlled, tooling can be on the order of about £$1200.
source_quote: Injection moulding and die casting for even relitivly small runs isnt as expensive as most people think as long as there are no undercuts or side pulls and the mold has a flat parting line, molds can be as cheap as £$1200 if the part is designed right.
example_value: The author cites molds "as cheap as £$1200" when the part is designed without undercuts/side pulls and with a flat parting line.
example_context: injection moulding and die casting

subject: process selection beyond CNC machining
main_point: Do not default to CNC machining as the only solution; evaluate alternative processes like casting, injection molding, laser/waterjet cutting, EDM, or 3D printing based on the part’s needs.
source_quote: CNC machining isn't a silver bullet either, you have casting, injection moulding, laser, waterjet, EDM and of course 3D printing.

subject: in-house small CNC investment for short-run production
main_point: For short-run production, the total cost of buying, setting up, and learning a small CNC often ends up at least 2–3× higher once you include labor time and schedule delays. This makes DIY machining uneconomical compared to external sourcing for limited batches.
source_quote: The cost of buying, setting up, learning how to properly use a small cnc machine will be at least 2 or 3 times greater if you factor in work hours, and delays.
example_value: The author characterizes a $25 per set quote as cheap relative to the true cost of DIYing a CNC for this job.
example_context: Bringing initial low-volume production (hundreds of sets) in-house on a small CNC machine

subject: material-dependent design under load
main_point: Because materials have different properties, a part that sees significant static or dynamic loads should be redesigned to suit the chosen material. Geometry, features, and details must reflect the material’s strengths and weaknesses to avoid failure.
source_quote: The options you mention, have very different properties and if there are any significant loads or dynamic loads, the design should be modified with respect to the material.
example_value: The author later cites plywood with sharp corners as a poor choice for one of the components if it carries load.

subject: plywood parts with sharp corners
main_point: Avoid designing plywood parts with sharp-cornered geometries, especially if the part carries load; this is likely to perform poorly and should be reworked to suit the material.
source_quote:
For example using plywood on the 
3rd component
 with those sharp corners would be a bad idea (however, as I said I don't know if this is supposed to take any significant load or if its just a stand/holder).
example_value: The author flags the OP’s “3rd component” with sharp corners as a bad idea in plywood.
example_context: Plywood components expected to carry any significant load or dynamic load

subject: DIY equipment investment break-even volume
main_point: Investing in DIY manufacturing equipment only starts to make economic sense when you plan to scale to the order of thousands of pieces. Below that volume, the payback is unlikely to justify the upfront cost and learning curve.
source_quote: A final thought, is that an investment on DIY equipment would make sense, if you are planning to scale production to probably something in the order of a few thousand pieces.
example_context: Production planning for scaling from pilot runs to several thousand units

subject: design for cost-effective manufacturing (DFM)
main_point: Redesign parts to suit more cost-effective manufacturing methods while preserving function. DFM-driven changes can significantly reduce production cost without sacrificing performance.
source_quote: it would probably make more sense to adjust design in order to accommodate for more cost effective manufacturing while maintaining function

subject: sheet fabrication vs machining from block
main_point: For suitable geometries, producing parts from sheet stock can be much cheaper than machining them from a solid block. Selecting a sheet-based process (e.g., cutting/forming) can dramatically lower cost relative to CNC milling billet.
source_quote:
You'd be surprised how much cheaper it would be to manufacture the 
2nd component
 from sheets of material rather than machining it with a cnc from a block.
example_value: The author points to the OP’s “2nd component” as a candidate to be made from sheet instead of machined from a block.
example_context: Flat or 2D-profile components that can be produced from sheet material via cutting processes

subject: grinder vs hand file for stainless stock removal
main_point: For removing about 1–2 mm of material from stainless steel, choose a grinder for efficiency; using a hand file will take many hours.
source_quote: Removing 1 or 2 mm of stainless would require a grinder unless you want to spend many hours with a file.
example_context: Hand-removing 1–2 mm from a stainless steel adapter or small part

subject: interpretation of unspecified hardness value '200'
main_point: A hardness value given simply as "200" is likely expressed on the Brinell or Vickers scale rather than Rockwell.
source_quote: "200" looks like Brinell or Vickers hardness
example_context: Interpreting a stainless steel part’s hardness when only the number 200 is provided without a scale

subject: ordinary hand file hardness
main_point: Ordinary hand files are roughly 600 on the Vickers/Brinell hardness scales, making them much harder than many stainless steels.
source_quote: still not much compared to the 600 Vickers or Brinell of an ordinary file.

subject: key size (length and depth) for load transmission
main_point: Dimension a key’s length and depth to carry the required transmitted load, and account for shock loads in addition to steady forces. Shock loading is a common cause of failure, so keys should be sized with sufficient margin for impact/overload conditions.
source_quote: The size (length) and depth of the key has to be sufficient for the force that has to be transmitted. Not only that force which might be easy to calculate but also any shock loads as most breakages tend to be from shock loading.

subject: integral gear-shaft vs separate gear on shaft
main_point: Integrating a gear as part of the shaft increases strength compared to a separate mounted gear. Separate gears on shafts are chosen when the gear must rotate independently, typically via intermediate gearing.
source_quote: Some gears are made as part of the shaft which makes them stronger, others need to rotate independent of the shaft they are on at times and are connected by intermediate gears.

subject: oversized key and keyway for worn keyway repair
main_point: When replacing a component that has a worn keyway, choose an oversized key and recut the keyway larger to take up the wear-induced clearance and restore a proper fit.
source_quote: If you're replacing a part with a worn keyway, you may want to go to an oversized key and keyway to accomodate any clearance that has been worn.
example_context: Repairing a worn keyway in a keyed shaft/hub connection.

subject: keyway clearance for frequent disassembly
main_point: For assemblies that will be taken apart often, specify increased keyway clearance to facilitate repeated assembly and disassembly.
source_quote: If the part is going to be disassembled frequently you'll want more clearance in the keyway.
example_context: Keyed shaft–hub assemblies that require frequent disassembly for maintenance.

subject: standard references for keyed shaft and hub fits
main_point: Machinery's Handbook provides recommended fit classes and actual keyway dimensions for designing keyed shaft–hub connections.
source_quote: There are recommended fits for keyed shafts and hubs in Machinery's Handbook as well as the actual keyway dimensions
example_context: Using Machinery's Handbook as a design reference for keyed shaft and hub geometry.

subject: oversize keystock hand-grinding practice
main_point: One effective way to achieve proper key fits is to buy oversize keystock and hand‑grind it to an exact fit, making the specific key callout on the drawing less critical from the builder’s perspective.
source_quote: As a machine builder, we purchase oversize key stock and always hand grind them to exact fits for the application, so from our standpoint, we don't care how the key is called out on the drawing.
example_context: machine building of keyed shaft/gear assemblies using oversize keystock hand-fit by grinding

subject: broached keyway dimensional sensitivity
main_point: When the mating part’s keyway is broached, the dimensions are generally not very critical as long as you use the correct shims and bushing for the specific broach.
source_quote: Most of the time the other part is broached so dimensions are not super critical if you have the correct shims/bushing for the particular broach.
example_context: broaching keyways with the appropriate broach, shims, and bushing

subject: slotting keyways using standard dimension charts
main_point: If you are slotting/milling a keyway, consult the standard dimension charts to determine the correct slot sizes.
source_quote: But if your slotting that keyway, then you'll need the charts.
example_context: milling (slotting) straight female key slots on shafts

subject: engineering drawings for keyways with tolerances
main_point: If you lack shop support to interpret or adjust fits, you should explicitly specify the keyway dimensions and include tolerances on both the shaft slot and the mating part’s slot.
source_quote: If you don't, then you'll have to call out exact dimensions WITH tolerances for the shaft slot, and part slot.
example_context: engineering drawings for keyed shaft and mating part without machinist/builder support

subject: idler gear effect on overall ratio in three-gear train
main_point: In a three-gear train, the tooth count of the middle idler does not change the overall gear ratio; the ratio depends only on the driver and driven gears.
source_quote: With 3 gears, the size of the idler in the middle does not affect the ratio
example_value: Example combinations like 20/X/40, 30/X/60, or 40/X/80 all yield the same 2:1 ratio regardless of idler tooth count X.

subject: change-gear selection strategy for manual lathes
main_point: When multiple gear combinations yield the same ratio on a manual change‑gear lathe, favor using the least‑used gears to spread wear and preserve commonly used gears. This helps keep frequently needed gears in better condition for other setups.
source_quote: So if you're using the geartrain the best option is to use some gear less usable (and with less wear) for other configurations.
example_value: Choosing among several gear combinations that all give a 2:1 ratio on a manual change‑gear lathe.
example_context: manual change‑gear lathes for threading/feed gearing

subject: replacement change‑gear material upgrade prioritization
main_point: When a worn change gear needs replacement, make the new gear from a better material and prioritize upgrading the gear that is most commonly used or interchangeable across your usual applications to maximize benefit.
source_quote: You want to create a new gear with better material and you'll select the oposite (the most interchangeable gear for all your common applications).
example_value: Upgrading a frequently swapped gear in the lathe’s change‑gear set to a stronger material when fabricating a replacement.
example_context: manual change‑gear lathes undergoing gear replacement due to wear

subject: minimum teeth to avoid undercut in 20° PA gears
main_point: For standard off‑the‑shelf 20° pressure‑angle gears, select gears with more than 24 teeth to avoid undercut tooth profiles. Choosing higher tooth counts reduces the risk of weak, undercut teeth.
source_quote: Generally you want more than 24 teeth in a gear to avoid having an undercut tooth profile, if you're using off the shelf 20 degree gears.
example_context: off-the-shelf 20° pressure-angle gears

subject: spur gear ratio limit
main_point: Limit the tooth count ratio of mating spur gears to a maximum of 5:1. Exceeding this can lead to unfavorable geometry or loading in the mesh.
source_quote: Spur gears you also want to have at most a 5:1 ratio between teeth.
example_context: spur gears

subject: pinion hardness selection vs gear
main_point: Specify the pinion in a harder material than its mating gear. This material pairing guideline improves durability of the gear set.
source_quote: Your smaller gear (pinion) should be of a harder material than it's mating gear.

subject: coprime gear tooth counts for even wear
main_point: Choose mating gears with coprime tooth counts (GCF = 1) so that every tooth eventually meshes with every tooth on the mate. This distributes contact and results in more even wear.
source_quote: If possible have the greatest common factor between the number of teeth be 1, this way every tooth on the gear will encounter every tooth on the pinion and wear will be more even than if the same pairs of teeth mesh every time.

subject: rack-and-pinion tangential force from torque
main_point: For a rack-and-pinion, the linear force transmitted to the rack equals the pinion’s tangential tooth force, which is computed as torque divided by the pinion pitch radius (F = T / r).
source_quote: Tangential force = torque/(pitch diameter/2).

subject: spur rack-and-pinion frictional losses
main_point: Spur rack-and-pinion meshes typically incur about 2–3% loss to friction, so actual linear force is slightly less than the ideal tangential force from torque-radius calculation.
source_quote: less power lost due to friction, typically 2-3% for spur tooth and racks
example_context: spur gear teeth meshing with a rack (spur rack-and-pinion)

subject: Lego knob diameter
main_point: The nominal diameter for a Lego stud/knob is 4.9 mm, which sets the target size for mating sockets and related features.
source_quote: The knob diameter is 4.9mm.
example_context: Lego system studs/knobs and compatible sockets

subject: 5 mm drilled socket fit for Lego knob
main_point: Drilling a socket with a 5.00 mm bit leaves too much clearance for a 4.9 mm Lego knob, resulting in a loose fit.
source_quote: A 5mm metric drill bit is too large and produces a loose, sloppy fit.
example_context: Drilling sockets in plastic to accept 4.9 mm Lego studs/knobs

subject: 3/16 in drill for Lego round axle hole
main_point: Using a 3/16 in (4.76 mm) drill creates a close-fit hole for Lego round axles/pegs, providing a better match than a 5 mm drill.
source_quote: A 3/16 inch imperial drill bit (4.76 mm) seems to be about perfect for a Lego round axle/peg shaft.
example_context: Creating smooth-bore round holes for Lego round axles/pegs

subject: Non-round knob geometry for interference fit
main_point: A slight noncircularity (on the order of ~0.1 mm) in a Lego-style knob promotes an interference fit by elastically deforming as it is inserted into the mating socket.
source_quote: For ideal results the knob should actually be slightly non-round (by a something like 100m) so it deforms slightly into place,
example_context: Lego-compatible stud/knob fit into sockets

subject: Undersize print then drill to final size
main_point: For FDM-printed parts, leaving holes slightly undersized with thicker walls and then drilling to final size yields a smooth, accurate bore and good fit.
source_quote: I can just print slightly undersized with thick walls, then drill it out and get a great result.
example_context: Finishing 3D-printed plastic parts to create smooth-bore Lego round axle holes

subject: button-plunger reach loss in incremental plunger mechanisms
main_point: In a dispenser where the plunger advances upward as fluid is dispensed, the actuator button can eventually lose physical contact with the plunger. When this happens, further pressing the button will not move the plunger, preventing additional dispensing even though fluid remains.
source_quote: After a certain level of fluid is gone but fluid still remains, the button won't be able to touch the plunger no matter how much I press the button.
example_value: In the described pen-like dispenser, once the plunger has moved up after dispensing some fluid, the button no longer reaches it, so pressing the button fails to actuate the plunger.
example_context: Pen-like dispenser concept using a clutch-held plunger that advances incrementally with decreasing fluid level

subject: silicone/caulking gun mechanism
main_point: A silicone (caulking) gun-style mechanism is a simple, practical, and proven approach to achieve the desired plunger-driven fluid dispensing function for this kind of device.
source_quote: Take a look at a silicone gun mechanism. Simple and practical and does exactly what you are trying to invent.
example_context: Handheld fluid dispensing mechanisms such as caulking/silicone guns

subject: hobbyist CAD for mechanisms
main_point: For hobbyists, designing mechanisms with gears, linkages, and actuators is challenging and generally requires professional, expensive CAD software.
source_quote: "it will entail gears, linkages and actuators" I believe is very difficult for the hobbyist.  This level of modelling requires professional design software costing ££££.
example_context: Hobbyist modelling of gears, linkages, and actuators

subject: FreeCAD 0.16 assembly capability
main_point: FreeCAD 0.16 lacks multi-part/assembly capability, limiting users to modeling single links rather than complete linkages.
source_quote: It also can't deal with more than one part, so can only try to model a link, not linkages.
example_value: The author tested FreeCAD 0.16 (the then-stable version) and found it could not handle more than one part.
example_context: FreeCAD 0.16 (2016 stable release) capability for assemblies

subject: student licenses for professional CAD
main_point: If you have academic affiliation, obtain a student/academic license for SolidWorks, Solid Edge, or Fusion 360; these tools are well-suited for linkage design and can model range of motion.
source_quote: As you're academically linked, might I suggest getting a student /academic license for something like SolidWorks or SolidEdge.  There might also be Fusion 360.  They work well and are of a suitable stature for linkages and such.  They also allow the range of motion to be modelled.
example_context: Academically affiliated users evaluating SolidWorks, Solid Edge, or Fusion 360 for linkage and motion modelling

subject: free 3D CAD availability on Linux
main_point: At the time of writing, Linux users did not have access to free 3D CAD packages the author considered usable.
source_quote: Unfortunately for me as a Linux user, there are no free usable 3D modelling packages at this time.
example_context: Linux users seeking free, usable 3D CAD software (circa 2016)

subject: parametric modeling in CAD
main_point: Use a parametric CAD approach where the model is generated from adjustable parameters (a "recipe"), so the design can be easily regenerated and tested iteratively. This supports efficient simulation and refinement before building hardware.
source_quote: Maybe this is because most of what I do is parametric modeling, e.g. describing the computer a recipe on how to produce a model from parameters, that can then be tested.

subject: rubber seal as indicator of non-tapered threads
main_point: The presence of a rubber seal suggests the joint seals via the gasket rather than thread interference, indicating the thread is likely straight (non-tapered).
source_quote: It does not appear to be tapered and the rubber seal would support this observation.
example_value: On the observed plug, a rubber seal was present and the threads did not appear tapered.

subject: parallel shafts power transmission
main_point: When the motor and driven shafts are parallel rather than coaxial, a direct coupling is not possible; motion must be transmitted through at least one intermediate stage such as a belt and pulleys or a pair of gears.
source_quote: I don't have a lot of space under the cylinder, so I decided to move that motor to make it parallel to the cylinder (and then to the cylinder shaft), this also means that I won't be able to direct drive the cylinder shaft and I will need to use at least a pair of pulleys (with belt :)) or gears.
example_value: Due to space constraints, the motor is relocated to be parallel to the cylinder shaft, necessitating a belt or gear stage instead of direct drive.

subject: belt pulley backlash
main_point: Pulley-driven transmissions generally introduce significant play/backlash. They are a poor choice when minimizing backlash is a primary requirement.
source_quote: Pulleys have a lot of play.

subject: single-stage 1:50 gear size vs backlash tradeoff
main_point: A single-stage 1:50 gear set minimizes play/backlash but requires substantial physical space. It is not well-suited to tight packaging constraints.
source_quote: You don't have a lot of space, so a single 1:50 gear, while optimal for play, would take a lot of space.

subject: worm gear axis reorientation limitation
main_point: Worm gears achieve high reduction ratios but rotate the output axis by 90°. If parallel shaft orientation must be maintained, you need two worm stages or an added bevel gear set.
source_quote: High ratios are easily obtainable with worm drive, but they turn the axis 90 degrees, so if the motor must be parallel, you'd need two sets of these (or one set + bevel gears to return to original direction).

subject: worm-based reduction minimal backlash
main_point: Using worm-based reduction (e.g., dual worm stages or worm plus bevel gears) tends to yield the least backlash among options that keep the motor parallel.
source_quote: Still, that would probably create least play while keeping the motor orientation.

subject: single worm drive for 1:50 with minimal backlash
main_point: If you can mount the motor at 90° to the driven axis, a single worm gear on the motor shaft can provide a 1:50 reduction with minimal backlash, in a straightforward setup.
source_quote: Although if you could install the motor 90 degrees to the cylinder axis, a single worm drive, with the worm directly on the motor axis, and firmly held with in a bearing would provide your 1:50 ratio with minimum backlash quite easily.

subject: PCB mounting to DIN rail clips
main_point: Avoid attaching DIN rail clips directly to a PCB to prevent twisting loads on the board during clip mounting and removal. Use an intermediate mounting approach to isolate the PCB from these torsional forces.
source_quote: I do not want the PCB directly attached to DIN rail clips because I don't want twisting forces applied to the PCB during DIN rail mounting/removal.
example_value: The PCB is spaced off a mounting plate by plastic board supports, and the DIN rail clips attach to the plate instead of the PCB.
example_context: Assemblies using DIN rail clips for mounting PCBs or electronics enclosures, where clips are engaged/disengaged from the rail.

subject: injection molding setup economics
main_point: Injection molding delivers very low per-part cost at high volumes (on the order of tens of thousands), but the mold’s upfront cost makes it uneconomical for small runs like ~500 units. Choose injection molding only when quantity is high enough to amortize the tooling cost.
source_quote: If you wanted to do 50,000 units, the answer is almost certainly injection molding of some kind.  You could make what you are describing easily for probably pennies per piece... but it would cost quite a bit to set up the mold.  That's probably not worth the setup cost just for 500 pieces.
example_value: At ~50,000 units, parts can be made for pennies each; at ~500 units, the mold setup cost is not worth it.
example_context: Process selection for plastic parts where injection molding is an option, comparing small (~500) vs large (~50,000) production volumes.

subject: bandsaw slicing of plastic sheet into blanks
main_point: For a few hundred simple flat parts, buy large plastic sheets and have a shop bandsaw them into 3-inch-wide blanks to reduce fabrication cost before drilling.
source_quote: Buy some big sheets and have a machine shop slice them into 3" sections with a band saw.
example_value: Cut 12"-long by 3"-wide strips from sheet as blanks for subsequent hole drilling.
example_context: Low-volume (hundreds) production of simple plastic mounting plates from sheet stock.

subject: acrylic sheet suitability and cost
main_point: Acrylic sheet is a very low-cost option (under about $1 per piece for this application) that is stiff enough and easy to drill for simple mounting plates.
source_quote: Looks like you could get the raw material in acrylic for less than $1 per piece.  That should be easily enough to drill holes in and should be stiff enough.
example_value: Acrylic blanks for the described plate can be sourced for under $1 each.
example_context: Simple 12" x 3" thin mounting plates requiring several drilled holes for PCB mounting hardware.

subject: physical spline lofting (thin flexible beam energy minimization)
main_point: A traditional lofting spline behaves as an interpolating curve through the sample points because the flexible strip assumes the minimum-energy shape of a thin elastic beam.
source_quote: This technique is a type of interpolation (curve exactly passes over sample points) using a physical analog model (minimal potential energy of a thin flexible beam).

subject: NURBS/control-point approximation vs interpolation
main_point: Digital CAD commonly represents shapes using control-point-based approximation (e.g., NURBS) rather than forcing curves to interpolate all given data points.
source_quote: instead of using a similar interpolation technique they chose an approximation technique by means of distant control points

subject: local support in NURBS/subdivision modeling
main_point: In NURBS and subdivision surface modeling, moving a control point influences only a local region of the surface, leaving the rest unchanged. This locality enables targeted edits without disturbing the overall shape.
source_quote: By contrast, with nurbs and subdivision surfaces, control points exercise local control, beyond which the surface is unaffected.
example_context: NURBS and subdivision surfaces in CAD modeling

subject: global support in physical drafting splines
main_point: With physical lofting splines held by weights, each defining point influences the entire curve. Adjusting any point changes the full length of the spline rather than a localized area.
source_quote: The defining points have support over the entire length of the spline, meaning moving one affects the entire length of the curve.
example_context: Physical lofting with flexible strip and ducks (weights) in drafting

subject: effort scaling with variation span/higher order NURBS
main_point: Interpolation and approximation can be used with both local and non-local support, but the required effort grows as the affected span increases. Higher-order NURBS generally demand more work to manage wider influence.
source_quote: These can apply to either case - local or non-local, but the effort required increases as the span of the variation increases (ie. using higher order nurbs).
example_context: Spline/NURBS interpolation or approximation in CAD surface algorithms

subject: optimization requirement for interpolating schemes
main_point: Implementing interpolating surface schemes typically requires solving an optimization problem, unlike approximation methods. This adds algorithmic complexity compared to approximation.
source_quote: It requires an optimization step not found in approximation schemes.
example_context: Interpolating spline/subdivision algorithms in CAD compared to approximation schemes

subject: approximating vs interpolating subdivision schemes
main_point: Approximating subdivision schemes tend to yield smoother surfaces, whereas enforcing exact positional constraints (as in interpolation) necessitates an optimization step. Thus smoothness comes more easily with approximation, but exactness requires added computation.
source_quote: In general, approximating schemes have greater smoothness, but editing applications that allow users to set exact surface constraints require an optimization step.
example_context: Subdivision surface refinement schemes in CAD/CG applications

subject: implementation simplicity of approximation for free-form design
main_point: For free-form surface design workflows, approximation methods are simpler to implement than interpolation. They avoid the extra optimization burden needed to meet exact constraints.
source_quote: For free-form design, the approximation technique is easier to implement.
example_context: Free-form CAD surface design tools and algorithms

subject: surface import using interpolation for initial mesh
main_point: When importing surfaces, prefer interpolation to recreate an initial coarse mesh that matches the source, then let an operator position the elements appropriately. This helps preserve the original shape during the transfer.
source_quote: For importing a surface from another format, interpolation techniques may be desirable, at least to form an initial coarse mesh, with an operator putting these in the right place for the job.
example_context: Importing surface geometry between formats and constructing a starting mesh in CAD

subject: eccentric spacer/bushing offset adjustment
