main_point: Avoid starting a loft directly on an existing part surface if that would require extending the loft just to make it intersect. Start the loft from a datum/reference plane instead to ensure clean intersection.
source_quote: I don't want to start this spoke at the surface of the hub as then my loft would need extending in order to fully intersect it. Instead, I will loft from the XZ plane.
example_value: The author chose to start the spoke loft from the XZ plane instead of the hub surface to avoid extending the loft.

subject: parallel plane creation via point and plane (Inventor)
main_point: In Autodesk Inventor, selecting a point and an existing plane when creating a work plane produces a plane parallel to the selected plane and passing through the chosen point. This is a quick way to place a plane offset at an arbitrary point.
source_quote: I created a plane by selecting the bottom point of my reference sketch, and the XZ plane before clicking plane. This automatically creates a plane that is parallel to the XZ plane and passes through that point.
example_value: A plane parallel to XZ was created by picking the reference sketch’s bottom point and the XZ plane.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor (including LT 2021) work plane creation tool

subject: reference sketches for loft sizing
main_point: Use separate reference sketches populated with the required dimensions to define the sizes of loft section profiles. This clarifies the intended thickness/width at each end before creating the loft.
source_quote: Create reference sketches, with the dimensioned values (11mm and 9.5mm in this view, and 22mm and 24mm in the other axis of the spoke).
example_value: Reference sketches used values 11 mm and 9.5 mm in one view, and 22 mm and 24 mm in the other axis.

subject: constraining ellipse profiles using projected geometry
main_point: To place ellipse profiles accurately for a loft, project key endpoints from reference sketches and constrain them coincident to the ellipse’s major and minor axes. This anchors the ellipses correctly to the predefined geometry.
source_quote: The two ellipses are easy to create by first projecting the endpoints of the reference sketches, and then making these coincident to the major and minor axes of the elipse.

subject: localized boundary stress as a modeling red flag in FEA
main_point: Strongly localized peak stresses right at a boundary are a warning sign of a modeling issue (e.g., constraints or mesh) rather than real material behavior. Treat such stress plots with suspicion and check your boundary conditions and mesh quality.
source_quote: First of all, whenever I see stresses so localised near the boundary, I always think that there is something wrong.

subject: overconstraining boundary conditions in FEA
main_point: Fully fixing an entire face can overconstrain a model, producing artificial stress components and inflated corner peaks that do not represent real stresses. Avoid blanket fixed constraints that suppress necessary degrees of freedom.
source_quote: IMHO, the max stress at corner is an artifact, probably due to overconstraining the model. I.e. I expect you have fixed the entire face, and as a result there is an additional (non-real) component of the stress.

subject: boundary condition strategy to prevent overconstraint in FEA
main_point: Instead of fixing the whole face, constrain only what’s needed: restrict the face’s normal translation, fully fix one corner, and fix the other corner in a single in‑plane direction. This prevents rigid-body motion without overconstraining the surface.
source_quote:
In any case, what you could do to test that is, change from fixing the entire surface to the following three conditions:

- fix the normal to the surface translation direction for the whole surface.
- fix one corner for all translation directions
- fix another corner to one of the inplane directions

subject: allowing Poisson contraction in FEA constraints
main_point: A constraint scheme that permits Poisson-driven in‑plane contraction/expansion provides adequate restraint while avoiding artificial stresses. With the same mesh, allowing these DOFs yields more reasonable stress results.
source_quote: That should provide adequate fixture to the model (I hope I am not forgetting a dof), and it will also let the model contract/expand due to the Poisson ratio. For the same mesh you should see more reasonable results.

subject: mesh refinement and stress convergence at corners (non-overconstrained model)
main_point: In a properly constrained model, coarse meshes under-report corner stresses due to averaging, while mesh refinement drives the stresses toward their converged values. This reflects expected FE convergence behavior when constraints are appropriate.
source_quote: Notice for the "not overconstrained model" that for the Coarse mesh, the stress at the corner is less (due to averaging). As the mesh becomes more refined, the stress converge to their "real" value.
example_value: In the author’s “not overconstrained” case, corner stress rose from about 24.8 kPa (5 mm) to ~26.7 kPa (2 mm) and ~26.1 kPa (1 mm), indicating convergence.

subject: fillet-region stress artifact in FEA
main_point: Apparent peak stresses near fillets can be artifacts of geometry/mesh that do not represent real material stresses. Treat fillet hot spots cautiously and verify whether they stem from modeling rather than physics.
source_quote: Additionally I expect that near the fillet area you also have a geometry/meshing artifact. I.e. the value does not correspond to real stresses.

subject: mesh refinement effect on fillet stress
main_point: Refining the mesh at a fillet often raises the reported peak stress, with the magnitude depending on the material model used. This behavior indicates a mesh/geometry-driven hot spot rather than a stable, physical stress value.
source_quote:
You can test that by refining the mesh size more (smaller elements). Depending on the material model you are using you should see 
a further increase
 (I did not misspell) of the stress at the fillet.
example_value: The author’s tables show max stress at a small-radius fillet increasing as element size decreases (e.g., from ~60.9 kPa at 5 mm to ~82.6 kPa at 1 mm for R=1).
example_context: FEA of fillet stress with different material models (e.g., linear elastic vs nonlinear)

subject: coarsening mesh to mitigate edge hot spots
main_point: Coarsening the mesh can suppress spurious edge hot spots by averaging, mitigating non-physical stress peaks. This is a numerical workaround to stabilize plots when investigating artifact-prone edges.
source_quote: By increasing the element size the problem should be mitigated around those edges.

subject: re-entrant fillet radius stress concentration
main_point: A small re-entrant fillet radius acts as a strong stress riser, producing a high localized stress concentration. Increasing the radius reduces the concentration and peak stress at that feature.
source_quote: You have a small re-entrant fillet radius which creates a large stress concentration.

subject: failure modes at stress concentrations
main_point: High stress concentrations at geometric discontinuities can trigger local failure modes: ductile materials may exhibit localized plastic yielding, while more brittle materials may initiate cracks.
source_quote: In real life, either there will be a small region of plastic yielding, or a crack will start to form.

subject: beam theory omission of stress concentrations
main_point: Simple hand calculations based on beam theory do not account for stress concentrations at geometric features, so they will underestimate peak stresses compared to FE results that resolve those details.
source_quote: If you are comparing the FE model with a hand calculation using beam theory (or something similar) the hand calculations ignore the stress concentration.

subject: rigid links with central load reactions
main_point: In a rigid-body model where two links are both fixed and a load is applied between them, the reactions are theoretically unbounded (tend toward infinity).
source_quote: when two rigid links are fixed and a force is applied in the middle, the reaction force in links tend to infinity.

subject: mesh density (node count) in FEA
main_point: If results look suspicious, refine the mesh by increasing the number of nodes to improve solution quality.
source_quote: Maybe you need to increase the number of nodes, avoid floating edges with restrictions or use fixed points not the entery plane.

subject: applying restrictions to floating edges in FEA
main_point: Avoid applying boundary-condition restrictions to floating edges in the model.
source_quote: Maybe you need to increase the number of nodes, avoid floating edges with restrictions or use fixed points not the entery plane.

subject: point constraints vs plane constraints in FEA
main_point: Use fixed-point constraints rather than constraining an entire plane when setting boundary conditions.
source_quote: Maybe you need to increase the number of nodes, avoid floating edges with restrictions or use fixed points not the entery plane.

subject: shear stress concentration at fillets
main_point: Filleted regions in a part develop localized increases in shear stress; the shear stress concentrates around the fillet geometry.
source_quote: there is shear stress concentration around the fillet.

subject: fillet radius effect on torsional stress concentration at a shoulder
main_point: In a stepped shaft under torsion, reducing the fillet radius at the shoulder increases shear stress concentration. A smaller radius makes the shear transition between the small and large diameters less gradual, elevating local stresses.
source_quote: the smaller the fillet radius, r the less ductility to transit gradually from high shear in smaller diameter shaft to the low shear in the larger shaft, the more stress concentration.
example_value: Transition from a smaller to a larger diameter shaft; decreasing fillet radius increases the stress concentration factor at the step.

subject: torsional failure risk at a stepped shaft shoulder
main_point: In a stepped shaft, the larger diameter section can behave as a rigid anchor under torque, causing the smaller diameter section to twist and fail near the shoulder if stresses concentrate there.
source_quote: Ultimately the larger D section can act as a rigid wise and just twist the small D part to failure.

subject: absence of fillet at diameter transition
main_point: A sharp corner (no fillet) at a diameter transition is highly prone to stress concentration and can easily fracture under load. Including a fillet at the shoulder mitigates this fragility.
source_quote: Imagine if there was no fillet that intersection would be so fragile it could easily break due to stress concentration as has been seen in many moving mechanical parts.

subject: shear stress line visualization
main_point: To visualize shear stress concentration, sketch shear stress flow lines and vary their density to represent the local stress magnitude. This provides an intuitive picture of where shear is higher or lower.
source_quote: There's nothing stopping you from drawing "shear stress lines" whose density corresponds to the stress magnitude.

subject: stress flow line quantitative limitations
main_point: Stress flow-line sketches are only qualitative; using them to predict or calculate quantitative stress values is unreliable. Rely on them for intuition, not for numerical results.
source_quote: These will have as much meaning as the "axial stress lines": useful for broad visualization and intuition but not really quantitatively predictive from a sketch.

subject: torque vector orientation in torsion
main_point: In torsion, the torque can be represented as a vector perpendicular to the plane of rotation, following the right-hand rule. Visualizing torque this way clarifies that the torsional moment is normal to the rotation plane.
source_quote:
The double curve sign notation is the vector of the torsional torque. That vector is normal to the plane of rotation. This is essentially an outcome of the 
right hand rule
.

subject: equivalence of torque sign conventions
main_point: The curved-arrow torsion symbol and the torque vector (double-arrow) notation are equivalent; both depict the same torsional loading on a beam.
source_quote: Both representations above represent the same loading condition on the beam.
example_value: Curved arrow indicating rotation vs a double-arrow/vector normal to the plane.

subject: visualizing shear stress using torque vector notation
main_point: Adopt the torque-vector notation for torsion to visualize shear stresses analogously to axial stress visualizations. This convention helps map stress directions in a way similar to axial loading.
source_quote: IF you use the second one you can visualise the shear stresses the same way you can for axial forces. i.e.
example_value: Using the vector-normal (second) representation instead of the curved arrow to reason about shear stresses.

subject: fillet root vs flat root spline root geometry
main_point: In spline design, fillet root splines blend the tooth space into the root diameter with a smooth curve, whereas flat root splines can include a flat section at the bottom of the tooth space.
source_quote: Fillet root splines have a smooth curve between adjacent teeth and the root diameter, flat root splines may not and will have a flat portion of tooth space between teeth.

subject: spline root fillet effect on bending strength and load capacity
main_point: Using a fillet at the spline tooth root increases bending strength at the root, which in turn raises the spline’s load capacity compared to flat-root forms.
source_quote: Fillet root teeth provide better bending strength and thus higher load capacity.

subject: fillet root spline definition
main_point: Per ISO 4156-1, a fillet root spline is defined such that both opposing flanks meet the root circle through one single continuous fillet.
source_quote:
spline having a tooth or space profile in which the opposing flanks are connected to the root circle (D
ei
 or D
ie
) by a 
single
 fillet.

subject: flat root spline definition
main_point: Per ISO 4156-1, a flat root spline is defined so that each opposing flank connects to the root circle via its own fillet, rather than a single shared fillet.
source_quote:
spline having a tooth or space profile in which 
each
 the opposing flanks are connected to the root circle (D
ei
 or D
ie
) by a fillet.

subject: flat root spline fillet presence
main_point: Flat root splines also include fillets at the root; the key difference from fillet root splines is not the presence of fillets but whether there is a single shared fillet or separate fillets per flank.
source_quote: The distinction is quite subtle, as even flat root splines have fillets.

subject: fillet radius and fatigue performance
main_point: Larger fillet radii at abrupt section changes reduce stress concentration and improve fatigue life. Increasing the radius at a step transition is a recognized method to enhance fatigue performance.
source_quote: Conventional engineering knowledge tells us that if we increase the fillet radii, we will get a better fatigue performance for this abrupt change in EI within this plate, which is great.
example_value: A steel plate with a milled step under load from above.

subject: mating part corner clearance limiting fillet radius
main_point: Increasing a pocket or step fillet radius can interfere with the mating part’s fit, making the mating component’s corner sharpness (or corner radius) the limiting factor for how large the fillet can be. Fillet sizing must balance stress reduction with assembly clearance at the interface.
source_quote: But a bigger fillet will also mean the item that this plate is supporting (which in this case fits into the milled area) becomes a limiting factor with how sharp their corners are.
example_value: The supported item fits into the milled area of the plate and its corner sharpness constrains the achievable fillet radius.

subject: hob cutter movement in gear hobbing
main_point: In typical gear hobbing, the hob remains fixed in position and only rotates on its own axis during cutting, with no translational motion relative to the work aside from depth feed.
source_quote: Other than turning so the cutting teeth can cut, the cutter in the hob doesn't normally move at all. It just sits in one spot, and turns on its axis.
example_context: typical gear hobbing operations

subject: gear tooth flank geometry from hobbing
main_point: Hob cutting yields a faceted approximation to the ideal curve, consisting of multiple straight-line facets tangent to the profile; with 3–5 facets (depending on gear size/pitch), the deviation is typically small.
source_quote: The teeth it produces don't really fit the curve you'd get in a normal drawing. Instead, you get a few (at least three, often 5, depending somewhat on the size/pitch of the gear you're cutting) straight lines that are tangent to the curve--and that's enough that the deviation from the curve is normally pretty minimal.
example_context: gear hobbing using typical hobs, with facet count depending on gear size/pitch

subject: indexed hobbing pass sequence
main_point: In the described method, each hob tooth cuts a single straight facet; the process is run through, the cutter is withdrawn, the gear is indexed by one tooth, and the cycle is repeated.
source_quote: So, each tooth of the hobb is cutting one straight facet. You run the cutter through to cut one set, pull it out, turn the gear one tooth, and repeat.
example_context: gear cutting operations where the hob creates discrete facets with indexing between passes

subject: running-in gears with abrasive to improve tooth form
main_point: A common practice is to lap gears by meshing them with abrasive and running them briefly, which rounds the faceted flanks toward a more accurate involute.
source_quote: Depending on how you're using the gear, you frequently want to "run it in"--mesh some gears together, add some grit, and spin them for a little bit, so the grit will round off the facets into something closer to a proper involute form.
example_context: post-processing of gears with faceted tooth flanks to improve form

subject: worm gear hobbing kinematics
main_point: In worm gear cutting, there is circular relative motion of the work, but the hob itself still spins in place; the cutter’s helical teeth drive the workpiece rotation as they cut.
source_quote: When you're cutting something like a worm gear, you do get "circular" movement, but in most cases that's more like your first picture--the hobb still just spins in place, but the angled teeth of the cutter turn the work-piece as they cut it.
example_context: cutting worm gears with a hob

subject: power transmission selection (gears vs chain/belt)
main_point: Use geared meshing or a chain/belt drive to couple offset shafts; select the transmission type based on the torque, speed, and power requirements. Adding teeth to the driver and a gear to the driven shaft enables direct gear mesh; otherwise use a chain or belt if better suited to the load/speed profile.
source_quote: Put teeth on the circumference of the driver and then a gear on the shaft of the driven. Either they can mesh or use a chain or belt drive - depends on the torque/speed/power...

subject: hydraulic link consideration for space-constrained drives
main_point: In space-constrained layouts, consider a hydraulic link, but first define how tightly the speed ratio must be maintained. If constant ratio is required, verify whether the hydraulic system can meet that tolerance.
source_quote: Of course if space is an issue consider a hydraulic link but is the speed ratio to be held constant or is there an acceptable tolerance.

subject: gear placement to couple offset shafts
main_point: Place gears on both shafts at a different axial position (e.g., below the wheels) to achieve meshing when the primary wheel positions are offset. This relocates the gear engagement without changing the wheel alignment.
source_quote: Another option is to put gears on both shafts but below the two existing wheels.

subject: chains/pulleys for fixed shaft positions
main_point: Use a chain or belt/pulley drive when the driver and driven shafts maintain a fixed relative position; it’s a straightforward way to transmit torque across an offset when alignment does not change.
source_quote: - chains/pulleys : if the position of the shafts is fixed
example_context: power transmission between two shafts whose relative positions are fixed

subject: Schmidt linkage for parallel-axis translation while coupled
main_point: Select a Schmidt linkage when one rotational axis must translate parallel to the other while remaining mechanically coupled to transmit rotation.
source_quote: - Schmidt linkage  ( Video for operation ): if you want to move parallel one axis of rotation with the others.
example_context: mechanisms requiring coupling between parallel but laterally offset shafts where one axis may move parallel to the other

subject: swivel joint + lever arm linkage for wheels
main_point: Use a swivel joint connector on the dependent wheel and link it to the driving wheel’s anchor point with a lever arm as the recommended linkage between the wheels.
source_quote: You should connect one of these swivel joint connectors, or similar, on the dependent wheel, and connect to the driving wheel's anchor point by a lever arm.
example_value: Reference to DSTI swivel joints as a candidate component.
example_context: Mechanical linkage between a driving wheel and a dependent wheel using a lever arm.

subject: shaft extension with coupling
main_point: A straightforward way to address an offset drive is to extend the motor shaft using a same-diameter shaft segment joined with a shaft coupling. This lets you relocate the drive point without complex linkages.
source_quote: It is easy to extend the shaft, all you need is a shaft of the same diameter and 25cm long and a coupling,
example_value: Author suggests a 25 cm long same-diameter shaft section joined via a coupling.

subject: chain drive suitability at high torque
main_point: For the torque level discussed, a chain drive is the preferred transmission choice. It is better suited to higher torque loads than alternatives considered in the thread.
source_quote: With that kind of torque a chain drive would be more suitable.
example_value: The post refers to about 50 Nm torque.
example_context: Power transmission selection for roughly 50 Nm torque applications

subject: torque-to-force equivalence at radius
main_point: A torque of 50 Nm produces a force roughly equivalent to lifting 50 kg when applied at a 0.1 m radius. This offers a quick way to gauge the load magnitude from torque.
source_quote: 50 Nm is quite a high torque, at 10 cm radius that's like lifting 50 kg!

subject: radial variation and step change of E and CTE in a cladded cylinder
main_point: In a bimetallic (cladded) cylinder, E and CTE vary with radius and jump at the interface, so they cannot be treated as constants when integrating to compute thermal stresses. The integration must explicitly handle the step change at the material boundary.
source_quote: It is made a bit more difficult than the case of a single material since the Young’s modulus (E) and coefficient of thermal expansion (cte) vary spatially as a function of the radial position; therefore it cannot be assumed constant and must be considered in the integration. At the boundary between the cladding and cylinder, there is a step change in the material properties due to the material discontinuity.
example_context: bimetallic/cladded cylinders with dissimilar materials across the wall thickness

subject: numerical evaluation of axial thermal-stress integral
main_point: The axial stress integral in this thermoelastic cylinder analysis is commonly evaluated numerically rather than in closed form, using methods like the trapezoidal or Simpson’s rule.
source_quote: and the integral is usually solved numerically using trapezoidal/simpson's rule.
example_context: evaluating the Hooke’s-law-based axial stress integral across a cylinder’s thickness from a through-wall temperature profile

subject: initial uniform temperature assumption
main_point: This class of analytical thermoelastic solutions requires the wall to start at a uniform reference temperature; if the initial temperature field is not homogeneous, the solution’s validity is compromised.
source_quote: The analytical solution is only valid in so far as the wall temperature is initially homogeneous at some reference temperature.
example_context: analytical transient thermoelastic stress solution for a thick-walled bi-metallic cylinder

subject: reference temperature for thermal strain integration
main_point: When computing thermal stresses, integrate using temperature relative to the initial reference (ΔT = T_current − T_ref), not the absolute temperature field.
source_quote: The temperature distribution used in the integration is therefore the temperature relative to this initial reference state (i.e. T = T_current - T_ref).
example_value: After switching to ΔT in the integration, the Hooke’s-law stress history matched the finite element solution almost exactly.

subject: percent thread depth selection in hard materials
main_point: For harder materials, target a lower percent thread (about 50–60%) so the fastener will fail in tension before the internal threads strip. This guides tap drill size selection to bias failure mode away from thread shear.
source_quote: It goes on to suggest using lower thread depths (50%-60%) for harder materials, to ensure the bolt breaks before the thread strips.
example_context: tapped internal threads in harder materials

subject: strength benefit vs thread percentage
main_point: Beyond roughly 75% thread engagement, further increasing percent thread provides little additional joint strength. This is why tap drill charts commonly target about 75% thread depth.
source_quote: The book explains that tap drill charts usually show a 75% thread depth, because a greater percentage of thread does not increase the strength appreciably.
example_context: tap drill chart recommendations for standard threads

subject: percent thread depth definition
main_point: Percent thread depth is the ratio of the actual cut thread height (trapezoid after crest truncation) to the height of the ideal theoretical thread form (full triangle), independent of the specific thread standard.
source_quote: thread percent should be the height of the trapezoid of the actual cut thread relative to the triangle of the theoretically ideal thread, regardless of how that ideal thread has been specified.

subject: tap drill size effect on thread percentage
main_point: Increasing the tap drill diameter reduces percent thread engagement because it removes more of the thread crest, decreasing the resulting thread height.
source_quote: If I drill a larger hole before tapping, then lower thread percentage because more of the peak forming the minor diameter is lopped off.

subject: condition for 100% thread engagement
main_point: A pre-drilled hole equal to the tap’s minor diameter yields 100% thread engagement since the thread crest is left intact.
source_quote: If I drill a hole to match the minor diameter of the tap then 100% thread because none of the peak has been removed.

subject: condition for 0% thread engagement
main_point: If the tap drill diameter equals the tap’s major diameter, the thread crests are completely removed and no thread forms (0% thread).
source_quote: 0% thread is where my tap drill is the same diameter as the major diameter of the tap. So much of the peak of the thread has been removed that there is no thread at all.

subject: percent thread depth calculation constant
main_point: Many reference tap drill/percentage tables, including Machinery’s Handbook, compute thread percentage using a 1.299 constant in their formulas.
source_quote: Just take note that a lot of tables (even the machinery's book) give the percentage result using 1.299
example_value: Machinery’s Handbook tables use 1.299 for thread percentage calculations.
example_context: tap drill charts and Machinery’s Handbook thread percentage tables

subject: FreeCAD Datum Line vs Sketcher Construction Geometry
main_point: In FreeCAD, a Datum Line exists at the body level, while analogous reference geometry within a sketch is provided by Sketcher’s Construction Geometry.
source_quote: I learned that a Datum Line is a body feature, and that the Sketcher has something similar in the Construction Geometry.
example_context: FreeCAD PartDesign/Sketcher usage

subject: Arc orientation via construction line angle constraint in FreeCAD Sketcher
main_point: To control an arc’s orientation in FreeCAD Sketcher, draw a line through the arc’s endpoints and constrain the angle of that line; then toggle the line to Construction Geometry so it drives the angle without becoming real model geometry.
source_quote: If I add a straight line through both end points of the arc, it is easy to add a constraint on the angle of that line. But I don't want that line there. With the Construction Geometry toggle button I can change the real line into a dotted line, which is not a real line, but still useful to create the desired angle constraint.
example_value: The line becomes a dotted construction line yet remains usable to enforce the desired angle constraint.
example_context: FreeCAD Sketcher with Construction Geometry

subject: equal planet spacing divisibility condition
main_point: For evenly spaced planets in a planetary gearset, the sum of the ring and sun gear tooth counts divided by the number of planets must be an integer. In other words, (R + S) must be exactly divisible by the number of planets.
source_quote:
There is another rule I've found that states that to allow equidistant spacing of the planets in the arrangement, 
R + S / number of planets
 must be an integer with no remainder.
example_value: With R=66, S=12, and 3 planets, (66 + 12) / 3 = 26 (an integer), so the spacing condition is satisfied.

subject: planetary gear pitch circle tangency
main_point: In a classic planetary gearset, each planet's pitch circle is tangent to both the sun and the ring gear pitch circles, implying perfect rolling at both meshes.
source_quote: Most of the literature an examples of planetary gearsets that I've seen so far have described a relationship where the pitch circle of the planet gear(s) is tangent to both the pitch circle of the sun gear and the ring gear simultaneously.

subject: ring-sun-planet tooth count relation
main_point: For a simple planetary gearset with planets tangent to both sun and ring, the ring gear tooth count equals the sun plus twice the planet tooth count (R = S + 2P).
source_quote:
Most examples also follow this relationship:

R = 2P + S

subject: gear profile shift
main_point: Using profile shift, a gear’s pitch circle can be intentionally shifted away from the standard reference diameter while still achieving proper mesh.
source_quote: Profile shift allows to move the pitch circle of a gear off the reference diameter.

subject: center distance vs gear ratio with profile shift
main_point: Applying profile shift makes it possible to design gears that mesh at a center distance different from the one implied by the nominal transmission ratio.
source_quote: Thus you can create a meshing pair of gears where the "center distance of a cylindrical gear pair" does not correspond to the transmission ratio.

subject: planet gear operating pitch diameters
main_point: A planet gear can be designed with different effective pitch diameters for its meshes with the sun and with the ring gear.
source_quote: The planet gears have two different pitch diameters.  One for the planet sun interface and one for the planet ring interface.
example_context: planetary gearsets where a planet meshes simultaneously with a sun (external) gear and a ring (internal) gear

subject: planetary gear interface pressure angles
main_point: The operating pressure angle at the planet–sun mesh can differ from that at the planet–ring mesh.
source_quote: Each interface will also have a different pressure angle.
example_context: planetary gearsets where a planet meshes with both a sun and a ring gear

subject: common base circle and conjugate meshing
main_point: Even with differing operating pitch diameters and pressure angles at the two interfaces, the design can use a single base circle and still achieve conjugate meshing.
source_quote: But there is one base circle.  The mesh can be conjugate.
example_context: planetary gearsets where a planet meshes simultaneously with a sun and a ring gear

subject: SolidWorks shell feature uniform offset on arcs
main_point: Using a 5 mm Shell operation applies a uniform 5 mm offset to arcs as well as straight edges, not a different arc offset.
source_quote: if you look at my drawing, i used shell with 5mm, this offsets even the arc with 5mm.
example_value: The user modeled the part and observed that applying a 5 mm shell offset also moved the arc inward by 5 mm.
example_context: SolidWorks part modeling using the Shell feature

subject: shaft key bearing stress calculation formula
main_point: A common design approach for keyed joints computes bearing (compressive) stress on the key as p = (M/R)/(Le·t), where torque divided by shaft radius gives the tangential force and Le·t is the projected bearing area on the key. This provides an approximate check against allowable compressive stress for the hub/shaft/key interface.
source_quote:
The usual formula is

$$p = rac{F}{A} = rac{rac{M}{R}}{L_e \cdot t}$$

subject: keyway depth approximation for bearing area
main_point: In bearing stress calculations for keys, the keyway depth t is often approximated as half the key height (t ≈ h/2) to estimate the loaded area.
source_quote: The $t$ can be sometimes replaced by $\frac{h}{2}$, where $h$ is key height.

subject: torsional shear stress formula
main_point: In the linear-elastic range, shear stress in a shaft under torque varies linearly with radius and is given by τ = (M/I_p)·r. This relation applies at a distance r from the shaft center when using the polar moment of inertia I_p.
source_quote:
In your particular case the stress is the shear stress from the torque, which can be calculated at a distance r from the center by the following equation (provided you are still in the elastic/linear region):

$$\tau = \frac{M}{I_p} r$$
example_context: linear-elastic torsion of shafts (using polar moment of inertia I_p)

subject: relation between stress and differential force
main_point: The differential force on a small surface element equals the local stress times the differential area: dF = τ·dA. This enables integrating distributed contact forces from a known stress field.
source_quote:
If you have the shear stress then you can calculate the force F  acting on a small area as:

$$dF(r) = \tau(r) dA$$

subject: polar moment of inertia for keywayed shaft geometry
main_point: For a solid circular shaft, the polar moment is I_p = (π/2)·r^4, but introducing a keyway makes determining I_p nontrivial. This added geometric complexity complicates torsional stress calculations.
source_quote:
The polar moment of inertia can be easily calculated for a circular disk 
$I_p = \frac{\pi }{2}r^4$
, however with the keyhole things get slightly complicated.
example_context: shafts with a key hole/keyway (non-circular cross-section)

subject: stress concentration at keyway corners
main_point: Keyway corners create stress concentrations whose magnitude depends on the fillet radius and is difficult to predict accurately, which can increase error in analytical stress/force estimates. Designs or calculations that ignore this effect risk underestimating local stresses.
source_quote: Near the corner of the key hole, there will be stress concentration which will be depending on the radius and cannot be accurately predicted, thus increasing the error.
example_context: keyway/key hole corner regions with finite fillet radii

subject: F=M/r force estimate in keyed shaft design
main_point: Using F = M/r to represent the force corresponding to applied torque is an adequate approximation for practical keyed-shaft design calculations, without resolving components.
source_quote:
The simple answer is

$$
F=M/r
$$

and that is acceptable for practical purposes.
example_context: shaft key design calculations for torque transmission

subject: treatment of force components in key design practice
main_point: Typical keyed-joint design practice does not separate total force from its normal component (Fx) when performing calculations.
source_quote: That distinction is not considered in typical design practice.
example_context: typical mechanical design practice for keyed shafts

subject: stress distribution across key contact
main_point: Contact pressure along a key is inherently non-uniform; assuming uniform compressive stress is an oversimplification.
source_quote: The complicated answer starts with noting that the stress distribution in keys is not uniform.

subject: midplane contact-induced stress singularity in keys
main_point: At the key’s midplane where it contacts both shaft and hub, the geometry/contact conditions cause singular stress concentrations, invalidating a uniform-stress assumption there.
source_quote: contact with the shaft and hub at the midplane of the key leads to singular stress concentrations.

subject: FEA for key stress analysis
main_point: For detailed, realistic assessment of non-uniform and concentrated stresses in keyed joints, prefer finite element analysis over textbook approximations.
source_quote: Finite element modeling is probably the best tool for answering your question with more sophistication than is offered by textbooks.
example_context: analyzing detailed stress distribution in keyed shaft–hub interfaces beyond uniform-stress assumptions

subject: spline-based CNC toolpaths for G2 continuity
main_point: Some CNC CAM-generated toolpaths use splines to achieve (approximate) G2 curvature continuity, yielding smoother machine motion than lower-continuity paths.
source_quote: I've heard of CNC tool paths using splines to approximate G2 continuity to create smoother motion.
example_context: CNC CAM toolpaths using spline curves for motion smoothing

subject: G2 curvature continuity in rollercoaster track design
main_point: Using G2 curvature continuity in rollercoaster track transitions avoids abrupt curvature jumps that a mere G1 join would cause, reducing shock/jerk on riders and structure.
source_quote: Also, rollercoaster designs use G2 continuity to reduce shock from sudden changes in curve radius that would otherwise result from a G1 curve between two sections.
example_context: Rollercoaster track geometry and transition design

subject: sweep profile orientation on helical path
main_point: Kinks can appear where coiled-pipe sections meet if the swept cross-section is kept vertical relative to the model rather than oriented perpendicular (normal) to the path. To maintain smoothness, orient the pipe’s circular profile normal to the end of the coil/path.
source_quote: they also had kinks in the pipe that should not be there.  I figured this was a mainly a result of the pipes circles remaining vertical instead of perpendicular to the end of the coil path.
example_value: The model visually matched views but showed kinks; the author suspects the pipe’s circular profiles remained vertical instead of being perpendicular to the helical path.

subject: helix uncoiling requires accounting for slope/pitch
main_point: Unrolling or "uncoiling" a helical segment cannot be based on circular arc length alone; you must account for the helix’s axial slope/pitch. Using only π/2·R for a quarter turn will misplace lengths or tangency points.
source_quote: Though as I just typed that I realize my simple uncoil may not have been correct as it did not account for the helix's slope, just the circle.
example_value: The author computed the 1/4-turn length as PI/2*Radius, then realized this ignored the helix’s slope.

subject: unrolling a helix quarter-turn length
main_point: For modeling a quarter turn transition of a helix, treating the unrolled length as one quarter of the helix’s base circumference can be used to locate geometry. This uses 1/4 of the helix diameter’s circumference as the linear measure for that segment.
source_quote: The methodology for unrolling the helix is valid.  Just needed to determine 1/4 of the circumference of the helix's diameter.
example_value: The author used 1/4 of the circumference of the helix’s diameter to place the unrolled point corresponding to a 1/4 turn.
example_context: Laying out coil end geometry when modeling a pipe helix transition in CAD

subject: centerline lying on offset extruded surface
main_point: If you extrude the end-arc and its tangent by the helix radius to form a curved surface, the pipe’s centerline must lie on that surface. This offset-surface construction constrains the centerline path for the transition.
source_quote: I then extruded the arc, and the tangent apparently (can't figure out how to limit the selection of joined lines), by the radius of the helix (and maybe a tad more to be on the safe side) to create a curved surface.  The centerline has to be somewhere on this surface.
example_value: The poster extruded the 35 mm radius arc and tangent by the helix radius to locate the centerline surface.
example_context: Constructing centerline paths for a coiled pipe end transition in CAD

subject: projecting 3D line onto curved surface to create path
main_point: To derive a transition curve constrained to a surface, draw a 3D straight line between key points and project it onto the previously created curved surface. This yields a surface-conforming path usable as a centerline.
source_quote: I then projected the straight line onto the arc's curved surface that was previous created and that resulted in a nice line (yellow) in my opinion.
example_value: A straight 3D line connecting the helix edge and arc bottom was projected onto the extruded curved surface to produce the path.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor 3D sketch workflow for pipe centerline creation on a curved surface

subject: Inventor projection behavior and 3D sketch project-to-surface workaround
main_point: In Inventor, projecting geometry while sketching on a plane projects normal to that plane; to control the projection onto a specific plane/surface, use a 3D sketch and Project to Surface, which accepts a constructed plane as the target.
source_quote: Attempt 1 was a failure as I decided to sketch on the plane and project geometry...while it did that, but it does it in the direction normal to the plane.  NOT what I wanted.  So I started a 3D sketch and tried to project sketch 3 on to a surface hoping the newly created plane would count as a surface.  I got lucky and it worked!
example_value: The author constructed a plane through three points; planar sketch projection was normal-only, so they switched to a 3D sketch and successfully projected the curve onto the plane treated as a surface.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor projection tools when mapping 2D geometry onto a plane not normal to the view

subject: creating a profile plane normal to a path endpoint
main_point: Create a construction plane normal to the path at its endpoint to place the sweep profile precisely perpendicular to the runout direction. Selecting the path segment and its end point defines this plane.
source_quote: I created a plane normal to an axis at a point.  I chose the 40 mm line and the end point of it.
example_value: They selected the 40 mm straight runout line and its endpoint to define a plane normal to that axis before sketching the pipe cross-section.
example_context: Autodesk Inventor sweep setup for pipe modeling

subject: outer-surface stress maxima under bending and torsion
main_point: For a loaded beam or shaft under combined bending and torsion, the critical points for maximum stresses are at the outer surface (top and bottom fibers). At these locations, bending normal stress and torsional shear stress are maximized, while transverse (vertical) shear stress goes to zero at the surface.
source_quote: I am assuming that the points that will experience the greatest stresses are most likely the top and bottom edges of the beam, where both bending and torsional stresses are maximised (and vertical shear stresses are zero).

subject: beam modeling choice (cantilever vs simply supported)
main_point: If the structure actually behaves as a cantilever, analyze it as a cantilever rather than as a simply supported beam; the bending moment at the fixed support then follows directly from the cantilever model.
source_quote:
Why don't you model the beam as a cantilever which it is? Or maybe I am confused and will try to modify my answer if you clarify in a comment.

In that case, the bending moment at C will simply be:

$$M_c = \frac{F}{2}C$$
example_value: For the OP’s geometry, the bending moment at support C is Mc = (F/2)·C.
example_context: beams fixed at one end (cantilever boundary condition)

subject: ASME alignment with ANSI drafting standard
main_point: ASME drafting conventions align with ANSI rather than ISO, meaning ASME-based drawings follow ANSI-style practices.
source_quote: ASME follows the ANSI drafting standard.
example_context: Engineering drawing standards (ASME Y14-series vs ANSI vs ISO)

subject: mixing of ANSI and ISO drafting conventions in company standards
main_point: Because ANSI and ISO each allow alternative practices from the other, many organizations combine elements of both and end up with hybrid, company-specific drafting standards.
source_quote: Both ANSI and ISO have adopted many of the other standard as an alternative, so many companies have mixed and matched the drafting standards to create their own, oddball standard.
example_context: Organizations implementing engineering drawing standards (ANSI and/or ISO)

subject: dimension text orientation (ANSI vs ISO)
main_point: ANSI requires dimension text to be read horizontally, whereas ISO aligns the text parallel to the dimension line.
source_quote: ANSI dimensions are read horizontally. ISO dimensions are parallel to the dimension line.
example_context: Dimensioning conventions in ANSI vs ISO drafting standards

subject: dimension text placement relative to dimension line (ANSI vs ISO)
main_point: ANSI centers dimension text on the dimension line, while ISO places the text above the dimension line.
source_quote: ANSI dimensions are centered on the dimension line. ISO dimension are placed above the dimension line.
example_context: Dimensioning conventions in ANSI vs ISO drafting standards

subject: abbreviations vs symbols in ANSI and ISO dimensioning
main_point: ANSI dimensioning favors textual abbreviations, whereas ISO relies on symbolic notation for features and counts.
source_quote: ANSI tends to use abbreviations. ISO uses symbols. (example: RAD, DIAM, 3 PLACES versus R, Ø, 3X)
example_value: Example given: ANSI uses RAD, DIAM, 3 PLACES; ISO uses R, Ø, 3X.
example_context: Dimensioning conventions in ANSI vs ISO drafting standards

subject: dimension callout syntax (ANSI vs ISO)
main_point: ANSI and ISO differ in the ordering and notation of dimension callouts, with ANSI placing the value and descriptor before multiplicity, and ISO placing multiplicity first followed by symbol and value.
source_quote:
dimensions have a different syntax.
ANSI: 1.000 DIAM 3 PLACES
ISO: 3X Ø 1
example_value: ANSI example: 1.000 DIAM 3 PLACES; ISO example: 3X Ø 1
example_context: Dimensioning conventions in ANSI vs ISO drafting standards

subject: internal pressure distribution in closed vessels
main_point: In a closed pressure vessel, the internal pressure is spatially uniform, so differences in stress between directions are not due to pressure gradients. Any directional stress differences arise from geometry and loading configuration, not from non-uniform pressure.
source_quote:
Actually, 
the pressure inside the vessel is uniform and constant everywhere
.

subject: hoop vs axial stress in thin-walled cylinders
main_point: For thin-walled cylinders under internal pressure, hoop (circumferential) stress exceeds axial (longitudinal) stress regardless of the pressure level. Design and failure assessment should therefore consider hoop stress as the governing stress direction.
source_quote: What you should understand is that independent of the pressure the stresses in the circuferential direction are always greater than the axial stresses.

subject: pressure-relief slits in thin-walled vessels
main_point: Introducing slits or vent features into a thin-walled, pressure-containing skin provides a path for pressure relief, reducing internal pressure buildup and lowering the driving stress for rupture.
source_quote:
What this do is:
a) They relieve internal pressure
example_value: Slitting a hot dog casing before heating prevents bursting by venting pressure.

subject: crack arrest features (slits)
main_point: Pre-made slits act as crack arrestors: if a crack initiates, it will terminate at the slit, limiting propagation and reducing the likelihood of catastrophic tearing.
source_quote: b) if crack start to develop, the slits arrest the development of the crack early on.
example_value: Pre-slit hot dog skins limit tearing by stopping cracks at the slit edges.

subject: hoop vs axial stress ratio in thin-walled cylinders
main_point: Using thin-walled cylinder formulas, the circumferential (hoop) membrane stress is twice the axial (longitudinal) stress; equivalently, hoop stress can be expressed as PD/(2t).
source_quote: In the old days we used the formula- Stress = PD/2t , and the hoop stress was twice the axial /longitudinal stress .

subject: pressure vessel head thickness vs shell thickness
main_point: A common design practice was to make pressure vessel heads about half the shell wall thickness, justified by the heads experiencing lower stress than the cylindrical walls.
source_quote: Pressure vessel heads were usually half the thickness of the walls because of the lower stress relative to the walls.
example_context: Conventional pressure vessel design where head stresses are lower than cylindrical shell stresses (e.g., standard head geometries under internal pressure).

subject: hidden lines in section views
main_point: There are two common drafting conventions for section views: one shows only the material at the cutting plane (no hidden lines), while the other also includes nearby hidden features that are relevant to the detail, omitting distant or irrelevant items.
source_quote: When it come to sections I have heard two schools of thought this. School A is basically just like the computer and you only include what is in the cutting plane. This means you would never have a hidden line in a section. Kind of the way computers cut sections through solids, at least in the early days. School B says when you have a section you also include include nearby hidden items, but not things that are far away/have no bearing on what you are trying to convey.

subject: CAD dashed linetype intersection behavior
main_point: In many CAD systems, dashed/dotted linetypes are generated between a line’s endpoints without adjusting at intersections, so a crossing can fall on a gap and leave a visible white space at the intersection.
source_quote: it appears to me that dashes and dots are just proportioned between end points of the lin with no regard if they intersect with a another dashed line. This mean you occasionally get white space where lines cross.
example_context: Many CAD programs' linetype generation behavior for dashed/dotted lines

subject: breaking dashed lines at intersections to control linetype phase
main_point: A common workaround for dashed-line crossings that show a gap is to split the line at the intersection so a dash starts there, which improves appearance but fragments the geometry and can complicate measuring the line’s total length.
source_quote: Alternatively one can break the line so it has an end point at the point of intersection. This forces a solid line to appear at intersection point. Looks better, but now if you want to get the length of the line the line is broken into small segments potentially.
example_context: CAD drafting where dashed linetype generation does not align with intersections

subject: 2D CAD drafting limitations
main_point: 2D CAD tools typically do not detect drafting issues such as hidden-line crossings or dimension lines touching object lines, so these errors can persist unless the drafter corrects them.
source_quote: Computer 2D drawing has limitations (no detection of crossing of invisible lines, dimension lines touching the solid lines, and lots of others), and cad programs simply don't care about these kind of things (and I hate this aspect, but we work with what we got).

subject: bending drafting rules for clarity
main_point: It is acceptable to relax strict drafting rules when it improves clear communication of the object and its details.
source_quote: Isn't uncommon to bend the rules a little bit maintainning this mindset.

subject: dimensioning to hidden lines
main_point: Do not dimension to hidden (invisible) lines; this is considered poor practice.
source_quote: Front view, dimensions using invisible lines, realy? This is one definite no-go by what I know.

subject: placing dimensions inside part boundaries
main_point: Avoid placing dimensions inside the part outline because it reduces readability.
source_quote: And dimensions inside of the piece is not a good idea too (dificult readability).

subject: hidden lines in section views
main_point: Section views should not include hidden lines, and near-miss or partial hidden lines are especially misleading and must be avoided.
source_quote: No invisible lines in section, and absolutelly no partial (only close) invisible lines this is asking for misunderstanding.

subject: hidden lines in hatched metal sections
main_point: For metal parts with hatched sections, omit hidden lines because they are harder to read within the hatch.
source_quote: No hidden lines shown. I'm from school A, but for metal hatching (like this piece) using hidden lines would be harder to locate, so not showing would be the best.
example_context: technical drawings of metal parts with hatched section views

subject: hatching of reinforcing parts in section
main_point: Reinforcing parts follow the same convention as bolts and rivets in sections and generally are not hatched when cut.
source_quote: For reinforcing parts in hatching the rule is the same as bolts and rivets, and don't need to hatch.
example_context: mechanical drafting conventions for sectioning of fasteners and reinforcing members

subject: dimension balancing across views
main_point: Distribute dimensions across different views to balance the drawing and improve readability.
source_quote: The secret here is dimension balancing, you distribute the dimensions between views to improve readability.

subject: minimum number of orthographic views
main_point: Provide three or more orthographic views, even for simple parts, to aid understanding.
source_quote: A good rule of thumb is ever use 3 or more views (even for simple objects).

subject: depicting countersinks in views
main_point: When a countersink is required, depict it explicitly in the top view and in the front view using hidden lines or a partial section.
source_quote: If the countersink is necessary then you show in the drawing. Show in top view (like you've done) and show in front view with invisible lines (or in partial cut like in the example you've seen)

subject: representing curved-surface intersections
main_point: Do not add intersection lines where a curved surface meets another if no true edge exists; draw only what is actually visible in the view.
source_quote: Is not true, the normal procedure is to draw as you see the view (no line because there's no real edge)

subject: inferring radii from multiple views
main_point: Providing at least three views allows readers to recognize curved features like radii without adding artificial lines.
source_quote: With at least 3 views (the minimum number of views necessary) the radius will be easily recognized even without a line.

subject: rack tooth flank flatness in involute meshing
main_point: In involute gear meshing, the common normal at the point of contact is a fixed straight line tangent to the base circles. When one member is a rack, its tooth flank must align with this contact normal, so the rack’s contact surface is flat rather than an involute curve.
source_quote: Standard (circular) involute gears have a stationary contact normal. It is usually a line, that is tangential to the base radii of the two gears. When you replace one gear with a rack, then for the meshing to be the same on the gear, the rack needs to be compliant to the given contact normal. From the stationary contact normal you can easily follow, that the contact surface must be flat.

subject: involute of infinite base circle interpretation for racks
main_point: Reasoning about a rack’s profile via an "infinite base circle" is misleading; the theoretical involute of an infinite-radius base circle collapses to a point. The rack’s straight flank comes from matching the stationary contact normal, not from an involute of an infinite circle.
source_quote: The observation of an infinite base radius (on the rack) may be misleading, because the (theoretical) involute of the racks (infinite) base circle would be a point.

subject: involute geometry at infinite base circle
main_point: In involute gearing, as the base circle diameter approaches infinity (the rack case), the involute profile becomes a straight line. This explains why rack teeth have straight flanks instead of curved involutes.
source_quote: If the diameter of the base circle of a gear is increased without limit, the base circle will become a straight line. If the "string" wrapped around this base circle to generate the involute were still in place after the base circle's enlargement to an infinite radius, the string would be pivoted at infinity and would generate an involute that is a straight line.

subject: metal pneumatic tubing fitting systems
main_point: For connecting metal pneumatic tubing, two commonly used fitting systems are cutting ring fittings and press fittings.
source_quote:
As far as I know, two commonly used systems are 
cutting ring fittings
 and 
press fittings
.
example_context: Pneumatic metal tubing connections using cutting ring fittings or press fittings

subject: installation clearance for cutting ring and press fittings
main_point: Cutting ring and press fittings require installation clearance; if the layout doesn’t allow enough space, you won’t be able to install them properly.
source_quote: Note that both need some space for installation.
example_context: Using cutting ring or press fittings in pneumatic tubing assemblies

subject: push-in connector systems for pipe
main_point: Push-in connector systems exist that allow a pipe to be inserted directly into the fitting without separate flaring or pressing steps.
source_quote: there are systems where you simply push the pipe into a connector
example_context: Pneumatic piping systems using push-in style connectors

subject: SolidWorks helix/spiral tool with global variables
main_point: In SolidWorks, drive the conical spring using the built‑in helix/spiral feature tied to global variables so that edits to those variables trigger an automatic rebuild.
source_quote: What I can do is demonstrate how you could apply your global variables to the built-in helix/spiral tool, such that the you can edit your variables in exactly the same way, and it automatically rebuilds whenever you edit a global variable value.
example_value: Applied to a conical spring model controlled by ri, rf, H, nc, and d.
example_context: SolidWorks helix/spiral feature driven by global variables

subject: SolidWorks Enter key behavior in value/equation boxes
main_point: Pressing Enter in a SolidWorks value/equation input box issues a standard rebuild (Ctrl+B), causing the model to update.
source_quote: (SW sends a CTRL+B when you press enter in the value/equation box).
example_context: SolidWorks value/equation input boxes

subject: Equation-driven curve vs helix/spiral rebuild performance in SolidWorks
main_point: An equation‑driven curve model for the spring rebuilt roughly four times slower than a helix/spiral‑based model.
source_quote:
Your supplied model using the equation curve takes almost 
four times
 as long to rebuild.
example_value: Measured on the OP’s provided conical spring model; later features were removed to compare initial sweep rebuild times fairly.
example_context: SolidWorks conical spring modeled with equation-driven curve versus helix/spiral feature

subject: SolidWorks Simulation failure with rubber material loads
main_point: The poster observed that their SolidWorks Simulation failed when a load was applied to a model with the material set to rubber, whereas switching to alloy steel allowed them to proceed. This suggests that, in their setup, analyses with rubber-like materials under load did not solve successfully.
source_quote: Below is an image using alloy steel because the simulation kept failing if I applied a load to rubber?
example_value: A bent right-angled tube model with material set to natural rubber failed to solve under load, so the user switched the material to alloy steel to generate an image.
example_context: SolidWorks Simulation on a bent right-angled tube with material set to natural rubber; applying a load to the model caused solver failure.

subject: PL annotation (number of identical feature locations)
main_point: In technical drawings, the PL (places) annotation indicates how many locations share the specified feature; for example, 0.430R 2PL means there are two arcs of radius 0.430 at different locations on the part.
source_quote: Your guess is correct. "0.430R 2PL" means there are two places where there is a curve with the given radius.
example_value: Annotation example: "0.430R 2PL" denotes two arcs with radius 0.430.

subject: Use of PL notation to avoid repeating identical dimensions
main_point: PL annotations are often applied to repeated small features (e.g., many identical holes) to show the count in one note instead of dimensioning each feature separately, such as 0.1R 36PL.
source_quote: This is more commonly used for things like small holes, where you might see something like "0.1R 36PL" rather than each one of the 36 holes being dimensioned individually.
example_value: Example note: "0.1R 36PL" for an array of 36 identical small holes.

subject: frictional torque capacity vs radius
main_point: Increasing the effective radius of the friction interface raises the moment arm, so a given torque can be resisted with less frictional force (and thus lower required clamp load). Therefore, making the flange contact diameter larger reduces the needed friction force to prevent slip under the same torque.
source_quote: it would be better to have the flange face diameters as wide as possible because it would require less frictional force to resist the torque at a wider radius.

subject: estimating flange torque capacity using bolt clamp load and bolt circle radius
main_point: Estimate slip resistance by converting the bolt’s tightening torque to clamp force and treating the bolt circle radius as the moment arm for frictional torque. Check that this capacity meets the gearbox’s rated torque and duty.
source_quote: The simplest way by far is to select a prospective bolt, calculate the clamping force this creates when it is torqued to rated torque, and use the bolt circle as an approximation of the moment arm. Compare this against the rated torque spec and duty type for the gearbox.

subject: bolt grade selection for industrial flanges
main_point: For most industrial applications, Grade 5 bolts are sufficient; use Grade 8 in harsher environments or on fussier machinery, and some designs tap the flange to enforce a specific fastener choice.
source_quote: Grade 5 bolts are ordinarily adequate for industrial uses. Some fussier machines or harsh environments may need grade 8. Most fussy ones would have the receiving flange tapped for a particular bolt.
example_context: industrial machinery and harsh-environment applications requiring fastener selection

subject: importance of dynamic loads in flange joint design
main_point: Prioritize dynamic effects—shock loads, engine torque pulses, vibration, and brake/clutch engagements—when designing flange joints, as these typically drive the required capacity more than steady torque.
source_quote: The real problem here is for shock load tolerance, torque pulses from diesels, vibration tolerance, brake and clutch engagement torques, etc.
example_context: torque-transmitting joints subject to shocks, diesel torque pulses, vibration, or brake/clutch events

subject: load factors overshadow precision of effective pressure radius
main_point: Because load factors for dynamic effects can be 3–4× in severe cases, small errors (e.g., 5%) in effective pressure radius are not critical to the overall design outcome.
source_quote: Since many of these issues are balled into load factor coefficients, and can be as high as 300% or 400% in severe cases, getting the effective flange pressure radius right to within 5% isn't very important to the big picture.
example_context: applications where shock/vibration load factors are applied to torque capacity calculations

subject: torque-controlled bolt tightening repeatability
main_point: Even with new, in-spec hardware and a calibrated torque wrench, torque tightening yields only about 10% repeatability in achieved clamp condition.
source_quote: Repeatability with new and to-spec hardware using a calibrated torque wrench is only 10%.
example_context: torque-controlled tightening of new, specification-compliant fasteners using a calibrated torque wrench

subject: designing bolted joints for field maintenance variability
main_point: Design bolted joints to tolerate future maintenance variability—unknown fastener substitution and improper tightening—which motivates conservative flange designs.
source_quote: Five years from now, some mechanic is going to replace a bolt with one pulled from a coffee can and tighten it with pliers. That's what you need to design for in most cases, and is why typical flanges are more than adequate.
example_context: field-maintained bolted flanges over long service intervals with non-controlled maintenance practices

subject: vacuum boundary penetrations
main_point: When a component must maintain an internal vacuum, drilling and tapping through its wall should be avoided because it introduces a leak path that compromises vacuum integrity. Penetrations of the vacuum boundary are therefore not an acceptable fastening approach in such designs.
source_quote: My first and normal approach would be to drill a tapped hole in the hollow tube; however this is not an option in this situation, as the inside of the cylindrical tube is kept in a vacuum, and has to be in order for the project we are working on to work.
example_value: The asker rejects drilling/tapping into a 1.9" hollow aluminum tube because its interior must remain under vacuum for the project to work.
example_context: Vacuum systems where the part’s wall serves as the vacuum boundary (e.g., a hollow aluminum tube acting as a vacuum vessel)

subject: two-piece shaft collar mounting method
main_point: To attach a component without breaching a tube’s wall, clamp a two-piece shaft collar around the pipe and tap the collar to accept fasteners for the add-on part. This provides a solid external mounting approach compatible with vacuum vessels.
source_quote: One way would be to clamp the outside of the pipe with a two-piece shaft collar. Properly tightened, a shaft collar will resist pretty heavy loads before it slips. You could tap the shaft collar and attach your plastic part as you normally would before attaching the collar to the pipe under vacuum.
example_context: Attaching parts to a pipe where penetrating the wall is not allowed (e.g., vacuum vessel).

subject: shaft collar compression on thin-walled pipe under vacuum
main_point: Clamping with a shaft collar compresses the tube and can crush a thin-walled pipe, a risk increased when the tube is under inward (vacuum) pressure. Check wall strength—at least roughly—before relying on a collar in such cases.
source_quote: Note that a shaft collar will compress the pipe, so there is some risk of crushing the pipe, especially since it is already under inwards pressure. I doubt this will be a practical concern, but it is worth doing at least a rough check if you are using a thinner pipe wall.
example_context: Thin-walled pipes under vacuum clamped with shaft collars.

subject: shaft vs pipe size mismatch for shaft collars
main_point: Commercial shaft collars are generally sized to shaft diameters rather than nominal pipe sizes, making an exact fit for pipe OD hard to find.
source_quote: One problem might be that shaft collars are typically manufactured for shaft sizes not pipe sizes, so you probably won't be able to find a perfectly sized collar.
example_context: Commercial shaft collars sized for shaft diameters rather than nominal pipe OD.

subject: machining a shaft collar ID to fit pipe
main_point: If a correctly sized collar isn’t available, either make a custom collar or rework a near-size commercial collar by enlarging its ID to match the pipe.
source_quote: Since you have access to a shop, you could machine your own from scratch just for the pipe, or you could buy an 1 7/8" collar (like McMaster Carr 6436K26) and machine the ID slightly larger.
example_value: Buy a 1 7/8 in collar (e.g., McMaster Carr 6436K26) and open the ID slightly to fit a 1.9 in OD pipe.
example_context: When a suitable pipe-size shaft collar is unavailable and you have machining capability to modify or make a collar.

subject: opening an ID: grinding vs turning/milling
main_point: Grinding can be used to enlarge an inner diameter in a pinch, but turning or milling is preferred for better results.
source_quote: In a pinch you could open up the ID with a grinder too, but turning or milling would be a much better option.

subject: shaft collar holding strength when properly tightened
main_point: A properly tightened shaft collar can transmit substantial load without slipping.
source_quote: Properly tightened, a shaft collar will resist pretty heavy loads before it slips.

subject: critical buckling pressure safety margin for vacuum cylinder design
main_point: Use a safety margin by sizing the wall so the predicted critical buckling pressure is about three times the expected external pressure. This provides a conservative thickness when designing an aluminum vacuum cylinder.
source_quote: So you should set $p_{crit}$ to about 3 atm to be safe, then find E and ν for your aluminum, plug those in along with your diameter, and length.
example_context: aluminum vacuum cylinders under external atmospheric pressure

subject: checking cylindrical shell buckling across circumferential mode numbers
main_point: When using the cylindrical shell buckling formula, evaluate multiple integer circumferential modes (n>1) and choose a wall thickness that meets the target pressure for every mode. This ensures the design covers the worst-case buckling mode.
source_quote: Then plug in a few integer values of n>1 to find a thickness t that is strong enough for all values of n.
example_context: cylindrical shell buckling calculations that include an integer mode number n parameter

subject: stainless thermal conductivity and tip material selection
main_point: Because stainless steel conducts heat poorly, consider attaching a higher-conductivity tip (such as copper), potentially with a stainless plating for surface properties. This can improve thermal response for a probe compared to an all-stainless tip.
source_quote: Stainless steel is not the greatest heat conductor so you might actually want to weld on be a reason to weld on a tip of a different material (i.e. solid copper but stainless plated).

subject: manufacturing methods for single-piece probe tips
main_point: Probe tips that appear to be single-piece in mass production are typically made by forming or extrusion processes rather than machining. These methods can create seamless-looking tips efficiently at volume.
source_quote: If the mass produced tips you saw are indeed single-piece then they are probably made with non-machining methods such as extrusions and forming which don't even fall under the purview of "machining".

subject: mass-production tooling amortization and low-volume economics
main_point: High-volume processes rely on expensive dedicated machines and tooling, so their upfront cost makes small production runs uneconomical even though the per-part cost is very low at scale. Low quantities cannot amortize the tooling investment.
source_quote: If you need less, the initial investment into the machine and other tooling is cost prohibitive.
example_value: The post notes machines and tooling can cost hundreds of thousands to millions, but make millions of identical parts so the cost is amortized and each part becomes dirt cheap.

subject: volume thresholds for dedicated tooling feasibility
main_point: For low- to medium-value parts, dedicated tooling like molds, dies, or extrusion is generally only economical at volumes in the thousands; runs around a hundred are typically too small to justify the setup cost.
source_quote: Unless your parts are high value, molds, dies, and extrusion machines are off the table unless you get thousands. Even a hundred might be too few.

subject: brazed tips on thermocouple probes
main_point: Some thermocouple probe tips that may look monolithic are actually brazed onto the tube. Visual inspection can reveal a brazed joint.
source_quote: Because I am holding a couple of thermocouple probes in my hand right now and the tip is clearly brazed on.

subject: shrink fitting a tip onto a tube
main_point: For low-volume probe tips, use a shrink-fit joint: it is robust, achievable with standard shop equipment, and allows flexibility in tip geometry, provided you hold tight tolerances.
source_quote: In your case I would just recommend a good shrink fit. It's never going to come out and you get more flexibility to make the head more suited to purpose. This should be well within reach of a machine shop and doesn't need crazy custom machines. It just needs careful tolerances.

subject: seam concealment by finish grinding and polishing
main_point: Finish grinding and polishing can hide the joint line of a brazed or shrink-fit tip so it appears seamless, with color potentially the only visible clue if dissimilar materials are used.
source_quote: And with appropriate finish grinding and polishing you won't even be able to see the seam line (apart from colour should you choose a different material).
example_value: The author notes their brazed thermocouples were finish ground to feel seamless, with only the filler metal’s different color revealing the joint.

subject: spin forming tube tip on lathe
main_point: Form the tapered tip by spin forming the stainless tube on a lathe to the desired profile. This achieves most of the geometry before any sealing or finishing.
source_quote: If you start with a stainless steel tube and spin form it on a lathe to the right profile you're 95% of the way there.
example_context: Forming stainless steel tube tips on a lathe

subject: sealing hollow tube tip by fusing or brazing/soldering
main_point: Seal the hollow end by using heat to fuse the tip closed or by applying a brazing or soldering process. Expect to experiment to dial in the method for your tube and profile.
source_quote: Some experimentation might be required, but you can likely use heat to melt the tip and seal it. Or perhaps some kind of brazing or solder.
example_context: Sealing the end of stainless steel tubing after forming

subject: finishing operations after sealing tube tip
main_point: Choose finishing based on how cleanly the tip was sealed. A precise seal may only need a quick polish, while a less precise seal may require a final machining pass.
source_quote: Depending on how precise the sealing method is, you might only need a quick polish to clean it up, or maybe a final machining step.
example_context: Post-sealing finishing of stainless tube tips

subject: unit notation on drawings vs specifications (mils vs decimal inches)
main_point: In US practice, engineering drawings generally present small dimensions in decimal inches (e.g., 0.002"), while specification documents may use either decimal inches or mils. This reflects differing conventions between drawings and specs rather than a strict universal rule.
source_quote: On a drawing it would always be 0.002".  In a specification document it could be either.
example_value: 50 μm may appear as 0.002" on a drawing or as 2 mils in a specification document.
example_context: US engineering drawings and specification documents for machining/mechanical parts

subject: symbol usage for mil/thou
main_point: There is no commonly used standalone symbol for mil/thou in US practice; the word "mils" is written out in documentation. The spelling is "mils," not "mills."
source_quote: I'm not aware of any.  We just always wrote "mils" (not "mills")
example_context: US engineering specifications and technical documents

subject: "tenths" terminology for 0.0001 inch
main_point: In US precision machining, 0.0001 inch (one ten-thousandth) is colloquially called a "tenth" (i.e., a tenth of a thousandth). This term is shop talk and not typically used in formal specifications.
source_quote: Colloquially, I know that people in precision machine shops refer to 0.1 mils (0.0001") as "tenths" (as in one ten thousandth of an inch).
example_context: US precision machine shops

subject: representation of sub-inch dimensions in US customary units
main_point: In US customary practice, sub-inch dimensions are expressed as decimal inches, with optional prefixes or scientific notation for very small values. There is no separate base unit below the inch.
source_quote: For US customary units, there's nothing smaller than an inch, you just start adding more zeros, applying prefixes, or using scientific notation.
example_value: 20 nm represented as 7.87e-7 inches.
example_context: US customary units in engineering documentation

subject: surface roughness units in US practice
main_point: In US documentation, surface roughness is commonly specified in microinches. This is a standard usage for expressing small-scale surface finish.
source_quote: For example, it would be common to specify surface roughness in microinches.
example_context: US engineering drawings and specifications for surface finish

subject: microinch (din)
main_point: A microinch equals one millionth of an inch (10^-6 in) and is denoted by the symbol din.
source_quote: A microinch is one millionth (¹⁄₁₀₀₀₀₀₀) of an inch. Labeled as din.

subject: remote monitoring and control via machine digital interfaces
