subject: time burden of mesh generation in industry
main_point: Industry experience reports that mesh generation is difficult enough to consume most of the project time in many FEA workflows.
source_quote: the authors noticed that mesh generation is so painful that it takes most of the time to achieve in the industry
example_context: industrial finite element analysis (FEA) workflows

subject: frequency of mesh convergence checks in industry
main_point: In many industrial FEA practices, mesh convergence verification is performed infrequently.
source_quote: mesh convergence is only rarely checked.
example_context: industrial finite element analysis (FEA) workflows

subject: adoption of IGA
main_point: Isogeometric Analysis is relatively new (about a decade old) and therefore not yet widely adopted.
source_quote: The method seems to be really interesting but not widely used since relatively new (10 years).
example_context: Isogeometric Analysis adoption in engineering industry

subject: automatic quadrilateral surface meshing software
main_point: Commercial meshing tools exist that can fully automatically generate all-quadrilateral meshes for planar or curved surfaces, even when the surface geometry is very complex. This eliminates the need for manual meshing on such surfaces when using these specialized products.
source_quote: there are several products that provide completely automatic meshing, delivering 100% quadrilateral meshes on surfaces of any degree of complexity.
example_value: Vendors offer tools advertised to create 100% quadrilateral meshes automatically for curved or planar surface models.
example_context: Commercial CAE meshing software for planar or curved surface meshing

subject: meshing software application specialization
main_point: Different meshing programs are optimized for specific application domains, so their suitability varies by use case (e.g., structural engineering versus PCB modeling). Users should expect specialization when selecting a meshing tool.
source_quote: some of those programs are best for structural engineering applications, other - for modeling of printed circuit boards, etc.
example_value: One program family targets structural engineering problems while another targets printed circuit board (PCB) modeling.
example_context: Commercial meshing software offerings segmented by application domain (structural analysis vs. PCB modeling)

subject: standardized gear tooth profiles
main_point: Designing gear teeth from first principles is complex, so most gears use standardized tooth profiles. Using standards avoids having to create unique tooth geometry for each design.
source_quote: Gear design from scratch is a fairly major process in itself and so the vast majority of gears are made to standardised tooth profiles.

subject: metric gear module system
main_point: Metric gears are commonly specified using the module system. This is the typical framework for defining spur gear geometry in metric practice.
source_quote:
Metric gears are usually designed to the 
module system
.
example_context: metric gear design using the module system

subject: module definition
main_point: In the module system, the module equals the pitch circle diameter divided by the number of teeth. This ties gear size directly to tooth count.
source_quote: the module number is the ratio between the two
example_context: metric gear module system

subject: gear standards covering tooth profile details
main_point: Standards cover gear tooth profile, clearances, and related calculations. Designers can rely on these standards rather than deriving tooth geometry each time.
source_quote: This means that the fiddly calculations of tooth profile, clearances etc are covered by the standard so you don't have to reinvent the wheel every time you design a part with gears in it.

subject: gear thickness and torque capacity
main_point: A key remaining design parameter is gear thickness, which determines torque capacity. Designers also specify how the gear is fixed to the shaft.
source_quote: This leaves the designer to specify thing like the thickness of the gear (which determines its torque capacity) as well as the arrangements for fixing it to a shaft.

subject: selecting stock gears vs custom manufacture
main_point: In practice, engineers often choose off-the-shelf gear sets instead of custom manufacturing. Stock gears typically satisfy most application requirements.
source_quote: Although in practice this often means picking an off the-shelf gear set rather than getting them manufactured as stock gears will cover almost all requirements.

subject: gear ratio by tooth count in module system
main_point: When using the module system, determine gear ratios by tooth counts rather than arbitrary diameters. You cannot specify fractional teeth on meshing spur gears.
source_quote: Note that in the module system you need to work out your gear rations by number of teeth, you can't just have arbitrary diameters as for obvious reasons you can't have fractions of teeth on meshing spur gears.
example_context: metric module-system spur gears

subject: assembly drawing practice for gears
main_point: In assembly drawings, represent meshing gears as circles at the pitch circle diameter and annotate the module. This conveys fit without detailing individual teeth.
source_quote: For assembly drawings it is common to draw meshing gears as circles of the appropriate PCD and use a note to specify the module.

subject: omitting gear tooth detail in drawings
main_point: Modern engineering drawings typically do not include full gear tooth detail. The gear’s specification is referenced elsewhere in documentation.
source_quote: In any case, in modern context,  it is not usually necessary to draw the detail of a gear in an engineering drawing as it will be specified elsewhere.

subject: scaling gear drawings across sizes
main_point: Do not scale a gear template to create other gear sizes. Meshing spur gears must share the same tooth dimensions and profile, so scaling will produce incompatible teeth.
source_quote: Also be aware that for meshing spur gears the dimensions and profiles of the teeth must be the same regardless of the diameter of the gear ie you cant just draw a template gear of one size and scale it to give different rations.

subject: minimum gear diameter for given tooth profile and tooth count
main_point: For a fixed tooth profile (module), there is a minimum gear diameter that can physically fit a required number of teeth. Below this limit the geometry will not accommodate the teeth.
source_quote: Similarly for a given tooth profile there will be a lower limit to the diameter which will physically accommodate the number of teeth required.

subject: using stock gears for academic projects
main_point: In academic projects, specifying suitable stock gears is generally sufficient. Document the selection criteria rather than designing tooth profiles from scratch.
source_quote: For an academic project, properly specifying stock gears should be perfectly adequate  as long as you set out the criteria used
example_context: academic engineering project requirements

subject: involute gear line of action
main_point: In involute spur gears, the contact point between meshing teeth travels along a straight line known as the line of action. This straight-line contact path arises from the involute tooth geometry.
source_quote: This means that the point of contact between meshing teeth will move in a straight line (called the line of action).
example_value: Visualized like a string unwound from one wheel and wound onto another.

subject: determinants of spur gear tooth shape
main_point: Spur gear tooth geometry is determined by the tooth count and the pressure angle (the angle of the line of action). Choosing these parameters defines the resulting involute profile.
source_quote: It is the number of teeth and the angle of that line that will decide the shape of the spurs.

subject: using woodgears.ca gear generator for DXF export
main_point: For a low-cost approach to creating gear geometry for AutoCAD, use the woodgears.ca gear generator and export the profile as a DXF. This avoids manually constructing the involute in CAD.
source_quote:
Is a cheap solution an option? If so there is a gear generator on 
woodgears.ca
 that can export to DXF.
example_context: Using the woodgears.ca online gear generator to create involute spur gears and exporting as DXF for AutoCAD or similar CAD tools.

subject: normal force sensitivity in shaft-part friction modeling
main_point: Modeling a shaft-part interface via a friction coefficient can be unreliable because the contact normal force depends strongly on tiny dimensional and material variations. If the CAD/FEA tool does not capture those dependencies, results from a fixed friction coefficient may be inaccurate.
source_quote: It is difficult to model with friction coefficients in this case, because the normal force is dependent on very small changes in dimensions and material strengths that your software may or may not support.
example_context: Simulating friction for a rotating part on a shaft in CAD using friction coefficients

subject: iterative calibration of friction coefficient in simulation
main_point: Calibrate the friction coefficient by iteratively matching simulation output to measured behavior. Start with a guessed coefficient, run the simulation, compare to the measured torque, and adjust the coefficient until the results converge.
source_quote: It may be more accurate and easier to just iterate to a solution. First you guess at a friction coefficient, insert it into your simulation, run your simulation, see if your result is higher or lower than amount you measured, then guess a new value and repeat until you feel that you are are close enough to your measured value.
example_context: Calibrating friction for a rotating part on a shaft by matching simulation to measured torque

subject: cam-ground piston ellipticity
main_point: Many modern internal combustion engine pistons are intentionally made slightly elliptical (cam-ground) rather than perfectly round.
source_quote: many modern pistons are cam ground--slightly elliptical in shape
example_context: modern internal combustion engine pistons

subject: cam-ground piston thermal expansion rationale
main_point: Cam-ground pistons are shaped so they become more nearly circular at operating temperature due to thermal expansion. The initial slight ellipticity compensates for in-service growth.
source_quote: As I currently understand it, the reason for this is so that when the piston heats up to the operating temperature, it forms a more precise circular shape.
example_context: pistons operating at engine running temperature

subject: piston ellipse orientation vs pin-connection restraint
main_point: Asymmetric restraint at the piston-to-rod pinned connection can cause the piston head to expand more along the axis with less constraint when it heats up. To compensate, the manufactured ellipse is oriented so its minor (smaller) axis aligns with the least-restrained direction, tending toward roundness at operating temperature.
source_quote: It is possible that at this connection, a great deal more restraint is provided in one direction compared with the other. I imagine that as the piston head heats up, it is inclined to expand more in the direction in which less restraint is provided by the (relatively) cooler piston rod/pinned connection. In that case, the minor axis of the elliptical piston head would coincide with this direction of least restraint.
example_value: At the wrist-pin/rod joint, the cooler, stiffer assembly may restrain one axis more than the other, so the piston expands preferentially along the less-restrained axis.
example_context: Pistons attached to connecting rods via a wrist pin where the pin boss/rod joint provides unequal stiffness/restraint by direction.

subject: eccentric cam adjuster
main_point: Rotating an eccentric element with an off-center hole changes the position of the attached shaft, allowing fine height adjustment. A lock (e.g., a knob) is loosened to rotate for adjustment and then tightened to hold the position.
source_quote: The purpose is that you can loosen the knob and rotate the piece to slightly raise and lower the shaft that is connected on the other end.
example_value: On a printing press, this mechanism adjusts the impression cylinder by a few thousandths of an inch.

subject: modified sine cam profile composition
main_point: A modified sine cam motion law is constructed by using cycloidal segments for the first and last one-eighth of the motion and a sinusoidal segment for the middle seven-eighths.
source_quote: The modified sine curve is actually a combination of cycloidal curve at the first and last 1/8 of the curve and a sine curve in the middle 7/8 of the curve.

subject: same-material bushing and housing interface during removal
main_point: When a press-fit bushing and its housing are made of the same material in a blind bore, grinding or cutting removal provides no clear boundary feedback, making non-damaging extraction very difficult and risky to the housing.
source_quote: This was very difficult to remove and especially to remove without damage. All kinds of Dremel tools (grinders, sanders, cutters, etc.) were used and while they did make "progress" on the material removed, it was impossible to tell where the bushing stopped and the housing started because they were the same material.
example_value: The OP tried various Dremel tools on a bronze bushing in a bronze water pump cap and could not discern when they were cutting the bushing versus the housing.
example_context: Press-fit bronze bushing in a blind bronze water pump cap bore

subject: center drill for removing press-fit bushing
main_point: A center drill can be used as an effective method to remove a stubborn press-fit bronze bushing when abrasive tools risk damaging the same-material housing.
source_quote: It ended up taking a center drill to remove it.
example_value: After failing with Dremel tools on a bronze bushing in a bronze pump cap, the OP successfully removed it using a center drill.
example_context: Press-fit bronze bushing in a blind bronze water pump cap bore

subject: grease and dowel hydraulic bushing removal
main_point: To remove a blind press-fit bushing without damaging the housing, pack the bushing with grease and drive a snug-fitting wooden dowel into it with light hammer taps; the tight dowel and grease create hydraulic force to push the bushing out.
source_quote: The tried and true method of backyard mechanics involves grease and a wooden dowel. Find a wooden dowel slightly larger than the inside diameter of the bushing. Sand the dowel so it fits snuggly in to the bushing. Pack the bushing full of grease. Insert the dowel and tap it with a hammer.
example_value: Described as analogous to removing a pilot bushing in a crankshaft.
example_context: press-fit bushings installed in blind bores (e.g., pilot bushings in a crankshaft or a pump cap)

subject: incompressible grease generating extraction force
main_point: When a blind bushing bore is tightly sealed by a dowel, hammering the dowel pressurizes the trapped, incompressible grease, which exerts force that drives the bushing out of the housing.
source_quote: The idea is that the grease will have no where to go and can't compress so it will force the bushing out.
example_context: blind bores where the bushing ID can be sealed by a close-fitting dowel

subject: threaded-ID bushing extraction via slide hammer or jacking bolt
main_point: You can tap internal threads in the bushing with a bottoming tap and extract it either by pulling with a slide hammer on a screwed-in bolt or by advancing the bolt to jack the bushing out of the blind bore.
source_quote: Or tap threads into the inside with a bottoming tap. Then either screw in a bolt and use a slide hammer to pull it out or continue screwing the bolt in until the bushing climbs the bolt and comes out.
example_context: press-fit bushings with enough wall thickness to tap and installed in a blind bore

subject: tapered pipe nipple as internal puller for blind bushing removal
main_point: For blind press-fit bushings, you can thread a tapered pipe nipple into the bushing to create an internal grip point, add a flange, and pull it using a three-jaw puller with the puller rod passing through the nipple and bearing on the housing. This setup provides axial extraction force and can remove the bushing cleanly when conventional methods fail.
source_quote: a 3 inch or so black pipe nipple with tapered pipe thread fit into the bushing. The taper allowed me to carefully thread the nipple into the bushing with pliers. I put a flange on the other end of the nipple, and then I could use a three jaw puller on the flange, with the puller rod through the hollow nipple and pushing on the outer case. Came right out.
example_value: On a water pump’s bronze bushing, a ~3 inch black pipe nipple with tapered threads was carefully threaded in with pliers, a flange was fitted to the nipple, and a three-jaw puller was used to extract the bushing easily.
example_context: Blind, press-fit bronze bushings (e.g., in a water pump housing) where a tapered pipe thread can bite into the bushing ID.

subject: combining machinist square with 36-inch straight edge
main_point: Use two tools—a machinist square and a 36-inch straight edge—to cover the majority of common inspection tasks with one purchase strategy.
source_quote: I would consider getting two. A straight edge flat steel square (machinist square) and a 36" straight edge should cover most standard applications.
example_context: automotive engine deck and head surface inspection tasks

subject: machinist square for small mating surfaces
main_point: A machinist (steel) square is well-suited for checking flatness/fit on small component mating surfaces.
source_quote: The steel square will be great for smaller applications like small component mating surfaces.
example_value: small component mating surfaces

subject: 36-inch straight edge coverage for engine surfaces
main_point: A 36-inch straight edge is an appropriate length to span and check larger engine surfaces such as blocks and cylinder heads.
source_quote: The 36" should cover the larger areas like block and head surfaces.
example_value: block and head surfaces
example_context: automotive engine block and cylinder head surfaces

subject: squareness checking with machinist square
main_point: Including a machinist square adds the ability to verify squareness (perpendicularity), which can be useful in inspections beyond flatness checks.
source_quote: Even being able to check squareness could be helpful.

subject: jointing compound thickness when installing cylinder liner without shim
main_point: Per Volvo truck service guidance, when a cylinder liner is installed without a shim, apply an even bead of jointing compound about 0.8 mm thick to the underside of the liner collar.
source_quote:
If the cylinder liner is 
installed without a shim
, an even strand of jointing compound, approximately 0.8 mm thick, should be applied to the underside of the cylinder liner collar.
example_context: Volvo truck engines (wet cylinder liner installation per OEM manual)

subject: file test for steel hardness
main_point: If a hand file quickly makes a noticeable dent in a steel axle with just a few strokes, the part is likely not hardened; a hardened surface should resist being easily cut by a file. Using a file as a quick hardness check can indicate whether heat treatment is present.
source_quote:
However I did the "file" test in the old axle, and with a couple of file strokes I could do a good dent in there, so I guess it is not 
hardened
.
example_value: On the old axle, a couple of file strokes produced a good dent, leading the poster to conclude it was not hardened.
example_context: Using a hand file to assess hardness of steel axles or similar steel components

subject: furnace size limits for heat treatment
main_point: Heat treating long axles may be impossible at a given vendor if the part exceeds the furnace’s working length; equipment envelope limits can prevent hardening operations. Always confirm furnace capacity against part length before planning heat treatment.
source_quote: The guys that can do me new axles say because their length, they can't fit it inside their furnace...
example_value: In this case, the shop could not fit the new axles in their furnace due to length.
example_context: Heat-treatment shops with furnaces whose internal length is shorter than the axle or shaft to be treated

subject: crankshaft balance axis (main journals)
main_point: Crankshafts are balanced about the central axis defined by the main journals’ circle. The main journal axis is the reference for rotational balance in design.
source_quote: The crankshaft is designed to be balanced when spun along it's central axis, which is the center of the circle made by the main journals.

subject: crankpin journal non-concentricity with main journals
main_point: Crankpin journals on a crankshaft are offset and do not share the same axis as the main journals. This non-concentric geometry distinguishes pins from mains.
source_quote: These are not concentric with the main journals

subject: crankshaft grinding equipment choice
main_point: Crankshaft journals are not reconditioned on a typical lathe; they are ground on a dedicated machine with a large grinding wheel.
source_quote:
First, it's not spun on a lathe to make it round again, at least not the typical machine lathe you'd think of. It's a machine which has a huge grinding wheel, thus the reason we call it 
grinding a crank
.

subject: crankpin grinding setup method
main_point: To grind an eccentric crankpin, the work is centered on the specific journal being machined so that journal becomes the rotation axis during grinding.
source_quote: The crankshaft is placed on the machine and centered on the journal which is being machined.

subject: work and wheel speed relationship in crank grinding
main_point: In crankshaft grinding, the workpiece rotates very slowly while the grinding wheel runs at speed and is fed into the journal face.
source_quote: The crankshaft is then set to spinning at a very slow speed. The grinding stone in the back is then spun up to speed and is then brought into contact with the journal face.

subject: dial indicator use during crankshaft grinding
main_point: A dial indicator is used against the journal to display in real time how much material has been removed relative to the original size during grinding.
source_quote: The gauge shows the machinist how much material is taken from the journal or the difference between what the journal size was and what the size is at any given time during the process.

subject: stopping short of final size in grinding
main_point: During crankshaft grinding, the operator monitors removal and stops slightly short of the final dimension rather than grinding directly to size.
source_quote: As material is removed through the grinding process, the machinist pays attention to how much is removed, then stops the process once just shy of the finished dimensions.

subject: matching journal sizes within groups
main_point: Although main and rod journals can be ground to different sizes, rebuilders typically keep all rod journals the same size and all main journals the same size within their respective groups.
source_quote: The main and rod journals can be ground independently, but are usually matched to sizes between themselves (rod size = rod size; main size = main size).
example_context: Automotive/engine crankshaft regrinding practice

subject: off-center mounting for crankpin grinding
main_point: Crankpin journals can be ground by mounting the crankshaft off-center on the grinder, setting up to the eccentric pin rather than the main journal axis. This offsets the workpiece so the pin can be machined despite its non-concentricity.
source_quote: You can install the crankshaft off-center on the grinding machine:
example_context: crankshaft crankpin journal grinding on a crankshaft/cylindrical grinding machine

subject: indexing per crankpin during grinding
main_point: Each crankpin journal requires its own setup; the crankshaft must be repositioned or re-indexed for every pin before grinding or polishing.
source_quote: You'd have to adjust the crankshaft for each crankpin journal.
example_context: crankshaft crankpin journal grinding on a crankshaft/cylindrical grinding machine

subject: DIN 874 straightness tolerance for 300 mm sharp-edged rule
main_point: Under DIN 874, a 300 mm sharp‑edged straightedge is specified to be straight within ±3 micrometres across its length.
source_quote: DIN 874 says less than +/- 3 microns over a 300mm
example_context: DIN 874 standard for sharp‑edged rules (straight edges)

subject: DIN 874 flatness grades for steel rules
main_point: DIN 874 classifies steel straightedges into four flatness grades (00, 0, 1, 2) with tolerance formulas that increase with length: 00: 1+L/150, 0: 2+L/100, 1: 4+L/60, 2: 8+L/40 (µm).
source_quote:
for a "
steel rule
" DIN 874 defines four grades

Flatness tolerances are

- Grade 00: 1+(L/150)
- Grade 0:  2+(L/100)
- Grade 1:  4+(L/60)
- Grade 2:  8+(L/40)

E.g. in microns 

Grade
Length     00       0       1        2
--------------------------------------
0.5m       4        7      12       21
example_value: At L = 0.5 m, the tolerances (µm) are: Grade 00: 4, Grade 0: 7, Grade 1: 12, Grade 2: 21.
example_context: DIN 874 steel straightedges/rules

subject: straightedge measurement support procedures
main_point: The accuracy/flatness assessment of a straightedge depends on how it is supported; proper metrology procedures using specific supports and auxiliary gauges (e.g., gauge blocks or specialized test gauges) are required.
source_quote: This also depends on how you support the straight edge. There are specific procedures to be followed, some procedures involve using gauge blocks and/or other specialised test gauges in conjunction with the specially supported straight edge.

subject: commercial straightedge compliance with DIN 874
main_point: Straightedges sold by engineering tool suppliers will generally meet the DIN 874 straightness specification.
source_quote: If you purchase a "straight edge" from an engineering tool company, it will most likely meet this specification.
example_context: Commercial straightedges from engineering tool companies

subject: head gasket sealing surface flatness
main_point: Machining the cylinder head/block mating surfaces restores flatness so the head gasket seals uniformly across its entire area, preventing leaks. Ensuring perfect flatness of these mating faces is fundamental to reliable gasket sealing.
source_quote: The reason to have the mating surfaces machine is to ensure they are perfectly flat and that you get a good seal on every part of the head gasket with no leaking.

subject: engine block mating surface inspection for straightness
main_point: Before deciding on further machining, clean the engine block’s mating surface and verify its straightness using a straightedge and feeler gauges. This basic inspection helps confirm the surface is within flatness limits for proper head gasket sealing.
source_quote: I assume that the repair procedure suggests thoroughly cleaning the engine block mating surface and checking it for straightness with a steel rule and feeler gauge or similar.

subject: skimping on cylinder head truing
main_point: If you skimp on ensuring the cylinder head is flat/true, you risk redoing the job and buying another gasket set. The rework and parts cost can exceed the cost of machining you tried to avoid.
source_quote: the potentially expensive bit isn't the engineering works but the risk that you'll end up having to do the job again with yet another new gasket set if you skimp on ensuring the cylinder head is true.

subject: cylinder head facing practice
main_point: Shops are more likely to resurface (face) cylinder heads on high-mileage engines or when an overheat is suspected to have warped the head. This increases the chance of proper sealing on reassembly.
source_quote: Facing is more common with higher time engines, or ones which are suspected of having a warped head after overheats.
example_context: automotive cylinder heads after overheating or high running hours

subject: head gasket sealing failure risk from uneven head surface
main_point: If a head is not resurfaced, it may fail to seal properly to the block, leading to a poor mating surface and forcing a repeat disassembly. Resurfacing is recommended to lower this rework risk.
source_quote: In your instance, the most likely reason for the recommendation from the shop was to reduce the probability of a disassembly caused by a head which did not seal and resulted in an unsatisfactory mating between the block and cylinder head.
example_context: automotive engine cylinder head reassembly and head gasket sealing

subject: cylinder head R&R vs skimming cost
main_point: Removing and refitting a cylinder head is typically much more expensive than performing a light resurfacing pass. This cost differential favors proactive skimming to avoid costly rework.
source_quote: Generally the R&R costs are pretty high for the head, compared to a small skimming of the head.
example_context: automotive cylinder head service/repair

subject: limited skim margin on some diesel cylinder heads
main_point: Certain cylinder heads—particularly some diesel designs—have minimal material allowance, limiting how much resurfacing can be done. This constrains or may preclude skimming to avoid exceeding minimum head thickness.
source_quote: However, there is a downside, and that is that some heads, especially on some diesels (VW IDI 1.588L come to mind) have very little margin to skim.
example_value: VW IDI 1.588L is cited as having very little margin to skim.
example_context: diesel cylinder heads (e.g., VW IDI 1.588L)

subject: preemptive head skimming for gasket sealing reliability
main_point: Some shops choose to skim every head to ensure a clean, smooth surface that seals head gaskets reliably and improves reassembly outcomes. This practice reduces post-assembly sealing issues.
source_quote: My normal machine shop insists on skimming all heads because they have virtually no problems getting good seals with the cylinder head gasket afterwards, and feel that a clean, smooth surface helps the reassembly reliability.
example_context: automotive cylinder head resurfacing to ensure gasket seal

subject: gear backlash design allowance
main_point: Gear backlash is an intentional clearance built into the design, independent of manufacturing tolerances, to ensure gears mesh freely.
source_quote: In gear design, the backlash is introduced in the design itself (not by tolerances of manufacturing) to allow free meshing of the gears.

subject: gear pitch vs backlash
main_point: Using a finer gear pitch reduces the designed backlash.
source_quote: The backlash in the design can be minimized by reducing the pitch of the gears.

subject: proportional effect of gear pitch on backlash
main_point: Halving a gear’s pitch can roughly halve the designed backlash, suggesting a proportional reduction with pitch.
source_quote: For example, If the pitch of a gear is halved the designed backlash can also be halved.

subject: gear pitch vs torque capacity
main_point: Reducing gear pitch decreases the gear’s torque capacity, creating a trade-off between backlash and load capability.
source_quote: Though the reduced pitch also reduces the torque capacity of the gear.

subject: small-quantity fabrication cost
main_point: For hobby projects with low quantities, outsourcing fabrication can have high per-piece costs because there is no volume to amortize setup and tooling. Low-volume piece production tends to remain expensive.
source_quote: The problem with this is that hobby projects almost never need large quantities and piece production can be still expensive.
example_value: Designing in CAD and sending parts to a third-party fabricator for one-offs.
example_context: hobby projects with low production quantities using third-party fabrication services

subject: hand-tool aluminum machining accuracy
main_point: Using cheap hand tools to machine aluminum can produce inaccurate parts, which jeopardizes the function of assemblies with moving parts that require precision. The inaccuracy becomes a functional risk in mechanisms.
source_quote: Moreover, the results might be inaccurate, which is a problem for designs with moving parts.
example_context: hand machining aluminum parts with inexpensive tools for moving assemblies

subject: outsourced CNC prototyping cycle time
main_point: Depending on someone else’s CNC machine to make your parts can slow iteration, leading to longer prototyping cycles. External scheduling and coordination add delay versus in-house capability.
source_quote: This would most likely result in very slow prototyping cycles though.
example_context: outsourcing part machining to another person or shop's CNC for prototypes

subject: desktop CNC/router/3D printer availability as assembled units or kits
main_point: There is broad market availability of desktop CNC, routers, mills, and 3D printers offered both as assembled machines and as kits, making procurement feasible for small users.
source_quote: Hundreds of companies do sell assembled unit and/or kits.

subject: desktop/DIY CNC and 3D printer performance for DIY-level use
main_point: For DIY, home, and high school applications, desktop CNC/routers/3D printers generally meet expectations for software, speed, and accuracy and can work with materials like metal, plastic, and wood across a range of price/performance.
source_quote: But since many people make/buy/sell them, it sure live up to expectation (software, speed, accuracy) at the DIY/home/hi school level. People does use metal, plastic and even wood and wide range of price and performance
example_context: DIY/home/high school level desktop CNC, routers, and 3D printers

subject: hand filing as substitute for milling operations
main_point: Many milling-like results can be achieved manually by carefully filing to dimension and checking with a micrometer, provided you are willing to spend the time required. This enables creation of precise features without powered milling equipment.
source_quote: Actually, you can perform most milling operations with a file, a micrometer, and patience.

subject: machine frame stiffness for metal cutting
main_point: Cutting metals imposes high forces, so an insufficiently stiff machine frame leads to chatter, which degrades cut quality, generates excess heat, and rapidly dulls the tool. Ensure the machine’s structure is rigid enough for metal cutting to avoid these failure modes.
source_quote: If you do not have a stiff enough frame the cutting tool will simply bounce off the surface of the metal (chatter) and will result with very poor cutting, extra heat, and fast dulling of the tool.

subject: wood router spindle speed vs metal cutting
main_point: Wood routers typically run around 10k RPM, which is too fast for metal cutting. Even if they can skim light cuts in aluminum, the tool will dull quickly and the router itself will wear out because it isn’t built for metal-cutting loads.
source_quote: A router designed to cut wood may run at 10K RPM which is way too fast for metal.  It may be able to take very light cuts off aluminium but the cutting tool will dull very quickly and the router itself is not designed to take the forces of cutting metal and will also not live for very long.
example_value: A wood router at 10,000 RPM taking very light cuts in aluminum leads to rapid tool dulling and short router life.
example_context: Using wood routers to cut aluminum or other metals.

subject: coolant/lubrication in metal cutting
main_point: Metal cutting commonly benefits from lubrication or cooling, unlike typical woodworking operations. Coolant use is part of standard metal machining practice.
source_quote: Metal cutting often requires lubrication/cooling that isn't used with wood.
example_context: Metal cutting operations versus woodworking.

subject: 2D locating with drilled plate
main_point: When only 2D positioning is needed, a simple plate with drilled holes can achieve reasonable accuracy without a milling machine. This reduces tooling requirements for basic layouts.
source_quote: E.g. if you're just trying to locate some objects in 2D you can get a plate and drill holes in it with reasonable accuracy without needing any fancy milling equipment.
example_value: Using a flat plate and drilled holes to position parts in 2D.
example_context: Projects that only require 2D positioning of components.

subject: using oversized holes for adjustability
main_point: You can trade precision machining for adjustability by designing slop into features (e.g., oversized holes) and then setting position during assembly. Measure and align parts before tightening fasteners to meet accuracy needs without tight tolerances.
source_quote: You can also sometimes substitute adjustability to accuracy/precision, the simplest example is drilling a large hole and using a caliper or micrometer to measure the position before tightening your bolts.
example_value: Drill a large hole, measure with a caliper or micrometer, then tighten bolts to lock the position.
example_context: Bolted assemblies where position can be adjusted during assembly.

subject: community makerspace equipment access
main_point: Community makerspaces can be a low-cost way to access CNC machines and laser cutters. After completing brief, inexpensive training, members are typically permitted to use the equipment for fabricating parts.
source_quote: they have various CNC machines, laser cutters, Etc. which with some simple low cost training you are allowed to use.
example_value: Artisan's Asylum in Boston offers member access to CNC machines and laser cutters following low-cost training.
example_context: Community makerspaces/fab labs (e.g., Artisan's Asylum in Boston) that provide equipment access after required training.

subject: linear rail and block hole pattern compatibility expectations
main_point: It’s common for off‑the‑shelf rails and bearing blocks to have non‑matching hole patterns unless they’re explicitly sold as predrilled, compatible sets. Don’t assume mounting holes will align unless compatibility is specified by the supplier.
source_quote: That doesn’t sound very unusual to me unless you purchased materials that specifically purported to be predrilled and compatible.

subject: manual creation of mounting holes (drill/tap/countersink)
main_point: If the rail and block mounting holes don’t align, a practical fix is to lay out and drill your own holes, and where required, tap or countersink them to suit the fasteners.
source_quote:
Sounds like you may need to manually mark out, drill and possibly 
tap
 or 
countersink
 the holes you need.
example_context: Mounting generic SBR linear rails and bearing blocks when predrilled hole patterns do not match.

subject: SW URDF exporter preview crash
main_point: When using the SolidWorks URDF exporter, attempting to preview after defining links and joints (with other settings automatic) resulted in a crash with an error. This indicates a potential stability issue in that workflow for the user's setup.
source_quote: SW crashes and throws error
example_value: User clicks preview after specifying link and joint in sw_urdf_exporter; the progress bar loads for a while, then SolidWorks crashes.
example_context: SolidWorks with sw_urdf_exporter plugin, preview step after defining links and joints; other settings automatic.

subject: STEP import lacks mates and reference geometry in SW
main_point: In a STEP-based model workflow, assembly mates and reference geometry like reference coordinate systems and axes are not present after import, so these features are unavailable for the URDF export setup.
source_quote: assembly relations, reference coordinate system and axis do not exist
example_value: The user's model is a STEP file rather than the original SolidWorks assembly.
example_context: STEP files imported into SolidWorks for use with the sw_urdf_exporter plugin.

subject: reference frames for URDF joints in SolidWorks exporter
main_point: To include joints in a URDF exported from SolidWorks, you must define the model's reference coordinate systems and axes (manually if they are missing).
source_quote: If you want to have joints in your exported URDF: yes.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter when exporting models for URDF with articulated joints

subject: using original SolidWorks assembly for URDF export
main_point: Using the original SolidWorks assembly (with its relations/mates intact) is the most straightforward approach for exporting a URDF, avoiding manual setup of references.
source_quote: That would certainly seem to be the most straightforward way of doing it, yes.
example_context: Exporting URDF from SolidWorks models via the URDF Exporter

subject: using URDF exporter with newer SolidWorks versions (unsupported)
main_point: Consider trying the URDF exporter on newer SolidWorks versions; it may work even though those versions are not officially supported or recommended.
source_quote: I would try the plugin with a newer version of SW. It can work, it's just not supported / recommended.
example_context: SolidWorks URDF Exporter compatibility across SW versions

subject: friction-fit servo coupler without matching spline
main_point: A tight, non-splined 3D-printed ring over a servo’s splined output shaft tends to slip and spin under load, failing to transmit torque effectively. Relying on friction alone without engaging the spline does not provide sufficient torque transfer.
source_quote: So far, I'm having difficulty of this setup working with any level for torque and not just spinning in place.
example_value: The author used a 3D-printed plastic ring that fits tightly around the servo output but lacks the matching spline, and it spins in place when torque is applied.
example_context: Hobby servo with a splined output shaft and a 3D-printed plastic attachment that does not include the mating spline

subject: FDM 3D print internal voids and reduced strength
main_point: FDM 3D-printed parts should not be treated as solid, full-strength components because internal voids reduce their mechanical strength. Designers must account for this reduced strength when transmitting loads.
source_quote: FDM parts are far from 'full strength' parts, nearly all 3D printing is. There are too many 'spaces' inside of the print itself.
example_value: A 3D-printed servo attachment with an embedded M3 nut failed to transmit torque.
example_context: FDM 3D-printed polymer parts

subject: lever arm effects in joint geometry
main_point: Large lever arms amplify forces and torques at an interface, worsening stress and deformation. Minimizing the distance between fasteners and the load path reduces leverage and helps prevent failure.
source_quote: This gets compounded by your design itself, since this part leaves quite a bit of room for leverage.
example_value: The holes/pins were spaced far from the nut, increasing leverage on the plastic around the embedded nut.

subject: embedded metal nut in plastic under torque
main_point: If torque is transmitted through an embedded metal nut in a plastic part, the plastic can deform and erode a cavity, allowing the nut to spin freely. This results in loss of torque transmission and component failure.
source_quote: The plastic is set up to destroy itself right now, and the nut will make itself a nice hole to spin inside of.
example_value: An M3 hex nut embedded in a printed plastic hub spun inside the softened plastic when torque was applied.
example_context: Plastic parts (e.g., FDM prints) used to transmit torque via an embedded metal nut

subject: material and geometry choice for torque-carrying parts
main_point: For torque-carrying interfaces, choose a metal part or, if you must use printed plastic, reduce the part size/lever arms to lower stresses. This mitigates deformation and failure at the interface.
source_quote: Either figure out a way to get it made from metal, or decrease the size of the printed part.
example_value: A smaller-diameter printed hub would reduce leverage on an embedded nut.
example_context: Torque-transmitting adapters made by 3D printing

subject: metal vs plastic for torque transmission
main_point: Prefer metal components for couplings that must transmit torque when weight allows, as metal resists deformation far better than printed plastics. This choice improves reliability under load.
source_quote: I would recommend metal if you can afford the weight and plan on applying any kind of torque to this system.
example_value: Switching a servo adapter from printed plastic to steel for torque handling.
example_context: Robotic assemblies where servos impart torque and mass budget permits metal parts

subject: accepting DFM suggestions from manufacturers
main_point: Collaborate with fabricators and accept their suggested design changes to improve manufacturability. Incorporating DFM feedback early reduces cost and increases the likelihood of successful parts.
source_quote: Just be willing to work with them, and take their advice if they suggest a design change to aid in manufacturability.
example_value: A machine shop proposes minor geometry changes to a steel part to ease machining.

subject: using the servo horn interface for torque
main_point: Design attachments to engage the servo horn spline rather than relying on clamped or embedded-nut geometries. The horn interface handles torque better across materials.
source_quote: All that said, you would be better off interfacing with the servo horn if you can fit it into your design IMO. It would be better able to handle any torque in the system, regardless of material.
example_value: A 3D-printed part keyed to the servo horn spline instead of gripping a smooth output.
example_context: Hobby servo-driven mechanisms using standard servo horns

subject: lightweight printer motors with reduction gearing for robot actuation
main_point: If a hobby servo lacks sufficient torque, consider using a lightweight motor (such as those from printers) paired with a reduction gear train to multiply torque. This can provide enough force to support the robot while keeping overall weight low.
source_quote: You may need to instead use a light interrupted motor as are found in printers combined with a series of reduction gears to allow the force needed to suspend your robot without adding much weight.
example_value: The author suggests motors from printers combined with a series of reduction gears to achieve the force needed to suspend a robot without adding much weight.
example_context: robot actuators where servos lack torque; lightweight DC/stepper motors from printers with added gear reduction

subject: EDM method for hard injection mold tooling
main_point: In EDM-based moldmaking, a CNC-machined carbon (graphite) positive is used as the electrode to erode the negative cavity into hardened steel. This process enables forming hard steel mold cavities that are difficult to mill directly.
source_quote: which requires first CNCing a carbon positive and then using that as an electrode to spark-burn out a negative mold from hard steel.
example_context: traditional injection moldmaking for hardened steel tooling using EDM

subject: soft steel mold longevity
main_point: Softer steels that are easy to machine tend to have short service life when used as injection molds due to wear. Choosing soft steel implies limited run lengths before the mold must be remade.
source_quote: I know that a soft enough steel to be CNCed will not last very long as an injection mold
example_value: The poster is willing to replace the mold about every 500 parts.
example_context: injection molding with CNC-machined soft steel molds

subject: GRBL backlash compensation support
main_point: GRBL firmware is believed not to include built-in backlash compensation functionality.
source_quote: As far as I'm aware GRBL does not support backlash compensation
example_context: GRBL firmware on Arduino-based CNC controllers

subject: separation of concerns for backlash compensation implementation
main_point: Backlash compensation should not be implemented in a high-level paint/drawing program; keep mechanical compensation separate from content-generation software to maintain clear separation of concerns.
source_quote: Should a paint program really be doing mechanical backlash compensation?
example_context: CNC/plotter workflows where G-code is generated by a paint or drawing program and executed by a controller like GRBL

subject: mechanical correction of backlash at the source
main_point: When backlash causes problems, prioritize fixing it mechanically at its source—such as by improving the drivetrain (e.g., using a better gearbox)—rather than relying on software compensation.
source_quote: If backlash is really an issue then the easiest solution would be to fix it where it originates - mechanically. Get a better gearbox.
example_context: CNC/plotter machines experiencing drivetrain/gearbox backlash

subject: single-direction toolpath to neutralize backlash
main_point: You can avoid backlash effects by planning toolpaths to engage the tool only in one direction and ensuring the return move takes up all backlash before re-engagement.
source_quote: If you only cut/draw in one direction then you wind up with no backlash effects, as long as you move far enough in the opposite direction that you run out the backlash before the tool engages.
example_value: Start at home, move right to draw, then return home with the tool disengaged before moving right again for the next pass.
example_context: Plotting or cutting operations where the tool can be disengaged on the return move (e.g., CNC plotters, light cutting)

subject: GRBL hard limit alarm behavior
main_point: With GRBL_ESP32 on an MKS DLC32 and hard limits enabled, a limit-switch hit stops all machine motion and requires moving off the switch position before the program can be restarted.
source_quote: When the any of the axes triggers limit switch, all the motion stop. I have to move the axis manually to a position to restart the program.
example_value: User reports that any axis triggering a limit halts motion and requires manual repositioning to continue.
example_context: GRBL_ESP32 firmware on MKS DLC32 with $21 (hard limits) and $22 (homing) enabled

subject: Hardware debounce effect on GRBL auto-recovery
main_point: Adding a capacitor for hardware debouncing on the limit switch did not cause the controller to automatically move off the switch after a limit-trigger alarm.
source_quote: I added a capacitor with the limit switch to debounce and automatically move from the triggering position but it does not do that.
example_value: A capacitor was added across a NO mechanical limit switch to achieve auto back-off, but the controller still did not auto-move.
example_context: GRBL_ESP32 firmware on MKS DLC32 using NO mechanical limit switches

subject: make-vs-buy decision for non-core parts
main_point: Avoid designing and fabricating components that are not the core focus of your project; default to buying existing solutions rather than making them in-house.
source_quote: So again, to summarize - if it's not the focus of your project, don't do it.

subject: machining setup cost amortization
main_point: Fixed setup activities (programming, jigs, stops) dominate machining cost at low volumes, so per-part cost drops mainly by amortizing these fixed costs over larger quantities.
source_quote: Most of the cost for getting parts made is the conversion from CAD to gcode or other machine programming, making jigs, setting machine stops, etc. These costs are fixed and you pay them regardless of the part quantity you order, so someone that orders 1,000 parts gets to amortize the machining setup cost across a larger number of items, resulting in a lower per-part cost.

subject: design/drafting errors in custom parts
main_point: Errors in GD&T, machine design, or drafting can render a custom part unusable, wasting money and stalling the overall project until reworked.
source_quote: If you mess up anything in points 3, 4, or 5, you wind up with a fancy paperweight. Because of point 2, you paid a lot for it. Because of point 1, the rest of your project is stalled until you get these issues resolved.

subject: iterative rework and reorder delays
main_point: Custom part mistakes often trigger multiple fabrication cycles and shipping waits, where each fix can reveal new or previously missed issues, compounding schedule delays.
source_quote: So you wind up fixing the problem you did notice, re-order the part(s), wait for fabrication and shipping, just to potentially discover either (1) issues you didn't notice that were already present in the first batch, or (2) issues that you introduced when resolving the issue(s) with the first batch.

subject: COTS part selection margin
main_point: Define your requirements, then choose a commercially available component that slightly exceeds those performance specs to simplify integration and avoid custom fabrication.
source_quote: It will be a lot easier for you to identify the specs you need, then find the commercially-available part that just exceeds the performance specs you need.
example_value: Using a higher-rated COTS part may add weight and drive a larger motor or different ballscrew choice, but you still avoid fabrication and QA burdens.

subject: custom build exception threshold
main_point: Default to buying commercially available components and only pursue a custom design once you have demonstrated that no COTS option meets your requirements.
source_quote:
buy the commercially available stuff until you can 
prove
 that whatever item isn't commercially available. Only then should you take on trying to do it yourself.

subject: D-shaped motor shafts
main_point: A D-profile shaft mated to a matching D-bore creates a geometric lock that resists rotational slip, improving torque transfer between shaft and hub.
source_quote: I find shafts with D profile are better to transfer the force and it greatly helps reduce slipping since matting a D shaft (on the motor side) with a D bore (on a pulley or wheel hub) creates a geometric lock between the matting components.

subject: motor shaft profile prevalence on high-torque motors
main_point: High‑torque motors commonly use D‑profile shafts, although this is not universal and exceptions exist.
source_quote: All high-torque motors come with such profiles in general. Of course, there are exceptions to everything.
example_context: high-torque electric motors

subject: D-shaft manufacturability and assembly
main_point: D‑profile shafts are straightforward to manufacture and facilitate easy assembly and disassembly with mating components, favoring them for practical, low‑effort interfaces.
source_quote: D-shaft is the most simplest one to manufacture and easy to assemble and disassemble with its counterparts.

subject: direct vs indirect mounting decision
main_point: Choose direct mounting to a motor shaft only if the shaft’s load‑bearing capacity can handle the applied loads; otherwise use an intermediate shaft or different arrangement.
source_quote: Mounting directly or indirectly depends on the load-bearing capacity of the motor shaft.

subject: sleeve and grub screw coupling suitability
main_point: Simple sleeve-and-set‑screw couplings are acceptable for low‑torque applications, but should not be relied on as torque increases.
source_quote: Eg: A shaft coupling using a sleeve and grub screw may be adequate if it is a low torque application.

subject: set-screw coupling on softer shafts
main_point: When a hard set screw bears on a softer shaft at high torque, the screw can gouge the shaft, causing backlash or even complete coupling failure. Avoid mismatched hardness or redesign the interface to prevent this.
source_quote: If the shaft material is weaker than the coupling material, say you are using a grub screw to lock the shaft and its counterparts, under high torque the screw can eat the shaft away resulting in a lot of backlashes or total failure of shaft-to-shaft coupling.

subject: stepper vs in-runner brushed motors
main_point: Steppers provide holding torque and precise positioning, while in‑runner brushed motors are high‑speed devices that require gear reduction to obtain useful torque, making them suitable for different applications.
source_quote: Both are two very different motors used for two very different applications, the first one is a stepper motor which has better-holding torque & precise control, and the second one is a high-speed in-runner brushed motor (hence all the step-down/ low gear setup to convert that high speed to high torque).

subject: actuator selection for precision and torque
main_point: For applications that demand good torque and positioning precision (such as robotic joints), a servo motor or stepper is generally an adequate choice.
source_quote: For your use case, I believe you need decent torque and good precision so a servo motor or stepper should be adequate.
example_context: robotic arm/SCARA joints requiring precision and torque

subject: AccelStepper/TeensyStep synchronized move profile
main_point: Using AccelStepper or TeensyStep to execute line-by-line targets produces a synchronized move for all axes with a per-move speed profile that accelerates from the current state to maxSpeed and then decelerates to the target position.
source_quote: With AccelStepper or TeensyStep library I can move to give code line(N00x) in a synchronous move. So when I feed this code lines it will go from current position accelerating-to maxSpeed- then deaccelerating to target position.
example_context: AccelStepper or TeensyStep libraries on Arduino/Teensy for 6-axis stepper control

subject: encoder fault symptoms
main_point: Asymmetric position increments per equal turns in opposite directions, combined with a rough mechanical feel, indicate the encoder is faulty.
source_quote: I have determined the Encoder is faulty as when i rotate it clockwise by one turn it increments by 5mm but when I rotate it anti-clockwise by 1 turn it increments by 10mm (approximately). It also feels quite clunky when i rotate it.
example_value: Clockwise one turn increments 5 mm; anti-clockwise one turn increments 10 mm; encoder feels clunky.
example_context: Encoder on a 1980s hydraulic press brake CNC backstop driven by a DC motor and screw drive

subject: OEM drop-in encoder replacement
main_point: Start by asking the original manufacturer if a drop-in replacement encoder is available. Even if it seems unlikely, drop-in replacements are common enough in CNC/automation that it’s worth checking first.
source_quote: - First of all ask, if they can provide a drop in replacement. It is a long shot, but not that uncommon in the automation/CNC world.
example_context: industrial CNC/automation encoders on legacy machines (e.g., press brake backgauge)

subject: encoder counts per revolution (CPR) and output voltage for replacement selection
main_point: When selecting a replacement encoder, prioritize matching the counts per revolution. Also verify the output signal voltage with the manufacturer, even if 5 V is likely.
source_quote: How many counts/revolution does the encoder output is the main important characteristic to choose a replacement. Voltage of the output signals is probably 5 V but it does not hurt to ask to make sure.
example_context: incremental rotary encoders used in CNC motion feedback

subject: using technical specifications to source compatible encoders
main_point: Obtain the encoder’s technical specification and use it to cross-shop among vendors. Provide the spec to sales engineers to identify compatible replacements.
source_quote: - The technical spec can help you shop around from other vendors. You can all sales people of different companies and ask them if they have something compatible to your spec sheet.
example_context: sourcing replacement encoders across multiple industrial suppliers

subject: stepper motor acceleration handling location
main_point: In a setup using a CNC Shield V3 with DRV8255 stepper drivers, motion acceleration and deceleration are implemented in software rather than handled by the driver hardware.
source_quote: On my experience working with stepper motor and CNC shield V3 with DRV8255 motor driver, acceleration and decelaration happen on software side.
example_value: The author reports that in their CNC Shield V3 + DRV8255 configuration, the motion profile is generated in software.
example_context: CNC Shield V3 with DRV8255 stepper driver controlled by software on a microcontroller/host

subject: trajectory planner and PD control producing acceleration for stepper motion
main_point: The author computes an acceleration command with a simple trajectory planner plus PD error control, integrates it to obtain the target velocity, and transmits that velocity to the microcontroller for execution.
source_quote: So I have simple trajectory planner and PD controller to handle the error which produce control signal in form of acceleration, then I simply integral and get the velocity at that time. The acquired velocity then send to microcontroller.
example_value: A software-side planner outputs acceleration, which is integrated to velocity and then sent to the microcontroller.
example_context: Software motion control for a stepper-driven CNC setup using a microcontroller and DRV8255 drivers

subject: CNC trajectory planner responsibility
main_point: In CNC systems, the controller’s trajectory planner generates the acceleration profile, but it must obey the CAM-provided waypoints and the machine’s dynamic limits.
source_quote: The main element responsible for the planning of the acceleration profile is the trajectory planner in the CNC. However this planner is limited by the waypoints it gets from the CAM tool and by the dynamical limits of the machine.
example_context: CNC controllers with built-in trajectory planning receiving G-code from CAM

subject: CAM waypoints and feed settings constrain acceleration
main_point: CAM-defined toolpath segmentation and assigned feed/speed values inherently bound the achievable accelerations before the CNC plans motion.
source_quote: When the waypoints are defined and the feeds and speed for the segments are set this already imposes some limits on the accelerations.
example_context: CAM-generated G-code segments for CNC machining

subject: speed transitions between segments require acceleration
main_point: Whenever adjacent path segments command different speeds, the machine must accelerate or decelerate between them, which constrains motion smoothness and peak acceleration demands.
source_quote: One such limitation comes from segments with different speeds, obviously there is an acceleration needed between these.

subject: path curvature determines axis accelerations at constant feed
main_point: Toolpath curvature dictates required axis accelerations even at constant feed; tighter curves force higher accelerations on specific axes.
source_quote: A second limitation comes from the curvature on which the waypoints are situated. Even if the feedrate is constant, the curve will determine the acceleration of the different axes.

subject: CNC interpolation and corner rounding
main_point: CNC controllers preprocess CAM paths by rounding sharp corners and inserting intermediate points using linear, circular, or spline interpolation before motion is timed.
source_quote: The CNC rounds sharp corners, adds in between waypoints based on a linear/circular/spline interpolation.
example_context: CNC motion controllers performing path interpolation from G-code waypoints

subject: definition of CNC trajectory
main_point: In CNC control, a trajectory consists of the spatial waypoints combined with time-domain velocity and acceleration profiles.
source_quote: The waypoints together with the velocity and acceleration profiles form the trajectory.
example_context: CNC trajectory planning in motion controllers

subject: interpolation cycle time for trajectory updates
main_point: CNC controllers stream trajectory setpoints to axis drives each interpolation cycle, which in modern systems can be on the order of a few milliseconds (≈2 ms).
source_quote: The trajectory is then sent each cycle (interpolation cycles can be as low as 2 ms)  to the axis controllers.
example_value: Interpolation cycles as low as 2 ms.
example_context: Modern CNC motion controllers and their axis control update rates

subject: CNC planner respects machine dynamic limits
main_point: CNC trajectory planners generally account for machine dynamic constraints so that the computed motion profiles are feasible to execute.
source_quote: Usually the trajectory planner in the CNC is aware of the dynamical limits of the system and plans only executable trajectories.
example_context: CNC controllers with built-in knowledge of axis acceleration/velocity/jerk limits

subject: stepper driver trajectory smoothness limitations
main_point: Basic stepper drivers limit achievable smoothness—position, velocity, and acceleration (jerk) continuity—constraining how finely a trajectory’s motion profile can be executed.
source_quote: A stepper motor driver is  a simplistic case, which has its inherent limitations in terms of smoothness (the first/second/third order continuity of the trajectory).
example_context: Stepper motor driven CNC axes using simple step/direction drivers

subject: software-based acceleration planning in modern CNC
main_point: In modern CNCs, acceleration profile planning and execution are handled in control software rather than by dedicated hardware components, aside from inherent motor limitations.
source_quote: In modern (probably since the `90s) CNC machine there are no HW components actively participating in the acceleration profile planning or execution (if we disregard the inherent limitations of stepper motors).
example_context: Modern CNC machines from the 1990s onward with digital motion control architectures

subject: string-based translation between G-code and eV+
main_point: Because G-code and eV+ have simple, regular syntax, you can translate motion commands with a lightweight script that performs straightforward string substitutions rather than building a full interpreter. Simple find/replace and token adjustments are typically enough to convert paths for robot execution.
source_quote: These programming languages have a very simple syntax, you can just do string manipulation (replace  substrings, add or remove , or ;) and it should work.
example_value: Swap G-code motion lines into eV+ Move statements by replacing command tokens and minor syntax elements, leaving the coordinates intact.
example_context: Converting CNC-style G-code output to Omron Adept eV+ robot programs

subject: coordinate-based motion command mapping between G-code and eV+
main_point: Both CNC G-code and eV+ robot programs drive motion via coordinates; the primary difference is the keyword used for linear moves (e.g., G01 in G-code versus Move in eV+). This lends itself to token-level translation between the two formats.
source_quote: Your robot is also controlled by coordinates, but instead of a G01 command (in G-Code) it has a Move command.
example_context: Mapping motion commands from G-code to Omron Adept eV+ for robot path execution

subject: availability of image-to-G-code converters
main_point: Numerous tools exist to convert images into G-code paths, providing a ready source of coordinate toolpaths from drawings or photos.
source_quote: There are many image to G-Code converters out there.

subject: breakaway torque approximation via static friction
main_point: Estimate breakaway torque by modeling only static friction. Use the lead screw’s static friction coefficient and the applied load to compute the nut’s static-friction torque.
source_quote: You can approximate the breakaway torque by considering static friction only. From the static friction coefficient of the lead screw (by knowing the maximum load on the spindle, coming from the application) you can calculate the static friction torque of the nut on the lead screw.

subject: summation of component friction torques for breakaway
main_point: Calculate the static-friction torque for each component in the axis (lead screw, linear guides, bearings) and sum them to obtain the overall breakaway torque.
source_quote: You should do the same with all linear guides and/or bearings that you have and sum them up. That will be your breakaway torque.

subject: lead screw static friction and torque conversion formula
main_point: For a lead screw, static friction force equals coefficient times normal force (F = c·N), and the corresponding torque is T = F × lead / (2π).
source_quote: For the lead screw: F = c*N where F is the static friction force, c is the static friction constant and N is the normal force. In this case you have to convert the Force to Torque Torque = Force x Lead /2pi.

subject: manufacturer-provided friction-to-torque constant
main_point: Lead screw manufacturers may provide a constant that directly relates static friction to torque, allowing you to bypass intermediate calculations.
source_quote: Or the lead screw manufacturer might give directly the constant which links static friction constant to torque.

subject: power supply sizing for stepper systems
main_point: When selecting a power supply for a stepper system, treat motor requirements and driver capabilities as distinct. Size the supply to meet the motors’ actual voltage and current needs rather than assuming the driver specs alone define the requirement.
source_quote: Number one you need to differentiate between the driver capabilities and the motors requirements.
example_context: Closed-loop stepper motors with external drivers in CNC machines

subject: NEMA 34 stepper drive voltage typical
main_point: NEMA 34 stepper motors are commonly operated at 48 V or higher, so power supply choices should consider a minimum around that voltage.
source_quote: though Nema34 are typically driven at at least 48v
example_context: NEMA 34 stepper motors used in CNC routers

subject: power supply current headroom
main_point: Include about 20% current headroom when sizing a power supply for stepper-driven systems to provide safe overhead beyond calculated demand.
source_quote: Most of the time a 20% overhead margin is recommended.
example_context: Power supply sizing for multiple stepper motors

subject: simultaneous axis loading in CNC machines
main_point: For typical CNC operation, not all axes draw peak torque simultaneously; expect at most about two axes at full load. You can size the power supply for the expected simultaneous load rather than the sum of all motor currents.
source_quote: it is very unlikely that you'll ever have more than 2 motors working fully at any given time
example_value: The answer estimates an equivalent of 2.5 motors at full torque to size a 48 V, ~18 A supply instead of 30 A for four motors.
example_context: CNC routers with multiple stepper axes

subject: constant-current stepper drivers and power supply wattage
main_point: Stepper drivers regulate winding current independent of input voltage, so raising the supply voltage requires a higher-wattage power supply to deliver the same output current. A higher-voltage supply of equal wattage will be insufficient.
source_quote: they are designed to hold a constant current regardless of input voltage. If you go up in voltage you'll need a higher wattage power supply to still be able to deliver the necessary current.
example_context: Stepper motor drivers in CNC applications

subject: unregulated power supply ripple under load
main_point: Using an unregulated supply under high load increases ripple, causing large output-voltage fluctuations that can destabilize a CNC machine. Avoid unregulated supplies for sensitive CNC electronics with ~15 A or higher draw.
source_quote: The higher the load on the supply the larger the ripple in the voltage, so with a potential draw of 15A or more, you'll see tremendous fluctuations in the output voltage.  This would be pretty disastrous on a CNC machine.
example_context: CNC machines drawing ~15 A from a DC power supply

subject: GRBL stepper holding current drop during pause
main_point: Pausing after a G0 move can cause the controller to cut motor current, which lets the stepper lose position and ruins scan accuracy. This makes precise holding at the target point unreliable when the motors are idled during the pause.
source_quote: 2. Using G0: I do get it to pause there, but it drops motor current, losing a step and making precise scanning impossible.
example_context: GRBL on an Arduino Uno with a CNC shield controlling a 2D scanner; rapid move (G0) to position followed by a pause.

subject: natural vibration excitation from instantaneous force change
main_point: An abrupt, step-like change in applied force will excite a mechanical system’s natural modes, producing ringing or oscillations. This is a fundamental response to discontinuous inputs in dynamic systems.
source_quote: In theory, an instantaneous change in force will also excite natural vibrations in a system as well (in the same way connecting an inductor/capacitor directly to a 12v source induces ringing).
example_value: Analogous to an LC circuit ringing when connected directly to a DC source via a step input.

subject: S-curve motion profiles
main_point: Jerk-limited S-curve motion profiles yield smoother motion and improve tracking accuracy compared to constant-acceleration profiles. They are generally advantageous for following commanded trajectories more precisely.
source_quote: Short version, yes having an s-curve profile is beneficial for smoother and more accurate tracking.

subject: instantaneous acceleration changes (infinite jerk)
main_point: If a motion profile commands instantaneous acceleration changes (infinite jerk), real hardware cannot realize them, and the control loop will not track accurately at those transition points. This leads to following error where acceleration steps occur.
source_quote: Instantaneous acceleration changes are not possible so the control system simply cannot track perfectly at those points in the profile).

subject: motion profile derivative consistency
main_point: Trajectory generation must be internally consistent: the time-derivative of the commanded position profile must equal the commanded velocity, and the derivative of velocity must equal the commanded acceleration. Violating these relationships creates unattainable commands that degrade tracking.
source_quote: By this I mean, the derivative of your profile needs to match your velocity and the derivative of your velocity profile needs to match your acceleration.

subject: lower-level jerk limiting controllers
main_point: Some motion controllers automatically smooth a step-acceleration (trapezoidal) command into an effective S-curve by enforcing a jerk limit at a lower control level. This embedded jerk limiting can make a non-jerk-limited plan behave like a jerk-limited one.
source_quote: Other systems have a lower-level controller that will effectively turn your step-acceleration profile into an s-curve by limiting jerk of the profile (often a lower-level system parameter.
example_context: Motion controllers with a configurable lower-level jerk limit parameter

subject: Phoenix Mecano 'Lambda' linear motors
main_point: Phoenix Mecano manufactures a product line of linear motors referred to as “Lambda.”
source_quote: Thouse motors are calles lamba motors and are made from phoenix mecano.
example_value: Author references using one on a wheelchair to push the seat up.
example_context: Phoenix Mecano Lambda linear actuators

subject: Lambda linear motor size/strength options
main_point: The Lambda linear motor line is available in multiple sizes and strength levels, allowing selection of a stronger unit when needed.
source_quote: The have smaller and bigger one, the new version of the wheelchair has 1 stronger one.
example_value: The author notes their new wheelchair version uses a stronger unit.
example_context: Phoenix Mecano Lambda linear actuators

subject: LinuxCNC open-source G-code to motor command conversion
main_point: LinuxCNC is an open-source system that performs the end-to-end task of translating G-code into machine motor commands. It can serve as a reference or solution for implementing G-code interpretation and motion control.
source_quote:
LinuxCNC
 is an open source project dedicated to "converting" G-code into motor commands.
example_context: LinuxCNC project (open-source CNC control software)

subject: G-code interpretation contents (motion, waypoints, branches/loops)
main_point: A G-code interpreter must parse motion commands and waypoints, and may also need to handle program flow constructs like branches and loops. Robust interpreters therefore implement both motion parsing and control-logic parsing.
source_quote: Interpret the G code (mostly motion commands and way points, but also branches and loops)
example_context: CNC G-code dialects with macro/flow-control features (branches and loops)

subject: CNC motion planning and time-parameterization
main_point: Converting G-code into motor commands requires first planning a continuous geometric path between waypoints, then time-parameterizing that path with velocities and accelerations. This trajectory generation precedes axis command generation.
source_quote:
3. Plan a continoupous path between the waypoints
4. Add the time dimention to your path (velocities and accelerations)

subject: Axis projection (kinematics) from trajectory
main_point: After generating a trajectory, its commanded positions/velocities must be projected into each motor axis (i.e., mapped through the machine’s kinematics) to produce per-axis setpoints.
source_quote: 5. Project values to your motor axis

subject: Motor controller dependence on motor/driver hardware
main_point: The implementation that makes motors track the reference trajectory is highly dependent on the specific motor and driver hardware. Control strategy and signaling must match the motor/driver (e.g., stepper with a parallel-port interface).
source_quote:
6. Make your motor controller follow the reference trajectory (this is the 
part which is heavily dependent on your motors and motor driver, in your ase the stepper motor with parallel port)
example_value: Example cited: stepper motor with a parallel port driver.
example_context: Stepper motors driven via parallel-port step/direction interfaces

subject: LinuxCNC and GRBL projects
main_point: LinuxCNC and GRBL are cited as examples of software for handling CNC motion from G-code, and GRBL runs on Arduino hardware.
source_quote: LinuxCNC is a good example.  A simpler example would be GRBL, which runs on Arduinos:
example_context: LinuxCNC (PC-based CNC control) and GRBL firmware on Arduino microcontrollers

subject: G-code parsing into machine commands
main_point: A typical G-code interpreter processes the program line-by-line, parsing each line and mapping it to a specific command the controller will execute. This line-to-command parsing is the core mechanism by which CNC firmware turns G-code text into actionable machine instructions.
